patterns.title: Crafted session id in a cookie escapes the session directory in CherryPy file-based sessions
patterns.cause: The _get_file_path function in CherryPy session handling (lib/sessions.py in 3.0.x up to 3.0.2, filter/sessionfilter.py in 2.x) derives a file location from a session id. That id comes from a client cookie. A crafted id lets a remote attacker reach files outside the session directory.
preconditions: A CherryPy version affected by the advisory is in use: 3.0.x up to 3.0.2, 2.1, or another 2.x release.
Sessions are stored as files, so the session id is used to compute a file path.
The session id is read from a cookie that the client controls and is not verified before it is used.
patterns.prevention: Treat the session id from a cookie as untrusted input. Before it is used to build a session file location, check that it has the expected form of a session identifier, and reject anything else. After building the path, confirm that it resolves to a location inside the configured session directory, for example by comparing the resolved path with the directory, and refuse the request if it does not. Upgrade to a CherryPy release that includes the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which characters or sequences in the id trigger the traversal, how the fix validates the id, or which release first contains it. The sources also do not describe other session back ends. This card gives only general direction and does not cover other path-handling code in the application.

fixtures.scenario: A web application on an affected CherryPy version keeps sessions as files. A client sends a cookie whose session id is crafted so that the path computed by _get_file_path points outside the session directory. The server then creates, deletes, reads or writes a file chosen by the attacker.

The same application checks that the session id from the cookie has the expected form and rejects any other value. It also confirms that the final file path resolves inside the session directory. A crafted cookie is refused and no file outside the session directory is touched.

citations.quote: CherryPy Malicious cookies allow access to files outside the session directory
Directory traversal vulnerability in the _get_file_path function in (1) lib/sessions.py in CherryPy 3.0.x up to 3.0.2
allows remote attackers to create or delete arbitrary files, and possibly read and write portions of arbitrary files

patterns.title: Roundup before 1.4.4: unspecified issues possibly including cross-site scripting
patterns.cause: The advisories say only that Roundup before 1.4.4 has multiple unspecified vulnerabilities, and that some may be related to cross-site scripting (XSS). The sources do not identify the vulnerable code path, the input involved, or the exact flaw.
preconditions: The deployment runs a Roundup version earlier than 1.4.4.
The deployment is a Roundup tracker instance, since the affected package is roundup.
patterns.prevention: Run Roundup 1.4.4 or later. The sources give no more specific mitigation, so a deployment cannot safely claim protection from configuration or input handling changes alone.
patterns.limitations: The sources call the impact and attack vectors unknown and the vulnerabilities unspecified. The XSS link is only described as possible (some may be related to XSS). They do not name the vulnerable component, the injection point, the affected output context, or how the fix changes behavior. A fix commit is referenced, but its content is not in the sources, so no root-cause or fix-direction claim is made. Any other issues fixed in 1.4.4 are not described.

fixtures.scenario: A team runs a Roundup tracker at a version earlier than 1.4.4 and exposes it to users. It may be affected by the unspecified vulnerabilities, some of which may involve cross-site scripting.
A team runs a Roundup tracker at version 1.4.4 or later, which is the release line the advisories identify as no longer affected.

citations.quote: Multiple unspecified vulnerabilities in Roundup before 1.4.4 have unknown impact and attack vectors, some of which may be related to cross-site scripting (XSS).
Roundup vulnerability related to Cross-site scripting (XSS)

patterns.title: Admin login form reflects the URI of an earlier request without neutralizing it (Django, CVE-2008-2302)
patterns.cause: The login form in the Django administration application used the URI of a previous request in the page it returned. That value is attacker-influenced, and it was not neutralized for HTML output. A remote attacker could therefore get arbitrary web script or HTML into the login page.
preconditions: Django 0.91 before 0.91.2, 0.95 before 0.95.3, or 0.96 before 0.96.2 is in use.
The administration application login form is reachable.
A previous request whose URI the attacker can influence is carried into the login form.
patterns.prevention: Treat the URI of an earlier request as untrusted input wherever the login form uses it. Encode it for the HTML context in which it is emitted, so that markup or script characters in the URI are shown as text and not interpreted by the browser. Upgrade to a patched release: 0.91.2, 0.95.3, or 0.96.2 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a one-sentence description. They do not say where in the login form the URI is placed, which characters are dangerous, or how the upstream fix works. This card therefore gives only the general direction of treating the URI as untrusted and encoding it on output, and it makes no claim about other admin pages or other Django versions.

fixtures.scenario: A user without a valid session opens an admin page. The request URI contains attacker-chosen markup. The login form that is shown includes that URI unescaped, and the markup runs in the browser on the admin site's origin.
The same request with markup in the URI leads to a login form. The form encodes the URI for HTML output, so the markup appears as inert text and no script runs.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via the URI of a certain previous request.
Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the login form in the administration application in Django 0.91 before 0.91.2, 0.95 before 0.95.3, and 0.96 before 0.96.2

patterns.title: Regex backtracking DoS in Django form validation of email and URL fields
patterns.cause: The forms library validated EmailField and URLField input with regular expressions that could backtrack heavily on crafted values. A remote attacker could submit such a value and consume a large amount of CPU time, causing denial of service through algorithmic complexity.
preconditions: Application runs Django 1.0 before 1.0.4 or Django 1.1 before 1.1.1
Application accepts untrusted input through forms using EmailField or URLField
Attacker can submit crafted email address or URL values remotely
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 1.0.4 or 1.1.1 or later, which address the issue. More generally, an implementation should avoid validation patterns that can backtrack excessively on adversarial input, and should test any email or URL validation expression against crafted long or malformed values to confirm that matching time stays bounded.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact regular expression flaw, the specific crafted inputs, or the way the upstream change reworked the validation, so this card gives only general direction. They do not mention input length limits or timeouts as mitigations, and do not state whether other field types are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A Django 1.1.0 site exposes a signup form with an email field and a profile form with a URL field. An attacker submits a crafted value that triggers heavy regular expression backtracking, and the request consumes large CPU time, degrading service for other users.

The same site runs Django 1.1.1 or later, or 1.0.4 or later on the 1.0 branch. The same crafted email and URL values are validated without excessive backtracking, so the form rejects or accepts them quickly and CPU use stays normal.

citations.quote: Algorithmic complexity vulnerability in the forms library in Django 1.0 before 1.0.4 and 1.1 before 1.1.1
cause a denial of service (CPU consumption) via a crafted (1) EmailField (email address) or (2) URLField (URL)
triggers a large amount of backtracking in a regular expression.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS through the template argument of the Roundup issue program
patterns.cause: In Roundup before 1.4.14, cgi/client.py lets remote attackers inject arbitrary web script or HTML through the template argument to the /issue program. The attacker-controlled template value is not treated as untrusted data on its way into the response. The sources do not say which code path emits it.
preconditions: The deployment runs Roundup older than 1.4.14.
The web interface is reachable by remote users who can send requests to the /issue program.
The request carries an attacker-chosen value in the template argument.
A victim's browser processes the response that contains the injected content.
patterns.prevention: Treat the template argument as untrusted input. Any content derived from it that reaches an HTML response must be encoded for the HTML context so it is shown as text and not run as markup or script. Restricting the argument to a known set of expected values before use is also consistent with this goal. The most direct step the sources support is to run Roundup 1.4.14 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a one-sentence description. They do not say which code path emits the value, whether the injection is reflected or stored, or how the fix works. The prevention above is therefore general guidance on output encoding and input handling. The only version-specific claim is that releases before 1.4.14 are affected. The sources do not describe other parameters or other Roundup components.

fixtures.scenario: A user follows a crafted link to the /issue program on a Roundup instance older than 1.4.14. The link's template argument contains script or HTML markup. The response includes that markup as active content, and it runs in the victim's browser.

The same crafted link is sent to a Roundup instance at version 1.4.14 or later, or to an implementation that encodes or validates the template value. The markup is not run as script or HTML in the victim's browser.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via the template argument to the /issue program.
Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in `cgi/client.py` in Roundup before 1.4.14

patterns.title: Django 1.2.x XSS via attacker-supplied CSRF token cookie
patterns.cause: In Django 1.2.x before 1.2.2, a crafted csrfmiddlewaretoken (aka csrf_token) cookie let a remote attacker inject arbitrary web script or HTML. The cookie value comes from the client, so it is attacker-influenced input that must not be trusted.
preconditions: The application runs Django 1.2.x earlier than 1.2.2.
An attacker can cause a victim's browser to send a crafted csrfmiddlewaretoken (csrf_token) cookie value.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Django to 1.2.2 or later, the first release the advisories do not list as affected. In application code, treat the CSRF token cookie as untrusted client data. Do not place its value into HTML output unless it has been validated or context-appropriately escaped.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say that XSS was possible via the csrfmiddlewaretoken cookie in Django 1.2.x before 1.2.2. They do not describe the vulnerable code path, the output context, or how the upstream fix works. The escaping and validation advice is a general safeguard, not a description of that fix. Other Django branches are not covered by the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A site runs Django 1.2.1. A request arrives with a csrfmiddlewaretoken cookie whose value contains HTML or script markup chosen by an attacker, and the markup can end up executing in the victim's browser.
The same site runs Django 1.2.2 or later. A request with a cookie containing HTML or script markup does not result in script execution in the browser.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via a csrfmiddlewaretoken (aka csrf_token) cookie.
Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in Django 1.2.x before 1.2.2

patterns.title: Script injection through file upload filenames in old Django releases
patterns.cause: The filename associated with a file upload is attacker-controlled. In Django 1.1.x before 1.1.4 and 1.2.x before 1.2.5, it could be used to inject arbitrary web script or HTML, which is a cross-site scripting weakness (CWE-79).
preconditions: The application runs Django 1.1.x before 1.1.4 or Django 1.2.x before 1.2.5.
A remote attacker can supply a file upload whose filename contains script or HTML markup.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 1.1.4, 1.2.5 or a later release. Treat an uploaded filename as untrusted data, and encode it for the output context wherever it is shown to a user instead of inserting it into a page as raw markup.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a one-sentence description. They do not say which Django component handled or displayed the filename, how the fix works, or whether versions outside 1.1.x and 1.2.x were affected. The application-level encoding advice is general guidance, not a description of the upstream change. This card does not cover other XSS vectors.

fixtures.scenario: An application on Django 1.2.4 accepts file uploads. An attacker submits an upload whose filename contains script or HTML markup, and the markup is treated as web content instead of plain text.

The same application runs Django 1.2.5 or later, or 1.1.4 or later on the 1.1 line. Uploaded filenames are treated as untrusted and encoded for the output context, so markup in a filename does not become active content.

citations.quote: inject arbitrary web script or HTML via a filename associated with a file upload.

patterns.title: Directory traversal via crafted image tarball or manifest in Nova S3/RegisterImage
patterns.cause: Nova before 2011.3.1 handled image data supplied through the S3/RegisterImage image-registration method in a way that allowed directory traversal. A crafted tarball or a crafted manifest could make the service write outside the location it intended, overwriting arbitrary files.
preconditions: Nova version is earlier than 2011.3.1.
The EC2 API is enabled.
The S3/RegisterImage image-registration method is enabled.
The attacker is a remote authenticated user who can supply a crafted tarball or manifest.
patterns.prevention: Treat every name or path taken from an uploaded tarball or an image manifest as untrusted input. Before writing any file, resolve the final destination path and confirm it stays inside the directory reserved for that image. Reject the request if it escapes that directory, rather than trying to clean the name. Upgrade to Nova 2011.3.1 or later. If upgrading is not possible, disabling the EC2 API or the S3/RegisterImage method removes the stated precondition.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a short description. They do not say which functions, fields or archive member types were vulnerable, and they do not describe how the fix works. The containment check above is a general direction and is not confirmed as the upstream approach. The sources also say nothing about other Nova components or other image-registration paths.

fixtures.scenario: A Nova deployment older than 2011.3.1 has the EC2 API and S3/RegisterImage enabled. An authenticated user registers an image with a tarball or manifest containing an entry whose path climbs out of the image directory. The service writes to that location and overwrites a file elsewhere on the host.

A Nova deployment at 2011.3.1 or later, or one with S3/RegisterImage disabled, receives the same crafted tarball or manifest. Each destination path is resolved and found to lie outside the image directory, so the request is rejected and no existing file is modified.

citations.quote: allow remote authenticated users to overwrite arbitrary files via a crafted (1) tarball or (2) manifest.
when the EC2 API and the S3/RegisterImage image-registration method are enabled

patterns.title: Incomplete sanitization of content shown in Zope error messages allows reflected script injection
patterns.cause: Zope did not fully sanitize content when building error messages, so a remote attacker could get arbitrary web script or HTML into the error output. The sources say this happened because the earlier fix for CVE-2010-1104 was incomplete.
preconditions: The application runs an affected Zope release: 2.8.x before 2.8.12, 2.9.x before 2.9.12, 2.10.x before 2.10.11, 2.11.x before 2.11.6, or 2.12.x before 2.12.3. The advisory also lists 3.1.1 through 3.4.1.
A request can trigger an error message whose text is influenced by the remote attacker.
The error message is rendered to a browser, where injected HTML or script can execute.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a fixed Zope release. When building error messages, make sure every piece of externally influenced text is sanitized or escaped for HTML before it is shown, and apply that on every code path that produces error output, not only the path covered by an earlier fix. After fixing one sanitization issue, review sibling error-reporting paths so a partial fix does not leave a variant open.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact input vector, which error messages are affected, or what the incomplete sanitization missed. They do not explain how the 3.x range relates to the 2.x fixed versions. The guidance on consistent escaping is a general direction, not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A site runs Zope 2.12.2. A remote user sends a request that causes an error, and attacker-chosen text appears in the error message with sanitization that does not fully neutralize HTML or script. The browser runs that script.
A site runs Zope 2.12.3 or later, or an equivalent fixed release. Attacker-influenced text in error messages is fully sanitized before display, so injected markup is shown as inert text.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via vectors related to the way error messages perform sanitization
this issue exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2010-1104
Zope 2.8.x before 2.8.12, 2.9.x before 2.9.12, 2.10.x before 2.10.11, 2.11.x before 2.11.6, and 2.12.x before 2.12.3

patterns.title: SQLAlchemy before 0.7.0b4: SQL injection through select limit and offset
patterns.cause: In SQLAlchemy before 0.7.0b4, the limit and offset keywords of the select function, and the select.limit and select.offset functions, could be used by remote attackers to run arbitrary SQL commands. Keystone is named as an affected consumer. The sources do not explain the internal mechanism.
preconditions: The application uses a SQLAlchemy release older than 0.7.0b4.
Values for limit or offset reach the select function, select.limit or select.offset.
Those values can be influenced by a remote attacker, for example through request parameters in a service like Keystone.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade SQLAlchemy to 0.7.0b4 or later, which is the first release not listed as affected. As defense in depth, treat pagination values from clients as untrusted data. Convert them to plain integers at the application boundary and reject anything else before building a select statement. Do not build limit or offset clauses by joining strings.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the injection works, which code path was changed, or what the fix does. They call some vectors unspecified. The advice to coerce values to integers is a general hardening step and is not confirmed by the sources as a complete mitigation. Upgrading is the only remedy the sources support, by implication of the affected version range.

fixtures.scenario: A web service runs SQLAlchemy 0.6.x and passes the page size and page offset query parameters from an HTTP request straight into the limit and offset keywords of a select call. A remote caller supplies crafted text instead of a number.

The service runs SQLAlchemy 0.7.0b4 or later. It also parses the page size and page offset parameters as integers, rejects the request if parsing fails, and only then passes the integers to the select call.

citations.quote: Multiple SQL injection vulnerabilities in SQLAlchemy before 0.7.0b4, as used in Keystone
allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary SQL commands via the (1) limit or (2) offset keyword to the select function

patterns.title: Untrusted guest console output in the Horizon log viewer refresh path enables XSS
patterns.cause: The refresh mechanism of the log viewer in the Horizon dashboard JavaScript handled guest console content in a way that let remote attackers inject arbitrary web script or HTML through that console. Guest console output is attacker-influenced data, and it was not kept inert when the log viewer displayed it.
preconditions: Horizon (OpenStack Dashboard) folsom-1, 2012.1, or an earlier release is in use.
The log viewer and its refresh mechanism are used to display guest console output.
An attacker can influence what the guest console contains.
patterns.prevention: Treat everything coming from the guest console as untrusted data on every display path, including the initial page render and later refreshes of the log viewer. Make sure the refresh code shows this content as plain text and never lets it be interpreted as HTML or script. Apply the same output handling to the refresh path as to the first render, so the two cannot differ. Use the project's standard output escaping, or a text-only way of inserting content into the page, rather than building markup from console content.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say that the XSS is in the log viewer refresh mechanism in the Horizon JavaScript file and is reachable via the guest console. They do not describe the exact vulnerable code, the payload form, or the exact fix. This card therefore gives only a general direction and does not say which escaping or insertion method the project adopted. It also does not cover other pages or components, or releases later than those listed.

fixtures.scenario: A user views an instance log in the dashboard while the log viewer auto-refreshes. The guest console contains markup that an attacker wrote. The refreshed content is treated as HTML, so the attacker's script runs in the dashboard session of the user viewing the log.

The same instance log is shown with the same attacker-written console content. Both the first render and each refresh show it as plain text, so the markup appears as literal characters and no script runs in the viewer's browser.

citations.quote: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the refresh mechanism in the log viewer
allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via the guest console
horizon/static/horizon/js/horizon.js in OpenStack Dashboard (Horizon) folsom-1 and 2012.1 and earlier

patterns.title: Directory traversal via dot-dot in file element path when writing into guest disk images (Nova, CVE-2012-3360)
patterns.cause: In virt/disk/api.py, the path attribute of a file element supplied by an authenticated user was used to decide where to write inside the guest disk image. A .. (dot dot) sequence in that path was not neutralized, so the write could land outside the intended location and put arbitrary files into the disk image.
preconditions: OpenStack Compute (Nova) Folsom (2012.2) or Essex (2012.1) is in use.
The deployment runs over libvirt-based hypervisors.
The attacker is a remote authenticated user who can supply a file element with a path attribute.
patterns.prevention: Treat the path attribute of a file element as untrusted input. Before any write, resolve the requested path against the intended base location inside the mounted disk image, for example with a canonicalizing call such as os.path.realpath(), and confirm that the resolved result still lies inside that base. Reject the request if the path contains .. components or resolves elsewhere. Perform the check on the final resolved target, not only on the raw string.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state the vulnerability class, the affected file and versions, and the .. vector. They do not describe the upstream fix, which exact checks it added, or how symbolic links inside the image are handled, so the prevention direction here is general guidance and may not match the upstream change. Hypervisor back ends other than libvirt-based ones are not addressed by the sources.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user submits a file element whose path attribute contains .. segments. The implementation joins it to the image mount point without resolving it, so the file is written outside the intended directory within the disk image.

An authenticated user submits the same file element. The implementation resolves the full target path, sees that it falls outside the permitted base location inside the image, and refuses the write. A file element with a plain path under the base location is accepted.

citations.quote: write arbitrary files to the disk image via a .. (dot dot) in the path attribute of a file element.
Directory traversal vulnerability in virt/disk/api.py in OpenStack Compute (Nova) Folsom (2012.2) and Essex (2012.1), when used over libvirt-based hypervisors

patterns.title: Redirect responses accepting unvalidated URL schemes enable data: URL XSS
patterns.cause: The redirect response classes HttpResponseRedirect and HttpResponsePermanentRedirect in affected Django versions did not validate the scheme of the redirect target. A target using the data: scheme was therefore accepted, which might allow remote attackers to conduct cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks.
preconditions: Application runs Django before 1.3.2, or a 1.4.x release before 1.4.1
Application issues a redirect using HttpResponseRedirect or HttpResponsePermanentRedirect
The redirect target can be influenced by a remote attacker, so it may carry a data: URL
patterns.prevention: Validate the scheme of every redirect target before issuing the redirect, and only allow schemes the application expects, such as http and https. Reject or replace targets that use data: or any other unexpected scheme. Upgrading Django to 1.3.2, or to 1.4.1 on the 1.4 series, is the direction of the upstream fix. Where attacker-influenced targets are used, also prefer redirecting to known internal destinations rather than raw user input.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that the scheme of the redirect target was not validated and that a data: URL could lead to XSS. They do not describe which other schemes were affected, the exact browser behavior that makes the attack work, or the details of the upstream scheme check. The advice to prefer known internal destinations is a general hardening suggestion and is not taken from the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A view takes a destination from a request parameter and passes it directly to HttpResponseRedirect on Django 1.4.0. An attacker supplies a data: URL as the destination, and the response redirects to it without any scheme check.

A view takes a destination from a request parameter and checks that its scheme is on an allowlist of http and https before calling HttpResponseRedirect. A data: URL is rejected, and the application falls back to a default internal page. The project also runs Django 1.4.1 or later.

citations.quote: do not validate the scheme of a redirect target, which might allow remote attackers to conduct cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks via a data: URL.
Django before 1.3.2 and 1.4.x before 1.4.1 do not validate the scheme of a redirect target

patterns.title: Unsafe pickle deserialization of memcached metadata in OpenStack Swift
patterns.cause: Swift before 1.7.0 used the loads function of the pickle Python module to read metadata that it had stored in and loaded from memcached. Pickle data can carry instructions that run code when it is loaded, so a crafted pickle object placed where Swift reads it is executed as code instead of being treated as plain data.
preconditions: The Swift version is earlier than 1.7.0.
Swift stores metadata in memcached and reads it back by deserializing with the pickle module.
A remote attacker can get a crafted pickle object into the data that Swift loads from memcached.
patterns.prevention: Do not deserialize data from a shared cache with a format that can encode executable behavior, such as pickle. Store cached metadata in a data-only serialization format that can represent only plain values like strings, numbers, lists and mappings, and parse it with a loader that cannot instantiate arbitrary objects. Treat everything read back from memcached as untrusted input, validate that the decoded structure has the expected shape, and upgrade to Swift 1.7.0 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that pickle loads was used unsafely for memcached metadata and that versions before 1.7.0 are affected. They do not describe how the attacker reaches memcached, which metadata fields are involved, or the exact replacement format used in the upstream change. Other hardening, such as restricting access to memcached, is not covered by the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A Swift service older than 1.7.0 caches object metadata in memcached and reads it back by running pickle loads on the stored bytes. An attacker who can influence the cached entry supplies a crafted pickle object, and the service executes attacker-chosen code when it loads that entry.

A Swift service at version 1.7.0 or later caches metadata in memcached using a data-only format and decodes it with a parser that yields only plain values. A crafted entry in the cache is either rejected as malformed or read as inert data, and no code runs.

citations.quote: uses the loads function in the pickle Python module unsafely when storing and loading metadata in memcached
which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a crafted pickle object

patterns.title: Roundup XSS through the @action request parameter (CVE-2012-6131)
patterns.cause: Roundup before 1.4.20 handles the @action request parameter in cgi/client.py in a way that lets a remote attacker inject arbitrary web script or HTML. The advisories do not say which code path emits the value, so the exact output location is not known from these sources.
preconditions: The deployment runs Roundup before version 1.4.20.
A remote attacker can send a request to a tracker page, such as support/issue1, with a crafted @action parameter.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Roundup 1.4.20 or later. In similar code, treat the @action parameter, like any request parameter, as untrusted data. Encode it for the HTML context wherever it could reach a response, so that markup is shown as text and never run as script.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a one-line description. They do not name the output context, the exact code path, or the mechanism of the fix, so this card cannot say how the parameter reached the page or which encoding the project chose. They also do not say whether other parameters or other versions are affected beyond the stated range.

fixtures.scenario: A tracker running a Roundup version before 1.4.20 receives a request to an issue page whose @action parameter contains script or HTML markup, and the response lets that markup execute in the visitor's browser.
The same request is sent to a tracker running Roundup 1.4.20 or later, and the @action value is not rendered as active script or HTML.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via the @action parameter to support/issue1.
Cross-site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability in `cgi/client.py` in Roundup before 1.4.20

patterns.title: XML Entity Expansion denial of service via Python XML libraries in Django
patterns.cause: The XML libraries for Python, as used in Django and other products, are susceptible to XML Entity Expansion (XEE). A remote attacker can send crafted XML that makes the parser consume excessive resources and crash the process, causing denial of service.
preconditions: The application, including Django code paths, parses XML with the standard Python XML libraries.
The XML comes from a remote party who may be an attacker.
The runtime is one of the affected Python versions named in the CVE record (2.6, 2.7, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4).
patterns.prevention: Do not hand untrusted XML to a parser that expands entities without limits. Where possible, configure parsing so that entity definitions in untrusted input are rejected or not expanded, or use a parser hardened against entity expansion. Apply the vendor or framework update that addresses this issue. Treat all remotely supplied XML as hostile input.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact fix, the specific Django components or functions affected, or which parser settings are safe. They do not specify fixed versions. They describe only a denial of service (resource consumption and crash), not data disclosure. The advice above is therefore general and should be checked against the vendor advisory and the Python and Django release notes.

fixtures.scenario: A service accepts XML from anonymous remote clients and parses it with the default Python XML libraries on an affected Python version. A client submits a small document that triggers entity expansion, and the worker process uses excessive resources and crashes.

A service accepts XML from remote clients only after the parsing path has been changed so that entity definitions in untrusted input are rejected or not expanded, and the vendor update is applied. The same crafted document is refused and the worker keeps running normally.

citations.quote: allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (resource consumption and crash) via an XML Entity Expansion (XEE) attack.
The XML libraries for Python 3.4, 3.3, 3.2, 3.1, 2.7, and 2.6, as used in

patterns.title: Do not let XML parsers resolve external entities in untrusted XML (Django XXE, CVE-2013-1665)
patterns.cause: The XML libraries for Python, as used in Django and possibly other products, process an XML external entity declaration together with an entity reference in the input. A remote attacker who controls the XML can use this to read arbitrary files (CWE-611, CWE-200).
preconditions: The application parses XML with the XML libraries for Python, as Django does.
The XML comes from a remote attacker or another untrusted party.
The input contains an external entity declaration and a matching entity reference, and the parser honors both.
patterns.prevention: Treat all externally supplied XML as hostile. Make sure the parsing path does not honor external entity declarations when it handles untrusted input. Do this by configuring the parser, by rejecting documents that declare entities, or by using a parser that does not resolve them. Do not rely on the default behavior of the Python XML libraries. Check every place the application deserializes or parses XML from outside, not only one entry point.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which Django components or parsers were affected, what the upstream change did, or which Django releases are fixed. They also do not cover entity expansion denial of service, network-based entity fetching, or other XML attack classes. They say only that Django and possibly other products are affected, so other code that uses the same libraries may be at risk. The prevention direction here follows from the described cause and is not a description of the actual patch.

fixtures.scenario: A Django application accepts XML from an anonymous remote client and parses it with the Python XML libraries using default settings. The client submits a document that declares an external entity pointing at a local file and then references that entity, so the attacker can read arbitrary files.

The same application parses untrusted XML only through a path that does not resolve external entity declarations. A submitted document that declares an external entity and references it is rejected or left unresolved, and no local file content reaches the attacker.

citations.quote: allow remote attackers to read arbitrary files via an XML external entity declaration in conjunction with an entity reference
The XML libraries for Python 3.4, 3.3, 3.2, 3.1, 2.7, and 2.6, as used in OpenStack Keystone Essex and Folsom, Django

patterns.title: Stored or reflected XSS through URLField values in the Django admin URL widget
patterns.cause: The AdminURLFieldWidget in contrib/admin/widgets.py, used for URLField inputs in the Django admin, allowed remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML through a URLField value. The sources do not describe the exact rendering mistake.
preconditions: Django 1.5.x earlier than 1.5.2, or 1.6.x earlier than 1.6 beta 2
The Django admin is in use and a model field is a URLField rendered by AdminURLFieldWidget
An attacker can supply a value for that URLField
patterns.prevention: Run a Django release that contains the fix: 1.5.2 or later on the 1.5 branch, or 1.6 beta 2 or later on the 1.6 branch. As a general design direction, any URL value shown by an admin widget should be treated as untrusted data and not as markup. The sources do not say how the upstream fix does this.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only the affected version ranges, the component and the attack outcome. They do not describe the vulnerable rendering step, which URL values trigger it, whether the injection is stored or reflected, or which other widgets are affected. Guidance beyond upgrading cannot be confirmed from them.

fixtures.scenario: A site runs Django 1.5.1 with the admin enabled. A model has a URLField, and an attacker supplies a value containing script or HTML. The admin widget renders that value, and the injected content can run in an administrator's browser.
The same site runs Django 1.5.2 or later, or 1.6 beta 2 or later. The same attacker-supplied URLField value is no longer an injection vector through AdminURLFieldWidget.

citations.quote: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the AdminURLFieldWidget widget in contrib/admin/widgets.py in Django 1.5.x before 1.5.2 and 1.6.x before 1.6 beta 2
allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via a URLField.

patterns.title: Redirect URL validation that accepts non-HTTP schemes enables XSS (CVE-2013-6044)
patterns.cause: The is_safe_url helper in Django utils/http.py treated a URL's scheme as safe even when it was not HTTP or HTTPS. A redirect target using a scheme such as javascript: could therefore pass validation, which might introduce cross-site scripting or other vulnerabilities. The login view in django.contrib.auth.views was the demonstrated case.
preconditions: Django 1.4.x before 1.4.6, 1.5.x before 1.5.2, or 1.6 before beta 2 is in use.
The application relies on is_safe_url to decide whether a user-supplied redirect target is acceptable, as the login view in django.contrib.auth.views does.
An attacker can supply a redirect target that uses a non-HTTP, non-HTTPS scheme such as javascript:.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a patched Django release (1.4.6, 1.5.2, or 1.6 beta 2 or later). In any code that validates redirect or link targets, allow only the HTTP and HTTPS schemes and reject every other scheme, including javascript:. Treat scheme validation as an allow-list check rather than assuming any parsed scheme is safe. Fall back to a fixed, known-good local destination when validation fails.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe only the scheme-handling flaw and the javascript: example. They do not detail other bypass forms, how the browser or user triggers the payload, or the exact structure of the upstream fix. They do not describe any host-matching behavior of the helper. Applications with their own custom redirect validation are not covered by the advisory text.

fixtures.scenario: A site on an affected Django version uses the stock login view. An attacker crafts a login link whose post-login redirect parameter carries a javascript: URL. The validation helper accepts it because it only checks that a scheme exists, so the unsafe target is used for the redirect.

The site runs a patched Django release, or its own redirect check allows only HTTP and HTTPS schemes. The same login link with a javascript: redirect parameter is rejected, and the user is sent to a default local page instead.

citations.quote: treats a URL's scheme as safe even if it is not HTTP or HTTPS
which might introduce cross-site scripting (XSS) or other vulnerabilities into Django applications that use this function

patterns.title: Django MySQL typecasting flaw in FilePathField and IP address model fields
patterns.cause: The FilePathField, GenericIPAddressField and IPAddressField model field classes in affected Django releases do not properly perform type conversion. The advisories tie this to MySQL typecasting and label it a MySQL injection issue (CWE-89), so a value for one of these fields may not be converted to the expected type before it reaches the database.
preconditions: The application uses Django before 1.4.11, 1.5.x before 1.5.6, 1.6.x before 1.6.3, or 1.7.x before 1.7 beta 2.
A model uses FilePathField, GenericIPAddressField or IPAddressField.
The database backend is MySQL, since the issue is described as related to MySQL typecasting.
A remote attacker can influence the value that is used for one of these fields.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Django to 1.4.11, 1.5.6, 1.6.3, 1.7 beta 2 or a later release, depending on the release line in use. When writing or reviewing field code, make sure values are converted to the intended type by the application layer before they reach the database. Do not rely on MySQL implicit typecasting to normalize them.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the impact and attack vectors only as unspecified. They do not say which queries or inputs are exploitable, how severe the effect is, or what the upstream change does. The advisory title says MySQL injection, while the CVE text says unspecified impact. Whether other database backends are affected is not stated. The guidance above is therefore limited to upgrading and to converting types explicitly.

fixtures.scenario: A site runs Django 1.6.2 on MySQL. A model has an IPAddressField, and its value is influenced by remote user input. The field class does not properly convert the type of that value, so MySQL typecasting may apply to it.

The same site runs Django 1.6.3 or later on MySQL, where the field classes perform type conversion properly. Any custom code that handles these field values also converts them to the expected type explicitly before use.

citations.quote: do not properly perform type conversion, which allows remote attackers to have unspecified impact and vectors
Django Vulnerable to MySQL Injection
model field classes in Django before 1.4.11, 1.5.x before 1.5.6, 1.6.x before 1.6.3, and 1.7.x before 1.7 beta 2

patterns.title: Control characters in link schemes bypass lxml HTML cleaner blacklist
patterns.cause: The lxml.html.clean module in lxml before 3.3.5 used an incomplete blacklist when checking link schemes. Control characters inside a link scheme allowed XSS payloads to get past the clean_html function.
preconditions: The application uses lxml.html.clean, for example the clean_html function, to sanitize untrusted HTML
The installed lxml version is earlier than 3.3.5
The sanitized output is rendered in a browser for other users
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to lxml 3.3.5 or later. Do not treat a blacklist of dangerous link schemes as complete. Make sure the scheme check accounts for control characters embedded in the scheme, so such links are not judged safe. Where practical, also apply defense in depth to sanitized output.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the specific control characters or schemes involved, and they do not describe how the upstream fix works. They do not say whether other bypasses exist, or whether other cleaning APIs in the module are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A web app runs user-submitted HTML through clean_html from lxml 3.3.4. An attacker submits a link whose scheme contains control characters. The cleaner lets it through and the page serves it, enabling XSS.
The same app runs lxml 3.3.5 or later. The same link with control characters in its scheme is handled by the updated cleaner and does not reach readers as an executable script link.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to conduct cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks via control characters in the link scheme to the clean_html function.
Incomplete blacklist vulnerability in the lxml.html.clean module in lxml before 3.3.5

patterns.title: Stored XSS in Horizon Orchestration through crafted template resource names
patterns.cause: The Orchestration/Stack section of the Horizon dashboard, when used with Heat, handles content taken from a user-supplied template, including resource names, as if it were trusted. A crafted template can therefore inject arbitrary web script or HTML into pages that other dashboard users view.
preconditions: Horizon is a vulnerable release: before 2013.2.4, 2014.1 before 2014.1.2, or Juno before Juno-2.
Horizon is used with Heat and its Orchestration dashboard.
An attacker who is an Orchestration template owner or catalog can supply a crafted template.
Another user opens the Orchestration/Stack pages that show the template-derived values.
patterns.prevention: Treat every value that comes from an orchestration template, resource names included, as untrusted data. Encode such values for the HTML context in which they are rendered, and never mark them as safe markup. Rely on the template engine's default escaping and review any place that bypasses it. Upgrade to a Horizon release that contains the fix: 2013.2.4, 2014.1.2, or Juno-2 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact rendering location, the full list of affected fields beyond the resource name mentioned in the title, or how the upstream fix works. The encoding guidance above is a general direction, not a description of the actual patch. Template-derived values shown in other dashboards or in other contexts, such as attributes or scripts, are not covered by the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A user with the ability to supply a template uploads one whose resource name contains script markup. Another user opens the stack pages on an unpatched Horizon, and the markup is inserted into the page unescaped and runs in that user's browser session.

The same crafted template is uploaded to a patched Horizon, or to one that encodes template-derived values for HTML output. The resource name is shown as literal text, and no script runs in the viewer's browser.

citations.quote: allows remote Orchestration template owners or catalogs to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via a crafted template.
Horizon-Orchestration Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability through resource name

patterns.title: Untrusted network name in the Horizon Launch Instance menu script
patterns.cause: The Launch Instance menu in OpenStack Dashboard (Horizon) uses a client-side script, horizon.instances.js, that handles network names. A remote authenticated user could supply a network name containing web script or HTML, and the affected versions allowed that content to be injected into the page.
preconditions: Horizon is running an affected version: before 2013.2.4, 2014.1 before 2014.1.2, or Juno before Juno-2.
An authenticated user can create or set a network name that contains script or HTML.
Another user opens the Launch Instance menu, where the network name is handled by the horizon.instances.js script.
patterns.prevention: Treat every network name as untrusted data. In the Launch Instance menu script, show the name only as plain text and never let it be interpreted as HTML or script. Upgrading to a fixed release (2013.2.4, 2014.1.2, or Juno-2 and later) removes the known issue. Any similar client-side code that displays user-chosen resource names should follow the same rule.
patterns.limitations: The sources only give the affected component, the affected versions, and the injection vector (a network name). They do not describe the exact unsafe code path, how the payload reaches the page, or what the fix changes. The advice to show names as plain text is a general direction and is not taken from the upstream fix. Other places that display network names are not covered by the sources.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user names a network with a value that includes HTML or script markup. A second user then opens the Launch Instance menu in an affected Horizon version, and the name is processed by the menu script in a way that lets the markup take effect in the second user's browser.

The same markup-bearing network name is created, but the Launch Instance menu shows it as literal text, or the deployment runs a fixed Horizon release. The second user sees the characters of the name and no script or HTML takes effect.

citations.quote: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in horizon/static/horizon/js/horizon.instances.js in the Launch Instance menu
allows remote authenticated users to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via a network name.

patterns.title: Stored XSS via host aggregate name in Horizon Host Aggregates interface
patterns.cause: The Host Aggregates interface in OpenStack Dashboard (Horizon) handled a user-supplied host aggregate name in a way that let script or HTML in the name reach the browser as active content. The sources describe the result as cross-site scripting through a new host aggregate name, but they do not detail the exact template or rendering path.
preconditions: The deployment runs an affected Horizon version: before 2013.2.4, 2014.1 before 2014.1.2, or Juno before Juno-3.
An administrator-level user can create a host aggregate and supply its name.
The host aggregate name is later displayed in the Host Aggregates interface.
patterns.prevention: Treat the host aggregate name as untrusted data wherever the interface displays it. Apply context-appropriate output encoding at render time so markup characters in the name are shown as text and never interpreted as HTML or script. Keep the framework's automatic escaping enabled for this field and avoid marking it as safe. Consider also validating the allowed character set for aggregate names as defense in depth. Upgrade to a patched Horizon release.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which views, templates, or widgets rendered the name unsafely, nor whether the name was stored or reflected. They do not describe the patch internals. Input validation alone is not described as the fix, and the defense-in-depth suggestion about character sets is not drawn from the sources. The sources only name remote administrators as the injecting party, so impact on other users is not stated.

fixtures.scenario: An administrator creates a new host aggregate whose name contains HTML or script markup. The Host Aggregates interface in an unpatched Horizon version displays the name without proper escaping, so the markup is treated as active content in the browser.

An administrator creates a host aggregate whose name contains HTML or script markup. The patched Horizon version encodes the name when rendering, so the browser displays the characters as literal text and nothing executes.

citations.quote: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the Host Aggregates interface in OpenStack Dashboard (Horizon)
allows remote administrators to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via a new host aggregate name.
before 2013.2.4, 2014.1 before 2014.1.2, and Juno before Juno-3

patterns.title: Redirect URL safety check bypassed by leading whitespace in Django (CVE-2015-0220)
patterns.cause: The Django is_safe_url helper did not properly handle leading whitespace in a URL. A crafted value that begins with a newline followed by a javascript scheme could therefore pass the safety check. This enables cross-site scripting through redirect URLs.
preconditions: The application runs Django before 1.4.18, 1.6.x before 1.6.10, or 1.7.x before 1.7.3.
The application relies on the is_safe_url helper to decide whether a redirect URL is acceptable.
An attacker can influence the redirect URL, and can include leading whitespace such as a newline before a javascript scheme.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a fixed Django release (1.4.18, 1.6.10, 1.7.3 or later). In any custom redirect validation, do not trust a URL whose leading characters have not been handled explicitly. Make sure leading whitespace cannot hide a dangerous scheme from the check, and validate the exact string that will be placed in the redirect. Reject any redirect target that is not clearly a safe local path or an explicitly allowed host.
patterns.limitations: The sources only describe leading whitespace and give a newline followed by a javascript scheme as the demonstrated case. They do not list which other whitespace or control characters were affected. They also do not explain how browsers interpret such URLs, and they do not describe the details of the upstream change. Other redirect validation weaknesses are out of scope here.

fixtures.scenario: A login view reads a next-page parameter from the query string and validates it with the vulnerable is_safe_url helper. An attacker supplies a value that starts with a newline character followed by the javascript scheme. The check accepts it and the application issues it as a redirect target.

The same view runs on a fixed Django release. The same crafted value with a leading newline and a javascript scheme is rejected as unsafe, and the application falls back to a default local page instead of redirecting to it.

citations.quote: does not properly handle leading whitespaces, which allows remote attackers to conduct cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks via a crafted URL
The django.util.http.is_safe_url function in Django before 1.4.18, 1.6.x before 1.6.10, and 1.7.x before 1.7.3

patterns.title: Full pathname in filesystem URL of image location enables arbitrary file read or delete in Glance V2 API
patterns.cause: The Glance V2 API accepted a filesystem URL in the image location property that contained a full pathname. A remote authenticated user could point an image at an arbitrary file on the server and then read or delete it. The sources say this exists because an earlier fix for CVE-2014-9493 was incomplete.
preconditions: Glance V2 API from a release before 2014.1.4, or a 2014.2.x release before 2014.2.2
The attacker is a remote authenticated user
The attacker can supply a filesystem URL containing a full pathname in the image location property
patterns.prevention: Treat the image location value as untrusted input. Do not accept a user-supplied full pathname in a filesystem URL as a location for a stored image. Make sure the check covers every way a client can set the location through the V2 API, not only the case handled by the earlier fix. Upgrade to a release that contains the fix. Where possible, resolve the final path and confirm it stays inside the directory configured for the filesystem store before any read or delete.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the fix works, which code paths were missed by the earlier fix, or the exact validation used. They do not say whether other URL schemes or API versions are affected. The advice to confine resolved paths to the store directory is a general design direction and is not taken from the sources.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user creates or updates an image through the V2 API and sets its location to a filesystem URL holding a full pathname to a sensitive file outside the image store. The service accepts it, and a later image download or image delete acts on that file.

An authenticated user submits the same filesystem URL with a full pathname. The service rejects the location because it does not refer to a file inside the configured image store, and no file outside the store is read or deleted.

citations.quote: allows remote authenticated users to read or delete arbitrary files via a full pathname in a filesystem: URL in the image location property.
this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2014-9493.

patterns.title: Django admin readonly_fields model attribute rendered without neutralizing script (CVE-2015-2241)
patterns.cause: The contents function in admin/helpers.py let attacker-influenced script or HTML reach the admin page through a model attribute listed in ModelAdmin.readonly_fields. The advisories give a property as the example.
preconditions: Django older than 1.7.6, or a 1.8 release older than 1.8b2
A ModelAdmin lists a model attribute, such as a property, in readonly_fields
The value of that attribute can be influenced by a remote attacker
The attribute is displayed on an admin page viewed by another user
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 1.7.6 or later, or to 1.8b2 or later, where the affected function is fixed. In application code, treat any model attribute shown in a read-only admin display as untrusted data. Make sure it is HTML-escaped on output rather than inserted as markup.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, which other output paths are affected, or whether workarounds exist. They name only the contents function in admin/helpers.py and the readonly_fields case. The escaping guidance is general XSS practice, not a statement of what the patch does. Releases between 1.8 and 1.8b2 are covered only as the sources state them.

fixtures.scenario: An admin site runs Django 1.7.5. A ModelAdmin lists a property in readonly_fields, and the property returns text that includes markup supplied by a remote user. A staff member opens the change page, and the markup is interpreted by the browser as script or HTML.

The same admin configuration runs on Django 1.7.6 or 1.8b2 or later. The staff member opens the same change page, and the attribute value does not result in script execution from attacker-supplied markup.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via a model attribute in ModelAdmin.readonly_fields
Django before 1.7.6 and 1.8 before 1.8b2

patterns.title: Control characters bypass redirect URL safety check in Django is_safe_url
patterns.cause: The utils.http.is_safe_url function in affected Django versions does not properly validate URLs that contain a control character. A URL such as one beginning with a backspace character followed by javascript: can pass the safety check, which allows cross-site scripting through a user-supplied redirect URL.
preconditions: Django before 1.4.20, 1.5.x, 1.6.x before 1.6.11, 1.7.x before 1.7.7, or 1.8.x before 1.8c1
Application relies on is_safe_url to vet a redirect URL that a user can supply
An attacker can supply a URL containing a control character, such as a backspace before a javascript: scheme
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a patched Django release: 1.4.20, 1.6.11, 1.7.7, or 1.8c1 or later. In custom code that vets redirect targets, do not trust a URL that contains control characters. Reject such input or strip it before parsing, and validate the scheme and host of the normalized value, not the raw string.
patterns.limitations: The sources only describe the control character issue and give a backspace javascript: URL as an example. They do not list which other control characters are affected, and they do not describe the details of the upstream fix. The 1.5.x line is listed as affected without a stated fixed version.

fixtures.scenario: A login view redirects to a next parameter checked only by an unpatched is_safe_url. An attacker sends a link whose next value starts with a backspace character before javascript:, and the check accepts it.
The app runs a patched Django release. A next value with a leading control character before a javascript: scheme is rejected, and the view falls back to a fixed default redirect target.

citations.quote: does not properly validate URLs, which allows remote attackers to conduct cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks via a control character in a URL
Django cross-site scripting (XSS) attack via user-supplied redirect URLs

patterns.title: Stored XSS via heat template description rendered as form field help text in Horizon
patterns.cause: The Orchestration/Stack section of Horizon takes the description value from a heat template and uses it as the help_text attribute of a form Field. That value was not properly handled, so script or HTML placed in the description could be delivered to the browser of a user viewing the stack form.
preconditions: Affected Horizon versions: 2014.2 before 2014.2.4, or 2015.1.x before 2015.1.1
The attacker can supply a heat template whose description parameter contains script or HTML
A user opens the Orchestration/Stack section, where the template description is shown through the help_text attribute of a Field
patterns.prevention: Treat template-derived text, such as a heat template description, as untrusted data. Make sure it is escaped or otherwise neutralized for the HTML context before it is rendered as field help text, so markup is displayed as plain text and not interpreted by the browser. Apply this at the point where the value becomes a form field attribute, and do not rely on the template author being trusted. Upgrading to Horizon 2014.2.4 or 2015.1.1 or later picks up the vendor fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a short description of the flaw. They do not describe the exact escaping mechanism used by the fix, other template fields or pages that might be affected, or any mitigations other than the fixed releases. The scope of this card is limited to the description parameter and help_text handling named in the advisory.

fixtures.scenario: A user uploads or supplies a heat template whose description contains HTML with an embedded script. When the stack creation form is displayed, the description is placed into the help_text of a field without proper handling, and the script runs in the browser of the person viewing the form.
The same heat template is submitted, but the description is treated as untrusted text and is escaped when rendered as help text. The form shows the markup as literal text and no script executes.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via the description parameter in a heat template
which is not properly handled in the help_text attribute in the Field class
OpenStack Dashboard (Horizon) 2014.2 before 2014.2.4 and 2015.1.x before 2015.1.1

patterns.title: Untrusted input in JSON error messages for the IPython /api/contents path enabled XSS
patterns.cause: IPython 3.x before 3.2 did not neutralize input when generating web page content. Remote attackers could inject arbitrary web script or HTML through vectors involving JSON error messages and the /api/contents path. This is the CWE-79 pattern, where attacker-influenced text appears in a response without being made safe for the context that interprets it.
preconditions: The deployment runs IPython 3.x older than version 3.2.
The notebook web service exposes the /api/contents path to requests an attacker can influence.
A JSON error message produced for that path carries attacker-influenced content, and a victim's browser then handles it as web script or HTML.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade IPython to version 3.2 or later. In similar designs, treat any request-derived text placed in an error message as untrusted data. Neutralize or encode it for the context where it is consumed. Make sure clients treat error responses as data and never as markup or script. Review every error path of a content API, not only the success path.
patterns.limitations: The advisories give only a short description. They do not state which field or parameter carried the payload, how the browser came to interpret the error message, or what the exact code change was. This card therefore cannot say whether the fix encoded server output, changed response handling, or both. The only version boundary the sources give is IPython 3.x before 3.2. They say nothing about other branches or other endpoints.

fixtures.scenario: An IPython 3.1 notebook server receives a request to a path under /api/contents that triggers an error. The JSON error message includes attacker-supplied text, and a victim's browser handles that text as web script or HTML.
An IPython 3.2 or later server handles the same request. The error message content is neutralized, so attacker-supplied text is not interpreted as web script or HTML in the victim's browser.

citations.quote: inject arbitrary web script or HTML via vectors involving JSON error messages and the /api/contents path
Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in IPython 3.x before 3.2
Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation in IPython

patterns.title: IPython before 3.2: XSS through JSON error messages on the /api/notebooks path
patterns.cause: IPython before 3.2 did not properly neutralize input during web page generation. Attacker-influenced content could appear in JSON error messages tied to the /api/notebooks path, and that content could carry web script or HTML.
preconditions: The deployment runs an IPython version earlier than 3.2.
Requests reach the /api/notebooks path of the IPython web service.
Attacker-influenced input can end up inside a JSON error message returned for such a request.
A victim's browser handles that error content in a way that lets embedded script or HTML take effect.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to IPython 3.2 or later. In your own code, treat any text echoed into an error message as untrusted data. Neutralize it for the context where it will be shown, for example by HTML-escaping it before it is placed in page content. Do not assume that wrapping a message in JSON makes it safe to display.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a one-line description. They do not say how the issue is triggered, which handlers or fields are involved, or how the 3.2 release changed the behavior. They also do not say whether the browser interprets the response directly or only after client-side rendering. This card therefore gives general direction and does not describe the exact fix.

fixtures.scenario: An IPython 3.1 notebook server receives a request on the /api/notebooks path with markup in the part of the request that the server echoes back in a JSON error message. A user's browser then processes that message and the markup is treated as active content.
The same request is sent to IPython 3.2 or later, or to a service that escapes echoed text for its output context. The markup is neutralized and is displayed as plain text, so no script runs.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via vectors involving JSON error messages and the /api/notebooks path.
Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation in IPython

patterns.title: Django 1.8.x URLValidator ReDoS causing CPU exhaustion before 1.8.3
patterns.cause: The URL validator in Django 1.8.x before 1.8.3 (validators.URLValidator) can be made to consume excessive CPU by remote attackers. The advisory titles the issue a ReDoS, which points to regular-expression evaluation cost. The sources do not describe the specific input pattern or the faulty expression.
preconditions: The application runs a Django 1.8.x release older than 1.8.3.
The application uses validators.URLValidator, directly or through a feature that relies on it.
Input that a remote party can influence reaches the validator.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Django to 1.8.3 or later, the first release the advisories list as not affected. Until the upgrade is deployed, treat every code path that passes externally supplied text to URLValidator as exposed to CPU-consumption denial of service. Inventory those paths so they can be re-tested after the upgrade.
patterns.limitations: The sources say the attack vectors are unspecified. They give no triggering input, no details of the vulnerable expression, and no description of the fix. This card therefore cannot recommend specific input limits or pattern changes, and it does not claim that other Django versions or other validators are affected or safe.

fixtures.scenario: A public web form on Django 1.8.2 checks a user-submitted link field with URLValidator. A remote client submits crafted values that tie up server CPU and slow or block other requests.
The same form runs on Django 1.8.3 or later. The deployment inventory confirms that no environment still uses an earlier 1.8.x release for URL validation.

citations.quote: validators.URLValidator in Django 1.8.x before 1.8.3 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (CPU consumption) via unspecified vectors.
Django ReDoS in validators.URLValidator

patterns.title: Folder names rendered unescaped in the Jupyter and IPython Notebook file browser enable XSS
patterns.cause: The notebook file browser builds web page content that includes a folder name without properly neutralizing it. A folder name containing script or HTML is therefore interpreted by the browser as active markup instead of being shown as text. The affected releases are IPython Notebook before 3.2.2 and Jupyter Notebook 4.0.x before 4.0.5.
preconditions: The server runs IPython Notebook before 3.2.2 or Jupyter Notebook 4.0.x before 4.0.5.
A folder exists whose name contains attacker-chosen script or HTML.
A user opens the file browser view that lists that folder name.
patterns.prevention: Treat every folder name as untrusted data wherever the file browser puts it into a page. Neutralize the name for the context it is placed in, so the browser shows it as plain text and never parses it as markup or script. Prefer a text-only insertion mechanism or the framework's automatic escaping over hand-built markup. Upgrade to IPython Notebook 3.2.2 or later, or Jupyter Notebook 4.0.5 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say the flaw is in the file browser in notebook/notebookapp.py and is triggered via a folder name. They do not describe the exact rendering path, the escaping context, or how a hostile folder name gets created. They also note the issue was first reported as CSRF, which may be inaccurate. This card therefore gives general direction only and no details of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A shared notebook server contains a folder whose name includes an HTML script payload. A user opens the file browser, the folder name is placed into the page as markup, and the payload runs in the user's browser session.
The same folder name is listed in the file browser, but it is neutralized for its page context. The browser shows the literal characters as text, and no script runs.

citations.quote: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the file browser in notebook/notebookapp.py in IPython Notebook before 3.2.2
allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via a folder name.
Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation in Jupyter Notebook

patterns.title: Plone URL checking accepts crafted URLs containing script markup, leading to XSS
patterns.cause: Plone's URL checking infrastructure includes a method that decides whether a URL is valid and located in the Plone site. It can be given a specially crafted URL that carries HTML, such as a script tag opener or a javascript scheme, in plain or percent-encoded form. The URL is not rejected, so cross-site scripting can be achieved.
preconditions: A vulnerable Plone release is in use: 3.3.0 through 3.3.6, 4.0.0 through 4.0.10, 4.1.0 through 4.1.6, 4.2.0 through 4.2.7, 4.3.x before 4.3.7, or 5.0rc1.
An attacker can supply a URL value to the Plone URL checking method.
The URL contains a script tag opener or a javascript scheme, either literal or percent-encoded.
patterns.prevention: Treat any URL passed to the validity and in-site check as untrusted data. Reject a URL as invalid if it contains a script tag opener or a javascript scheme, in both literal and percent-encoded forms, before reporting it as a valid in-site URL. Upgrade to a Plone release that includes the upstream fix; 4.3.7 is the first fixed 4.3.x release named in the advisory data.
patterns.limitations: The sources name the vulnerable method only generically and list the four trigger patterns. They do not describe the exact fix, the entry points that reach the method, how the payload is rendered, or the fixed versions for the 3.3, 4.0, 4.1, 4.2 and 5.0 lines. A denylist of known patterns may not cover every encoding variant, and the sources do not say whether other markup is also affected.

fixtures.scenario: A request passes a URL containing a percent-encoded script tag opener, or a javascript scheme, to the Plone URL checking method on an affected version. The method does not reject it, and the script content can run in a visitor's browser.

The same request, with a URL containing a script tag opener or a javascript scheme in literal or percent-encoded form, is rejected as invalid by the URL check on a fixed Plone version. No script content is accepted as a valid in-site URL.

citations.quote: Plone's URL checking infrastructure includes a method for checking if URLs valid and located in the Plone site.
By passing HTML into a specially crafted url containing
Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in Plone 3.3.0 through 3.3.6, 4.0.0 through 4.0.10, 4.1.0 through 4.1.6, 4.2.0 through 4.2.7, 4.3.x before 4.3.7, and 5.0rc1.

patterns.title: Shell metacharacters in a font name reach command execution in Pygments image formatter
patterns.cause: The FontManager._get_nix_font_path function in formatters/img.py in Pygments 1.2.2 through 2.0.2 lets shell metacharacters in a font name lead to execution of arbitrary commands. The font name is untrusted input, and the affected code does not keep it from being interpreted as shell syntax.
preconditions: The application runs Pygments 1.2.2 through 2.0.2.
The image formatter's font handling on a Unix-like system is used (the function name suggests this, but the sources do not say so explicitly).
An attacker can influence the font name that is passed to the formatter.
patterns.prevention: Treat the font name as data and never as part of a command line. An implementation should avoid building a shell command string from the font name. If an external program must be consulted, pass the name as a separate, literal argument with no shell interpretation. It should also reject or constrain font names that contain unexpected characters. Upgrading to a Pygments release newer than 2.0.2 is the direct remedy implied by the affected version range. Do not let untrusted users choose font names.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only the affected function, the affected version range, and the attack vector of shell metacharacters in a font name. They do not describe the exact vulnerable call, which external program is involved, which release first fixed the issue, or how the upstream change works. The prevention guidance is therefore a general direction and not a description of the upstream fix. The sources also do not say how an attacker typically supplies the font name.

fixtures.scenario: A web service uses Pygments 2.0.2 to render code as images. It accepts a font name from a request parameter and passes it to the image formatter. A user submits a font name containing shell metacharacters followed by an extra command, and that command runs on the server.

The same service uses a Pygments version newer than 2.0.2, or only accepts font names from a fixed server-side list. A font name containing shell metacharacters is rejected or treated as a literal name that matches no font, and no extra command runs.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands via shell metacharacters in a font name.
The FontManager._get_nix_font_path function in formatters/img.py in Pygments 1.2.2 through 2.0.2

patterns.title: Unescaped exception messages in the Werkzeug debugger page enable XSS
patterns.cause: The debugger in Pallets Werkzeug before 0.11.11 builds its error page in the render_full function in debug/tbtools.py. A field containing an exception message could carry script or HTML that ended up in the page, so a remote attacker able to influence that message could inject arbitrary web script or HTML.
preconditions: Werkzeug version earlier than 0.11.11 is in use, directly or through a product such as Flask.
The Werkzeug debugger is active and renders its error page through render_full.
An exception message contains content that a remote attacker can influence.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Werkzeug to 0.11.11 or later. In any code that builds an error or traceback page, treat exception messages as untrusted data and apply output encoding for the HTML context before inserting them into the page, so that markup in a message is displayed as text and never interpreted by the browser.
patterns.limitations: The sources only name the affected function, file and version range, and the exception message field as the injection vector. They do not describe the exact fix, which other fields might be affected, or whether other deployment conditions matter, so this card makes no claims on those points.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs on Werkzeug 0.10 with the debugger enabled. A request makes the application raise an exception whose message includes attacker-supplied markup. The debugger error page inserts that message without encoding, so the markup runs in the browser of whoever views the page.
The same application runs on Werkzeug 0.11.11 or later. The same exception is raised, and the message is shown in the debugger page as inert text instead of executing as script or HTML.

citations.quote: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the render_full function in debug/tbtools.py in the debugger in Pallets Werkzeug before 0.11.11
allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via a field that contains an exception message.

patterns.title: Windows path traversal in Radicale filesystem storage backend via crafted request path
patterns.cause: The filesystem storage backend in Radicale before 1.1 on Windows lets a crafted request path reach files outside what the server is meant to serve. The advisory's example is a path that begins with a drive-letter-style component, /c:/file/ignore.
preconditions: Radicale before version 1.1 is in use
The server runs on Windows
The filesystem storage backend is in use
A remote attacker can send requests with a chosen path
patterns.prevention: Do not trust the request path when choosing a file location. Before any read or write, check that the final filesystem location is still inside the configured storage area, and reject request paths that point elsewhere, including drive-letter-style paths like the advisory's example. Upgrade to Radicale 1.1 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a one-line description and one example path. They do not explain the exact parsing or path-joining flaw, list other path forms that may be affected, or say how the upstream fix works. The checks above are a general direction, not a description of the actual patch. Whether non-Windows systems are affected is not stated beyond the Windows scope.

fixtures.scenario: A Radicale server before 1.1 on Windows uses the filesystem storage backend. A remote client requests the path /c:/file/ignore, and the server reads or writes a file outside its intended storage area.
