A Radicale server at version 1.1 or later, or an implementation that confirms the final location stays inside the storage area, receives the path /c:/file/ignore and rejects it without touching any file outside that area.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to read or write to arbitrary files via a crafted path, as demonstrated by /c:/file/ignore.
The filesystem storage backend in Radicale before 1.1 on Windows

patterns.title: Redirect target check in is_safe_url accepts URLs with basic authentication
patterns.cause: In Django before 1.8.10 and 1.9.x before 1.9.3, the utils.http.is_safe_url function could be fooled by a URL containing basic authentication. A target that looks like it points to the local site but actually leads to an attacker's host could be accepted as safe.
preconditions: The application runs Django before 1.8.10, or a 1.9.x release before 1.9.3
The application uses is_safe_url to decide whether a redirect target is trusted
An attacker can influence the redirect target, for example through a link the victim follows
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 1.8.10, 1.9.3 or later. Treat redirect targets as untrusted input. Do not accept a target just because it starts with the expected host name. Reject targets that embed credentials, and fall back to a fixed local default when validation fails.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works internally, which other URL forms are affected, or how the XSS outcome occurs. They say only that XSS is possible. The sources also do not say which application views pass user input to is_safe_url. Only the demonstrated URL form is documented.

fixtures.scenario: An application takes a user-supplied redirect target and checks it with is_safe_url on Django 1.9.2. An attacker supplies a URL like http://mysite.example.com\@attacker.com, the check passes, and the victim is sent to the attacker's site.

The application runs Django 1.9.3 or later, or 1.8.10 or later, and still validates the redirect target. A URL containing basic authentication is not trusted, and the user is sent to a default local page.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to redirect users to arbitrary web sites and conduct phishing attacks
via a URL containing basic authentication, as demonstrated by `http://mysite.example.com\@attacker.com`.
Django before 1.8.10 and 1.9.x before 1.9.3

patterns.title: Authenticated users injecting AngularJS templates through Horizon dashboard forms (CVE-2016-4428)
patterns.cause: Horizon 8.0.1 and earlier, and 9.0.0 through 9.0.1, let a remote authenticated user inject an AngularJS template through a dashboard form. The injected content was then handled as script or HTML in the browser instead of as inert text, which is cross-site scripting (CWE-79).
preconditions: The deployment runs an affected Horizon version: 8.0.1 or earlier, or 9.0.0 through 9.0.1.
The attacker is an authenticated user who can submit values through a dashboard form.
The submitted value is later rendered in a page where an AngularJS template can take effect.
patterns.prevention: Treat every value entered in a dashboard form as plain data and never let it be interpreted as an AngularJS template or as markup. Where user-supplied text is shown in a page that AngularJS processes, make sure the framework does not evaluate it as a template. Upgrade Horizon to a release that includes the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a one-sentence description. They do not name the vulnerable form, field or template, and they do not describe how the upstream fix works. The prevention direction here is therefore general. They do not say whether the payload is stored or reflected, and they do not give the first fixed release number. Check the vendor advisory and release notes for those details.

fixtures.scenario: A user with a valid Horizon login enters text containing an AngularJS template into a dashboard form field. The page that later displays the value lets AngularJS process it, so attacker-chosen script or HTML runs in the browser of whoever views that page.

A user enters the same template-like text into the same form field. The page shows it as literal text, AngularJS does not evaluate it, and no script or HTML from the input runs in any viewer's browser.

citations.quote: allows remote authenticated users to inject arbitrary web script or HTML by injecting an AngularJS template in a dashboard form.
OpenStack Dashboard (Horizon) 8.0.1 and earlier and 9.0.0 through 9.0.1

patterns.title: Admin related-object popup callback inserting data through Element.innerHTML (Django XSS)
patterns.cause: The dismissChangeRelatedObjectPopup function in the Django admin script RelatedObjectLookups.js made unsafe use of Element.innerHTML. Markup in data handled by that function could be interpreted as HTML or script by the browser instead of being treated as plain text.
preconditions: The application runs Django before 1.8.14, a 1.9.x release before 1.9.8, or a 1.10.x release before 1.10rc1.
The Django admin is in use and serves the RelatedObjectLookups.js script.
Attacker-influenced data reaches the Element.innerHTML usage inside dismissChangeRelatedObjectPopup.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 1.8.14, 1.9.8, 1.10rc1 or later, which address this issue. In any custom admin JavaScript derived from this file, do not build page content from data by assigning it to Element.innerHTML. Write such data into the page in a way that the browser treats as text, not markup.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which input an attacker controls, how the popup flow is triggered, or what the upstream change does. They also do not describe any workaround other than moving to fixed releases. The text-insertion guidance above is a general direction and is not taken from the advisory wording.

fixtures.scenario: A site runs Django 1.9.7 with the admin enabled. Data containing HTML markup reaches the related-object popup dismissal handling, and the script places it into the page through Element.innerHTML, so the browser runs the injected script in the admin user's session.
A site runs Django 1.9.8 or later, or a project with customized admin scripts that avoid Element.innerHTML for data. The same markup-bearing data is shown as inert text and no script runs.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via vectors involving unsafe usage of Element.innerHTML.
Django before 1.8.14, 1.9.x before 1.9.8, and 1.10.x before 1.10rc1

patterns.title: Unsanitized fact variables from the Ansible controller allow command execution on clients
patterns.cause: Ansible before version 2.2.0 did not properly sanitize fact variables sent from the controller to its clients. Specially crafted variable values could therefore be treated as commands instead of plain data.
preconditions: The deployment runs Ansible before version 2.2.0.
Fact variables are sent from the Ansible controller to Ansible clients.
An attacker can create special variables on the controller.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Ansible 2.2.0 or later, which is the first version not listed as affected. In any similar design, treat variable and fact values that cross from a controller to a client as untrusted data. Sanitize them before they can influence command execution, so a value can never be interpreted as a command. Also limit who can create or modify variables on the controller, since that ability is the attacker's entry point.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the vulnerable code path, the characters or constructs that are dangerous, or how the fix sanitizes values. They give no workaround for systems that cannot upgrade. This card therefore stays at the level of direction and does not describe the exact validation to apply.

fixtures.scenario: A controller running Ansible before 2.2.0 sends fact variables to a client. An attacker who can create a special variable on the controller supplies a crafted value, and the client runs arbitrary commands as the user Ansible runs as.

The controller and clients run Ansible 2.2.0 or later, and fact variables received from the controller are sanitized. A crafted variable value is handled as data and no arbitrary command runs on the client.

citations.quote: Ansible before version 2.2.0 fails to properly sanitize fact variables sent from the Ansible controller.
An attacker with the ability to create special variables on the controller could execute arbitrary commands on Ansible clients as the user Ansible runs as.

patterns.title: Open redirect through the came_from parameter after Plone login
patterns.cause: After a login-required visit, Plone sends the user to the login form with a came_from parameter holding the previous URL, then redirects back to it after login. Plone already used a same-site check to block most malicious values. A few more ways of tricking that check into accepting a malicious link were found, so a crafted came_from value could still send an authenticated user to an attacker's site.
preconditions: The application redirects to a came_from style URL taken from the request after a successful login.
The only protection is a same-site check on that URL, and the check can be fooled by crafted links.
An attacker can get a user to click a specially crafted link that leads to the login form.
The deployment runs an affected Plone version (2.5 through 5.1rc1) without the hotfix.
patterns.prevention: Treat the came_from value as untrusted input. Before redirecting, confirm that it points to a page on the same Plone site, using a same-site check that is hardened against crafted links. Apply the vendor hotfix or upgrade past the affected versions. Where the check cannot be trusted, fall back to a fixed default landing page rather than the supplied value.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe which crafted link forms bypassed the original check or how the hotfix changes the check, so this card cannot list specific bypass patterns. They also do not say whether other redirect parameters are affected. They name only Plone 2.5 through 5.1rc1 as affected.

fixtures.scenario: A user opens a link to the Plone login form whose came_from value is crafted so the same-site check accepts it, although it points to an attacker's site. The user logs in and is redirected to the attacker's page, which looks like the original site.

The same crafted link is used against a site with the hardened same-site check. The came_from value is rejected, so the user lands on a page inside the Plone site after login and is not sent to the attacker's site.

citations.quote: Plone 2.5-5.1rc1 sends you to the login form with a 'came_from' parameter set to the previous url.
You would login, and get redirected to the site of the attacker, letting you think that you are still on the original Plone site.
But a few more ways of tricking Plone into accepting a malicious link were discovered, and fixed with this hotfix.

patterns.title: Stored XSS via user-controlled profile home page link
patterns.cause: A member profile property named home_page accepted a javascript value, and the author page rendered it as a link target. When a visitor clicked the home page link, the script ran in the visitor's browser.
preconditions: The application lets members edit a profile property that holds a home page address
The property value is not restricted to safe URL schemes before it is rendered as a link
Other users view the author page and click the link
patterns.prevention: Treat profile fields as untrusted input. Before rendering a member-supplied address as a link target, allow only safe schemes such as http and https, and reject or neutralize javascript values. Apply the check where the link is rendered as well as where the value is saved, so that previously stored values are also covered.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact fix, so the specific validation or escaping used upstream is not stated. They name only the home_page property and the author page, and do not say whether other profile fields or views were affected. The advice to check at both save and render time is general guidance, not taken from the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A member sets the profile home page to a javascript scheme value. A visitor opens the author page and clicks the home page link, and the script runs in the visitor's session.
A member sets the home page to a javascript scheme value. It is rejected or neutralized, so the author page shows no active link and clicking never runs script. A normal https address still works.

citations.quote: A member of the Plone site could set javascript in the `home_page` property of their profile
have this executed when a visitor click the home page link on the author page.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS in certain Apache Airflow 404 pages
patterns.cause: Certain 404 pages in Apache Airflow could be exploited to perform a reflected cross-site scripting attack. The sources do not say which input was reflected or which code path produced the pages.
preconditions: A vulnerable Apache Airflow version earlier than 1.9.0 is running.
A user opens a crafted link that leads to an affected 404 page.
The user's browser does not block reflected XSS. Chrome detects the attempt and stops the page from loading, but Firefox and other browsers do not.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Apache Airflow to 1.9.0 or above, which is the mitigation the advisories give. In general, an implementation should treat any request-derived text shown on a not-found or other error page as untrusted. It should be encoded for HTML output rather than relied on a browser's reflected-XSS filter. The sources do not describe the upstream change itself.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the affected URL, parameter, template or handler, and they do not describe how the upstream fix works. They say only that certain 404 pages were affected. They do not describe versions before 1.9.0 in more detail, and they offer no workaround other than upgrading. Chrome blocking the attack is a browser-side behavior, not a defense the application provides.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow deployment older than 1.9.0 is used with Firefox. A user follows a crafted link that triggers an affected 404 page, and the browser does not block the reflected script.
The deployment runs Airflow 1.9.0 or above. The same crafted link to a not-found page no longer yields an XSS, and reviewers also confirm that error pages encode any request-derived text.

citations.quote: It was noticed an XSS in certain 404 pages that could be exploited to perform an XSS attack.
Firefox and other browsers don't, and are vulnerable to this attack.
The fix for this is to upgrade to Apache Airflow 1.9.0 or above.

patterns.title: Minion ID validation must reject directory traversal in Salt master authentication
patterns.cause: Salt's minion id validation was vulnerable to directory traversal. A remote minion could present a crafted minion ID and authenticate to a master even though its credentials were incorrect. The validation did not stop an identifier supplied by an untrusted peer from being treated as more than a plain name.
preconditions: A Salt master running a release before 2016.11.7, or a 2017.7.x release before 2017.7.1
The master accepts connection attempts from remote minions that supply their own minion ID
The attacker can send a crafted minion ID to the master
patterns.prevention: Treat a minion ID as untrusted input and validate it strictly before the master uses it for authentication decisions. Accept only a plain identifier and reject any value that could traverse directories. Upgrade to Salt 2016.11.7, 2017.7.1 or later, which address the flaw. In your own code that takes peer-supplied identifiers, apply the same rule: validate the identifier first, and do not let it select or alter a location outside the intended storage area.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say that minion id validation was vulnerable to directory traversal and that a crafted ID let a minion with incorrect credentials authenticate. They do not describe which files or directories were reached, the exact characters involved, or how the validation was changed. The exact checks to apply are therefore not specified here. Version coverage comes only from the advisory ranges.

fixtures.scenario: A remote minion connects to a vulnerable master with wrong credentials and a minion ID built to include directory traversal elements. The master's validation lets it pass, and the minion is authenticated.

The same minion connects to a patched master. The master's validation rejects the crafted ID because it is not a plain identifier, and the minion is not authenticated. A minion with a plain ID and correct credentials still authenticates normally.

citations.quote: Directory traversal vulnerability in minion id validation in SaltStack Salt before 2016.11.7 and 2017.7.x before 2017.7.1
allows remote minions with incorrect credentials to authenticate to a master via a crafted minion ID.

patterns.title: Disabled autoescaping in Django technical 500 debug page enables XSS
patterns.cause: In Django 1.10.x before 1.10.8 and 1.11.x before 1.11.5, HTML autoescaping was turned off for one portion of the template that renders the technical 500 debug page. Content rendered in that portion was not HTML-escaped, so under the right circumstances it allowed a cross-site scripting attack.
preconditions: Django 1.10.x earlier than 1.10.8, or Django 1.11.x earlier than 1.11.5, is in use.
Debug mode is enabled, which makes the technical 500 debug page accessible.
The 'right circumstances' named in the advisories are met; the sources do not say what they are.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 1.10.8, 1.11.5, or later. When writing or reviewing error-page and debug templates, keep autoescaping enabled for every region that renders dynamic data, and do not switch it off for a portion of a template unless the content is known to be safe. Do not run production sites with debug mode enabled, since that is what exposes the technical 500 page.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify which portion of the template lost autoescaping, which data reached it, or how an attacker would supply that data, so this card cannot describe the exploit path. They also say most production sites should be unaffected because debug mode should be off there. They do not describe the upstream changes, so this card gives only the general direction of the fix.

fixtures.scenario: A project runs Django 1.11.4 with debug mode enabled. An error produces the technical 500 page, and a portion of that page's template renders with autoescaping disabled, so content that should have been HTML-escaped is emitted raw into the page.

A project runs Django 1.11.5 or later, or 1.10.8 or later, where autoescaping is no longer disabled in that portion of the debug page template. Production also keeps debug mode off, so the technical 500 page is not reachable.

citations.quote: HTML autoescaping was disabled in a portion of the template for the technical 500 debug page.
Given the right circumstances, this allowed a cross-site scripting attack.
This vulnerability shouldn't affect most production sites

patterns.title: Incomplete minion ID validation allows directory traversal and authentication bypass on a Salt master
patterns.cause: The Salt master validated the minion ID supplied by a remote minion, but the validation was incomplete and a crafted minion ID could still perform directory traversal. A minion with incorrect credentials could then authenticate to the master. The advisory says this was an incomplete fix for CVE-2017-12791.
preconditions: A Salt master accepts a minion ID chosen by a remote minion.
The master runs a release before 2016.3.8, 2016.11.8 (2016.11.x line), or 2017.7.2 (2017.7.x line).
The minion ID validation does not fully reject crafted IDs, for example because an earlier fix for CVE-2017-12791 covered only some cases.
patterns.prevention: Treat the minion ID as untrusted input and validate it strictly before it is used for authentication or anywhere else. Accept only a conservative set of identifier characters and reject anything that could be read as a path component. When an earlier traversal fix exists, review it for gaps and test it against varied crafted IDs, not only the original exploit string. Upgrade to a release that contains the corrected validation.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which crafted ID forms bypass the earlier fix. They do not say which files or directories the ID reaches, or exactly how traversal leads to authentication. This card therefore gives only general guidance on validating the ID and cannot list specific rejected patterns. Backported fixes in other branches or distribution packages are not covered.

fixtures.scenario: A remote minion with incorrect credentials connects to a master on an affected version and presents a crafted minion ID. The incomplete validation lets the ID through and the minion authenticates to the master.
The master runs a fixed release with complete minion ID validation. The same crafted ID is rejected, so a minion with incorrect credentials cannot authenticate.

citations.quote: Directory traversal vulnerability in minion id validation in SaltStack Salt before 2016.3.8, 2016.11.x before 2016.11.8, and 2017.7.x before 2017.7.2
allows remote minions with incorrect credentials to authenticate to a master via a crafted minion ID.
this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2017-12791.

patterns.title: Mistune XSS via newline in link scheme and crafted email autolinks
patterns.cause: Mistune 0.7.4 mishandled input in its escape and autolink functions. An unexpected newline inside a scheme-like string, such as one splitting the word javascript, or a crafted email address could produce output that leads to cross-site scripting.
preconditions: The application renders untrusted Markdown with Mistune 0.7.4
The rendered HTML is served to users in a browser
Autolinks or links in the input are converted to HTML without further sanitization
patterns.prevention: Do not render untrusted Markdown with the affected 0.7.4 release without extra protection. Treat link targets and email autolinks as hostile. Make escaping and autolink handling robust to embedded newlines, so a scheme split across lines is not treated as harmless. Escape email-derived text before placing it in HTML. Sanitize the final HTML output as defense in depth.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say version 0.7.4 is affected and name the escape and autolink functions. They do not give the fixed version, the exact payloads, or the precise code change, so the details of a complete fix are unspecified here.

fixtures.scenario: A web app renders user comments with Mistune 0.7.4. A comment has a link whose target splits the word javascript across two lines. The output keeps the link and a click may run script in the viewer's browser.
The same app uses a release that is not 0.7.4 and sanitizes the final HTML. The split-scheme link and a crafted email autolink are neutralized or escaped, so no script runs when a viewer clicks.

citations.quote: mistune.py in Mistune 0.7.4 allows XSS via an unexpected newline
or a crafted email address, related to the escape and autolink functions.

patterns.title: Directory traversal through the static file route in Sanic before 0.5.1
patterns.cause: Sanic before 0.5.1 allowed arbitrary file reads through directory traversal. The advisories demonstrate it with a request path containing the substring /static/..%2f, so a crafted URL under the static route could reach files outside the intended directory.
preconditions: The application runs Sanic before version 0.5.1.
The application serves files through a static route such as /static.
An attacker can send a request path containing an encoded traversal sequence such as ..%2f.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Sanic 0.5.1 or later. In any code that maps URL paths to files, treat the request path as untrusted, including percent-encoded separators. Resolve the final file location to its canonical form and confirm it stays inside the configured static directory before opening it. Reject the request if it does not. Add a regression test that sends a path like /static/..%2f and expects a rejection.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say that versions before 0.5.1 allow arbitrary file reads and give one example substring. They do not describe the internal root cause, how the fix works, or whether other encodings or routes were affected. The canonicalize-and-confine approach is a general defensive direction, not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs Sanic 0.5.0 with a static route. A client requests a path beginning with /static/..%2f followed by the name of a file outside the static directory, and the server returns that file's contents.

A service runs Sanic 0.5.1 or later. The same request containing /static/..%2f is rejected or does not return any file outside the static directory, while normal requests for files inside the directory still work.

citations.quote: Sanic before 0.5.1 allows reading arbitrary files with directory traversal, as demonstrated by the /static/..%2f substring.

patterns.title: Unescaped key argument in Mistune _keyify enables XSS
patterns.cause: In Mistune before 0.8.1, the _keyify function in mistune.py does not escape its key argument. Attacker-influenced text that reaches this argument can carry web script or HTML into the output.
preconditions: The application uses Mistune before version 0.8.1.
Attacker-controlled content can reach the key argument handled by the _keyify function.
The generated output is delivered to users as HTML, for example in a web page.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Mistune 0.8.1 or later. In any code that handles key values like this, treat the key as untrusted data and escape it for the HTML context before it is placed in output. Do not rely on the key being harmless. Where practical, also sanitize or restrict the final rendered HTML for untrusted input.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which Markdown constructs supply the key argument, where the key appears in the output, or what payloads work. They also do not describe the exact upstream change, so this card gives only the general direction of escaping the key. Whether other Mistune code paths have similar gaps is not covered.

fixtures.scenario: A site renders user-submitted Markdown with a Mistune release older than 0.8.1. A submission supplies a key containing HTML or script markup, the unescaped key reaches the page, and the markup runs in a visitor's browser.
The same site runs Mistune 0.8.1 or later, so the key argument is escaped. The same submission appears as inert text and no script or HTML from the key is interpreted by the browser.

citations.quote: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the _keyify function in mistune.py in Mistune before 0.8.1
allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML by leveraging failure to escape the

patterns.title: Avoid arbitrary code execution from yaml.load() on untrusted YAML in PyYAML before 5.1
patterns.cause: In PyYAML before 5.1, the yaml.load() API could execute arbitrary code when it parsed untrusted YAML. Applications that deserialize YAML strings with this general-purpose loader, instead of the safe loading API, let attacker-controlled input trigger code execution (CWE-502).
preconditions: The application uses a PyYAML version older than 5.1.
The application calls the yaml.load() API.
The YAML input comes from an untrusted source.
The safe loading function, yaml.safe_load, is not used.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to PyYAML 5.1 or later, which contains the patch for this CVE. Version 4.1 was intended to carry the fix but was yanked because of breaking changes, so do not rely on it. Parse untrusted YAML with yaml.safe_load rather than yaml.load(). Treat the 5.1 deprecation of load() as a prompt to review every call site. Do not use the UnsafeLoader, which was introduced only for backward compatibility with the old load() behavior, for data that is not fully trusted.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which YAML constructs or tags enable code execution, so this card cannot list specific payload types. They do not describe the default behavior of load() in 5.1 beyond its deprecation, or the exact safety properties of UnsafeLoader. They give no guidance on trust boundaries for YAML that is considered trusted. Applications that depend on legacy load() behavior may need migration work, and the sources do not detail it.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs PyYAML 5.0 and parses YAML configuration or documents uploaded by external users with the yaml.load() API. A crafted document causes arbitrary code to run in the service process.

A service runs PyYAML 5.1 or later and parses externally supplied YAML only with yaml.safe_load. Any remaining uses of the legacy load behavior via UnsafeLoader are limited to fully trusted, internally controlled files.

citations.quote: In PyYAML before 5.1, the yaml.load() API could execute arbitrary code if used with untrusted data.
The load() function has been deprecated in version 5.1 and the 'UnsafeLoader' has been introduced for backward compatibility with the function.
PyYAML insecurely deserializes YAML strings leading to arbitrary code execution

patterns.title: Cross-site scripting in the MoinMoin GUI editor link dialogue
patterns.cause: MoinMoin versions before 1.9.10 have a cross-site scripting flaw in the link dialogue of the GUI editor. Remote attackers can inject arbitrary web script or HTML through it. The sources do not say which input, field or output path is responsible.
preconditions: The wiki runs MoinMoin older than 1.9.10.
The GUI editor and its link dialogue are reachable by users.
A remote attacker can supply input that reaches the link dialogue; the exact vector is unspecified in the sources.
patterns.prevention: Run MoinMoin 1.9.10 or later, since the advisories list earlier releases as affected. Because the sources do not describe the defect, do not assume a narrower mitigation. Until an upgrade is possible, treat the GUI editor link dialogue as an untrusted-input surface and review it for unescaped output.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say the vectors are unspecified. They do not name the vulnerable parameter, the context where script runs (stored or reflected), or what the fix changes. The sources do not say whether disabling the GUI editor is an effective workaround, so this card makes no claim about it. Review the upstream release notes before relying on any more specific guidance.

fixtures.scenario: A wiki runs a MoinMoin release older than 1.9.10. A user opens the GUI editor and uses the link dialogue. Attacker-influenced input is handled there and can result in script or HTML running in the victim's browser.
A wiki runs MoinMoin 1.9.10 or later. The GUI editor link dialogue is used in the same way, and the affected version range no longer applies.

citations.quote: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the link dialogue in GUI editor in MoinMoin before 1.9.10
allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via unspecified vectors.

patterns.title: Glance v1 copy_from URL enables masked internal port scanning (SSRF)
patterns.cause: The Image Service API v1 copy_from feature makes the Glance service fetch a user-supplied URL, such as one pointing at localhost on port 22, without restricting the destination. The request then appears to originate from the Glance service, so an attacker can probe internal hosts and ports while hiding their own origin.
preconditions: Glance before Newton with the Image Service API v1 enabled
The copy_from feature accepts a user-supplied URL when an image is created
The Glance service host can reach internal or loopback network destinations that the attacker cannot reach directly
patterns.prevention: Do not let user-supplied URLs drive server-side fetches to arbitrary destinations. Validate the target of any copy_from style URL against an allowlist or deny internal and loopback addresses and unexpected ports before the service connects. Alternatively, disable the v1 copy_from feature where it is not needed, and prefer API versions that do not offer it.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change, which versions or settings control the feature, or which address ranges and ports are blocked. They also do not cover redirects, DNS rebinding, or other bypasses, so those are not addressed here.

fixtures.scenario: An attacker creates an image through API v1 with a copy_from value of http://localhost:22. Glance connects from its own host, and the response lets the attacker infer whether that internal port is open.
The service checks the copy_from target against an allowlist and rejects loopback and internal destinations before connecting, so the attacker gets no signal about internal ports.

citations.quote: The 'copy_from' feature in the Image Service API v1 allowed an attacker to perform masked network port scans.
it is possible to create images with a URL such as 'http://localhost:22'.
the scan would appear to originate from the Glance Image service.

patterns.title: Open redirect via numeric URLs accepted by Django is_safe_url
patterns.cause: The redirect safety check django.utils.http.is_safe_url() treated some numeric URLs as safe when they were not. User-supplied on-success redirect targets could therefore send users to an unintended destination. A URL that passed the check and was placed in a link could also lead to XSS.
preconditions: Django 1.10 before 1.10.7, 1.9 before 1.9.13, or 1.8 before 1.8.18 is in use
The application takes a post-action redirect target from user input
The application relies on is_safe_url() to decide whether that target is safe
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 1.10.7, 1.9.13, 1.8.18 or later. Treat any user-supplied redirect target as untrusted and pass it through the safe-URL check before redirecting. Do not place a value into a link just because it passed the check; keep output escaping in place. Fall back to a fixed internal default when the check rejects a target.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which numeric URL forms were wrongly accepted, so this card cannot list exact bypass inputs. They also do not describe how the fix changed the check. Fixed versions are known only for the 1.8, 1.9 and 1.10 branches; other branches are not covered.

fixtures.scenario: A login view on an unpatched Django 1.10.6 reads a next parameter from the request. It passes the check in is_safe_url() and redirects there. An attacker supplies a numeric URL the check wrongly accepts.
The same view runs on Django 1.10.7 or later. It validates the next parameter with the patched is_safe_url() and redirects to a fixed internal default page when validation fails.

citations.quote: considered some numeric URLs "safe" when they shouldn't be
they could suffer from an XSS attack

patterns.title: Open redirect through the Django static serve view in unpatched releases
patterns.cause: In Django 1.10 before 1.10.7, 1.9 before 1.9.13, and 1.8 before 1.8.18, the django.views.static.serve() view could be made to redirect to any other domain by a maliciously crafted URL. The sources do not describe the internal mechanism.
preconditions: The site runs Django 1.10 before 1.10.7, 1.9 before 1.9.13, or 1.8 before 1.8.18.
The site uses the django.views.static.serve() view to handle requests.
An attacker can get a victim to open a maliciously crafted URL on the affected site.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Django to a patched release: 1.10.7 or later on the 1.10 series, 1.9.13 or later on the 1.9 series, or 1.8.18 or later on the 1.8 series. After upgrading, check that crafted URLs sent to the serve view no longer produce a redirect to an external domain.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say what makes a URL maliciously crafted, which request shapes trigger the redirect, or how the fix works. They do not mention workarounds other than upgrading, and they do not cover releases outside the listed ranges. This card therefore gives no input-validation guidance beyond applying the patched versions.

fixtures.scenario: A site on Django 1.10.6 serves files through the django.views.static.serve() view. A user opens a crafted link to the site and is redirected to an unrelated external domain.
The same site is upgraded to Django 1.10.7 or later. The same crafted link no longer sends the user to another domain.

citations.quote: A maliciously crafted URL to a Django (1.10 before 1.10.7, 1.9 before 1.9.13, and 1.8 before 1.8.18) site
could redirect to any other domain, aka an open redirect vulnerability.

patterns.title: Open redirect in Django CommonMiddleware on unpatched 1.11.x and 2.0.x releases
patterns.cause: The CommonMiddleware component of Django (django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware) contains an open redirect (CWE-601) in Django 1.11.x before 1.11.15 and in 2.0.x before 2.0.8. The sources do not describe the internal mechanism.
preconditions: The application runs Django 1.11.x earlier than 1.11.15 or Django 2.0.x earlier than 2.0.8.
The application uses django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Django to 1.11.15 or later on the 1.11 line, or to 2.0.8 or later on the 2.0 line, since the advisories mark every earlier release in those lines as affected. After upgrading, confirm the deployed version in each environment, including build images and pinned dependency files, so no unpatched copy remains.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only the affected version ranges and the affected component. They do not say which requests or inputs trigger the redirect, how severe it is, whether any configuration-only workaround exists, or whether Django releases outside the 1.11 and 2.0 lines are affected. This card therefore recommends only upgrading and does not describe the internal fix.

fixtures.scenario: A web application runs Django 2.0.7 with CommonMiddleware enabled in its middleware settings. It falls in the affected range and is exposed to the open redirect.
A web application runs Django 2.0.8 or later, or 1.11.15 or later, with CommonMiddleware enabled. It is outside the affected ranges named in the advisories.

citations.quote: in Django 1.11.x before 1.11.15 and 2.0.x before 2.0.8 has an Open Redirect.
django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware in Django 1.11.x before 1.11.15 and 2.0.x before 2.0.8 has an Open Redirect.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS via crafted URL in Flask-Admin 1.5.2 helpers module
patterns.cause: The helpers.py module in Flask-Admin 1.5.2 has a reflected cross-site scripting flaw that can be triggered through a crafted URL. The sources do not say which function or URL component is affected, or how the unsafe data reaches the page.
preconditions: The application runs Flask-Admin 1.5.2.
A victim opens a crafted URL that targets the affected code path in helpers.py.
The application serves the resulting response to the victim's browser.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Flask-Admin to a release that contains the fix for CVE-2018-16516. In your own code, treat any value derived from the request URL as untrusted. Escape it for the HTML context where it is output, and do not mark it as safe markup. Review any custom views or templates that reuse values from the URL.
patterns.limitations: The advisories give only one sentence and do not name the vulnerable function, the URL component, or the exact fixed version. This card therefore cannot describe the precise flaw or confirm that a given upgrade removes it. Check the project's release notes and the linked fix to confirm the fixed version. The output-escaping advice is general guidance, not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: An administrator of an application running Flask-Admin 1.5.2 follows a link in a message. The link is a crafted URL aimed at the helpers.py code path, and the response reflects attacker-influenced content that the browser treats as active content.

The application runs a Flask-Admin release that includes the fix for CVE-2018-16516. Custom views escape any URL-derived values on output, so a crafted URL is shown as inert text and does not run in the administrator's browser.

citations.quote: helpers.py in Flask-Admin 1.5.2 has Reflected XSS via a crafted URL.

patterns.title: Untrusted notebook XSS through nbconvert responses served without a Content Security Policy
patterns.cause: In Jupyter Notebook before 5.7.1, nbconvert responses are treated as having the same origin as the notebook server. The NbconvertFileHandler and NbconvertPostHandler in notebook/nbconvert/handlers.py do not set a Content Security Policy. JavaScript in an untrusted notebook can therefore run through the nbconvert endpoints with access to the server API.
preconditions: The deployment runs Jupyter Notebook before 5.7.1.
A user opens or converts an untrusted notebook that contains script content.
The conversion output is returned by an nbconvert endpoint on the same origin as the notebook server.
The nbconvert response carries no Content Security Policy.
patterns.prevention: Treat converted output from untrusted notebooks as active content that must not share the server's privileges. The fix direction is for the nbconvert file and post handlers to attach a Content Security Policy to their responses, so that script in the converted document cannot run with access to the server API. Upgrade to Jupyter Notebook 5.7.1 or later, where this is addressed.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not give the exact policy directives used in the fix. They do not say whether other handlers or content types need the same treatment. They do not describe other mitigations, such as serving converted output from a separate origin, or how well they work. This card covers only the missing policy on the two named handlers.

fixtures.scenario: A user asks the server to convert a notebook from an untrusted source that embeds JavaScript. The nbconvert endpoint returns the result with no Content Security Policy. The browser treats the response as same-origin with the notebook server, so the script can reach the server API.

A user asks the server to convert the same untrusted notebook. The nbconvert endpoint returns the result with a Content Security Policy that stops the embedded script from executing with server API access. The converted document is delivered without exposing the server API.

citations.quote: nbconvert endpoints can execute JavaScript with access to the server API.
NbconvertFileHandler and NbconvertPostHandler do not set a Content Security Policy to prevent this.
Jupyter Notebook before 5.7.1 allows XSS via an untrusted notebook because nbconvert responses are considered to have the same origin as the notebook server.

patterns.title: Cross-site scripting through crafted directory names in the Jupyter Notebook file listing
patterns.cause: In Jupyter Notebook before 5.7.2, the file browser script notebook/static/tree/js/notebooklist.js handles certain URLs unsafely. A crafted directory name can therefore lead to cross-site scripting (CWE-79).
preconditions: The notebook package is a version before 5.7.2.
A directory with a crafted name exists in a location the notebook file browser displays.
A user opens the file browser page, where notebooklist.js processes URLs that involve that directory name.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade the notebook package to 5.7.2 or later. In similar file browser code, treat directory names, and any URLs derived from them, as untrusted data. Handle them in a way that keeps them from being interpreted as active page content, and do not trust URLs built from user-controllable names.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say that notebooklist.js handles certain URLs unsafely when given a crafted directory name. They do not say which URLs or code paths are affected, which payloads work, or whether the fix uses encoding, validation or another method. They also do not say who can create such a directory or what the attacker gains. The general handling advice above is a direction, not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A notebook server runs a version before 5.7.2. A directory with a crafted name is placed where the file browser lists it, and a user opens the listing page, so the browser script handles URLs tied to that name unsafely.

A notebook server runs version 5.7.2 or later, or the listing code treats every directory name and derived URL as untrusted data. Opening the listing page with the same crafted directory name does not run attacker-supplied script.

citations.quote: Jupyter Notebook before 5.7.2 allows XSS via a crafted directory name because notebook/static/tree/js/notebooklist.js handles certain URLs unsafely.

patterns.title: lxml HTML cleaner misses escaped javascript: URLs, enabling XSS
patterns.cause: In lxml before 4.2.5, the lxml.html.clean module did not remove javascript: URLs that use escaping. An example is the spaced-out form j a v a s c r i p t: which Internet Explorer treats as a script URL. The cleaned output therefore still carried an active script URL.
preconditions: The application uses the lxml.html.clean module to sanitize untrusted HTML.
The installed lxml version is older than 4.2.5.
The cleaned HTML is rendered in a browser, such as Internet Explorer, that interprets the escaped form as a javascript: URL.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade lxml to version 4.2.5 or later. When sanitizing URLs, an implementation should treat escaped or obfuscated spellings of the javascript: scheme as equivalent to the plain scheme and remove them, rather than matching only the literal text. Test the cleaner with escaped and spaced-out scheme variants as well as the plain form.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which escaping forms the fix covers, which tags or attributes are affected, or how the fix works internally. The only demonstrated browser is Internet Explorer. The advisory says this is similar to CVE-2014-3146 but gives no further detail. Other XSS vectors are not covered.

fixtures.scenario: A comment form passes user HTML through the lxml cleaner on lxml 4.2.4. A link whose address is written as j a v a s c r i p t: with a payload survives cleaning and is shown to Internet Explorer users.
The same form runs on lxml 4.2.5 or later. The escaped javascript: link is removed during cleaning, and a test with escaped scheme variants confirms none remain in the output.

citations.quote: does not remove javascript: URLs that use escaping, allowing a remote attacker to conduct XSS attacks
This is a similar issue to CVE-2014-3146.

patterns.title: Stored XSS from edited metadata database objects in Apache Airflow page views
patterns.cause: Apache Airflow before 1.10.2 rendered certain page views from object state held in its metadata database in a way that let script content in that state run in the browser. A malicious admin user could edit that state to plant the script. The sources do not name the specific pages, fields, or templates involved.
preconditions: Apache Airflow older than 1.10.2 is in use.
An attacker holds admin-level access and can edit the state of objects in the metadata database.
Another user opens one of the affected page views, which displays the edited state.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 1.10.2 or later. In any similar application, treat values read from the metadata database as untrusted, even when only privileged users can write them. Encode or escape them for the HTML context where they are displayed, and avoid inserting them into pages as raw markup or script.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which page views or object fields were affected, nor how the fix works, so the output-encoding guidance is general direction rather than a description of the upstream change. The issue is limited to a malicious admin user, so it does not cover unauthenticated or low-privilege attackers. The sources give no workaround other than the fixed version.

fixtures.scenario: A malicious admin user edits the state of an object in the metadata database so it contains script content. A colleague later opens a page view that displays that object, and the browser runs the script in the context of the Airflow web interface.
The deployment runs Airflow 1.10.2 or later. An admin edits the same object state to include script-like text, and the page view shows it as inert text rather than running it in the viewer's browser.

citations.quote: a malicious admin user could edit the state of objects in the Airflow metadata database to execute arbitrary javascript on certain page views

patterns.title: Serve user files under a CSP header so they are treated as a separate origin (Jupyter Notebook XSS via SVG)
patterns.cause: Jupyter Notebook before 5.5.0 did not send a CSP header that makes the browser treat served files as belonging to a separate origin. A file such as an SVG document could therefore carry an XSS payload and be handled as part of the application's own origin.
preconditions: The application serves user-supplied or user-editable files, such as SVG documents, over HTTP.
The responses for those files carry no CSP header that isolates them from the application origin.
The deployment runs Jupyter Notebook before version 5.5.0.
patterns.prevention: Attach a Content-Security-Policy header to every response that serves a user file, so the browser treats those files as a separate origin from the application and not as trusted application content. Apply it in the shared file-serving path, so file types that can embed active content, such as SVG, are covered along with the rest. Upgrade to Jupyter Notebook 5.5.0 or later, which the advisories identify as the first version past this issue.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not give the exact CSP directives, the affected URL paths or handlers, or how the fix is implemented. They do not describe other file types beyond the SVG example. They do not say whether a CSP header alone is enough, or whether other mitigations such as a separate serving domain are needed.

fixtures.scenario: A notebook server of a version before 5.5.0 serves a user-uploaded SVG document with no CSP header. The SVG contains an XSS payload, and the browser treats the file as part of the application's origin.

A notebook server at version 5.5.0 or later serves the same SVG document with a CSP header that makes the browser treat served files as a separate origin from the application. The embedded payload does not run with the application's origin.

citations.quote: Jupyter Notebook before 5.5.0 does not use a CSP header to treat served files as belonging to a separate origin.
an XSS payload can be placed in an SVG document.

patterns.title: Browsable API templates with autoescaping disabled allow XSS in Django REST framework
patterns.cause: In Django REST framework versions before 3.9.1, the default Browsable API view templates disable autoescaping. Content rendered through those templates is therefore not HTML-escaped by default, so attacker-influenced data shown in the browsable interface can be interpreted as markup or script by the browser.
preconditions: The application uses django-rest-framework before version 3.9.1
The default Browsable API view templates are in use
Data that an attacker can influence is rendered through those templates and viewed by another user in a browser
patterns.prevention: Upgrade django-rest-framework to version 3.9.1 or later, where the default Browsable API templates no longer disable autoescaping. In any custom or overridden Browsable API templates, keep the template engine's autoescaping enabled so that dynamic values are HTML-escaped on output, and avoid turning escaping off for values that may carry user-controlled content.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that the default Browsable API templates disable autoescaping before 3.9.1. They do not identify which template fields or inputs are exploitable, give attack payloads, or describe the exact upstream change. Whether the Browsable API renderer is enabled in a given deployment, and whether custom templates are affected, is not covered and must be checked separately.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs django-rest-framework 3.9.0 with the default Browsable API renderer enabled. A user-controlled value reaches the default templates, where autoescaping is disabled, and a second user who opens the browsable page in a browser has the unescaped content treated as markup.

An application runs django-rest-framework 3.9.1 or later, and any customized Browsable API templates leave autoescaping on. The same user-controlled value is HTML-escaped on output and displayed as plain text.

citations.quote: allows XSS because the default DRF Browsable API view templates disable autoescaping.
Django REST framework (aka django-rest-framework) before 3.9.1 allows XSS

patterns.title: Authorization header forwarded on cross-origin redirect in urllib3
patterns.cause: urllib3 before 1.24.2 did not remove the authorization HTTP header when following a redirect that differs in host, port, or scheme. The issue exists because an earlier fix for CVE-2018-20060 was incomplete: it was case-sensitive.
preconditions: The application uses urllib3 before version 1.24.2
A request carries an authorization HTTP header
The server answers with a redirect to a different host, port, or scheme
The client follows the redirect automatically
patterns.prevention: Upgrade urllib3 to 1.24.2 or later. In any redirect-following code, compare the origin (host, port, and scheme) of the original request with the redirect target. If they differ, drop the authorization header before resending. Match the header name case-insensitively, because the earlier case-sensitive fix was incomplete.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say how the 1.24.2 fix is implemented. They do not cover other sensitive headers such as cookies, or how same-origin redirects are handled. They also give no detail on which header spellings bypassed the earlier fix.

fixtures.scenario: A client on urllib3 1.24.1 sends a request with an authorization header. The server redirects to a different host, port, or scheme, and the header is forwarded to that unintended destination, exposing the credentials.
A client on urllib3 1.24.2 or later follows the same cross-origin redirect, but the authorization header is removed before the request is resent, so the other host never receives the credentials.

citations.quote: does not remove the authorization HTTP header when following a cross-origin redirect
this issue exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2018-20060 (which was case-sensitive)

patterns.title: Unsafe pickle deserialization in Superset before 0.23 allows remote code execution
patterns.cause: Superset versions prior to 0.23 used an unsafe load method from the pickle library to deserialize data. Deserializing untrusted data this way can lead to possible remote code execution.
preconditions: The deployment runs a Superset version prior to 0.23.
A code path deserializes data with the pickle library's unsafe load method.
The data being deserialized can come from an untrusted source, as the advisory title Deserialization of Untrusted Data indicates.
patterns.prevention: Run Superset 0.23 or later. In any code that handles data crossing a trust boundary, do not pass that data to the pickle library's unsafe load method. Review other code paths that deserialize data in the same way.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which Superset features or data paths used the unsafe load, how an attacker could supply the data, or what replaced it in the fix. They also do not describe any mitigation short of upgrading. They note only that 0.23 was released before any Apache Software Foundation release of Superset, so version numbering may be confusing when checking affected installs.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs a Superset release older than 0.23. A component deserializes stored or received data with the pickle library's unsafe load method, so a crafted payload could trigger remote code execution.
A deployment runs Superset 0.23 or later. A review of the code finds no use of the pickle library's unsafe load method on data that an untrusted party could influence.

citations.quote: Versions of Superset prior to 0.23 used an unsafe load method from the pickle library to deserialize data leading to possible remote code execution.
Deserialization of Untrusted Data in superset
Note Superset 0.23 was released prior to any Superset release under the Apache Software Foundation.

patterns.title: Stored XSS from admin-editable metadata database state shown in Airflow page views
patterns.cause: Object state held in the Airflow metadata database can be edited by an admin user. That stored state is later shown on certain page views, where it can run as arbitrary javascript in the browser of whoever opens the page. The advisory classes this as stored cross-site scripting.
preconditions: The attacker is a malicious admin user who can edit the state of objects in the Airflow metadata database.
Certain page views display that stored state to other users.
A victim opens an affected page view after the stored state was modified.
patterns.prevention: Treat values read from the metadata database as untrusted, even when only admin users can write them. Wherever stored object state is placed into a page view, encode it for the HTML context it lands in, so the browser treats it as text and not as script. Review every page view that renders database-backed object state, not only the ones known to be affected. Upgrade to an Airflow release that includes the fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a one-sentence description. They do not name the affected page views, the object fields, the exact rendering flaw, or the first fixed version. The guidance above is therefore general output-encoding direction and not a description of the upstream change. The sources also do not say whether non-admin write paths to this state exist.

fixtures.scenario: An admin user changes the stored state of an object in the metadata database so that it contains script content. A second user opens a page view that displays that object, and the script runs in the second user's browser session.
The same modified object state is displayed on the page view only after being encoded for HTML output. The browser shows the content as inert text and no script runs for the second user.

citations.quote: A malicious admin user could edit the state of objects in the Airflow metadata database to execute arbitrary javascript on certain page views.
Apache Airflow vulnerable to Stored XSS

patterns.title: SQL injection through a crafted password in the Salt MySQL module user_chpass function
patterns.cause: The mysql.user_chpass function in the Salt MySQL module is vulnerable to SQL injection through a specially crafted password string. The sources do not say how the statement is built or which characters are dangerous.
preconditions: Salt 2018.3 or 2019.2 is in use, in a version earlier than the fixed release 2018.3.4
The mysql.user_chpass function from the Salt MySQL module is called
An attacker can influence the password string passed to that function
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Salt to 2018.3.4 or later. In code that sets MySQL account passwords, treat the password as untrusted data and never let it change the structure of the SQL statement. Keep values separate from SQL text, using the database driver's parameter handling or correct escaping for the value's context. Also restrict who can supply passwords to this function.
patterns.limitations: The sources give no detail on the vulnerable query construction, the exact fix, or which inputs are dangerous. They also do not say whether 2019.2 has a separate fixed version. The advice on handling input is general and is not taken from the upstream patch.

fixtures.scenario: A Salt 2018.3 master runs mysql.user_chpass with a password string from an untrusted source. The string is crafted so the MySQL server runs attacker-chosen SQL, which can escalate privileges.
A Salt release at or above 2018.3.4 runs mysql.user_chpass with the same crafted password. The password is handled purely as a value, so it is stored as the password and no extra SQL runs.

citations.quote: The component is: The mysql.user_chpass function from the MySQL module for Salt. The attack vector is: specially crafted password string.
An attacker could escalate privileges on MySQL server deployed by cloud provider. It leads to RCE.
The fixed version is: 2018.3.4.

patterns.title: Open redirect after login via crafted links to the login page
patterns.cause: The login page of Jupyter Notebook and JupyterHub could be reached through a crafted link that, after a successful login, sent the user's browser to a malicious site instead of a page on the same server. The sources do not say which input or code path caused this.
preconditions: Jupyter Notebook before 5.7.8 (the CVE record says before 5.7.7), or JupyterHub before 0.9.6 (the CVE record says before 0.9.5)
The server is not running under a base_url prefix, because servers with a prefix are reported as not affected
For JupyterHub, the user's browser is one of the affected ones (Chrome or Firefox); for Notebook, all browsers are affected
A user is lured into following a crafted link to the login page and then logs in successfully
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a fixed release of the notebook and jupyterhub packages (at least 5.7.8 and 0.9.6 per the advisory). In general, an implementation should decide where to send a user after login by checking that the destination stays on the same server, and should fall back to a safe default page when it does not. Pay particular attention to deployments without a base_url prefix.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the vulnerable parameter, the exact validation flaw, or the fix, so the redirect-validation guidance above is a general direction and not a description of the upstream change. The advisory and the CVE record give different fixed versions (5.7.8 and 0.9.6 versus 5.7.7 and 0.9.5); check the project release notes before relying on either. The sources do not explain why a base_url prefix avoids the issue, so it should not be treated as a mitigation.

fixtures.scenario: An unprefixed Jupyter Notebook server older than the fixed release receives a login link crafted by an attacker. The user logs in with valid credentials and the browser is then redirected to an attacker-controlled site.

The server runs a fixed release, or checks that the post-login destination stays on the same server. The same crafted link leads to a normal on-server landing page after login, and the user is not sent to an external site.

citations.quote: allows crafted links to the login page, which will redirect to a malicious site after successful login.
Servers running on a base_url prefix are not affected.

patterns.title: Open redirect in Jupyter Notebook via empty netloc in redirect target validation
patterns.cause: Jupyter Notebook before 5.7.8 could be made to issue an open redirect when the redirect target had an empty netloc. The sources say this was an incomplete fix for CVE-2019-10255, meaning the earlier redirect validation did not cover this case.
preconditions: The application is Jupyter Notebook before version 5.7.8.
A redirect target is taken from a request-supplied value and checked before redirecting.
The supplied target has an empty netloc, a case the earlier check for CVE-2019-10255 did not handle.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Jupyter Notebook to 5.7.8 or later. In code that redirects to a user-supplied target, make the validation handle a target whose parsed netloc is empty explicitly, rather than assuming an empty netloc is safe. Only allow redirects that are clearly local to the application. After fixing one bypass, re-check the whole validation path for similar variants, since this CVE exists because an earlier fix was incomplete.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not give the exact request format that triggers the redirect, the affected endpoints, or how the upstream check was changed. They also do not say whether other malformed targets bypass validation. This card describes the direction only and does not claim the full set of unsafe inputs.

fixtures.scenario: A Notebook server older than 5.7.8 receives a login or similar request carrying a redirect target that parses with an empty netloc. The earlier validation for CVE-2019-10255 lets it through, and the server redirects the user to a location the attacker chose.

A Notebook server at 5.7.8 or later receives the same request. Validation handles the empty netloc case, so the target is not treated as a safe local redirect and the user is not sent to an attacker-chosen location.

citations.quote: In Jupyter Notebook before 5.7.8, an open redirect can occur via an empty netloc.
This issue exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2019-10255.

patterns.title: Object.prototype pollution through jQuery deep extend in versions before 3.4.0
patterns.cause: In jQuery before 3.4.0, the deep-copy mode of the extend function mishandles a source object that has an enumerable __proto__ property. The copy can then extend the native Object.prototype, which pollutes the prototype shared by all objects.
preconditions: The application uses a jQuery version before 3.4.0, for example one bundled with a product such as Drupal or Backdrop CMS.
Client code calls jQuery extend in deep mode, with true as the first argument, to merge a source object into a target.
The source object is unsanitized and contains an enumerable __proto__ property.
patterns.prevention: Use jQuery 3.4.0 or later, and check that any copy of jQuery bundled with a product or framework is also upgraded. Do not feed unsanitized objects into a deep merge. Treat a __proto__ key in untrusted data as hostile and reject or strip it before merging.
patterns.limitations: The sources only describe the prototype pollution flaw in jQuery. They do not say how the pollution leads to cross-site scripting, and they do not state which Django components bundle jQuery or how Django changed. The upstream fix is not described here, and the sources give no other mitigation.

fixtures.scenario: A page runs on jQuery 3.3.1 and deep-merges a parsed request object into its defaults. The object has an enumerable __proto__ property, so the merge extends Object.prototype for all objects.
The page runs on jQuery 3.4.0 or later and removes any __proto__ key from untrusted objects before a deep merge, so Object.prototype is not extended.

citations.quote: If an unsanitized source object contained an enumerable __proto__ property, it could extend the native Object.prototype.
jQuery before 3.4.0, as used in Drupal, Backdrop CMS, and other products, mishandles

patterns.title: Unvalidated Current URL link in Django AdminURLFieldWidget enables clickable JavaScript links
patterns.cause: The AdminURLFieldWidget shows a clickable Current URL value and displays the provided value without validating it as a safe URL. A value that carries a JavaScript link therefore becomes a clickable script link in the admin page (CWE-79).
preconditions: Django 1.11 before 1.11.21, 2.1 before 2.1.9, or 2.2 before 2.2.2 is in use.
The admin renders a URL field through AdminURLFieldWidget, which shows the clickable Current URL value.
The displayed value is unvalidated, either stored in the database or supplied as a URL query parameter payload.
A user must interact with the rendered link for the script to run.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a patched Django release (1.11.21, 2.1.9, 2.2.2 or later). In general, an implementation that shows a value as a clickable link should first validate that the value is a safe URL. A value that fails validation should be shown as plain, escaped text and not as a link. This applies to values read from the database and to values taken from URL query parameters.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the flaw and the affected versions but not the exact validation rules, the permitted URL schemes, or how the upstream fix works. They do not say which users or pages are exposed beyond the admin widget, or whether other widgets are affected. Treat the safe-URL check described here as a direction, not a full specification.

fixtures.scenario: An admin change form for a model with a URL field renders the Current URL link from a stored value that uses a JavaScript URL scheme, or from a query parameter payload with the same content. The link is clickable and runs script when an administrator clicks it.

The same admin change form runs on a patched Django release, or the value is checked as a safe URL before being linked. A value using a JavaScript URL scheme is not turned into a clickable link and is displayed only as escaped text.

citations.quote: The clickable Current URL value displayed by the AdminURLFieldWidget displays the provided value without validating it as a safe URL.
an unvalidated value stored in the database, or a value provided as a URL query parameter payload, could result in an clickable JavaScript link.

patterns.title: Stored XSS via editable metadata database object state in Airflow page views
patterns.cause: Object state held in the Airflow metadata database could be edited by a malicious admin user. That state was then shown on certain page views in a way that let arbitrary javascript run. The same issue also exposed local files readable by the webserver process.
preconditions: An attacker holds an admin user role and can edit the state of objects in the Airflow metadata database
A page view displays that stored state to other users
The webserver process can read local files, which bounds what the file disclosure can reach
patterns.prevention: Treat every value read from the metadata database as untrusted data, even when only admins can edit it. Encode values for the output context of each page view so stored content is shown as text and never run as script. Do not let stored values choose which local files the webserver reads. Review every view that renders database-backed object state, not only one page.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the affected page views or fields. They also do not explain how the local file disclosure worked, or how the upstream fix changed the code. The guidance here is therefore general and may not cover every affected view. The sources also give no details on affected or fixed versions.

fixtures.scenario: An admin edits a stored object state in the metadata database so it contains script content. Another user opens a page view that displays that object, and the script runs in that user's browser.
The same edited state is displayed on the page view, but the value is treated as untrusted data and encoded for its output context. It appears as plain text and no script runs.

citations.quote: A malicious admin user could edit the state of objects in the Airflow metadata database to execute arbitrary javascript on certain page views.
This also presented a Local File Disclosure vulnerability to any file readable by the webserver process.

patterns.title: Archive extraction path traversal in NLTK Downloader packages
patterns.cause: The NLTK Downloader before version 3.4.5 mishandled entries in a downloaded NLTK package, which is a ZIP archive, during extraction. An entry name containing dot dot slash sequences could place files outside the intended location, so an attacker who controls the package contents could write arbitrary files.
preconditions: The NLTK Downloader of a version before 3.4.5 is used to fetch and extract a package.
The package is a ZIP archive that contains an entry name with a dot dot slash sequence.
The attacker can influence the package content that the downloader extracts.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade NLTK to version 3.4.5 or later. In any code that extracts archives, do not trust entry names from the archive. Before writing each entry, resolve its final destination path and confirm it stays inside the intended extraction directory. Reject or skip any entry whose resolved path falls outside that directory, rather than writing it.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that extraction mishandled dot dot slash in ZIP entries and that versions before 3.4.5 are affected. They do not describe the exact upstream change, other traversal forms such as absolute paths or symlinks, or what the downloader does with untrusted package sources. Those points are not covered here.

fixtures.scenario: A user on NLTK 3.4.4 downloads a package whose ZIP archive contains an entry named with leading dot dot slash components. During extraction the entry is written outside the data directory, overwriting a file elsewhere in the user's file system.
A user on NLTK 3.4.5 or later downloads the same package. Each entry is checked against the extraction directory, and the entry with dot dot slash components is not written outside it.

citations.quote: NLTK Downloader before 3.4.5 is vulnerable to a directory traversal, allowing attackers to write arbitrary files
in an NLTK package (ZIP archive) that is mishandled during extraction

patterns.title: Untrusted zone name used in a remote ps check allows command injection in solaris_zone
patterns.cause: The solaris_zone module checks the zone name by listing processes with the ps command on the remote Solaris host. The zone name is attacker-influenced input, and a crafted name can lead to arbitrary commands running on that host. The advisory title lists OS command injection and improper input validation as the weaknesses.
preconditions: The solaris_zone module from the Ansible Community modules is used to set a zone name on a Solaris host.
An attacker can influence the zone name value that is passed to the module.
The Ansible Engine version is 2.7.15, 2.8.7, 2.9.2 or an earlier version.
patterns.prevention: Treat the zone name as untrusted data. Validate it against a strict allow-list of characters and length before use. Do not let it be interpreted as shell syntax when the remote process check runs. Pass it as a plain argument or compare it against process output inside the module, instead of building a command line from it. Update to a release that contains the fix referenced for this CVE.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact vulnerable code, the specific characters that trigger the injection, or how the upstream fix works. The validation and argument-handling guidance above is general direction for this weakness class, not a description of the upstream change. The sources do not say which releases are fixed beyond naming 2.7.15, 2.8.7 and 2.9.2 and earlier as affected.

fixtures.scenario: A playbook takes a zone name from an external or untrusted variable and passes it to solaris_zone on an affected Ansible version. The module checks the name with a bare ps command on the remote host, and a crafted name causes extra commands to run there.

A playbook restricts the zone name to a short allow-list of plain characters before calling solaris_zone. It runs a patched Ansible version, so the name is never interpreted as shell syntax by the remote process check.

citations.quote: the zone name is checked by listing the process with the 'ps' bare command on the remote machine
An attacker could take advantage of this flaw by crafting the name of the zone and executing arbitrary commands in the remote host.

patterns.title: Path traversal via Content-Disposition filename in pip URL installs
patterns.cause: When pip installed from a URL, it took the download filename from the Content-Disposition response header. That header can contain ../ sequences, so the saved file could land outside the intended download location and overwrite files such as an SSH authorized_keys file. The sources place the flaw in _download_http_url in _internal/download.py. It was fixed in pip 19.2.
preconditions: A tool or installer is given a URL and downloads the file itself
The local filename is taken from the server-supplied Content-Disposition header
The header filename is joined to a destination directory without removing directory components
The process has write access to sensitive paths outside the download directory
patterns.prevention: Treat the filename from a Content-Disposition header as untrusted input. Reduce it to a bare file name with no directory parts or ../ sequences before building the destination path. Then resolve the final path, for example with os.path.realpath(), and confirm it still lies inside the intended download directory, rejecting the download otherwise. Upgrade pip to version 19.2 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so the checks above are general hardening direction rather than a description of that change. They also do not cover other filename sources, such as the URL path, or other attack vectors. Platform-specific separators and encodings are not discussed.

fixtures.scenario: A user runs an install command with a URL. The server replies with a Content-Disposition filename containing ../ segments. The client joins it to the download directory unchecked and writes outside it, overwriting a file in the home directory.

The same server reply arrives, but the client keeps only the final name component and confirms the resolved path stays inside the download directory. The file is saved safely there, or the download is rejected.

citations.quote: a Content-Disposition header can have ../ in a filename, as demonstrated by overwriting the /root/.ssh/authorized_keys file
This occurs in _download_http_url in _internal/download.py.

patterns.title: Ansible fetch module writes outside the destination when an absolute path is not restricted
patterns.cause: The fetch module in Ansible before 2.5.15, 2.6.14 and 2.7.8 did not restrict an absolute path. A path that should have stayed under the specified destination could therefore point elsewhere on the local controller host. This allowed files to be copied and overwritten outside that destination.
preconditions: The controller runs an Ansible version before 2.5.15, 2.6.14 or 2.7.8 (depending on the release line).
A task uses the fetch module to copy a file to the local controller host.
An absolute path is accepted without restriction when the local write location is determined.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Ansible 2.5.15, 2.6.14, 2.7.8 or later. In similar code, do not let an absolute path override or escape the configured destination directory. Before writing, confirm that the final local location is still inside the specified destination, and reject or neutralize absolute paths that fall outside it.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which input carried the absolute path, such as the remote source path or a destination value. They do not describe the exact upstream check, so the validation approach here is a general direction rather than a description of the fix. They give no detail on exploitation conditions, privileges, or other affected modules or versions.

fixtures.scenario: A playbook on an affected Ansible version runs the fetch module with a specified local destination directory. The path in use is absolute and unrestricted, so the file is written to a location outside that directory on the controller host and overwrites an existing file there.
