The controller runs a fixed release, or the fetch logic restricts absolute paths. The file is written only inside the specified destination directory, and a path that would resolve outside it is rejected or confined.

citations.quote: Ansible fetch module before versions 2.5.15, 2.6.14, 2.7.8 has a path traversal vulnerability
allows copying and overwriting files outside of the specified destination in the local ansible controller host, by not restricting an absolute path.

patterns.title: SQL injection through the order_by parameter in SQLAlchemy before 1.3.0b3
patterns.cause: SQLAlchemy releases through 1.2.17 and 1.3.x through 1.3.0b2 allow SQL injection via the order_by parameter. The sources do not describe the internal mechanism, so the exact flaw is not stated here.
preconditions: The application uses a SQLAlchemy version in the affected range: 1.2.x, or 1.3.x up to 1.3.0b2.
The application uses the order_by parameter in its queries.
Input that an outside party can influence may reach the order_by parameter (inferred from the injection description; the sources do not spell out the data path).
patterns.prevention: Move to a SQLAlchemy release that contains the upstream fix, which first appears in 1.3.0b3. The fix was applied only to the main branch and was never backported to the 1.2.x line, so staying on 1.2.x does not remove the exposure. Until the upgrade is done, treat any value that reaches the order_by parameter as untrusted and do not let outside input control it directly.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which inputs or API paths trigger the flaw, or what the fix changes. They also word the affected range differently: one says before 1.3.0b3, another says through 1.2.17 and 1.3.0b2, and a third says all 1.2.x versions remain vulnerable. Because of that, the exact boundary is unclear. The sources name only a beta release as fixed and say nothing about later stable releases. They give no workaround, so the interim advice above is a cautious inference, not a verified mitigation.

fixtures.scenario: A web service runs SQLAlchemy 1.2.x and builds a listing query whose order_by parameter is influenced by a request value chosen by the client. A crafted value could inject SQL, and no 1.2.x release has the fix.
The service runs SQLAlchemy 1.3.0b3 or later, which contains the upstream fix. Request values do not control the order_by parameter directly.

citations.quote: SQLAlchemy through 1.2.17 and 1.3.x through 1.3.0b2 allows SQL Injection via the order_by parameter.
all 1.2.x versions remain vulnerable.

patterns.title: Archive member names must be sanitized when extracting ansible-galaxy collection tarballs
patterns.cause: When ansible-galaxy installs a collection from a .tar.gz file, it creates a directory from a name stored in the archive without sanitizing that name. A crafted archive can therefore make the extraction step write outside the intended location.
preconditions: ansible-engine 2.9.x prior to 2.9.7 is in use
A collection is installed with the ansible-galaxy collection install command
The collection .tar.gz file is attacker-controlled or comes from an untrusted source
patterns.prevention: Treat every filename inside an archive as untrusted input. Before creating a directory or file for an archive member, sanitize the name and confirm that the final destination stays inside the intended extraction directory. Reject or skip members whose names would escape it. Upgrading to ansible-engine 2.9.7 or later is the vendor-side remedy implied by the affected version range.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a brief description. They do not say which sanitization method the fix uses, whether other member types such as links are affected, or which platforms are affected. The advice to confirm the destination stays inside the extraction directory is a general direction, not a description of the upstream change. Versions outside the 2.9.x range are not addressed.

fixtures.scenario: An installer on an affected 2.9.x version is given a collection tarball whose member names contain parent-directory components. It creates the directory from the unsanitized name, so extraction writes outside the collection install path and can overwrite an existing file on the system.

An installer sanitizes each member name and checks that the destination stays inside the collection install directory. When given the same tarball, it rejects the offending members and leaves files outside the install path untouched.

citations.quote: When extracting a collection .tar.gz file, the directory is created without sanitizing the filename.
An attacker could take advantage to overwrite any file within the system.

patterns.title: Stored XSS in the Wagtail admin page revision comparison view
patterns.cause: The page revision comparison view in the Wagtail admin can be made to run attacker-supplied script. A low-privilege editor crafts a page revision history, and the script runs in the browser of a higher-privileged user who views it. The sources do not say which revision field or rendering step is responsible.
preconditions: The attacker has a limited-permission editor account for the Wagtail admin.
A user with higher privileges opens the revision comparison view for a page whose revision history the attacker crafted.
The deployment runs Wagtail before 2.7.2 on the 2.7 branch or before 2.8.1 on the 2.8 branch.
patterns.prevention: Treat page revision content as untrusted, even when it was written by authenticated editors. Make sure every revision value shown in the comparison view is encoded for the HTML context it appears in, so it displays as text and never runs as script. Upgrade to Wagtail 2.7.2 on the LTS 2.7 branch or Wagtail 2.8.1 on the 2.8 branch. If an upgrade is not possible, the advisory's workaround is to disable the revision comparison view by routing its URL to a redirect to the admin home page, placed ahead of the other routes.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the affected field, the missing escaping step, or the code-level fix, so this card cannot confirm which output paths were unsafe. The redirect workaround only turns off the comparison view and does not fix the underlying rendering. The sources state that ordinary site visitors without admin access cannot exploit the issue. They say nothing about other admin views.

fixtures.scenario: A low-privilege editor saves a page revision whose content includes script-bearing markup. A superuser later opens the comparison view for that page on Wagtail 2.8.0, and the script runs with the superuser's credentials.

The same editor saves the same revision, but the site runs Wagtail 2.8.1 or 2.7.2, or the comparison route is redirected to the admin home page. When the superuser views the comparison, no attacker script runs and the content cannot act with the superuser's credentials.

citations.quote: A cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability exists on the page revision comparison view within the Wagtail admin interface.
could potentially craft a page revision history that, when viewed by a user with higher privileges, could perform actions with that user's credentials.
The vulnerability is not exploitable by an ordinary site visitor without access to the Wagtail admin.
Patched versions have been released as Wagtail 2.7.2 (for the LTS 2.7 branch) and Wagtail 2.8.1 (for the current 2.8 branch).

patterns.title: Command injection in an example DAG shipped with Apache Airflow
patterns.cause: An example DAG bundled with Apache Airflow 1.10.10 and below contained a remote code/command injection flaw. Any authenticated user could use it to run arbitrary commands as the user running the airflow worker or scheduler, depending on the executor. The sources do not describe the exact data flow inside the DAG.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version 1.10.10 or below is deployed.
Example DAGs are loaded, which is the default unless example loading is switched off in the configuration.
The attacker holds a valid authenticated account on the Airflow instance.
patterns.prevention: Do not load the bundled example DAGs in any deployment that serves real users. Turn example loading off through the load_examples configuration option, which the advisory says removes the exposure. Upgrade to a release newer than 1.10.10. When writing DAGs or operators, do not build shell command text from values an authenticated user can influence. Keep such values separate from the command, or validate them strictly, so they are never interpreted as shell syntax.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the vulnerable example DAG, the input an attacker supplies, or the code change in the fix. They do not say which release first contains the fix, only that 1.10.10 and below are affected. The general advice about handling user-influenced values in commands is a design direction and is not taken from the advisory text. Disabling examples only removes this particular exposure and does not address other command injection risks in custom DAGs.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 1.10.10 deployment keeps example loading enabled. An authenticated low-privilege user triggers the vulnerable example DAG and gets arbitrary commands executed as the worker or scheduler user.

An Airflow deployment has example loading disabled in its configuration, or runs a release newer than 1.10.10. The vulnerable example DAG is not available, so an authenticated user cannot use it to run commands.

citations.quote: A remote code/command injection vulnerability was discovered in one of the example DAGs shipped with Airflow
would allow any authenticated user to run arbitrary commands as the user running airflow worker/scheduler

patterns.title: Command injection through a directly reachable Celery broker in Apache Airflow
patterns.cause: With CeleryExecutor in Apache Airflow 1.10.10 and below, the Celery worker acts on what arrives through the message broker. An attacker who can connect to the broker (Redis or RabbitMQ) directly can inject commands, and the worker then runs them as arbitrary commands.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version 1.10.10 or below is deployed.
The deployment uses CeleryExecutor.
An attacker can connect directly to the message broker, such as Redis or RabbitMQ.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to an Airflow release newer than 1.10.10. Until then, do not let untrusted parties reach the broker: limit network and authentication access to the scheduler and the workers. Do not treat content received from the broker as trusted input to a command.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the injection mechanism, the message fields involved, or how the fixed releases change the worker. They do not name the first fixed version, only that 1.10.10 and below are affected. They say nothing about brokers other than Redis and RabbitMQ or about executors other than CeleryExecutor. Broker access control is a reasonable mitigation inferred from the stated precondition, not a measure the sources endorse.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 1.10.10 deployment uses CeleryExecutor with a Redis broker that other hosts on the network can reach. An attacker connects to the broker directly and injects a command, and a Celery worker runs it.
An Airflow deployment runs a release newer than 1.10.10. Its broker accepts connections only from the scheduler and worker hosts, so an outside party cannot connect to the broker to inject commands.

citations.quote: When using CeleryExecutor, if an attacker can connect to the broker (Redis, RabbitMQ) directly, it is possible to inject commands
resulting in the celery worker running arbitrary commands.

patterns.title: Celery worker deserializes malicious broker payloads in Apache Airflow CeleryExecutor (CVE-2020-11982)
patterns.cause: In Apache Airflow 1.10.10 and below, the default Celery worker configuration was insecure. A payload inserted directly into the broker could be deserialized by the worker, which allowed remote code execution on the worker.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version 1.10.10 or below
CeleryExecutor is in use with a broker such as Redis or RabbitMQ
An attacker can connect to the broker directly
patterns.prevention: Treat everything read from the broker as untrusted input. Do not let workers deserialize arbitrary broker payloads under the insecure default Celery configuration. Upgrade to an Airflow release that fixes the default worker configuration. Also restrict network access to the broker so that only trusted Airflow components can reach it.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact configuration change in the fix, the specific serializer settings, or the first fixed version. They also do not say whether broker authentication alone is enough. Network restriction reduces exposure but does not remove the unsafe worker default.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 1.10.10 deployment uses CeleryExecutor with a Redis broker reachable by an attacker. The attacker inserts a crafted payload into the broker and the worker deserializes it, which leads to code execution.

A patched Airflow deployment uses CeleryExecutor with a broker reachable only by trusted Airflow components. Workers do not deserialize arbitrary payloads, so a crafted broker message is not executed.

citations.quote: Insecure default config of Celery worker in Apache Airflow
if an attack can connect to the broker (Redis, RabbitMQ) directly, it was possible to insert a malicious payload directly to the broker

patterns.title: Unencoded query parameters in Django admin ForeignKeyRawIdWidget enable XSS
patterns.cause: The Django admin ForeignKeyRawIdWidget generated query parameters that were not properly URL encoded. This created a possibility of cross-site scripting (CWE-79).
preconditions: The application runs Django 2.2 before 2.2.13 or Django 3.0 before 3.0.7.
The Django admin is used with a field rendered by ForeignKeyRawIdWidget, which generates query parameters.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 2.2.13, Django 3.0.7, or a later release, where the generated query parameters are properly URL encoded. In custom code that builds URLs or query strings, encode every parameter name and value with a standard URL-encoding routine at the point where the query string is assembled. Do not concatenate raw values into URLs that are rendered in pages.
patterns.limitations: The advisories give no detail on which inputs reach the widget, where the injection occurs, or how an attack would be carried out. They do not say whether Django versions outside the listed ranges are affected, or whether other widgets share the problem. This card therefore stays at the level of the stated cause and the fixed versions.

fixtures.scenario: An admin site runs Django 3.0.6 and a model form uses the raw ID widget for a foreign key. The widget builds query parameters that are not properly URL encoded, so the page is exposed to XSS.
The same admin site runs Django 3.0.7 or later. The query parameters generated by the raw ID widget are properly URL encoded, so the XSS exposure described in the advisory does not apply.

citations.quote: Query parameters generated by the Django admin ForeignKeyRawIdWidget were not properly URL encoded, leading to a possibility of an XSS attack.
An issue was discovered in Django 2.2 before 2.2.13 and 3.0 before 3.0.7.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS through the origin parameter on Airflow endpoints such as /trigger
patterns.cause: In Apache Airflow before 1.10.12, the origin parameter passed to some endpoints, such as /trigger, was vulnerable to cross-site scripting (CWE-79). The sources do not say how the value was used or where it was rendered.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version earlier than 1.10.12 is deployed.
A user-facing endpoint such as /trigger accepts an origin parameter supplied by the requester.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 1.10.12 or later, the first version the sources do not list as affected. In your own code, treat any origin-style parameter as untrusted input. Do not let a request-supplied value become active markup in a page.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the other affected endpoints, the exact sink, the payload shape, or the fix mechanism. The advice to treat the parameter as untrusted is a general direction, not a description of the upstream change. Whether any other parameters were affected is unknown.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow deployment running a version earlier than 1.10.12 receives a request to the /trigger endpoint. The origin parameter holds attacker-chosen content instead of a normal return location.
The same request is sent to a deployment running Airflow 1.10.12 or later, where the origin parameter is no longer reported as vulnerable to XSS.

citations.quote: In Apache Airflow < 1.10.12
was vulnerable to XSS exploit.

patterns.title: Unescaped form field help text in Wagtail form pages enables editor-driven XSS
patterns.cause: When a form page type is exposed to editors through the wagtail.contrib.forms app and its template uses Django's standard form rendering helpers such as form.as_p, HTML tags in a form field's help text are rendered unescaped. Django allows this by design, but Wagtail policy does not let editors insert arbitrary HTML, so editors could inject script, including for privilege escalation.
preconditions: A form page type is made available to editors through the wagtail.contrib.forms app.
The page template renders the form with Django's standard helpers such as form.as_p.
An editor can author the help text of form fields.
Wagtail version is before 2.7.4 on the 2.7 branch or before 2.9.3 on the 2.9 branch.
patterns.prevention: Treat editor-authored help text as untrusted and escape it on output so HTML tags are not interpreted. Upgrade to Wagtail 2.7.4 or 2.9.3 or later, which escape help text by default. If an upgrade is not possible, render the form field by field in the template and do not apply the safe filter to the help text. Enable the opt-in setting that allows HTML in help text only if editors are fully trusted with that risk.
patterns.limitations: The sources say the flaw is not exploitable by ordinary visitors without Wagtail admin access, so the threat is limited to editor-level users. They do not describe the exact code change in the fix. Sites that re-enable HTML in help text through the opt-in setting accept the risk again. Behavior in other releases is not covered.

fixtures.scenario: A site uses an older Wagtail with a form page whose template calls form.as_p. An editor puts a script tag in a field's help text. Visitors, including administrators, load the page and the markup is output unescaped.
The site runs a patched Wagtail release, or renders fields one by one without the safe filter on help text. The same script tag appears as visible escaped text and is not executed by the browser.

citations.quote: any HTML tags used within a form field's help text will be rendered unescaped in the page.
In these versions, help text will be escaped to prevent the inclusion of HTML tags.
as a matter of policy Wagtail does not allow editors to insert arbitrary HTML by default
omitting the |safe filter when outputting the help text.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through SVG attachments uploaded to a MoinMoin wiki
patterns.cause: MoinMoin before version 1.9.11 let a user with write permissions upload an SVG attachment containing malicious javascript. The script ran in the browser of any user who viewed that SVG file on the wiki. The sources do not say which code path was at fault.
preconditions: The wiki runs MoinMoin before version 1.9.11.
The attacker has write permissions, which include uploading attachments.
A victim views the uploaded SVG file on the wiki in a browser.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade MoinMoin to version 1.9.11 or later, which the advisory says contains the necessary fixes. The advisory advises upgrading over working around the flaw. Two interim measures are named: a Content Security Policy set in the web server, which it says might be possible, and granting write permissions only to trusted users. Treat any user-uploaded SVG as able to carry executable script.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the technical fix, so this card cannot say how 1.9.11 handles SVG files. They do not say which Content Security Policy directives would work or how well they would. They give no detail on other attachment types or on content already uploaded before patching. The advisory says only that upgrading is advised, so existing SVG attachments may need to be reviewed separately.

fixtures.scenario: A wiki runs a MoinMoin version older than 1.9.11 and gives write access to many contributors. One contributor uploads an SVG attachment containing javascript. When another user opens that SVG on the wiki, the script runs in their browser.

The wiki is upgraded to MoinMoin 1.9.11 or later, and write permissions are limited to trusted users. An SVG attachment containing javascript is no longer exploitable against viewers, and a Content Security Policy in the web server adds a further layer.

citations.quote: In MoinMoin before version 1.9.11, an attacker with write permissions can upload an SVG file that contains malicious javascript.
This javascript will be executed in a user's browser when the user is viewing that SVG file on the wiki.
a work around via a Content Security Policy in the web server might be possible.
MoinMoin Wiki 1.9.11 has the necessary fixes and also contains other important fixes.

patterns.title: Unescaped Ansible facts reaching the pipe lookup plugin shell command
patterns.cause: The pipe lookup plugin runs its command through the subprocess Popen call with the shell option enabled. If a variable placed in that command is not escaped by the quote plugin, an attacker who can overwrite ansible facts can control what the shell executes. This is OS command injection (CWE-78).
preconditions: A playbook or template uses the pipe lookup plugin.
The command string given to the plugin includes a variable or fact value.
That variable is not escaped by the quote plugin.
An attacker is able to overwrite the ansible facts that supply the value.
patterns.prevention: Treat every fact or variable that reaches the pipe lookup command as untrusted data. Escape each interpolated value with the quote plugin before the command string is built, so the shell reads it as one literal argument and not as shell syntax. Where possible, avoid building shell command strings from variable data at all. Review existing uses of the pipe lookup plugin and check that each interpolated value is escaped. Also upgrade to an ansible release that contains the fixes referenced for this CVE.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say how facts get overwritten in practice, which ansible versions are affected, or what the upstream change does internally. The advice above is a direction drawn from the stated cause (a missing quote escape with the shell enabled), not a description of the upstream fix. Escaping with the quote plugin may not cover every other plugin or module that handles untrusted facts, and the sources do not address those.

fixtures.scenario: A playbook uses the pipe lookup plugin with a command that embeds a fact value directly and does not pass it through the quote plugin. An attacker overwrites that fact with text containing shell metacharacters and a second command. The shell runs the injected command on the controller.

A playbook uses the pipe lookup plugin, and every fact or variable in the command string is first escaped with the quote plugin. When an attacker overwrites the fact with shell metacharacters, the shell treats the whole value as one literal argument and no extra command runs.

citations.quote: A flaw was found in the pipe lookup plugin of ansible.
the variable is not escaped by quote plugin
An attacker could take advantage and run arbitrary commands by overwriting the ansible facts.

patterns.title: Fetch module lets an intercepted or injected path choose the destination on the controller
patterns.cause: When the Ansible Engine fetch module is used, an attacker who intercepts the module can inject a new path and choose a new destination path on the controller node. The advisory text does not say which value is trusted wrongly, so the exact mechanism is not described in the sources.
preconditions: The fetch module is used to copy files from a managed host to the controller node.
An attacker is able to intercept the module and inject a new path.
The Ansible Engine version is in the 2.7.x, 2.8.x or 2.9.x branches, which are believed to be vulnerable.
patterns.prevention: Do not let a path that comes back from the module or the remote side decide where a file is written on the controller. Derive the controller destination from values the controller itself controls. Before writing, resolve the final destination to its canonical form and confirm it stays inside the intended destination directory, rejecting anything that falls outside. Also move to an Ansible release that includes the upstream fix for CVE-2020-1735.
patterns.limitations: The sources are short and do not describe the vulnerable code path, the exact injected field, the fixed versions, or the upstream fix. The prevention direction here is general path-confinement guidance and is not a description of the actual patch. The sources also do not say how an attacker gains the ability to intercept the module.

fixtures.scenario: A playbook runs the fetch module against a managed host. An attacker who intercepts the module injects a new path, and the file is written to a destination of the attacker's choosing on the controller node, outside the directory the playbook author intended.

A playbook runs the fetch module and the controller computes the destination from its own configured destination directory. It resolves the final path and refuses to write if the result is outside that directory, so an injected path cannot redirect the file.

citations.quote: An attacker could intercept the module, inject a new path, and then choose a new destination path on the controller node.
All versions in 2.7.x, 2.8.x and 2.9.x branches are believed to be vulnerable.

patterns.title: Zip extraction in win_unzip writing outside the destination folder
patterns.cause: The Extract-Zip function in the Ansible win_unzip module did not check whether each extracted file belongs to the destination folder. An archive crafted with path traversal entries can therefore place files outside the intended extraction directory.
preconditions: Ansible 2.7.17 and prior, 2.8.9 and prior, or 2.9.6 and prior is in use.
Archives are extracted with the Extract-Zip function of the win_unzip module.
The archive is attacker-crafted and uses path traversal in its entry paths.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Ansible 2.10 or later, where the issue is reported as fixed. In any archive extraction code, resolve the final target path of every entry and confirm it lies inside the intended destination folder before writing. Reject or skip entries that fall outside it. Treat entry names inside the archive as untrusted input.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the fix works, which traversal forms are affected (relative sequences, absolute paths, or others), or whether other archive formats or modules are affected. The check direction above follows from the stated flaw and is not a description of the upstream change. Backports to the 2.7, 2.8 and 2.9 lines are not mentioned.

fixtures.scenario: A playbook uses win_unzip on a Windows host to extract an archive from an untrusted source. One entry in the archive has a path that climbs out of the destination folder. The extraction writes that file to a location outside the destination because no containment check is made.

The same playbook runs on Ansible 2.10 or later. An entry whose path would land outside the destination folder is not written there, and only files that belong to the destination folder are extracted.

citations.quote: the extracted file(s) are not checked if they belong to the destination folder
An attacker could take advantage of this flaw by crafting an archive anywhere in the file system, using a path traversal.
This issue is fixed in 2.10.

patterns.title: Stale persistent domain definition after live migration exposes destination host devices
patterns.cause: Live migration did not update the persistent domain XML of the guest. After a soft reboot, the guest could reach destination host devices whose paths matched host devices that its old definition referenced on the source host. Those paths can map to different Cinder volumes on the destination.
preconditions: The instance has previously undergone live migration
A user performs a soft reboot of that instance
The deployment allows host-based connections, such as root and ephemeral devices
Device paths on the destination host match paths referenced on the source host but map to different volumes
patterns.prevention: Make sure the persistent domain definition is brought in line with the destination host as part of live migration, so a later soft reboot does not reuse device references from the source host. Run a Nova release that includes the fix (19.3.1, 20.3.1 or later). Treat device paths as host-specific and never assume they refer to the same backing volume on another host.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, so the exact fields updated during migration are not stated. Despite the XXE and CWE-611 labels, the sources describe a stale-definition problem, not XML external entity parsing. Fixed versions are inferred from the affected-version ranges. Deployments without host-based connections are stated as unaffected.

fixtures.scenario: A guest is live migrated, then soft rebooted. Its persistent definition still names device paths from the source host, and on the destination those paths map to other volumes.
After live migration the persistent definition is updated for the destination host, so a soft reboot only reaches the devices intended for this guest.

citations.quote: OpenStack Nova Live migration fails to update persistent domain XML
By performing a soft reboot of an instance that has previously undergone live migration, a user may gain access to destination host devices
Only deployments allowing host-based connections (for instance, root and ephemeral devices) are affected.

patterns.title: Attacker-selected backend module via facts when the use parameter is omitted in Ansible package and service modules
patterns.cause: When the package or service module is used without the 'use' parameter, the module that actually runs is chosen from the Ansible facts file. If an earlier task was run with a malicious user, that user can influence the facts and so select the module that is sent. The advisory titles this an argument injection (CWE-88).
preconditions: The package or service module is used in a task.
The 'use' parameter is not specified in that task.
A previous task was executed with a malicious user who can affect the facts file.
Ansible Engine 2.7.x, 2.8.x or 2.9.x, all believed vulnerable.
patterns.prevention: Specify the 'use' parameter explicitly on package and service tasks so the backend module is not picked from facts. More generally, treat the facts file as untrusted input that an earlier task or user may have written, and do not let it alone decide which module is dispatched. Move to a release that contains the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which Ansible version contains the fix or how the fix works. They do not describe the exact payload or what the selected module can do. They do not say whether setting the 'use' parameter fully removes the risk in every configuration. The facts-handling guidance above is a general hardening direction, not a statement from the advisories. Only 2.7.x, 2.8.x and 2.9.x are named, and they are described as believed vulnerable.

fixtures.scenario: A playbook runs the package module without the 'use' parameter. An earlier task was run with a malicious user, who left facts that name a module of their choosing. The later task then runs the module the attacker selected.
The same playbook sets the 'use' parameter explicitly on the package task, so the backend module is fixed by the playbook author and not taken from the facts file.

citations.quote: A flaw was found in Ansible Engine when the module package or service is used and the parameter 'use' is not specified.
the module sent can be selected by the attacker using the ansible facts file.
Argument Injection in Ansible

patterns.title: SSRF in the Charts and Query View of the old Apache Airflow UI
patterns.cause: In Apache Airflow versions prior to 1.10.13, the Charts and Query View of the old Flask-admin based UI were vulnerable to server-side request forgery (CWE-918). The sources do not describe the code path or the mechanism.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version prior to 1.10.13 is deployed
The old Flask-admin based UI is the interface in use
The Charts and Query View of that UI are part of the deployment
patterns.prevention: Run Apache Airflow 1.10.13 or later, which is the first version the sources identify as not affected. The sources give no details of the fix, so no implementation-level guidance is given beyond the version boundary.
patterns.limitations: The sources are brief and give no attack vector, required privileges, request parameters, or affected internal targets. They do not say whether any configuration or workaround reduces exposure short of upgrading. They also do not describe how the fix works. This card covers only the version boundary and the named UI components.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs apache-airflow at a version earlier than 1.10.13 and exposes the Charts and Query View of the old Flask-admin based UI.
A deployment runs apache-airflow at version 1.10.13 or later, which is not listed as affected for the Charts and Query View issue.

citations.quote: In Apache Airflow versions prior to 1.10.13, the Charts and Query View of the old (Flask-admin based) UI were vulnerable for SSRF attack.

patterns.title: Incomplete fix leaves the origin parameter open to XSS in Apache Airflow endpoints
patterns.cause: The origin parameter passed to some Airflow endpoints, such as the trigger endpoint, was vulnerable to cross-site scripting. The same weakness was reported earlier as CVE-2020-13944. The fix shipped in Airflow 1.10.13 did not fully close it, so the issue remained exploitable.
preconditions: The deployment runs Apache Airflow in a version affected by this CVE (see limitations for the version range).
An endpoint such as the trigger endpoint accepts an origin parameter from the request.
The deployment relies only on the earlier, partial fix for CVE-2020-13944.
patterns.prevention: Treat the origin parameter as untrusted input on every endpoint that accepts it, not just the one named in the first report. When fixing an XSS report, check that the fix covers all endpoints and all ways of supplying the value, and re-test after the change, because the first fix here was incomplete. Operators should upgrade to Apache Airflow 1.10.15 or later, the version the GHSA advisory gives as the end of the affected range.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact injection point, payload shape, or output context. They also do not describe the code change, so this card gives no specific encoding or validation technique. The sources disagree on the affected range: GHSA says versions prior to 1.10.15, while PYSEC and the CVE record say prior to 1.10.13. The list of affected endpoints is open-ended (some endpoints like the trigger endpoint). Nothing is stated about severity or required user interaction.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs an Airflow version that includes only the 1.10.13 fix. A request to the trigger endpoint carries an attacker-chosen origin value, and the application still treats that value as trustworthy, so the XSS remains exploitable.

A deployment runs Airflow 1.10.15 or later. The origin value on the trigger endpoint and on other endpoints that accept it is handled as untrusted data, and a test with attacker-chosen origin values confirms that none of them lead to script execution.

citations.quote: This is same as CVE-2020-13944 but the implemented fix in Airflow 1.10.13 did not fix the issue completely.
This issue affects Apache Airflow versions prior to 1.10.15.
Apache Airflow cross-site scripting due to incomplete fix for CVE-2020-13944

patterns.title: Flask-CORS resource matching on non-canonical paths allows ../ traversal
patterns.cause: In Flask-CORS before 3.0.9, resource matching does not ensure that request pathnames are in a canonical format. A path containing ../ segments can therefore be handled differently from the canonical path it resolves to, which gives access to private resources.
preconditions: The application uses a Flask-CORS release older than 3.0.9.
Flask-CORS resource matching is used to decide how a request path is treated.
A request path can contain ../ segments that have not been reduced to canonical form before matching.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Flask-CORS to 3.0.9 or later. In any code that matches request paths against resource rules, put the pathname in canonical form first, so that ../ segments are resolved before the match decides how the request is treated. Do not treat a raw, non-canonical path as equivalent to the canonical path it resolves to. Review private routes to confirm that no non-canonical spelling of their path is handled under a different rule.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that resource matching does not ensure canonical pathnames and that ../ traversal reaches private resources. They do not describe the exact matching logic, which CORS settings are affected, what data is exposed, or how the upstream change works. Applications that use their own path matching should verify canonicalization themselves, because the sources do not cover that case.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs Flask-CORS older than 3.0.9 and has private routes. A client sends a request whose path includes ../ segments that resolve to a private route. Resource matching does not canonicalize the path, so the private resource is accessed.

An application runs Flask-CORS 3.0.9 or later. Request paths containing ../ segments are put in canonical form before resource matching, so the request is treated as the private route it resolves to and is not reached through a differently matched rule.

citations.quote: It allows ../ directory traversal to access private resources because resource matching does not ensure that pathnames are in a canonical format.
An issue was discovered in Flask-CORS (aka CORS Middleware for Flask) before 3.0.9.

patterns.title: Directory traversal in the MoinMoin cache action leading to remote code execution
patterns.cause: The cache action in action/cache.py in MoinMoin through 1.9.10 accepts a crafted HTTP request that makes it reach files outside the location it is meant to serve. The request is not confined to the intended directory. Combined with attachment upload, this gives an attacker remote code execution.
preconditions: MoinMoin version 1.9.10 or earlier is running.
The cache action is reachable by HTTP request.
The attacker can upload attachments to the wiki, for example through write permission and the AttachFile action.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to MoinMoin 1.9.11 or later, which contains the fixes. Any code that maps a request-supplied name to a file path should keep the resulting path inside its intended directory. The advisory says a workaround is not advised, but disabling the cache action or the AttachFile action might be possible. It also says to grant write permission, which includes uploading attachments, only to trusted users.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the vulnerable request parameter, the exact traversal technique, or how the upload leads to code execution. They do not describe the code-level fix. The workarounds are described only as possibly effective and are not recommended over upgrading. Versions are stated only as 1.9.10 and earlier being affected and 1.9.11 being patched.

fixtures.scenario: A wiki runs MoinMoin 1.9.10 with the cache action and attachment uploads enabled. A user with write permission uploads an attachment, then sends a crafted HTTP request to the cache action that traverses directories, which can lead to remote code execution.
A wiki runs MoinMoin 1.9.11 or later. Write permission is limited to trusted users, and the same crafted request to the cache action does not escape the intended directory.

citations.quote: The cache action in action/cache.py in MoinMoin through 1.9.10 allows directory traversal through a crafted HTTP request.
An attacker who can upload attachments to the wiki can use this to achieve remote code execution.
MoinMoin Wiki 1.9.11 has the necessary fixes and also contains other important fixes.

patterns.title: Jupyter Notebook open redirect through crafted server links (CVE-2020-26215)
patterns.cause: Jupyter Notebook before version 6.1.5 could be reached through a maliciously crafted link to a notebook server that redirected the browser to a different website. The sources do not name the endpoint, parameter or code path involved.
preconditions: The notebook server runs a Jupyter Notebook version earlier than 6.1.5.
The attacker knows or can guess the host of a notebook server, since crafted links can only reasonably be made for known hosts.
A user follows the crafted link, which looks like it points at the trusted notebook server.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade notebook to version 6.1.5 or later, where the issue is patched. When building a server that redirects, do not let a link to your own host send the browser to an arbitrary external site. Check the destination of any redirect before sending it, as the OWASP guidance on unvalidated redirects and forwards describes. The sources do not describe how the upstream patch works.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify the vulnerable route, the input that carries the destination, or the validation the patch adds, so this card gives no implementation detail beyond upgrading. They state that all notebook servers are technically affected but that practical attacks need a known server host. They do not mention other mitigations or workarounds.

fixtures.scenario: A notebook server runs a version before 6.1.5. An attacker crafts a link that begins with the known address of that server. A user opens it believing it is safe and ends up on a spoofed server on the public internet.

The notebook server runs version 6.1.5 or later. A link of the same crafted style that begins with the server address is not expected to send the user to a different website, because the issue is patched in that release.

citations.quote: a maliciously crafted link to a notebook server could redirect the browser to a different website.
A link to your notebook server may appear safe, but ultimately redirect to a spoofed server on the public internet.
The issue is patched in version 6.1.5.

patterns.title: Open redirect via crafted links to Jupyter Server before 1.0.6
patterns.cause: Jupyter Server before version 1.0.6 could be reached through a maliciously crafted link that sent the browser to a different website. The sources do not name the endpoint or parameter involved.
preconditions: The server runs Jupyter Server older than version 1.0.6.
An attacker knows the host of the target jupyter server, which is needed to build a believable link.
A user opens the crafted link in a browser.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to jupyter_server 1.0.6 or later, which the advisory lists as the patched release. In general, an implementation should not send a browser to a destination taken from a request without checking it. Treat any externally supplied redirect target as untrusted, as the OWASP guidance on unvalidated redirects and forwards describes.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which request input drives the redirect, how the patch validates targets, or which exact checks are needed. The general guidance above is a direction only, not a description of the upstream fix. The advisory also says all jupyter servers are technically affected, but crafted links are only reasonably made for known hosts.

fixtures.scenario: A server running a version older than 1.0.6 is reachable at a known host. An attacker sends a link that looks like it points to that server, but following it redirects the browser to a spoofed server on the public internet.
The server runs jupyter_server 1.0.6 or later. A link to it that carries an off-site destination does not send the browser to an attacker-controlled website.

citations.quote: a maliciously crafted link to a jupyter server could redirect the browser to a different website
A link to your jupyter server may appear safe, but ultimately redirect to a spoofed server on the public internet.
jupyter_server 1.0.6

patterns.title: Open redirect in Jupyter Server links sends browsers to a spoofed site
patterns.cause: In Jupyter Server before 1.1.1, an open redirect let a crafted link to a legitimate server host send the browser to a different, attacker-chosen website. The sources do not name the affected endpoint, parameter, or the exact input check that was missing.
preconditions: Jupyter Server older than version 1.1.1 is running.
The server runs without a base_url prefix.
An attacker knows or can guess the host of the target server, so a believable link can be built.
A user opens the crafted link in a browser.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade jupyter-server to 1.1.1 or later. If upgrading is not possible, the advisory's workaround is to run the server under a url prefix through the base_url setting instead of at the root. More generally, an implementation that issues redirects should not send the browser to a destination it has not verified as belonging to the server. The advisory points to the OWASP guidance on unvalidated redirects and forwards.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the vulnerable code path or the upstream fix, so this card cannot say which inputs must be validated or how. The url prefix workaround is a mitigation, not a fix, and the sources do not explain why it helps. The same flaw was reportedly patched in upstream notebook v5.7.8, but the sources give no details of that patch. The advisory also says only servers without a base_url prefix are technically affected, and it does not say how reliable a prefix is as a defense.

fixtures.scenario: A Jupyter Server older than 1.1.1 runs at the root path with no base_url prefix. An attacker sends a user a link that appears to point at the known server host. After the user opens it, the server redirects the browser to a spoofed server on the public internet.

The server is upgraded to 1.1.1 or later. Alternatively, an older server runs under a url prefix as the advisory's workaround. A link to the server host then does not send the browser to an outside site.

citations.quote: an open redirect vulnerability could cause the jupyter server to redirect the browser to a different malicious website.
All jupyter servers running without a base_url prefix are technically affected
A link to your jupyter server may *appear* safe, but ultimately redirect to a spoofed server on the public internet.
This is fixed in jupyter_server 1.1.1.

patterns.title: Sanitizer and browser parse HTML differently in the lxml clean module (CVE-2020-27783)
patterns.cause: The parser in the lxml clean module did not properly imitate browsers. The sanitizer and the user's page could therefore interpret the same markup differently. Markup the sanitizer judged safe could behave differently when a browser rendered it, which allowed cross-site scripting.
preconditions: The application uses the lxml clean module to sanitize untrusted HTML.
The sanitized output is later rendered by a browser on a user's page.
An attacker can supply the HTML that gets sanitized.
patterns.prevention: Make sure the sanitizer reads markup the way the target browser does, so that what it inspects matches what the browser executes. Keep lxml updated to a release that includes the upstream fix for this issue. Treat sanitizer output as only one layer of defense and test it with inputs that parse differently across parsers. Include inputs that browsers handle in unusual ways.
patterns.limitations: The advisories are brief. They do not name the specific markup constructs that trigger the parser mismatch, the affected or fixed version numbers, or the exact change made. This card therefore cannot list which inputs are dangerous or which release is safe. Check the lxml release notes for the fixed version. Any additional defense layers are general practice and are not described in the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A web application passes user-submitted HTML through the lxml clean module and inserts the result into a page. An attacker submits markup that the sanitizer parses as harmless but a browser parses differently, so script runs in the visitor's browser.

The same application uses a patched lxml release and also tests its sanitizer against inputs that parsers handle differently. The sanitizer and the browser agree on how the markup is structured, so no script from the attacker's input executes.

citations.quote: The module's parser didn't properly imitate browsers, which caused different behaviors between the sanitizer and the user's page.
A remote attacker could exploit this flaw to run arbitrary HTML/JS code.

patterns.title: Open redirect via unvalidated next parameter in Horizon workflow forms
patterns.cause: Horizon accepted a next parameter from the request and used it as a redirect target without validating it. An attacker could supply a malicious URL in that parameter, and Horizon would automatically redirect the user to it.
preconditions: The application reads a redirect destination from a next request parameter
The supplied destination is not validated before it is used for a redirect
An attacker can get a user to follow a link carrying a crafted next value
The affected workflow form is in a Horizon version before 15.3.2, 16.x before 16.2.1, 17.x, 18.x before 18.3.3, 18.4.x, or 18.5.x
patterns.prevention: Validate the next parameter before redirecting. Accept only destinations that are known to be safe, such as relative paths within the application or hosts the deployment explicitly trusts. If the value fails validation, ignore it and redirect to a fixed default page. Apply the same check everywhere a user-supplied redirect target is consumed, including workflow forms. Upgrade to a fixed Horizon release.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say that the next parameter lacked validation and that this allowed redirection to a malicious URL. They do not describe the exact code paths, which forms or views are affected beyond workflow forms, or the specific validation the fix uses. They do not say how the affected version ranges map to individual fixes. The exact allowlist or validation rules are therefore left to the implementer.

fixtures.scenario: A user receives a link to a Horizon workflow form with the next parameter set to an external attacker-controlled URL. After the user completes the form, Horizon redirects the browser to that external URL without checking it.

A user opens the same link with an external URL in the next parameter. Horizon validates the value, finds that it is not a safe destination, discards it, and redirects to the default in-application page.

citations.quote: There is a lack of validation of the "next" parameter
would allow someone to supply a malicious URL in Horizon that can cause an automatic redirect to the provided malicious URL.

patterns.title: Mutation XSS in bleach.clean when noscript and a raw-text tag are both allowed
patterns.cause: bleach.clean is vulnerable to a mutation XSS when the allowed tags option includes noscript together with a raw-text tag. The sources name the issue as mutation XSS but do not describe the parsing behavior behind it.
preconditions: The application calls bleach.clean on untrusted input with a bleach version older than 3.1.1.
The allowed tags option includes noscript.
The allowed tags option also includes at least one of these raw tags: title, textarea, script, style, noembed, noframes, iframe, xmp.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade bleach to 3.1.1 or later. Where an upgrade is not possible, do not allow noscript together with any of the listed raw tags in bleach.clean calls. Review allowed-tag lists so that none combine noscript with title, textarea, script, style, noembed, noframes, iframe or xmp. A strong Content-Security-Policy that avoids unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval in script-src is an additional mitigation, not a replacement for the first two steps.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not explain the exact mutation mechanism, so this card cannot say why the combination is unsafe or whether other tag combinations are affected. The advisory and fix reference give 3.1.1 as the patched release, while the PYSEC and CVE texts say before 3.11, so check the installed version against 3.1.1. A Content-Security-Policy only reduces risk and does not remove the flaw. The card covers only the bleach.clean usage described in the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A web application sanitizes user comments with bleach.clean on an old bleach release. Its allowed tags list contains noscript and style, so the unsafe combination is permitted and a crafted comment can produce a mutation XSS.

The application runs bleach 3.1.1 or later, and its allowed tags list does not combine noscript with any of the listed raw tags. The page also sends a strict Content-Security-Policy as defense in depth.

citations.quote: a mutation XSS affects users calling bleach.clean with noscript and a raw tag in the allowed/whitelisted tags option.
will also help mitigate the risk.

patterns.title: Open redirect via aiohttp normalize_path_middleware before 3.7.4
patterns.cause: A bug in the normalize_path_middleware middleware of aiohttp allowed a maliciously crafted link to an aiohttp-based web server to redirect the browser to a different website, which is an open redirect (CWE-601).
preconditions: The application runs aiohttp older than version 3.7.4.
The application uses the normalize_path_middleware middleware from the aiohttp web middlewares module.
A user's browser follows a maliciously crafted link that points at the affected server.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade aiohttp to version 3.7.4 or later, where the advisory states the problem is fixed. If upgrading is not possible, stop using normalize_path_middleware in the application, which the advisory names as a workaround.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact crafted input, the internal mechanism of the bug, or how the fix changes the middleware, so this card cannot say which URL shapes are dangerous. They also do not say what behavior is lost when the middleware is removed. Applications that do not use this middleware are not described as affected by this issue.

fixtures.scenario: A web service runs aiohttp 3.7.3 with normalize_path_middleware enabled. An attacker sends a victim a crafted link to the service, and the victim's browser is redirected to a different website.

The same service runs aiohttp 3.7.4 or later, or runs an older version with normalize_path_middleware removed. The crafted link no longer sends the browser to a different website through this middleware.

citations.quote: A maliciously crafted link to an aiohttp-based web-server could redirect the browser to a different website.
This security problem has been fixed in v3.7.4.
If upgrading is not an option for you, a workaround can be to avoid using

patterns.title: Mutation XSS in bleach.clean() when SVG or MathML, paragraph or break, and raw-text tags are allowed with comments kept
patterns.cause: In Bleach before 3.3.0, bleach.clean() is exposed to a mutation XSS when a risky combination of allowed tags is used and HTML comment stripping is turned off. The sources do not describe the internal mutation mechanism.
preconditions: The allowed tags include svg or math.
The allowed tags include p or br.
The allowed tags include at least one of style, title, noscript, script, textarea, noframes, iframe, or xmp.
The strip_comments option is explicitly turned off. It is on by default, and none of the listed tags are in the default allowed tags.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Bleach 3.3.0 or later, which escapes HTML comments by default. If upgrading is not possible, break the combination: do not allow the raw-text tags listed above, do not allow svg or math, do not allow p or br, or leave comment stripping on. A strong Content-Security-Policy that avoids unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval in script-src also helps reduce risk.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not explain the mutation mechanism or the exact payloads. The Content-Security-Policy is only a mitigation, not a fix. Version 3.3.0 is a breaking change because comments are now escaped by default, so output that relied on kept comments will differ.

fixtures.scenario: An app runs bleach.clean() on user content with svg, p, and style allowed and comment stripping turned off, on a Bleach release older than 3.3.0. Crafted markup can trigger a mutation XSS.
The same app upgrades to Bleach 3.3.0 or later, or stops allowing svg and math, or leaves comment stripping at its default of on, so the risky combination no longer exists.

citations.quote: Users are encouraged to upgrade to bleach v3.3.0 or greater.
bleach v3.3.0 introduces a breaking change to escape HTML comments by default.
none of the above tags are in the default allowed tags and strip_comments defaults to True.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through SVG profile picture upload in CKAN
patterns.cause: CKAN versions 2.9.0 to 2.9.3 let users upload an SVG file as their profile picture. An SVG file can carry malicious scripts, and these scripts ran in another user's browser when that user opened the picture. The sources name SVG upload of the profile picture as the vector but do not say which code path failed.
preconditions: The application runs CKAN 2.9.0 to 2.9.3.
A low privileged user can upload a profile picture and chooses an SVG file containing scripts.
A victim opens the malicious profile picture in a browser.
patterns.prevention: Do not let user-uploaded SVG content from a profile picture run scripts in the browser of any user who opens it. An implementation should treat the uploaded picture as untrusted data, and should either refuse SVG as a profile picture format or ensure that scripts inside it cannot execute when it is opened. Upgrading to a CKAN release later than 2.9.3 is the direction implied by the affected version range.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a short description. They do not describe the upstream fix, so they do not say whether the fix rejects SVG, sanitizes it, or changes how the file is served. They also do not say whether other upload fields or file types were affected, or which fixed version first resolves the issue. The advice above is therefore general and may need checking against the CKAN release notes.

fixtures.scenario: A low privileged user uploads an SVG file containing a script as their profile picture. Another user opens that picture, and the script executes in the second user's browser.

A low privileged user tries to upload an SVG file containing a script as their profile picture. The application either refuses the file or stops its script from running, so nothing executes in the browser of a user who opens the picture.

citations.quote: versions 2.9.0 to 2.9.3 are affected by a stored XSS vulnerability via SVG file upload
This allows low privileged application users to store malicious scripts in their profile picture.

patterns.title: Open redirect through a URL shortener that accepts unchecked external URLs
patterns.cause: The URL shortener functionality did not check user input for open redirects. This let a user create a short URL that pointed to an external, potentially malicious URL, even though the short link appeared to belong to the trusted application.
preconditions: The application offers a URL shortener feature that creates short links from user-supplied input
The user-supplied target is not checked to confirm it is an internal destination, so an external URL is accepted
A victim can be convinced to click the resulting short link, for example one presented as a dashboard link
patterns.prevention: Check every user-supplied target before the shortener stores it or redirects to it. Accept only destinations that belong to the application itself, and reject any URL that points to an external host. Apply the same check at the point where the short link is created, so a malicious external URL is never stored in the first place.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say how the upstream fix validates URLs, which URL forms were abused, or whether the check runs at creation time, at redirect time, or both. They give no detail on handling of relative paths, scheme-relative URLs, or encoded input. Affected versions are stated as up to and including 1.0.1 in some sources and as prior to 1.1.0 in others. The sources do not describe any impact beyond tricking a user into clicking a link.

fixtures.scenario: A malicious user submits an external URL to the shortener. The application creates a short link for it without checking the destination. The link is presented as a dashboard link, and a victim who clicks it is taken to the external site.

A user submits an external URL to the shortener. The application checks the input, finds that it does not point to an internal destination, and refuses to create the short link. A user who submits a destination inside the application gets a working short link.

citations.quote: By not checking user input for open redirects the URL shortener functionality would allow for a malicious user to create a short URL
Apache Superset up to and including 1.0.1 allowed for the creation of an external URL that could be malicious.

patterns.title: Unsafe handling of the origin parameter on Airflow endpoints such as trigger leads to reflected XSS
patterns.cause: The origin parameter passed to some Apache Airflow endpoints, such as the trigger endpoint, was vulnerable to cross-site scripting. This was a repeat of CVE-2020-13944 and CVE-2020-17515, because the earlier fix did not fully close the issue.
preconditions: Apache Airflow 1.x release older than 1.10.15, or Airflow 2.0.0 or 2.0.1.
An endpoint such as the trigger endpoint accepts an origin parameter supplied in the request.
A user's browser can be induced to send a request carrying an attacker-chosen origin value.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Airflow 1.10.15 or 2.0.2, which the advisories name as the fixed releases. Also move to the latest patch release of the installed Python minor version, as the advisories recommend. In your own code, treat the origin request parameter as untrusted data on every endpoint that accepts it, not only the endpoints named in earlier advisories. After fixing a reported XSS, re-check the whole class of inputs, since a partial fix left this issue open.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say how the origin value was used (for example, where it was placed in a page or a redirect). They do not list every affected endpoint beyond the trigger example, and they do not describe the code change in the fix. Concrete validation or encoding guidance therefore cannot be drawn from them. The Python update advice is tied to a separate CVE, CVE-2021-23336, and its relation to this XSS is not explained.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 2.0.1 deployment exposes the trigger endpoint. A user opens a link whose origin parameter holds attacker-chosen content, and the deployment does not treat that value as untrusted.
The deployment runs Airflow 2.0.2 or 1.10.15 or later. The origin parameter is handled as untrusted input on the trigger endpoint and on other endpoints that accept it.

citations.quote: parameter passed to some of the endpoints like '/trigger' was vulnerable to XSS exploit.
the implemented fix did not fix the issue completely.
Update to Airflow 1.10.15 or 2.0.2.

patterns.title: lxml Cleaner leaves formaction attribute when forms and safe_attrs_only are disabled
patterns.cause: The lxml clean module Cleaner class does not remove the formaction attribute when the safe_attrs_only and forms arguments are both disabled. Attacker-supplied HTML can therefore carry script-capable content past the sanitizer, which allows cross-site scripting.
preconditions: The application sanitizes untrusted HTML with the lxml clean module Cleaner class
The Cleaner is configured with both safe_attrs_only and forms disabled
The installed lxml version is earlier than 4.6.3
Users interact with the sanitized HTML output
patterns.prevention: Upgrade lxml to version 4.6.3 or later, which patches this issue. Until then, avoid disabling both safe_attrs_only and forms together on content from untrusted sources. Treat any Cleaner configuration that relaxes attribute filtering as a risk and review it for untrusted input.
patterns.limitations: The sources only describe the formaction attribute and the configuration with safe_attrs_only and forms disabled. They do not say whether other settings are affected, whether enabling only one of the two options is enough, or what other attributes may bypass the Cleaner. They do not describe the patch internals, so nothing beyond upgrading is verified here.

fixtures.scenario: A web app cleans user-submitted HTML with an lxml Cleaner older than 4.6.3 that has safe_attrs_only and forms both disabled. The submitted markup keeps a formaction attribute, and a user who interacts with the page may run attacker JS.

A web app cleans user-submitted HTML with lxml 4.6.3 or later. Even if safe_attrs_only and forms are disabled, the Cleaner handles the formaction attribute, so the output no longer lets it bypass the sanitizer.

citations.quote: When disabling the safe_attrs_only and forms arguments, the Cleaner class does not remove the formaction attribute allowing for JS to bypass the sanitizer.
A remote attacker could exploit this flaw to run arbitrary JS code on users who interact with incorrectly sanitized HTML.
This issue is patched in lxml 4.6.3.

patterns.title: Missing server-side link protocol validation in Wagtail rich text fields allows javascript: URLs
patterns.cause: When saving a rich text field in the admin interface, Wagtail did not apply server-side checks to ensure that link URLs use a valid protocol. The server accepted whatever URL the submitted data contained, so a crafted POST request could store links with javascript: URLs containing arbitrary code (CWE-79).
preconditions: The site runs an affected Wagtail version, earlier than 2.11.7 on the 2.11 LTS branch or 2.12.4 on the 2.12 branch.
The attacker is a user with access to the Wagtail admin interface.
The attacker submits a hand-crafted POST request that saves rich text content with a link whose URL uses an unsafe protocol such as javascript:.
patterns.prevention: Do not rely on the editor user interface to restrict link URLs. When rich text is saved, validate every link URL on the server and accept only valid protocols, so content with javascript: URLs is never stored or published. The advisory workaround does this by passing external link URLs through Wagtail's whitelist URL check when converting editor content to the database format. The permanent remedy is to upgrade to Wagtail 2.11.7 or 2.12.4 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not list which protocols count as valid, do not describe how already-stored content is handled, and do not describe the internals of the official fix. Exposure is limited to users with Wagtail admin access; the advisory says ordinary site visitors cannot exploit it. Sites that cannot upgrade should follow the workaround in the GitHub advisory, but the sources do not say whether it covers every rich text entry path.

fixtures.scenario: An editor with admin access sends a crafted POST request that saves a rich text field containing a link whose URL starts with javascript: and carries script code. The server stores and publishes it without checking the protocol, so the script can run when someone follows the link.

The same crafted POST request is sent, but the server checks each link URL for a valid protocol when saving the rich text. The javascript: link is not accepted as valid link content, and only links with valid protocols are stored.

citations.quote: Wagtail does not apply server-side checks to ensure that link URLs use a valid protocol
The vulnerability is not exploitable by an ordinary site visitor without access to the Wagtail admin.
Patched versions have been released as Wagtail 2.11.7 (for the LTS 2.11 branch) and Wagtail 2.12.4 (for the current 2.12 branch).

patterns.title: Indirect access to untrusted modules through allowed modules in through-the-web TAL expressions
patterns.cause: Zope restricts which Python modules can be used directly in TAL expressions, for example in Zope Page Templates added through the web, to avoid file system access via modules such as os. However, some untrusted modules were reachable indirectly by traversing through Python modules that are available for direct use, so the restriction could be bypassed. The sources do not describe the exact traversal mechanism.
preconditions: Zope version prior to 4.6 (4.x line) or prior to 5.2 (5.x line)
The site allows users to add or edit Zope Page Templates through the web
Untrusted users can author TAL expressions, for example because they hold the Manager role or were granted the add/edit permission
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Zope 4.6 or 5.2 or later, where the problem is fixed. An implementation that restricts module access in template expressions should enforce the allow list on everything reachable from an allowed module, not only on modules named directly, so that an allowed module cannot be used as a stepping stone to modules that are deliberately blocked. As a workaround, use the standard Zope user/role permission mechanisms to limit adding and editing Zope Page Templates through the web to trusted users, and do not assign the Manager role to untrusted users.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the specific modules or traversal paths involved, and they do not explain how the fix works internally, so this card cannot say which indirect routes were closed. The sources describe impact as reaching untrusted modules and the GHSA title mentions remote code execution; they give no further detail. Only sites that let untrusted users edit templates through the web are described as at risk, and the sources say nothing about other exposure. The workaround reduces who can exploit the issue but does not remove the flaw.

fixtures.scenario: A Zope 4.5 site grants template add/edit permission through the web to a group of semi-trusted users. One of them writes a TAL expression that starts from a module permitted for direct use and reaches an untrusted module that is blocked for direct import, gaining file system access.

The site runs Zope 5.2 or 4.6 or later, and template add/edit permission through the web is limited to trusted administrators. Expressions cannot reach blocked modules through allowed ones, and untrusted users do not hold the Manager role.

citations.quote: some of the untrusted modules are available indirectly through Python modules that are available for direct use.
Only sites that allow untrusted users to add/edit Zope Page Templates through the web are at risk.
The problem has been fixed in Zope 5.2 and 4.6.
Untrusted users should not be assigned the Zope Manager role and adding/editing Zope Page Templates through the web should be restricted to trusted users only.

patterns.title: Untrusted modules reachable through TAL expression traversal in through-the-web Zope Page Templates
patterns.cause: Zope restricts which Python modules TAL expressions in through-the-web templates can use directly, which keeps them away from file system access via modules such as os. Some untrusted modules can still be reached indirectly through Python modules that are available for direct use. This extends an earlier advisory with additional traversal cases. The advisory title describes the impact as remote code execution via traversal in TAL expressions.
preconditions: The site runs a Zope version before the fixed releases.
Users can add or edit Zope Page Templates through the web.
Some of those users are untrusted, for example by being granted the Manager role or an equivalent permission.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a fixed Zope release. Restrict adding and editing of Zope Page Templates through the web to trusted users with the standard Zope user and role permission mechanisms, and do not give untrusted users the Manager role. When designing expression evaluation, treat a module that is allowed directly as a potential bridge to modules that are not allowed. Check what a traversal step can reach, not only which names are allowed at the top level.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact traversal paths or the code change, so this card cannot say which modules or steps are involved. They give the fixed version as 5.21 in the GitHub advisory and PYSEC entry, and as 5.2.1 in the CVE text, so check the release notes for the correct number. The 4.6.1 fix for the 4.x line is stated consistently. Sites where only trusted users can edit templates are described as not at risk, and the sources do not cover any other exposure.

fixtures.scenario: A Zope site on an unpatched version lets a less-trusted user edit Page Templates through the web. That user writes a TAL expression that starts from an allowed module and traverses onward to a module that is not meant to be usable, such as one giving file system access.
The site runs a patched Zope release, and only trusted administrators hold the permission to add or edit Page Templates through the web. Untrusted users cannot author TAL expressions.

citations.quote: But some of the untrusted modules are available indirectly through Python modules that are available for direct use.
Only sites that allow untrusted users to add/edit Zope Page Templates through the web are at risk.
Most Python modules are not available for using in TAL expressions that you can add through-the-web, for example in Zope Page Templates.

patterns.title: Unsanitized form action attribute in untrusted notebook HTML enables code execution on load
patterns.cause: JupyterLab did not sanitize the action attribute of html form elements in notebook content. This made it possible to trigger form validation outside of the form itself, so an untrusted notebook could execute code when it was opened. The advisories classify the issue as XSS leading to remote code execution.
preconditions: The user runs an affected JupyterLab version, meaning one older than the patched releases 3.1.4, 3.0.17, 2.3.2, 2.2.10 or 1.2.21.
The user opens an untrusted notebook, since the attack requires user action.
The notebook contains html with a form element whose action attribute is not sanitized.
patterns.prevention: Treat all notebook-supplied html as untrusted. When rendering it, sanitize the action attribute of form elements so that attacker-chosen values are removed or restricted rather than passed through. Do not allow form behavior in untrusted content to be triggered from outside the form. Also restrict form submissions with a Content Security Policy, as the advisory's OWASP reference suggests. Upgrade to a patched release for your version line.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact mechanism by which the form validation leads to code execution, nor which attribute values are dangerous. They do not say whether the classic notebook package is affected or which notebook version fixes it, and the patched versions listed are JupyterLab releases. They do not specify the sanitization rules or the Content Security Policy directives to use. The Content Security Policy point rests only on the advisory's OWASP reference title. Exploitation still requires the user to open the notebook.

fixtures.scenario: A user on an affected JupyterLab version opens a notebook from an unknown source. Its html output contains a form whose action attribute is passed through unsanitized, so form validation is triggered outside the form and code runs on load.

A user opens the same notebook in a patched JupyterLab release, or in a deployment that sanitizes the form action attribute of untrusted html and restricts form submissions. The form action is neutralized and no code runs on load.

citations.quote: Untrusted notebook can execute code on load. This is a remote code execution, but requires user action to open a notebook.
Using this it is possible to trigger the form validation outside of the form itself.
Patched in the following versions: 3.1.4, 3.0.17, 2.3.2, 2.2.10, 1.2.21.
OWASP Page on Restricting Form Submissions

patterns.title: Sanitizer bypass in untrusted notebook HTML output leads to XSS and code execution on load
patterns.cause: Jupyter Notebook relied on a deprecated version of Google Caja to sanitize user input. A public Caja bypass let crafted HTML in a notebook output evade sanitization and run script when the notebook was opened. The script could then use Jupyter APIs to execute code.
preconditions: The victim runs a Notebook version older than the patched releases 5.7.11 or 6.4.1
The victim opens a malicious ipynb document, which is the required user action
Untrusted notebook content is sanitized with the deprecated Caja library
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Notebook to 5.7.11 or 6.4.1 or later. Do not treat a deprecated, bypassable sanitizer as the only barrier for HTML in untrusted notebooks. Treat all content in a notebook from an unknown source as attacker-controlled, and follow the injection prevention rules in the OWASP cheat sheet that the advisory references.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the patch works, which Caja bypass was used beyond the public example, or which versions before the fixes are affected. They do not cover other notebook front ends or other XSS paths. The advisory states that the attack needs user action to open the notebook.

fixtures.scenario: A user on an unpatched Notebook opens an ipynb file from an unknown sender. A code cell holds a display output with crafted HTML that bypasses the Caja sanitizer, so script runs on load and can call Jupyter APIs.
The user runs Notebook 5.7.11 or 6.4.1 or later and opens the same file. The crafted HTML output no longer runs script on load.

citations.quote: Jupyter Notebook uses a deprecated version of Google Caja to sanitize user inputs.
A public Caja bypass can be used to trigger an XSS when a victim opens a malicious ipynb document in Jupyter Notebook.
Untrusted notebook can execute code on load.

patterns.title: Open redirect through crafted URLs in Flask-AppBuilder OAuth (CVE-2021-32805)
patterns.cause: In affected Flask-AppBuilder versions that use OAuth, a crafted URL pointing at the trusted application domain can send a user on to a malicious site. This is an open redirect (CWE-601). The advisory workaround refers to the next query parameter carrying a site on a different domain from the protected application.
preconditions: The application is built with Flask-AppBuilder and uses its OAuth support.
The installed Flask-AppBuilder version is older than 3.2.2.
