An attacker can share a crafted URL on the application's trusted domain, and a user follows it.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Flask-AppBuilder to 3.2.2 or above. If upgrading is not feasible, filter incoming HTTP traffic whose next parameter names a domain different from the application being protected. In general, an implementation should not send users to a post-login destination on a domain other than its own.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the vulnerable code path, the exact validation that was missing, or the mechanics of the fix, so this card does not either. The traffic filter is only a stop-gap named by the advisory, and its coverage of other URL shapes is not stated. The sources do not say whether non-OAuth login flows are affected, and the exact earliest affected version is not given beyond 'affected versions'.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs a Flask-AppBuilder version older than 3.2.2 with OAuth login enabled. An attacker sends a victim a link on the application's own trusted domain whose next parameter names an external attacker-controlled site. The victim follows it and lands on the malicious site.

The application runs Flask-AppBuilder 3.2.2 or above. Alternatively, a gateway in front of an older version drops requests whose next parameter names a domain different from the application's own, so a crafted link no longer sends the user off-site.

citations.quote: an attacker can share a carefully crafted URL with a trusted domain for an application built with Flask-AppBuilder
Install Flask-AppBuilder 3.2.2 or above

patterns.title: Template injection in Ansible via facts placed in multi-line YAML strings
patterns.cause: Ansible's controller can be exposed to template injection when facts are used inside templates written as multi-line YAML strings. Facts that do not routinely contain special template characters are handled without sufficient scrutiny, so attacker-influenced content in them can be evaluated as template code, leading to command injection.
preconditions: Templates are placed in multi-line YAML strings
Fact values are interpolated into those templates
The facts handled do not routinely include special template characters
An attacker can influence the content of a fact used by the template
patterns.prevention: Treat fact values as untrusted data and never allow them to be evaluated as template code. Validate input and keep fact content separate from template syntax, so that special template characters inside a fact cannot be interpreted. Be careful when writing templates in multi-line YAML strings, and upgrade to an Ansible release that includes the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources are brief and do not describe the exact code path, the affected or fixed version numbers, or the precise mechanism of the fix. This card therefore gives only general direction and does not specify which Ansible components or settings must change.

fixtures.scenario: A playbook writes a template in a multi-line YAML string and inserts a fact value. A managed host reports a fact containing template syntax, and the controller evaluates it as template code, running attacker-chosen commands.
A playbook uses fact values only as plain data. Template syntax inside a fact is not evaluated, and the controller runs an Ansible version containing the upstream fix.

citations.quote: A flaw was found in Ansible, where a user's controller is vulnerable to template injection.
This issue can occur through facts used in the template if the user is trying to put templates in multi-line YAML strings
This flaw allows attackers to perform command injection, which discloses sensitive information.

patterns.title: Regular expression denial of service in the NLTK comparative sentences corpus reader
patterns.cause: The function _read_comparison_block() in nltk/corpus/reader/comparative_sents.py uses a regular expression with inefficient complexity. When an attacker controls the input that reaches this function, matching can consume excessive CPU time. The sources do not describe the exact pattern or the input shape that triggers the slowdown.
preconditions: The application uses the NLTK comparative sentences corpus reader, which contains _read_comparison_block().
An attacker can supply the input that is passed to _read_comparison_block().
The installed nltk version is one that predates the fix referenced for CVE-2021-3828.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade nltk to a release that includes the upstream fix for CVE-2021-3828. Do not pass untrusted text to the comparative sentences reader. Where untrusted corpus data must be processed, cap input size and enforce a CPU or wall-clock time limit on the parsing step so that a slow match cannot exhaust the service. When writing similar parsing code, avoid regular expressions with ambiguous or nested repetition, or replace them with simple linear string handling.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not state which nltk versions are affected or which version contains the fix. They also do not give the vulnerable pattern, an example payload, or how severe the slowdown is. The size cap and time limit are general mitigations and are not described in the sources, so they may not fit every deployment. This card covers only the reader named in the advisory and does not claim that other NLTK readers are safe or unsafe.

fixtures.scenario: A web service accepts user-uploaded text files and passes their contents to the NLTK comparative sentences reader. An attacker uploads a crafted file, and the call to _read_comparison_block() uses excessive CPU, so other requests are delayed or time out.

The service runs a patched nltk release and loads the comparative sentences corpus only from trusted, bundled files. Any user-supplied text is size-limited and parsed in a worker with a timeout, so a slow parse is stopped without affecting other requests.

citations.quote: The nltk package is vulnerable to ReDoS (regular expression denial of service).
may cause an application to consume an excessive amount of CPU.
nltk is vulnerable to Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity

patterns.title: Inefficient regular expressions in nltk RegexpTaggers allow ReDoS
patterns.cause: Some RegexpTaggers used by the nltk functions get_pos_tagger and malt_regex_tagger rely on regular expressions with inefficient complexity. This makes them vulnerable to regular expression denial of service (ReDoS). The advisories do not say which patterns are involved or what input triggers the slowdown.
preconditions: An affected nltk release is installed.
The application calls get_pos_tagger or malt_regex_tagger, or otherwise uses the RegexpTaggers they rely on.
Text passed to these taggers can be influenced by an untrusted party, since a ReDoS needs crafted input.
patterns.prevention: Move to an nltk release that contains the upstream fix for this CVE. In your own tagger rules, avoid regular expressions with inefficient complexity and review them for that weakness before use. Treat text fed to regex-based taggers as untrusted when it comes from outside your system.
patterns.limitations: The sources are vague. They do not name the vulnerable patterns, the affected or fixed version numbers, the exact input shapes that cause the slowdown, or how the upstream change resolves the problem. They also do not list any mitigation other than the fix, so any workaround such as limiting input size is not supported by them. Check the project's release notes for the exact fixed version.

fixtures.scenario: A web service runs an affected nltk release and calls get_pos_tagger on text submitted by anonymous users. A crafted submission makes the regex-based tagger consume excessive CPU time, and the service becomes unresponsive to other requests.

The same service runs an nltk release that includes the upstream fix for CVE-2021-3842. Any custom RegexpTagger rules it adds have been reviewed for inefficient regular expression complexity, so tagging untrusted text does not cause a CPU exhaustion.

citations.quote: NLTK is vulnerable to REDoS in some RegexpTaggers used in the functions
nltk is vulnerable to Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity

patterns.title: Directory traversal in Babel Locale loading leads to code execution
patterns.cause: In Babel before 2.9.1, Babel.Locale could be made to load arbitrary locale .dat files through directory traversal. These files contain serialized Python objects, so loading an attacker-chosen file can lead to code execution.
preconditions: The application uses a Babel version before 2.9.1.
An attacker can influence which locale Babel.Locale loads.
A .dat file containing serialized Python objects, chosen by the attacker, is reachable by the traversal.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Babel to 2.9.1 or later. In an implementation of locale loading, treat the locale identifier as untrusted input. Make sure it can only select files inside the intended locale data directory, and never let it resolve to a path outside that directory. Reject identifiers that contain path separators or parent directory references before any file is opened. Do not deserialize data files that come from outside the trusted locale data set.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state the vulnerable version range and the general impact. They do not describe the exact vulnerable code path, how locale names reach the file loader, or how the upstream fix works. The validation guidance above is a general direction and not a description of the upstream change. The sources also do not say whether other Babel entry points are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A web application runs Babel before 2.9.1 and passes a user-supplied locale string to Babel.Locale. The string contains traversal sequences that point at a locale .dat file outside the locale data directory. Babel loads the file, and the serialized Python objects in it can run code.

The application runs Babel 2.9.1 or later and only passes locale identifiers that it has checked against the locales it expects. A request with traversal sequences in the locale value is rejected and no file outside the locale data directory is loaded.

citations.quote: Babel.Locale in Babel before 2.9.1 allows attackers to load arbitrary locale .dat files (containing serialized Python objects) via directory traversal, leading to code execution.
allows attackers to load arbitrary locale .dat files (containing serialized Python objects) via directory traversal

patterns.title: lxml HTML Cleaner lets crafted script and SVG data URI script through
patterns.cause: The HTML Cleaner in lxml.html, used to sanitize untrusted markup, failed to remove certain crafted script content. It also let script content through when it was inside SVG files embedded using data URIs. Markup that the application treats as cleaned can therefore still carry executable script (cross-site scripting).
preconditions: The application uses the HTML Cleaner in lxml.html to sanitize untrusted HTML.
The installed lxml version is older than 4.6.5.
The cleaned output is used in a security relevant context, such as being rendered to other users in a browser.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade lxml to version 4.6.5 or later anywhere the HTML Cleaner handles untrusted input. Until the upgrade is deployed, do not treat Cleaner output from older versions as safe to render in a security relevant context. The sources list no workarounds, so the upgrade is the only remediation they support. After upgrading, confirm the deployed environment, including any pinned or vendored copies, actually resolves to the patched version.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe which crafted script patterns were missed or how the patch changes the Cleaner, so this card cannot say what input to filter or test for beyond SVG content in data URIs. They state there are no known workarounds, so no interim mitigation is documented. They say nothing about versions or code paths outside the HTML Cleaner, and they do not say whether upgrading alone is enough defense for every use of cleaned output.

fixtures.scenario: A web application accepts user-submitted HTML, passes it through the lxml.html Cleaner on lxml 4.4, and shows the result to other users. An attacker submits an SVG file embedded as a data URI, or other crafted script content, and the Cleaner leaves the script in the output.
The same application runs lxml 4.6.5 or later, verified in the deployed environment, so the Cleaner no longer lets the crafted script content or the SVG data URI script pass through.

citations.quote: The HTML Cleaner in lxml.html lets certain crafted script content pass through, as well as script content in SVG files embedded using data URIs.
Users that employ the HTML cleaner in a security relevant context should upgrade to lxml 4.6.5.
There are no known workarounds available.

patterns.title: Unrestricted file paths in Gradio static file serving expose host files
patterns.cause: In gradio versions before 2.5.0, file paths requested through the interface were not restricted. Static files were served in a way that let a remote user who received a shared Gradio link read arbitrary files on the host, limited only by operating system permissions.
preconditions: Running a gradio version prior to 2.5.0
The interface is publicly shared through a generated Gradio link while the link is active
The attacker knows the exact file name or relative file path on the host
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to gradio 2.5.0 or later. In similar file-serving code, restrict requested paths to an intended directory: resolve the requested path to its canonical absolute form, then confirm it lies inside the allowed base directory before opening it. Reject anything outside that directory. Add regression tests for traversal attempts so the check is not reverted.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact vulnerable code path, the endpoint involved, or the mechanics of the patch, so the canonicalization guidance is a general direction and not a description of the upstream fix. Access was read-only, and no evidence of exploitation is reported.

fixtures.scenario: A user shares a public link from an older gradio release. A remote visitor requests a path pointing outside the served folder, and the server returns that host file because paths are unrestricted.
A patched gradio release or a similar server resolves each requested path, checks it is inside the allowed base directory, and refuses requests that resolve elsewhere.

citations.quote: File paths are not restricted and users who receive a Gradio link can access any files on the host computer
An attacker would be able to view the contents of a file on the computer if they knew the exact relative filepath.
Paths are opened in read only mode. The problem has been patched in gradio 2.5.0.

patterns.title: Untrusted origin query argument on the Trigger DAG with config screen leads to XSS in Apache Airflow
patterns.cause: The Trigger DAG with config screen in Apache Airflow was susceptible to cross-site scripting through the origin query argument. A value supplied in the request URL could affect the page in a way that allowed script injection.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version 2.2.3 or below is in use.
The Trigger DAG with config screen is reachable by a user.
The origin query argument can be set by whoever builds the URL that the user opens.
patterns.prevention: Treat the origin query argument as untrusted input. An implementation should ensure that its value is never interpreted as markup or script when the screen is rendered, and should apply the same care to any other query argument that is echoed into a page. For deployments, use an Airflow release newer than 2.2.3.
patterns.limitations: The sources only name the affected screen, the origin query argument and the affected versions (2.2.3 and below). They do not say where on the page the value is used, whether it is reflected into HTML, an attribute or a link target, what the maintainers changed, or which release first contains the fix. Any more specific mitigation than treating the value as untrusted is therefore not supported here.

fixtures.scenario: A user follows a crafted link to the Trigger DAG with config screen in Airflow 2.2.3 or earlier. The origin query argument in the link carries attacker-chosen content, and the screen handles it in a way that lets script run in the user's browser session.
The same link is opened, but the screen treats the origin query argument as untrusted data and does not let its content be interpreted as markup or script, so no attacker-controlled script runs.

citations.quote: screen was susceptible to XSS attacks via the
This issue affects Apache Airflow versions 2.2.3 and below.

patterns.title: Open redirect in archivy web application redirects
patterns.cause: Archivy before the fixed release was vulnerable to open redirect (CWE-601), meaning the application could send users to a destination that was not confined to the application itself. The sources do not say which endpoint or parameter was affected.
preconditions: The application issues HTTP redirects to a target that can be influenced by the request
The target is not restricted to a trusted set of destinations before the redirect is sent
A victim follows a link that points at the legitimate application but leads to an attacker-chosen destination
patterns.prevention: Do not redirect to a caller-supplied destination as-is. Prefer fixed, server-side redirect targets or a short allow-list of known internal destinations. If a caller-supplied target is unavoidable, validate it before use and accept only relative paths on the same site, rejecting any value that names another host or scheme. Upgrade archivy to a release that includes the fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that archivy is vulnerable to open redirect. They do not name the affected route, parameter or validation flaw, so the cause and the validation guidance above are the general CWE-601 pattern rather than confirmed details of this bug. The advisories disagree on the fixed version: one says prior to 1.7.1 and the others say prior to 1.7.0. Check the upstream release notes before choosing a version.

fixtures.scenario: A user opens a link to the archivy site that carries a destination value pointing to an external host. After the action completes, the application redirects the browser to that external host without checking it, so the user lands on an attacker-controlled page.

The same link carries a destination value. The application accepts it only if it is a relative path inside the site or is on a fixed allow-list. An external host is rejected and the user is sent to a default internal page instead.

citations.quote: archivy prior to version 1.7.1 is vulnerable to open redirect.
Open Redirect in GitHub repository archivy/archivy prior to 1.7.0.

patterns.title: DOM-based XSS on the OctoPrint login endpoint before version 1.8.0
patterns.cause: OctoPrint versions prior to 1.8.0 have a DOM-based cross-site scripting flaw in the login endpoint. The endpoint allows javascript injection, so attacker-influenced content can run as script in the browser of a user who opens the login page.
preconditions: The deployment runs OctoPrint prior to 1.8.0.
The login endpoint is reachable by the victim's browser.
An attacker can get a victim to interact with an attacker-influenced login request, as in the phishing scenario the advisory describes.
patterns.prevention: Run OctoPrint 1.8.0 or later, which is the first version not listed as affected. In any similar login flow, treat everything the browser-side login page takes from the request or the server as untrusted text. It should never be interpreted as markup or script, so use text-only DOM operations or context-appropriate output encoding rather than HTML-parsing sinks.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the vulnerable parameter, the DOM sink, or how the upstream change works. The advice on text-only handling is a general direction for DOM XSS, not a description of the actual fix. The sources also do not say whether authentication state, cookies, or other defenses such as a content security policy change the impact. Account takeover is described only as possible in a phishing scenario.

fixtures.scenario: An administrator running OctoPrint prior to 1.8.0 follows a link crafted by an attacker to the login page. Injected javascript runs in the page, and the attacker may use it to take over the account in a phishing scenario.

The same administrator opens a crafted link to the login page of an OctoPrint instance at 1.8.0 or later. The advisory lists no javascript injection for that version, so the attacker-supplied content is not expected to execute.

citations.quote: The login endpoint allows for javascript injection which may lead to account takeover in a phishing scenario.
Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - DOM in GitHub repository octoprint/octoprint prior to 1.8.0.

patterns.title: OctoPrint Stream URL value can execute an XSS payload (CVE-2022-1432)
patterns.cause: In OctoPrint versions before 1.8.0, the Stream URL value was handled in a way that allowed an XSS payload placed in it to execute. The sources do not say where or how the value is rendered.
preconditions: OctoPrint is a version prior to 1.8.0.
A payload can be supplied through the Stream URL value.
The Stream URL value is later used in a way that lets the payload run in a user's browser.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade OctoPrint to 1.8.0 or later, which is the first version not listed as affected. When building similar features, treat a user-configurable stream address as untrusted data. Make sure it is never interpreted as executable script content wherever it is displayed or used.
patterns.limitations: The sources give no detail on the injection point, whether the payload is stored or reflected, the privileges needed to set the value, or the exact change made in 1.8.0. The general handling advice above is a direction only and is not a description of the upstream fix.

fixtures.scenario: An OctoPrint instance older than 1.8.0 has a Stream URL value containing an XSS payload, and the payload executes.
An OctoPrint instance at version 1.8.0 or later is configured with the same kind of Stream URL value, and the value does not result in script execution.

citations.quote: The Stream URL of octoprint application allowing a xss payload to execute.
Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Generic in GitHub repository octoprint/octoprint prior to 1.8.0.

patterns.title: Unencoded context output from the Django debug template tag leads to XSS
patterns.cause: The debug template tag in Django 2.2 before 2.2.27, 3.2 before 3.2.12, and 4.0 before 4.0.2 does not properly encode the current context when it renders it. Context values that contain markup can therefore reach the page unescaped, which may lead to cross-site scripting (CWE-79).
preconditions: The application runs Django 2.2 before 2.2.27, 3.2 before 3.2.12, or 4.0 before 4.0.2.
A rendered template uses the debug template tag.
The current template context holds values that contain HTML-significant characters, for example values influenced by users.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 2.2.27, 3.2.12, 4.0.2 or later within the matching release line. The general principle is that any dump of the template context must be HTML-encoded before it is written into a page, so that values are shown as text and never interpreted as markup. Until the upgrade is applied, avoid rendering the debug tag in templates that are served to users.
patterns.limitations: The advisories are brief. They do not say which context values are attacker-controllable, whether a particular setting such as DEBUG is needed for the tag to produce output, or how the upstream change implements the encoding. The advice to avoid the tag until upgrade is a conservative workaround inferred from the description, not stated in the sources. Only the three listed release lines are named as affected.

fixtures.scenario: A site on Django 3.2.11 includes the debug template tag in a page template. A context value contains script markup supplied by a user, and the tag writes it into the response without proper encoding, so the browser may execute it.
The same site runs Django 3.2.12 or later, or its templates do not use the debug tag. Context values that contain markup are shown as inert text and no script runs.

citations.quote: does not properly encode the current context. This may lead to XSS.
Django 2.2 before 2.2.27, 3.2 before 3.2.12, and 4.0 before 4.0.2

patterns.title: Spaces in temporary pathnames can lead to unintended file deletion in Pillow before 9.0.1
patterns.cause: Pillow before 9.0.1 mishandled spaces in temporary pathnames. Because of this, an attacker could cause files to be deleted. The advisories classify the issue as path traversal (CWE-22).
preconditions: The application uses a Pillow version older than 9.0.1.
A temporary pathname handled by Pillow contains one or more spaces.
An attacker can influence the situation so that the mishandled pathname results in a file deletion.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Pillow 9.0.1 or later. In any code that builds or consumes temporary pathnames, treat a name containing spaces as one complete path. Do not let the spaces change which file is acted on, and make sure a delete or cleanup step only ever targets the temporary file that was actually created.
patterns.limitations: The advisories are brief. They do not name the affected module, the exact mechanism of the mishandling, the attacker's required level of control, or the details of the fix. This card therefore cannot say which code paths are exposed, and the guidance on pathname handling is general rather than specific to Pillow internals.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs Pillow before 9.0.1 and works with a temporary pathname that contains a space. The space is mishandled, and a file other than the intended temporary file is deleted.
An application runs Pillow 9.0.1 or later. Temporary pathnames containing spaces are handled as single complete paths, so cleanup removes only the intended temporary file.

citations.quote: Pillow before 9.0.1 allows attackers to delete files because spaces in temporary pathnames are mishandled.
Path traversal in Pillow

patterns.title: Open redirect on the Flask-AppBuilder database authentication login page
patterns.cause: Flask-AppBuilder versions below 3.4.5 contain an open redirect vulnerability (CWE-601) when the database authentication login page is used. The advisories do not say which parameter or code path is affected.
preconditions: The application runs Flask-AppBuilder at a version below 3.4.5.
The application uses database authentication and exposes its login page.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Flask-AppBuilder to version 3.4.5 or later, which the advisories name as the fixed release. The advisories list no workarounds, so the upgrade is the only prevention they support. Until the upgrade is done, treat the database authentication login page as able to redirect users to destinations the application did not intend.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the redirect parameter, the exact flow, how the redirect target is checked, or how the fix works. They also do not say whether other authentication types are affected. They state only that the problem occurs with the database authentication login page. This card cannot offer a more specific mitigation than upgrading.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs Flask-AppBuilder 3.4.4 with database authentication enabled, so its login page is exposed to the open redirect described in the advisories.
A deployment runs Flask-AppBuilder 3.4.5 or later with database authentication enabled, which is the fixed release named in the advisories.

citations.quote: Flask-AppBuilder contains an open redirect vulnerability when using database authentication login page on versions below 3.4.5.
There are no known workarounds. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 3.4.5 or later.

patterns.title: Catastrophic backtracking in mistune inline markup regular expressions
patterns.cause: In mistune through 2.0.2, support for inline markup is implemented with regular expressions that can involve a high amount of backtracking on certain edge cases. This behavior is commonly called catastrophic backtracking (CWE-1333), so some inputs can make the regex engine consume far more work than their size suggests.
preconditions: The application uses mistune version 2.0.2 or earlier.
Text is parsed with inline markup support, which relies on the affected regular expressions.
The parsed text includes input that hits the edge cases that cause heavy backtracking.
patterns.prevention: Move to a mistune release newer than 2.0.2, since the advisories describe the affected range as through 2.0.2. When writing or reviewing inline markup parsing, avoid regular expressions whose matching work can grow sharply on edge-case input. Where untrusted text is rendered, consider bounding the input size and the time spent parsing it as defense in depth.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the problem only in general terms. They do not name the exact patterns, the triggering inputs, the first fixed version, or the specific change made upstream. They also do not say whether the backtracking cost is polynomial or exponential. The size and time limits suggested above are general hardening and are not described in the sources as fixes for this issue.

fixtures.scenario: A web service renders user-submitted comments with mistune 2.0.2 and inline markup enabled. A comment containing an edge case that triggers heavy backtracking in the inline regular expressions makes the parser use excessive time on that request.

The same service runs a mistune release newer than 2.0.2, and inline markup parsing no longer relies on the regular expressions that backtrack heavily. It also caps the length of submitted comments before parsing.

citations.quote: support of inline markup is implemented by using regular expressions that can involve a high amount of backtracking on certain edge cases
This behavior is commonly named catastrophic backtracking.

patterns.title: Directory traversal through custom component file serving in Streamlit
patterns.cause: The Streamlit server handled URLs for custom components by processing file paths taken from the request and returning the contents of the named file. File operations were not confined to the custom component directory, so a crafted URL could reach files elsewhere on the web server file system. One source also says existing files could be overwritten.
preconditions: The Streamlit app is hosted with custom components in use.
The Streamlit version is older than 1.11.1, the release that resolved the issue.
An attacker can send a crafted URL containing file paths to the Streamlit server.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Streamlit 1.11.1 or later. In any code that serves or writes files based on request paths, restrict every file operation to one designated base directory, here the custom component directory. Make sure a requested path cannot traverse outside that directory, and reject requests that would. As defense in depth, run the web server with low privileges and place it behind a firewall, which reduces the impact of any such exploit. Review custom components before using them.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact path forms an attacker used or the precise check added in the patch, so this card gives only the general direction of confining operations to the component directory. They state there are no workarounds, so upgrading is the only remedy they name. Low privileges and firewalls reduce severity but do not remove the flaw. The sources are inconsistent on impact: the advisory and CVE text mention only reading files, while the PYSEC entry also mentions overwriting files. The sources say Streamlit continued to check for other occurrences of the flaw, so other code paths are not ruled out.

fixtures.scenario: A team hosts a Streamlit app on Streamlit 1.10 that uses a custom component. An outside user sends a request to the component route with a file path that points outside the component directory, and the server returns the contents of a server log or another world readable file.

The same app runs Streamlit 1.11.1 or later, so file operations for custom components are limited to the component directory. The same request with an outside file path does not return the file. The server also runs under a low privilege account behind a firewall.

citations.quote: Users hosting Streamlit app(s) that use custom components are vulnerable to a directory traversal attack
This patch ensures that any file operations are restricted only to the custom component directory and cannot traverse outside of that.
return the contents of that file or overwrite existing files on the web-server
This issue has been resolved in version 1.11.1. Users are advised to upgrade.

patterns.title: Sanic static file serving exposes lateral directories via encoded slash URLs
patterns.cause: Per the advisories, the static file feature of Sanic (app.static) lets requests that use encoded %2F URLs reach lateral directories. The sources do not explain the internal mechanism. They say that parent directory traversal is not affected.
preconditions: The application serves files through app.static.
A request URL uses encoded %2F sequences.
The running Sanic version is older than the patched releases 20.12.7, 21.12.2 or 22.6.1, depending on the release line.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Sanic to a patched release: 20.12.7 or 21.12.2 on the LTS lines, or 22.6.1 on the current line. The advisories state that no workaround is known, so upgrading is the only documented mitigation.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the root cause or the fix logic, so this card gives no implementation-level guidance beyond upgrading. They do not say which versions are affected beyond listing the patched ones. They name no interim workaround, and they do not say how far the exposed lateral directories extend.

fixtures.scenario: An application on an unpatched Sanic release serves a directory with app.static. A client sends a request whose URL contains encoded %2F sequences, and the server returns content from a lateral directory.
The same application runs a patched Sanic release (20.12.7, 21.12.2 or 22.6.1 or later on its line). The same encoded %2F request no longer yields access to lateral directories.

citations.quote: Affected versions of sanic allow access to lateral directories when using
Parent directory traversal is not impacted.
There is no known workaround for this issue.

patterns.title: Malicious IPv6 redirect URI can cause denial of service in oauthlib URI validation
patterns.cause: An OAuth2.0 provider built on oauthlib accepts a redirect URI from the client and passes it to oauthlib's URI validation helpers, such as the absolute-URI check in the uri_validate module. A crafted URI with a malformed bracketed IPv6 host can make these helpers cause denial of service in the web application. The sources do not explain the internal mechanism of the slowdown.
preconditions: The application uses oauthlib OAuth2.0 provider support, or calls the uri_validate functions directly.
An attacker can supply the redirect URI, for example as a request parameter to the authorization flow.
The oauthlib version is in the affected range, 3.1.1 up to 3.2.1 according to the CVE record.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade oauthlib to 3.2.2 or later, which the advisory names as the fixed release. Until then, check the redirect URI in the web toolkit layer (for example the integration library in front of oauthlib) before oauthlib is called, and reject URIs that contain a colon, but only if the application needs neither ports nor IPv6 hosts in redirect URIs. Treat any user-supplied URI that reaches a validation helper as untrusted input and keep validation of it cheap and bounded.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe a denial of service and say nothing about how the redirect itself is abused, so the open redirect classification is not explained here. The root cause inside the validation code is not described. The CVE record says version 3.2.1 contains a patch and that there are no known workarounds, while the GitHub advisory says the fix is in 3.2.2 and offers a pre-check workaround, so the exact fixed version should be confirmed. The colon-based pre-check would also reject legitimate redirect URIs that use a port or an IPv6 host.

fixtures.scenario: An OAuth2.0 provider built on an affected oauthlib version receives an authorization request whose redirect URI has a bracketed IPv6 host made of a long run of colons. The URI is passed straight into oauthlib's absolute-URI validation, and the web application becomes unresponsive to other users.

The provider runs a fixed oauthlib release (3.2.2 or later). Where it cannot upgrade yet and needs no ports or IPv6 hosts, its web layer rejects any redirect URI containing a colon before oauthlib is called. The same malicious request is refused quickly and the application stays responsive.

citations.quote: Attacker providing malicious redirect uri can cause DoS to oauthlib's web application.
OAuthLib applications using OAuth2.0 provider support or use directly
Issue fixed in 3.2.2 release.
assuming no port or IPv6 is fundamentally required.

patterns.title: SSRF in Label Studio Data Import allows arbitrary file access
patterns.cause: In Label Studio Community Edition 1.5.0 and earlier, the Data Import module has a server side request forgery flaw. An authenticated user can use it to access arbitrary files on the system where the server runs. The sources do not describe the internal mechanism.
preconditions: Label Studio Community Edition version 1.5.0 or earlier is deployed.
The attacker has an authenticated account.
Self-registration is enabled, which is the default in the affected versions, so a remote attacker can create an account themselves.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to version 1.6.0 or later, where the issue is fixed. When building an import feature, make sure a user-supplied source cannot make the server read arbitrary files on its own system. Treat every authenticated user, including self-registered ones, as untrusted for this purpose.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which input forms or URL schemes are abused, or how version 1.6.0 changes the import behavior. They do not say whether disabling self-registration or other configuration changes reduce the risk. They also do not say whether network requests to internal services are possible beyond the file access described. Upgrading is the only remediation the sources confirm.

fixtures.scenario: A Label Studio 1.5.0 server keeps the default self-registration setting. A remote person creates an account, uses the Data Import module, and reads arbitrary files from the server's file system.
The deployment runs Label Studio 1.6.0 or later. A newly registered user who tries the same import cannot use the Data Import module to read arbitrary files on the system.

citations.quote: allows an authenticated user to access arbitrary files on the system
self-registration is enabled by default in these versions of Label Studio
This issue is fixed in version 1.6.0.

patterns.title: OS command injection in the Apache Airflow Pinot Provider task execution context
patterns.cause: The Apache Airflow Pinot Provider before version 4.0.0 improperly neutralizes special elements used in an OS command. As a result, an attacker can control commands executed in the task execution context without write access to DAG files.
preconditions: The Apache Airflow Pinot Provider is installed at a version prior to 4.0.0.
Airflow versions prior to 2.3.0 are affected whenever the Pinot Provider is installed.
Pinot-related tasks run in the task execution context, where the attacker-influenced command is executed.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade the Pinot Provider to version 4.0.0 or later. Airflow 2.3.0 or later is required for that provider version, so older Airflow deployments must be upgraded first. On Airflow 2.3.0 and later, the provider is not upgraded automatically, so install version 4.0.0 explicitly. In general, an implementation that builds OS commands must neutralize special elements in any externally influenced value before it reaches the command.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which operator, hook, parameter or input channel is vulnerable. They also do not describe how the attacker supplies the input, what privileges are needed, or how the provider neutralizes input in version 4.0.0. This card therefore gives only version-level guidance and a general principle, not a code-level remedy.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs Apache Airflow with the Pinot Provider at a version before 4.0.0. A user without write access to DAG files influences a value that a Pinot task turns into an OS command, so the attacker controls the commands the task executes.

A deployment runs Airflow 2.3.0 or later with the Pinot Provider explicitly installed at version 4.0.0 or later. Externally influenced values are not passed unneutralized into OS commands in the task execution context.

citations.quote: allows an attacker to control commands executed in the task execution context, without write access to DAG files
Apache Airflow Pinot Provider 4.0.0 can only be installed for Airflow 2.3.0+
you need to manually install the Pinot Provider version 4.0.0 in order to get rid of the vulnerability

patterns.title: Unescaped Host header reflected in NameVirtualHost 404 page enables HTML injection
patterns.cause: When the Host header does not match a configured host, twisted.web.vhost.NameVirtualHost returns a NoResource resource. That resource renders the attacker-supplied Host header into the 404 HTML response without escaping it. Markup or script in the header therefore reaches the response body as live HTML.
preconditions: The application uses twisted.web.vhost.NameVirtualHost to serve a Twisted web site.
The Twisted version is 0.9.4 or later and earlier than 22.10.0rc1.
A request arrives whose Host header matches no configured virtual host, so the 404 NoResource path is taken.
The attacker can control the Host header of a request whose response is rendered by a victim or client.
patterns.prevention: Treat the Host header as untrusted input. Any HTML page that echoes it, including error pages, must encode HTML-significant characters first, or must not echo it at all. Upgrade Twisted to 22.10.0rc1 or later, which contains the fix. The advisory lists no workarounds, so upgrading is the documented remedy.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so no implementation detail is given here. The CVE text says exploitation should be very difficult in practice, because modifying the Host header of a normal request implies a privileged position. The sources cover only the NameVirtualHost 404 path and do not say whether other Twisted components echo the Host header.

fixtures.scenario: A site is served through a NameVirtualHost with no matching host entry. A request arrives with a Host header containing an HTML heading element. The 404 body echoes the header value as live markup, so the injected element is interpreted by the browser.

The same request is sent to a site running Twisted 22.10.0rc1 or later, or to a site that encodes HTML-significant characters before echoing the header. The 404 page shows the header only as inert text, and no injected element is parsed.

citations.quote: renders the Host header unescaped into the 404 response allowing HTML and script injection.
In practice this should be very difficult to exploit as being able to modify the Host header
This issue was fixed in version 22.10.0rc1. There are no known workarounds.
first appeared in the 0.9.4 release.

patterns.title: Regular expression denial of service in Mako Lexer parsing before 1.2.2
patterns.cause: Mako versions before 1.2.2 are vulnerable to regular expression denial of service when the Lexer class is used to parse template text. The sources do not say which expression is responsible or what input triggers the slowdown. The babelplugin and linguaplugin components are also affected.
preconditions: The installed Mako version is earlier than 1.2.2.
Template text is parsed through the Lexer class, directly or through the babelplugin or linguaplugin integrations.
The text being parsed can be influenced by an untrusted party.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Mako to version 1.2.2 or later, which is the release the advisories name as the boundary for this issue. Apply the upgrade to every environment that runs Lexer-based parsing, including message extraction through babelplugin and linguaplugin. Until the upgrade is possible, avoid passing template text from untrusted sources to the Lexer class.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the vulnerable expression, the input shape that triggers it, or the change made in the fix. They give no guidance on input size limits or timeouts, and they do not say whether anything other than upgrading mitigates the issue. This card therefore only covers upgrading and limiting exposure of the parsing path to untrusted text.

fixtures.scenario: A service uses a Mako release earlier than 1.2.2 and feeds template text supplied by an outside party into the Lexer class, so a crafted input can make parsing consume excessive time.
The same service runs Mako 1.2.2 or later, and its Lexer, babelplugin and linguaplugin parsing paths use that patched release.

citations.quote: Sqlalchemy mako before 1.2.2 is vulnerable to Regular expression Denial of Service when using the Lexer class to parse.
This also affects babelplugin and linguaplugin.

patterns.title: Untrusted run_id in Airflow example DAGs enables command execution
patterns.cause: In Apache Airflow versions before 2.4.0, the example DAGs let a user who can trigger DAGs from the UI supply a run_id by hand. That value led to arbitrary command execution. The run_id is attacker-controlled input and was not kept apart from command execution.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version earlier than 2.4.0 is running.
The example DAGs are available in the deployment.
The attacker has UI access and can trigger DAGs.
The attacker can type in a run_id value when triggering a DAG manually.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 2.4.0 or later. In any DAG code you write, treat run_id as untrusted user input. Do not let its content become part of command text that a shell or other interpreter will run. Keep it as plain data, and validate or restrict its content before using it in any operation that runs commands.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which example DAG was affected or how run_id reached command execution. They do not describe the upstream change or give workarounds other than the fixed version boundary. This card gives only a general direction and is not a complete audit of how run_id is used elsewhere. The sources do not cover custom DAGs, but any code that handles run_id the same way should be reviewed.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow deployment on a version before 2.4.0 has example DAGs available. A user with UI access triggers one manually and enters a run_id containing command text instead of a normal identifier. The command runs on the Airflow host.
The deployment runs Airflow 2.4.0 or later. A user triggers a DAG with an unusual run_id, and the value is treated only as data, so no command from it is executed.

citations.quote: allows an attacker with UI access who can trigger DAGs, to execute arbitrary commands via manually provided run_id parameter
This issue affects Apache Airflow versions prior to 2.4.0.
Apache Airflow vulnerable to OS Command Injection via example DAGs

patterns.title: OS command injection via Apache Airflow Pig Provider before 4.0.0
patterns.cause: The Pig Provider did not properly neutralize special elements used in an OS command (CWE-78). An attacker could therefore control commands executed in the task execution context, without needing write access to DAG files.
preconditions: The Apache Airflow Pig Provider is installed at a version prior to 4.0.0.
Apache Airflow is a version prior to 2.3.0 with the Pig Provider installed, which also impacts such deployments.
On Airflow 2.3.0 or later, Pig Provider 4.0.0 or newer has not been manually installed.
patterns.prevention: Move to Pig Provider 4.0.0 or later. The advisory says this version must be installed manually, even on Airflow 2.3.0 or later, and can only be installed on Airflow 2.3.0 or later, so older Airflow deployments must be upgraded first. In general, an implementation that builds OS commands must neutralize special elements in any externally influenced value before it reaches the command.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the affected parameters, the entry point an attacker uses, or the code-level change in the fix. They also do not say how the neutralization is implemented. This card therefore only describes the version-based remediation and the general principle, not a verified code-level mitigation.

The sources do not say how Airflow implemented its fix, so this is the general direction for the weakness class and not a description of the patch.

patterns.title: ReDoS in setuptools package_index when parsing untrusted index HTML
patterns.cause: In setuptools 65.5.0 and earlier, package_index.py uses a vulnerable regular expression on HTML fetched from a package page or a custom PackageIndex page. Crafted HTML can make the match take excessive time, which causes denial of service.
preconditions: setuptools version 65.5.0 or earlier is in use
The package_index code fetches HTML from a PyPI package page or a custom PackageIndex page
An attacker can influence the HTML content, for example through a crafted package or a malicious custom index
patterns.prevention: Upgrade setuptools to 65.5.1 or later, which patches the vulnerable regular expression. Treat HTML fetched from package indexes as untrusted input. Do not run backtracking-prone regular expressions over it without safeguards. Where possible, restrict which index servers a build or install process contacts.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the exact regular expression, the input shape that triggers the slowdown, or how the patch changes the matching logic. They give no measurements of impact. Guidance beyond upgrading and treating fetched HTML as untrusted is therefore general and not confirmed by the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A build environment runs setuptools 65.5.0 and fetches a package page from a custom index. The page contains crafted HTML, and the regular expression in package_index.py consumes excessive processing time, so the process stalls.
A build environment runs setuptools 65.5.1 or later and fetches the same crafted page. The patched matching does not cause a denial of service, and the process continues normally.

patterns.title: OS command injection in the Apache Airflow Spark Provider (CVE-2022-40954)
patterns.cause: The Spark Provider did not properly neutralize special elements used in an OS command (CWE-78). An attacker could therefore read arbitrary files in the task execution context without having write access to DAG files.
preconditions: Apache Airflow Spark Provider is installed at a version prior to 4.0.0.
Alternatively, Airflow is a version prior to 2.3.0 with the Spark Provider installed, since Spark Provider 4.0.0 can only be installed on Airflow 2.3.0 or later.
An Airflow 2.3.0 or later deployment still carries the risk if it keeps a lower Spark Provider version, so the provider must be upgraded manually.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade the Spark Provider to version 4.0.0 or later, which requires running Airflow 2.3.0 or later. Do not assume that upgrading Airflow alone is enough, because a lower Spark Provider version may remain installed and must be upgraded explicitly. Code that builds OS commands from external values should neutralize special elements before they reach the command.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which operator, hook or parameter is affected, or how the attacker supplies the malicious input. They also do not describe the upstream code change. The only impact they state is arbitrary file read in the task execution context. They say nothing about other providers or any workaround short of upgrading.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs Airflow 2.2.x with an older Spark Provider installed. An attacker without write access to DAG files can read arbitrary files in the task execution context.
A deployment runs Airflow 2.3.0 or later and has manually installed Spark Provider 4.0.0, so the vulnerable provider version is no longer present.

patterns.title: Locale parameter in internationalized URLs interpreted as a regular expression (Django ReDoS)
patterns.cause: In affected Django releases, the locale parameter used by internationalized URLs was treated as a regular expression. Because the value was interpreted as a pattern rather than matched as plain text, it could be used for a potential denial of service attack (CWE-1333, inefficient regular expression complexity).
preconditions: The application runs Django 3.2 before 3.2.16, 4.0 before 4.0.8, or 4.1 before 4.1.2.
The application uses internationalized URLs.
A locale parameter value that an attacker can influence reaches the code that treats it as a regular expression.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 3.2.16, 4.0.8, 4.1.2 or a later release. In any code that builds URL patterns from locale values, do not let a locale value be interpreted as regular expression syntax. Treat it as literal text, either by matching it as a plain string or by escaping it fully before it is combined into a pattern. Where practical, compare it against a fixed list of configured language codes instead of a pattern.
patterns.limitations: The advisories are brief. They do not say which Django component or function was affected, what pattern shape triggers the slowdown, how severe the slowdown is, or how the upstream change works. They do not say whether any input other than the locale parameter is affected. This card does not claim that input length limits or other mitigations are sufficient. The upgrade is the only remedy named by the version ranges in the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A site on Django 4.0.7 serves internationalized URLs. A remote client supplies a crafted locale value, and the framework treats it as a regular expression, so request handling can be slowed enough to deny service to other users.

The same site runs Django 4.0.8 or later, or any code that handles locale values treats them as literal text or checks them against a fixed list of configured languages. A crafted locale value is matched as ordinary text and gets no regular expression interpretation.

citations.quote: internationalized URLs were subject to a potential denial of service attack via the locale parameter, which is treated as a regular expression.
In Django 3.2 before 3.2.16, 4.0 before 4.0.8, and 4.1 before 4.1.2

patterns.title: WsgiDAV directory browser can render untrusted data as cross site scripting
patterns.cause: When directory browsing is enabled, WsgiDAV's directory browser user interface can be exploited for cross site scripting if untrusted data is displayed in it. The advisory names the realm and the user name as examples. The sources do not describe the exact code path.
preconditions: WsgiDAV is used with its directory browsing feature enabled.
The deployment displays untrusted data in the directory browser user interface, for example a realm or user name.
A version of WsgiDAV earlier than 4.1.0 is in use.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade WsgiDAV to version 4.1.0 or later. If an upgrade is not possible, turn off the directory browser in the library configuration, which is the workaround the advisory gives. Treat any value shown in the directory browser interface, such as a realm or user name, as untrusted input and do not let outside parties control it.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not explain the vulnerable code path or how version 4.1.0 changes it, so this card does not describe the fix internals. The advisory says an attacker cannot exploit this simply by uploading a file or folder with a manipulated name. The sources do not list every field that may be affected beyond the realm and user name examples. Disabling the directory browser removes that feature, and the sources say nothing about other WsgiDAV features.

fixtures.scenario: A WsgiDAV server older than 4.1.0 has directory browsing enabled. Its realm or user name values come from a source that outsiders can influence, and these values are shown in the directory browser page.
The same server runs WsgiDAV 4.1.0 or later, or it has the directory browser disabled in its configuration, so the page that displays those values is not exposed in a vulnerable form.

citations.quote: Implementations using this library with directory browsing enabled may be susceptible to Cross Site Scripting (XSS) attacks.

This issue has been patched, users can upgrade to version 4.1.0.

patterns.title: Open redirect via the success_url parameter in Horizon Web Dashboard
patterns.cause: Horizon Web Dashboard versions 19.4.0 through 20.1.4 are affected by an open redirect (CWE-601) reachable through the success_url parameter. The advisories give no further mechanism, so the likely cause is that a caller-supplied destination is used for a redirect without enough restriction. That reading is an inference from the weakness class, not something the sources state.
preconditions: The deployment runs Horizon Web Dashboard in the affected range, 19.4.0 through 20.1.4.
A request can carry a success_url parameter whose value an outside party can choose or influence.
A user can be induced to follow a link or submit a request that carries that value.
patterns.prevention: Do not send users to a redirect target taken from the success_url parameter unless it has been validated first. Accept only destinations the application trusts, such as relative paths on its own host or an explicit allow list of hosts. Otherwise ignore the supplied value and use a fixed default page. Run the check on the final, fully parsed target, not on the raw string. Upgrading to a Horizon release that includes the vendor fix for the referenced bug is the direct remedy.
patterns.limitations: The sources only name the affected version range and the success_url parameter. They do not say which views or forms use the parameter, how the vulnerable code handles it, what the impact is beyond an open redirect, or which release fixes it. The validation guidance above is general CWE-601 practice, not a description of the upstream change. Check the linked bug report and the vendor release notes before relying on a specific fixed version.

patterns.title: XXE in OpenStack Swift S3 API allows arbitrary host file read via crafted XML
patterns.cause: The S3 compatibility layer of OpenStack Swift (s3api and swift3) accepted XML supplied by authenticated users and parsed it in a way that let crafted XML make the service return arbitrary file contents from the host server. The sources classify this as XML external entity injection but do not describe the exact parser or configuration involved.
preconditions: The deployment runs OpenStack Swift before 2.28.1, a 2.29.x release before 2.29.2, or version 2.30.0.
The S3 API is enabled, either through s3api (Rocky or later) or swift3 (Queens and earlier).
The attacker is an authenticated user able to submit crafted XML files to the S3 API.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a fixed Swift release (2.28.1, 2.29.2, or a later version). In general, an implementation that parses XML from API clients should not let that XML cause external resources or local files to be resolved, so that file contents from the host can never appear in a response. Treat all client-supplied XML as untrusted input, including requests from authenticated users.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the vulnerable XML parser, the specific S3 operations or XML elements affected, or the exact hardening used in the fix, so this card gives only general direction. They also do not say whether network-based entity resolution is possible, or whether any workaround exists short of upgrading. The swift3 project is described as no longer actively developed, and the sources do not say whether it receives a fix.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user sends the S3 API an XML document containing an external entity declaration that points to a local file on the Swift host, and the service returns that file content in its response.
The same authenticated user sends the same crafted XML to a patched Swift release, and the service does not resolve the external entity, so no host file contents are returned.

citations.quote: By supplying crafted XML files, an authenticated user may coerce the S3 API into returning arbitrary file contents from the host server
This impacts both s3api deployments (Rocky or later), and swift3 deployments (Queens and earlier, no longer actively developed).
An issue was discovered in OpenStack Swift before 2.28.1, 2.29.x before 2.29.2, and 2.30.0.

They also do not say whether any workaround exists short of upgrading. This card therefore cannot say which inputs to encode or sanitize, and it is not a complete defense against stored XSS in general.

patterns.title: Remote file existence check via absolute path traversal in mlflow server and mlflow ui
patterns.cause: In the MLflow Model Registry served by the mlflow server or mlflow ui commands, an absolute path traversal flaw (CWE-36) lets a remote actor check whether arbitrary files exist on the host or in remote storage the host can reach. The files need not be related to MLflow. The check works when the server is not restricted to trusted callers.
preconditions: The MLflow Model Registry is hosted with the mlflow server or mlflow ui command on a version older than the patched release.
Callers are not limited, for example by a cloud VPC, an IP allowlist, or authentication and authorization middleware.
The server has access to files outside MLflow's own data, including remote locations such as cloud blob storage.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a patched MLflow release; the advisory names 2.2.1 and the CVE record names 2.2.2. Limit who can query Model Registry and Tracking servers with a VPC, an IP allowlist, authentication or authorization middleware, or another access restriction. Reduce the impact of any remaining flaw by scoping the server's cloud credentials so it can only reach files and directories related to MLflow. Integrations that do not run mlflow server or mlflow ui are not affected.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the vulnerable code path, the request parameter involved, or how the upstream fix works, so no code-level mitigation is stated here. They disagree on the fixed version: the advisory says 2.2.1 and the CVE and PYSEC records say prior to 2.2.2. Treat 2.2.2 or later as the safer target. Access restriction and credential scoping are workarounds that limit exposure and do not remove the flaw. The sources describe the impact as existence checks only and do not discuss reading file contents.

fixtures.scenario: A team runs mlflow server on an older version with the Model Registry reachable by any host on a broad network. There is no authentication, and the server uses cloud credentials that can read many buckets. A remote caller can learn whether arbitrary local or remote files exist.

The team runs a patched MLflow release, places the server behind a VPC with an IP allowlist and authentication middleware, and scopes the server's cloud credentials to MLflow artifact locations only. Unrelated files cannot be probed by outsiders.

citations.quote: enables an actor to check the existence of arbitrary files unrelated to MLflow from the host server

restrict the scope of your server's cloud credentials such that it can only access files and directories related to MLflow

patterns.title: Path traversal in MLflow server and UI lets remote callers read files outside MLflow storage
patterns.cause: In MLflow versions before 2.2.1, the mlflow server and mlflow ui commands accepted a path value containing traversal elements, such as a backslash followed by two dots and a file name. This let a remote actor download arbitrary files unrelated to MLflow from the host, including files in remote locations the host can reach. The sources do not describe the exact vulnerable code path.
preconditions: The deployment runs the mlflow server or mlflow ui command with an MLflow version older than 2.2.1.
The MLflow Model Registry is hosted through those commands.
Untrusted parties can query the server because there is no VPC, IP allowlist, or authentication or authorization middleware.
The server has access to files beyond MLflow data, such as local host files or remote storage reachable with its credentials.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to MLflow 2.2.1 or later, which patches this issue. Until then, limit who can reach the Model Registry and Tracking servers with a cloud VPC, an IP allowlist for inbound requests, or authentication and authorization middleware. Also restrict the server's remote credentials, for example cloud blob storage credentials, so they only reach files and directories related to MLflow. In general, an implementation should not let a caller-supplied path escape the intended MLflow storage location, and its checks should cover backslash-style traversal as well as forward-slash forms.
patterns.limitations: The sources give no details of the vulnerable code path, the affected endpoints, or how the patch validates paths, so the general guidance on path checks is inferred from the weakness label and not from the fix. Network restrictions and credential scoping reduce exposure but do not remove the flaw in unpatched versions. Integrations that do not use mlflow server or mlflow ui, such as Databricks Managed MLflow and MLflow on Azure Machine Learning, are reported as unaffected.

fixtures.scenario: An MLflow 2.2.0 instance started with mlflow server is exposed to a wide network with no authentication. A remote caller sends a request whose path value uses backslash and two-dot traversal elements to name a file outside MLflow storage, and the server returns that file.

The same deployment runs MLflow 2.2.1 or later. The server sits inside a VPC with an inbound IP allowlist and uses cloud credentials scoped to MLflow artifact locations only, so a traversal-style request cannot reach unrelated files.

patterns.cause: The URL value submitted through the Add a new change detection watch function is stored and later shown on the main page. A crafted payload in that value can run as script or HTML in the browser of anyone who views the page. The sources do not name the exact rendering code path.
preconditions: The application accepts a user-supplied value in the URL parameter of the Add a new change detection watch function.
The stored value is later shown on the main page to users.
The affected version is older than the fixed release (see limitations for the version discrepancy).
patterns.prevention: Treat the watch URL as untrusted data at every point where it is shown. Encode it for the HTML context on output so that markup and script in the value display as plain text instead of executing. Also validate the value on input so that only well-formed URLs are stored. Review every other place that shows the stored URL, not only the main page. Upgrade to a release that contains the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the vulnerable code, the specific payload forms, or the exact upstream change, so the output encoding and validation advice is general direction rather than a confirmed description of the fix. The sources disagree on the affected range: one says before 0.40.2, the others say before v0.40.1.1. Confirm the fixed version against the project release notes. The sources do not say whether other fields or pages are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A user adds a new watch and enters a URL value containing a crafted script or HTML payload. The value is stored. When anyone opens the main page, the payload is rendered as active content and runs in their browser.

A user adds a new watch and enters the same crafted payload. The application rejects it as an invalid URL, or stores it and encodes it on output. The main page shows it as inert text and no script runs.

citations.quote: Changedetection.io before 0.40.2 was discovered to contain a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the main page.
execute arbitrary web scripts or HTML via a crafted payload injected into the URL parameter
Changedetection.io before v0.40.1.1 was discovered to contain a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the main page.

patterns.title: Shell command injection through the terminal title helper in IPython on Windows without ctypes
patterns.cause: The IPython terminal title helper, set_term_title in IPython.utils.terminal, can let text passed as the title be run as shell commands. This happens on Windows when ctypes is unavailable. Untrusted text such as a directory name can then become commands executed with the privileges of the current process.
preconditions: The code runs on Windows in a Python environment where ctypes is not available.

set_term_title is called directly, for example by a tool that uses IPython as a library. The ipython binary itself does not reach the vulnerable code, because the ctypes dependency in IPython.utils._process_win32 blocks it.
Attacker-influenced text, such as a directory name the user is induced to enter, reaches the title argument.
An affected IPython release is installed.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade IPython to a patched release. Until then, make sure every call to set_term_title uses only trusted or filtered input. Do not pass attacker-influenced strings such as folder names, paths or user-supplied labels as the title. Library authors who call this helper should treat the title as untrusted data and must not rely on the ctypes dependency to make the vulnerable path unreachable.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the patch changes the code, so this card does not either. They also do not say exactly how the shell command is built. The advisories disagree on the fixed version: the CVE and PYSEC text say prior to 8.1.0, while the GitHub advisory says prior to 8.10.0. Check the installed version against the GitHub advisory. The sources do not say what filtering is sufficient. The impact is limited to the scope of the current process.

fixtures.scenario: A Windows tool built on IPython as a library runs in an environment without ctypes. It calls set_term_title with the current working directory, and an attacker has created a folder whose name contains shell command text. When the user changes into that folder, the text can run as commands.

The same tool runs on a patched IPython release, or it only calls set_term_title with a fixed trusted title or a value filtered against shell metacharacters. A folder name containing command text is not executed.

citations.quote: Should an attacker get untrusted input to an instance of this function they would be able to inject shell commands as current process
Users are only vulnerable when calling this function in Windows in a Python environment where
Users of ipython as a library are advised to upgrade.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS from URL payloads rendered as-is in hosted Streamlit apps
patterns.cause: In Streamlit versions 0.63.0 through 0.80.0, a hosted app could be reached through a crafted URL carrying Javascript payloads. The server then rendered the malicious payload as-is instead of treating it as inert data, so the script ran in the victim's browser.
preconditions: The app runs a Streamlit version from 0.63.0 through 0.80.0 inclusive.
The app is hosted so that other users reach it over a network.
An attacker can craft a URL with Javascript payloads that points at the app.
A user is tricked into visiting the malicious URL.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Streamlit 0.81.0 or later, which contains the patch. Any component that echoes URL-supplied content back to a page should treat that content as untrusted data and never render it as-is. Retire unsupported versions, since the affected range is no longer supported, and run a current supported release.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the URL parameter, page, or component that rendered the payload, and they do not describe how the patch works. This card therefore gives only the general direction of not rendering URL-borne content as-is. The advisory rates severity as moderate, with a maximum CVSSv3 base score of 5.9. Versions before 0.63.0 and after 0.80.0 are stated to need no action.

fixtures.scenario: A team hosts an internal dashboard on a Streamlit release between 0.63.0 and 0.80.0. An attacker sends a colleague a link to the dashboard with a Javascript payload in the URL. The colleague opens it and the server renders the payload as-is, so the script executes in the colleague's browser.

The same dashboard runs Streamlit 0.81.0 or later. The same crafted link is opened, but the patched version does not render the payload as executable script, so nothing runs in the colleague's browser.

citations.quote: An attacker could craft a malicious URL with Javascript payloads to a Streamlit app.
the server would render the malicious javascript payload as-is, leading to XSS.
Version 0.81.0 contains a patch for this vulnerability.

patterns.title: Open redirect in Tornado 6.3.1 and earlier via a crafted URL
patterns.cause: Tornado versions 6.3.1 and earlier can be made to send a user to an arbitrary web site when the user opens a specially crafted URL. The sources do not name the affected handler, parameter, or the exact validation that is missing.
preconditions: The application runs Tornado version 6.3.1 or earlier.
A remote, unauthenticated attacker can craft a URL that the target application will process.
A user can be induced to access that crafted URL, for example through a phishing message.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a Tornado release newer than 6.3.1, since the advisories list 6.3.1 and earlier as affected. Do not let the destination of a redirect be controlled by data in an incoming URL unless it is confirmed to point to a site the application trusts. Review any place where the application redirects based on request input.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a one-sentence description. They do not identify the vulnerable component, the URL shape that triggers the issue, the first fixed version, or the upstream change. The version guidance is inferred from the affected range. The destination-checking advice is a general direction and is not described in the sources.

fixtures.scenario: An application on Tornado 6.3.1 receives a link with a crafted URL, sent by an attacker in a phishing message. A user opens it and is redirected to an attacker-chosen web site.

An application on a Tornado release newer than 6.3.1 receives the same crafted URL. Any redirect destination derived from request input is confirmed to be a trusted site, so the user is never sent to the attacker's site.

citations.quote: Open redirect vulnerability in Tornado versions 6.3.1 and earlier allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to redirect a user to an arbitrary web site
conduct a phishing attack by having user access a specially crafted URL.

patterns.title: Stored XSS in Wagtail ModelAdmin parent chooser and document inspect views
patterns.cause: Two Wagtail ModelAdmin admin views displayed attacker-influenced page and document data without safe HTML escaping. The sources describe the workaround as patched HTML escaping, using plain-text breadcrumbs for pages and escaped link markup for documents. A low-privilege editor could store content that ran script when a higher-privileged admin opened these views.
preconditions: Wagtail ModelAdmin is enabled, with Wagtail from version 1.5 and before 4.1.4 or 4.2.2
For pages, ChooseParentView is reachable because pages are managed through ModelAdmin
For documents, the ModelAdmin InspectView is enabled and shows document fields
A limited-permission editor can create pages or documents that a higher-privileged user later views
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Wagtail 4.1.4 or 4.2.2 or later. If upgrade is not possible, disable ModelAdmin for page models, or use a custom ChooseParentView that shows page breadcrumbs as plain text. For documents, disable InspectView, exclude document fields from it, or use a custom view that builds document link markup with escaped values. Treat content written by editors as untrusted in every admin view.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the exact fields that carry the payload, nor describe the upstream fix in detail. They cover only ChooseParentView and InspectView, so other admin views are not assessed. Ordinary site visitors without admin access are stated as not affected. The workaround must be applied to each ModelAdmin class concerned.

fixtures.scenario: A site runs an affected Wagtail with ModelAdmin managing a page model. A limited editor saves a page with script-bearing content. An administrator opens the Choose a parent page view, and the script runs with the administrator's credentials.
The site runs Wagtail 4.1.4 or 4.2.2 or later. The same editor content is shown in the Choose a parent page view and the document Inspect view as inert text, and no script runs for the administrator.

citations.quote: could potentially craft pages and documents that, when viewed by a user with higher privileges, could perform actions with that user's credentials
The vulnerability is not exploitable by an ordinary site visitor without access to the Wagtail admin, and only affects sites with ModelAdmin enabled.
Site owners who are unable to upgrade to the new versions can disable or override the corresponding functionality.
Patched versions have been released as Wagtail 4.1.4 and Wagtail 4.2.2.

patterns.title: Starlette StaticFiles path traversal via character-wise prefix check
patterns.cause: The static file handler decided whether a requested file was inside the served directory by calling os.path.commonprefix(). That function compares paths one character at a time and does not treat its arguments as paths. A dot-dot request that resolves to a sibling whose name begins with the served directory name (for example static1.txt next to static) therefore passes the containment check.
preconditions: The application serves files with StaticFiles from a directory such as static.
A sibling file or directory exists whose name starts with the same characters as the served directory name.
An attacker can send a request path containing dot-dot segments unchanged, for example with curl --path-as-is.
patterns.prevention: Check containment by comparing whole path components, not characters. Resolve the requested path to a normalized absolute form, then use os.path.commonpath() against the served directory, as the advisory recommends, and reject the request if the common path is not the served directory itself. Upgrade Starlette to 0.27.0 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the fixed version handles symbolic links, Windows path forms, or other normalization edge cases. They do not say whether the check alone is sufficient for every deployment. Only the dot-dot sibling-prefix case is documented.
