The affected range is stated as 0.13.5 up to, but not including, 0.27.0.

fixtures.scenario: A service mounts a static files handler on a directory named static. A sibling file named static1.txt and a sibling directory named static_disallow exist. A request using a dot-dot path, sent as-is, reaches the sibling and its content is returned.

Same layout, but the containment check compares whole path components after resolving the request path. The dot-dot request resolves outside the static directory and is rejected as not found, while files inside static are still served.

citations.quote: it does not treat the arguments as paths.
Confidentiality is breached: An attacker may obtain files that should not be open to the public.
allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to view files in a web service which was built using Starlette.

patterns.title: Stored XSS on the Airflow task instance details page (CVE-2023-29247)
patterns.cause: The task instance details page in the Apache Airflow UI is vulnerable to stored cross-site scripting. Stored XSS means persisted content is later delivered to a user's browser as active content instead of inert text. The sources do not say which stored field or which rendering step is responsible.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version is earlier than 2.6.0.
A user opens the task instance details page in the web UI.
Some content that an attacker can influence has been stored and is shown on that page. This follows from the stored XSS classification, and the sources do not name the field.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Apache Airflow to 2.6.0 or later, since the advisories state that versions before 2.6.0 are affected. When implementing similar pages, treat every stored value shown on the task instance details view as untrusted data. Encode it for the HTML context where it appears, so the browser displays it as text and never runs it as markup or script. The sources do not describe the actual upstream change, so this encoding guidance is the general direction for CWE-79 and not a description of that change.
patterns.limitations: The sources are brief and do not identify the vulnerable field, the data source, the required privileges for writing the malicious content, or the exact rendering flaw. They give no workaround other than the fixed version boundary. They do not confirm that all other UI pages are free of similar issues. This card does not describe or reproduce the upstream fix.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow deployment running a version earlier than 2.6.0 shows the task instance details page to operators. Attacker-influenced stored content appears on that page, and the browser treats it as active content when an operator views it.
An Airflow deployment runs version 2.6.0 or later. Stored values on the task instance details page are displayed as plain text, so an operator viewing the page does not trigger script execution.

citations.quote: Task instance details page in the UI is vulnerable to stored cross-site scripting.
This issue affects Apache Airflow before 2.6.0.

patterns.title: Directory traversal through the path parameter of the mlflow get-artifact endpoint
patterns.cause: The /get-artifact API method of mlflow accepts a client-supplied path parameter. The advisories say this lets attackers read arbitrary files on the server, so the requested path was not confined to the intended artifact location.
preconditions: The mlflow server exposes the /get-artifact API method to callers who are not fully trusted.
The server runs an affected mlflow version. The advisories give prior to v2.0.0 or up to v2.0.1.
The path parameter from the request is used to locate a file on the server.
patterns.prevention: Treat the path parameter as untrusted input. Before reading anything, resolve the requested location to its canonical form, for example with os.path.realpath(), and confirm it still lies inside the intended artifact root. Reject the request if it does not, including absolute paths and parent-directory references. Upgrade to an mlflow release that contains the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that the path parameter allows reading arbitrary files. They do not describe the exact validation that was missing or how the upstream fix works, so the confinement check above is a general direction and not a description of that fix. The advisories also disagree on the affected range: prior to v2.0.0 in one, up to v2.0.1 in the others. Check the fixed version against the project's own release notes.

fixtures.scenario: A client calls the /get-artifact endpoint with a path value that points outside the artifact store, and the server returns the contents of an arbitrary file from its filesystem.

A client calls the /get-artifact endpoint with a path value. The server resolves it to a canonical location and confirms it is inside the artifact root. A value that points elsewhere is rejected and no file content is returned.

citations.quote: A directory traversal vulnerability in the /get-artifact API method of the mlflow platform up to v2.0.1
allows attackers to read arbitrary files on the server via the path parameter.

patterns.title: Prompt-injected arbitrary URL retrieval (SSRF) in Langchain before 0.0.329
patterns.cause: In affected Langchain versions, prompt injection lets an attacker force the service to retrieve data from an arbitrary URL. The URL that gets fetched is influenced by attacker-controlled prompt content instead of being fixed by the application. This gives the attacker SSRF and a way to inject fetched content into downstream tasks.
preconditions: The application uses a Langchain version before 0.0.329 (the CVE record itself says through 0.0.155).
Attacker-influenced text reaches the prompt processed by the service.
The service can retrieve data from a URL as part of handling that prompt.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Langchain to 0.0.329 or later. Do not let text from a prompt alone decide which URL the service fetches, so the destination of any retrieval stays under application control. Treat retrieved content as untrusted input, because it can be injected into downstream tasks.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the vulnerable code path, the specific component involved, or how the upstream fix works, so this card gives no implementation-level guidance beyond upgrading. The advisories and the CVE record give different affected ranges (before 0.0.329 versus through 0.0.155), and the sources do not explain the difference. Whether any other mitigation, such as an allowlist or network egress controls, is sufficient is not established by the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A service built on a Langchain version before 0.0.329 accepts user text. An attacker embeds an instruction in that text that makes the service retrieve data from an attacker-chosen URL, and the fetched content then flows into later processing steps.
The service runs Langchain 0.0.329 or later. The destination of any retrieval is not decided by prompt text alone, and fetched content is handled as untrusted data before it reaches downstream tasks.

citations.quote: In Langchain before 0.0.329, prompt injection allows an attacker to force the service to retrieve data from an arbitrary URL
potentially injecting content into downstream tasks.
prompt injection allows an attacker to force the service to retrieve data from an arbitrary URL, essentially providing SSRF

patterns.title: Crafted input to the LangChain JIRA API wrapper can lead to OS command injection and remote code execution
patterns.cause: Versions of langchain before v0.0.225 contain a remote code execution flaw in the JiraAPIWrapper component. Attackers can execute arbitrary code by supplying crafted input. The advisory classifies it as OS command injection. The sources do not describe the exact code path or how the input reaches execution.
preconditions: The application uses langchain at a version before v0.0.225.
The application uses the JiraAPIWrapper component, also called the JIRA API wrapper.
An attacker can influence the input that is passed to that wrapper.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade langchain to v0.0.225 or later, where a fix is available. Until the upgrade is done, treat every value that reaches the JIRA API wrapper as untrusted, including text produced by users or by a language model acting on their behalf. Do not let such input be interpreted as executable code or as an operating system command. Where the wrapper is not needed, do not expose it to untrusted callers.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which parameter, method or code path is vulnerable, or how crafted input becomes code execution. They give no detail on what the fix changes. One source lists langchain 0.0.171 as vulnerable to arbitrary code execution, and its relationship to the JIRA wrapper issue is not stated. Input handling advice here is general and is not confirmed as sufficient without upgrading.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs langchain at a version before v0.0.225 and exposes the JIRA API wrapper to requests that carry attacker-controlled text. The attacker submits crafted input and arbitrary code runs on the host.

A service runs langchain v0.0.225 or later. Input to the JIRA API wrapper is still treated as untrusted, and the wrapper is only reachable by trusted callers, so crafted input does not lead to code execution.

citations.quote: Langchain before v0.0.225 was discovered to contain a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in the component JiraAPIWrapper (aka the JIRA API wrapper).
This vulnerability allows attackers to execute arbitrary code via crafted input.
Langchain OS Command Injection vulnerability
Langchain 0.0.171 is vulnerable to Arbitrary Code Execution.

patterns.title: ReDoS in Django EmailValidator and URLValidator via many domain name labels
patterns.cause: In affected Django releases, EmailValidator and URLValidator are subject to regular expression denial of service when the value contains a very large number of domain name labels. The validators' regular expression matching can be driven into excessive work by such crafted emails or URLs.
preconditions: The application runs Django 3.2 before 3.2.20, Django 4.1 before 4.1.10, or Django 4.2 before 4.2.3.
EmailValidator or URLValidator is applied to a value, for example through email or URL form and model fields.
An attacker can supply an email address or URL with a very large number of domain name labels.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Django to a release that includes the fix: 3.2.20 or later in the 3.2 series, 4.1.10 or later in the 4.1 series, or 4.2.3 or later in the 4.2 series. Confirm the deployed version after upgrading, including in container images and pinned requirements.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state the affected versions and that the attack uses a very large number of domain name labels. They do not describe the root regular expression flaw, the upstream code change, any interim workaround such as input length limits, or how much input is needed to cause a noticeable slowdown. Older Django series not listed are not addressed by the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A public signup form validates the email field with EmailValidator on Django 4.2.2. An attacker submits an address whose domain part has a very large number of labels, and the validation work ties up the worker handling the request.
The same signup form runs on Django 4.2.3 or later, which is outside the affected range, so an email with a very large number of domain labels is not subject to this ReDoS.

citations.quote: potential ReDoS (regular expression denial of service) attack via a very large number of domain name labels of emails and URLs.
In Django 3.2 before 3.2.20, 4 before 4.1.10, and 4.2 before 4.2.3

patterns.title: SQL injection via SQLDatabaseChain in langchain before v0.0.247
patterns.cause: The langchain SQLDatabaseChain component in versions before v0.0.247 contains a SQL injection flaw (CWE-89). A remote attacker can use it to obtain sensitive information. The sources do not describe the exact code path or how attacker input reaches the SQL layer.
preconditions: The application uses langchain at a version before v0.0.247.
The application uses the SQLDatabaseChain component.
A remote attacker can supply input that reaches that component.
The connected database holds data that is sensitive.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade langchain to v0.0.247 or later, which is the first version the CVE record does not list as affected. Until the upgrade is done, do not expose SQLDatabaseChain to input from untrusted remote users. Where it must stay exposed, connect it with database credentials limited to the minimum data needed, so a successful injection reveals as little as possible.
patterns.limitations: The sources are brief and give no root-cause detail, no description of the upstream change, and no list of unsafe usage patterns. They do not say whether other langchain SQL components are affected, or whether the least-privilege and exposure-limiting advice fully contains the issue. PYSEC-2023-110 names v.0.0.64, while the CVE record says all versions before v0.0.247. Check the vendor advisory for the exact affected range.

fixtures.scenario: A public web service runs langchain v0.0.64 and passes user-submitted text to SQLDatabaseChain over a database that holds customer records. A remote attacker crafts input that triggers SQL injection and reads data the service was never meant to return.
The service runs langchain v0.0.247 or later, and SQLDatabaseChain uses a database account limited to the minimum data needed. The same crafted input does not expose the sensitive records.

citations.quote: SQL injection vulnerability in langchain before v0.0.247 allows a remote attacker to obtain sensitive information via the SQLDatabaseChain component.
SQL injection vulnerability in langchain v.0.0.64 allows a remote attacker to obtain sensitive information via the SQLDatabaseChain component.

patterns.title: Low-privilege role can test database connections through default REST API permission
patterns.cause: The default permission set in Apache Superset up to and including 2.1.0 let the Gamma role use the REST API function that tests database connections. This function was not limited to roles meant to manage databases, so an authorization gap left an outbound-connection feature open to low-privilege users.
preconditions: Apache Superset version 2.1.0 or earlier is deployed.
The attacker holds an authenticated account with the Gamma role.
The default REST API permissions for the Gamma role have not been tightened.
patterns.prevention: Grant any API function that makes the server connect to a configurable database target only to roles that are meant to manage database connections. Do not include it in the default permissions of low-privilege roles such as Gamma. Audit role-to-permission mappings after install and after upgrade, and move to a Superset release newer than 2.1.0 that corrects the default permission. Keep an authorization check on the connection-test endpoint itself, so it does not rely on the user being logged in.
patterns.limitations: The advisories give only a one-sentence description. They do not name the endpoint, the permission name, the fixed release, or the exact network behavior. The server-side request forgery classification comes from the CWE metadata, not from the source text. This card therefore cannot say which internal targets are reachable or what a tester can learn from the responses.

fixtures.scenario: A Superset 2.1.0 instance runs with default role permissions. A user logged in with only the Gamma role calls the REST API to test a database connection, and the request is accepted although the user has no database management duties.

The same instance has the connection-test permission removed from the Gamma role, or runs a release newer than 2.1.0 that corrects the default. The Gamma user's request to test a database connection is denied as unauthorized, and only database-management roles can run it.

citations.quote: An improper default REST API permission for Gamma users in Apache Superset up to and including 2.1.0
allows for an authenticated Gamma user to test database connections.

patterns.title: Apache Airflow before 2.6.3: crafted input from an authenticated user makes a request hang
patterns.cause: Improper input validation in Apache Airflow versions before 2.6.3 lets an authenticated user send crafted input that makes the current request hang. The sources give no further detail on the mechanism.
preconditions: The deployment runs Apache Airflow at a version before 2.6.3.
The attacker is an authenticated user who can submit input to the affected request path.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Apache Airflow to 2.6.3 or later, a version that is not affected. Treat user-supplied input as untrusted and validate it before processing, since the issue is classed as improper input validation. Do not rely on authentication alone to limit who can trigger the hang.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the affected endpoint, parameter, or code path. They do not describe the hang mechanism, such as a backtracking pattern, and do not say whether the impact is a single stalled request or wider resource exhaustion. The redos family label and the CWE-1333 tag suggest an inefficient-complexity cause, but the sources do not confirm it. The only concrete remediation they state is upgrading, so no code-level fix or input constraint is given here.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow deployment on a version before 2.6.3 accepts input from an authenticated user. That user submits crafted input and the current request hangs.
An Airflow deployment runs version 2.6.3 or later. The same crafted input from an authenticated user does not cause the request to hang.

citations.quote: an authenticated user can use crafted input to make the current request hang
It is recommended to upgrade to a version that is not affected

patterns.title: Airflow test connection feature abused by users with Connection edit privileges
patterns.cause: In Apache Airflow before 2.7.0, an authenticated user with Connection edit privileges can read connection information and abuse the test connection feature. Sending many requests can cause denial of service, and the server can be made to establish harmful connections.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version earlier than 2.7.0 is deployed
The attacker is authenticated and holds Connection edit privileges
The test connection feature is reachable by that user
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Apache Airflow to version 2.7.0 or newer. Review and narrow user permissions so that only trusted administrators can edit Connections or reach sensitive functionality. Treat the test connection feature as a sensitive operation that makes the server open outbound connections on behalf of the user.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the internal flaw or what the upstream fix changed. They do not say whether rate limiting or destination filtering was added, or whether the test connection feature is disabled by default in 2.7.0. They name no workaround other than upgrading and reducing permissions. Permission review lowers exposure but is not shown to remove the flaw on older versions.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 2.6 deployment grants Connection edit rights to many users. One user repeatedly submits test connection requests with chosen settings, exhausting the server and making it open unwanted connections.
Airflow 2.7.0 or newer is deployed, and Connection edit rights are limited to a few trusted administrators who have reviewed their access to sensitive functions.

citations.quote: can be exploited by an authenticated user possessing Connection edit privileges
exploit the test connection feature by sending many requests, leading to a denial of service (DoS) condition on the server
administrators are encouraged to review and adjust user permissions to restrict access to sensitive functionalities, reducing the attack surface.

patterns.title: Absolute path traversal in mlflow before 2.5.0 (CVE-2023-3765)
patterns.cause: The advisories classify the flaw as an absolute path traversal in the mlflow project. In this class of bug, a caller-supplied path that is already absolute is used to reach files directly, instead of being kept inside an intended base location. The sources do not name the affected function, endpoint, or parameter.
preconditions: The deployment runs mlflow at a version earlier than 2.5.0.
A path value comes from an untrusted party and is used for file access.
The path is not confined to an intended base directory before it is used.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mlflow to version 2.5.0 or later. In any code that accepts file locations from untrusted input, refuse absolute paths. Resolve the final path with a canonicalizing call such as os.path.realpath(). Then confirm the resolved result is still inside the intended base directory before any read or write. Reject the request if it is not.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that this is an absolute path traversal in mlflow prior to 2.5.0. They do not identify the vulnerable component, the entry point, the impact (read, write, or both), or the exact fix. The generic hardening steps above are the standard defense for this weakness class, not a description of the upstream change. Check the mlflow release notes and advisory details before treating any specific code path as affected or fixed.

fixtures.scenario: A service running an mlflow version older than 2.5.0 accepts a file location from a remote user. The user supplies an absolute path that points outside the intended storage area, and the service uses it as given.

A service runs mlflow 2.5.0 or later. Any custom code that handles user-supplied locations rejects absolute paths, resolves the final path, and verifies it lies under the intended base directory before accessing the file.

citations.quote: Absolute Path Traversal in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.5.0.
Absolute Path Traversal in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.5.0.

patterns.title: Command injection in PaddlePaddle fs.py before version 2.5.0
patterns.cause: PaddlePaddle releases before 2.5.0 contain a command injection flaw in the fs.py module. It allowed arbitrary commands to run on the host operating system. The sources do not describe the exact code path or which inputs reach it.
preconditions: A PaddlePaddle release earlier than 2.5.0 is installed.
The fs.py module is present and in use in the affected deployment.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade PaddlePaddle to version 2.5.0 or later, which is the release boundary named in the advisories. In general, for this weakness class (CWE-78), an implementation avoids the problem by never letting externally supplied text be interpreted as part of an operating system command. Review any local code that builds command invocations from data it does not control.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that fs.py has a command injection and that it enables arbitrary command execution. They do not identify the vulnerable function, the attacker-controlled input, the required privileges, or how the upstream change works. The prevention guidance beyond upgrading is general to CWE-78 and is not confirmed against the actual fix.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs PaddlePaddle older than 2.5.0 and uses its fs.py functionality with values that an outside party can influence, so an attacker may be able to run arbitrary commands on the host.
The same service runs PaddlePaddle 2.5.0 or later, and any custom code that invokes operating system commands keeps untrusted data out of command interpretation.

citations.quote: PaddlePaddle before 2.5.0 has a command injection in fs.py.
This resulted in the ability to execute arbitrary commands on the operating system.

patterns.title: Open redirect after login in Jupyter Server via crafted login links
patterns.cause: The login flow could send a user to an arbitrary site after a successful login, or when a session was already logged in. The redirect destination was not limited to URLs served by Jupyter Server itself, so a maliciously crafted login link could point the browser anywhere.
preconditions: The attacker knows the address of a Jupyter Server.
The victim follows a maliciously crafted login link for that server.
The login succeeds, or the victim already has a logged-in session, and the server then redirects the browser.
patterns.prevention: Treat any post-login redirect destination taken from a request as untrusted input. Before redirecting, confirm that the destination is a URL served by the same Jupyter Server, and refuse or replace any other destination with a safe default page on the server. Apply the same check whether the login just succeeded or the session was already authenticated. Upgrade jupyter-server to release 2.7.2 or later, which contains the fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the specific request parameter, the exact validation rules, or how the fix works internally, so this card cannot describe them. They also report no workarounds, so upgrading is the only remediation they confirm. They do not say what an attacker could do on the destination site, beyond the redirect itself.

fixtures.scenario: A user receives a login link for a known Jupyter Server that carries a destination pointing to an external site. The user logs in, or is already logged in, and the server sends the browser to that external site.
A user receives the same kind of login link, but the server accepts only destinations served by the Jupyter Server. The external destination is rejected and the browser lands on a page on the server.

citations.quote: Maliciously crafted login links to known Jupyter Servers can cause successful login or an already logged-in session to be redirected to arbitrary sites
which should be restricted to Jupyter Server-served URLs
There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

patterns.title: Incomplete cross-site credential checks on the jupyter-server files endpoint
patterns.cause: The handler serving the /files/ URLs did not apply proper cross-site credential checks. The earlier upstream patch for CVE-2019-9644 was not applied completely, so part of that vulnerability stayed open. As a result, certain file contents could be exposed to cross-site requests, or files could be accessed when a user opened untrusted files via Open image in new tab.
preconditions: jupyter-server older than release 2.7.2 is in use
The /files/ URLs are served by the default files handler, not the alternative handler the advisory says implements the correct checks
A user can be induced to open untrusted content or an attacker-controlled page while having access to the server
patterns.prevention: Upgrade jupyter-server to 2.7.2 or later. If an upgrade is not possible, set the ContentsManager files handler class option to the FilesHandler class in jupyter_server.files.handlers. It is slower but implements the correct checks. In general, any handler that serves user files, including a performance-oriented replacement for a standard handler, should enforce the same cross-site credential checks as the reference handler. A security patch should also be applied to every handler path that serves the same data, so no variant is left unprotected.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which checks are missing, which request properties are validated, or how the faster default handler differs from FilesHandler. They do not describe a concrete exploit chain or the exact file types affected. This card gives only the general direction and the documented workaround, and it does not cover other endpoints.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs a jupyter-server version older than 2.7.2 with the default files handler. A user opens an untrusted file or a cross-site page, and a request to a /files/ URL is served without the proper cross-site credential check, exposing file contents.
A deployment runs jupyter-server 2.7.2 or later, or sets the files handler class option to the FilesHandler class. Cross-site requests to /files/ URLs are subject to the correct credential checks.

citations.quote: Upstream patch for CVE-2019-9644 was not applied completely, leaving part of the vulnerability open.
Improper cross-site credential checks on
which implements the correct checks.
Jupyter Server 2.7.2

patterns.title: Unblocked non-multi options in GitPython clone and clone_from allow command injection
patterns.cause: GitPython before 3.1.32 did not block insecure non-multi options in clone and clone_from. The library makes external calls to git without sufficient sanitization of input arguments, so attacker-influenced input such as a crafted remote URL can reach the git command line and lead to remote code execution. The advisory describes this as an incomplete fix for CVE-2022-24439.
preconditions: The application uses GitPython older than 3.1.32.
The application calls clone or clone_from.
An attacker can influence the remote URL or the options passed to the clone call.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade GitPython to 3.1.32 or later. Treat any remote URL or clone option that comes from users or other untrusted input as hostile. Do not let such input choose which git options are passed to clone or clone_from. Allow only a fixed, reviewed set of options and validate the repository URL against an expected form (for example, permitted schemes and hosts) before calling the library.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not list which options are considered insecure, do not describe the exact validation the fixed release performs, and do not give the precise exploit payload. This card therefore cannot say whether an input filter alone is sufficient, and it does not replace upgrading. The sources also do not cover other GitPython entry points beyond clone and clone_from.

fixtures.scenario: A web service lets users submit a repository address and optional clone settings. It passes them straight to clone_from on GitPython 3.1.31. A crafted remote URL or option value is forwarded to git and executes attacker-chosen commands on the server.

The same service runs GitPython 3.1.32 or later. It accepts only a repository URL that matches an allowlist of expected hosts and schemes, and it ignores any user-supplied clone options, so untrusted input cannot add options to the git invocation.

citations.quote: GitPython before 3.1.32 does not block insecure non-multi options in clone and clone_from.
the library makes external calls to git without sufficient sanitization of input arguments
which makes it possible to inject a maliciously crafted remote URL into the clone command

patterns.title: OS command injection in mlflow versions prior to 2.6.0 (CVE-2023-4033)
patterns.cause: The advisories classify the flaw as OS command injection (CWE-78) in the mlflow/mlflow project and say it affects versions prior to 2.6.0. They do not say which component, parameter or code path is affected.
preconditions: The deployment uses the mlflow package.
The installed mlflow version is older than 2.6.0.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mlflow to version 2.6.0 or later, since the advisories list only versions prior to 2.6.0 as affected. Confirm the installed version in every environment that runs mlflow, including servers, build images and developer machines.
patterns.limitations: The sources give no detail on the vulnerable entry point, the attacker-controlled input, the required privileges or how the command is built. They also give no code-level mitigation or workaround beyond the version boundary. This card therefore cannot say which features are exposed or how to harden code short of upgrading. Check the project's release notes for specifics.

fixtures.scenario: A team runs an mlflow installation whose version is older than 2.6.0, and it is within the range the advisories list as affected by OS command injection.
A team runs mlflow 2.6.0 or later, which is outside the affected range stated in the advisories.

citations.quote: OS Command Injection in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.6.0.
OS Command Injection in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.6.0.

patterns.title: Static view path traversal up one directory through null-byte handling in Python 3.11 path normalization
patterns.cause: On affected Python 3.11 and 3.12 pre-release versions, the path normalization function os.path.normpath truncates its input at the first null byte. A Pyramid static view that serves files from a full filesystem path can then resolve a request to a location one directory above the static root. The only file the sources say could be exposed this way is index.html in the parent directory. The sources do not describe the exact request form that triggers this.
preconditions: Pyramid 2.0.0 or 2.0.1 is in use.
The runtime is an affected Python version: 3.11.0 to 3.11.4, or 3.12.0a1 to 3.12.0rc1.
A static view is configured with a full filesystem path.
An index.html file sits exactly one directory above the static view's filesystem path.
patterns.prevention: Reject any requested path that contains a null byte before it is normalized or joined to the static root, so that truncation during normalization cannot change the resolved location. Run a Python version in which normalization no longer truncates at the first null byte, such as 3.11.5 or later in the 3.11 series, or temporarily use the 3.10 series. Use a Pyramid release that rejects null-byte paths, which is 2.0.2 per the advisory. Treat null bytes in file and directory names as invalid for static serving.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say how the null byte reaches the static view or which request encodings are affected, so a general input-validation review is still advisable. They state that exposure is limited to index.html one level up. They give no further detail on other deployment layouts. Null-byte rejection in Pyramid is described as a precaution and not as the root-cause fix, which the sources place in Python itself. The sources do not say whether other Python versions or other frameworks behave the same way.

fixtures.scenario: A Pyramid 2.0.1 application runs on Python 3.11.4 and serves a static view from an absolute directory. An index.html file exists in that directory's parent. A request containing a null byte in the path is normalized with truncation, and the parent index.html may be served.
The same application uses Pyramid 2.0.2 on Python 3.11.5 or later. Any request path containing a null byte is rejected before normalization, and the parent index.html is never served.

citations.quote: Pyramid now will reject any path that contains a null-byte out of caution.
impacts users of Python 3.11 that are using a Pyramid static view with a full filesystem path
Use a version of Python 3 that is not affected.
returning the behavior to pre-3.11 Python

patterns.title: Reference names joined to the .git directory can escape it and read arbitrary files
patterns.cause: To resolve some git references, the library reads files from the .git directory. In some places the file name comes from the user. The code joins the base directory with that user-given string and does not check whether the final path is outside the base directory. A name containing parent-directory segments can therefore point at any file on the system.
preconditions: The application passes user-controlled strings as reference or revision names to repository lookups such as commit, tree, or index diff.
The library joins the string to the .git directory path without confirming the result stays inside it.
The installed GitPython version predates 3.1.37.
patterns.prevention: Treat reference names as untrusted. After joining a name to the base directory, confirm the final path is still inside the repository's .git directory before opening it, ideally after resolving symlinks. Also validate that reference names are well formed and reject those containing traversal segments or absolute paths. Upgrade to GitPython 3.1.37 or later. In application code, validate user-supplied revision strings before handing them to the library.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the issue as blind: file contents could not be shown. Impact is limited to things like probing whether a file exists, or a denial of service from reading a large or endless file. The reporter says other code paths may also reach the flaw, and only three were confirmed. The sources do not describe the upstream fix in detail. One advisory says the issue was not yet addressed, while the CVE record says it was addressed in 3.1.37.

fixtures.scenario: An application passes a user-supplied revision string with parent-directory segments to a repository commit lookup. The library joins it to the .git directory and reads a file outside that directory.
The application validates the reference name, and the library confirms the resolved path is inside the .git directory before reading. Traversal names are rejected.

citations.quote: That code joins the base directory with a user given string without checking if the final path is located outside the base directory.
This allows an attacker to make GitPython read any file from the system.
This issue has been addressed in version 3.1.37.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through uploaded SVG images in Zope
patterns.cause: Zope stores SVG images uploaded by users, and an SVG image can contain malicious code. If an attacker uploads such an image and a user is tricked into following a specially crafted link, the code can run in the context of the site. Embedding the same image through an image tag with the SVG as its source is never vulnerable, so the risk comes from the user following a crafted link to the stored image rather than from the image tag.
preconditions: The Zope version is older than 4.8.10 (4.x line) or older than 5.8.5 (5.x line).
The site allows untrusted users to upload images, which means the permission to add documents, images, and files is held by untrusted roles.
An attacker uploads an SVG image that contains malicious code.
A user is tricked into following a specially crafted link.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Zope 4.8.10 or 5.8.5 or later, which contain the patches. Until then, or in addition, assign the permission named Add Documents, Images, and Files only to trusted roles. By default only the Manager role holds it. Do not grant it to roles that untrusted users can obtain. Review which roles currently hold it on every site.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the patch works, which links or URL forms trigger the issue, or what the crafted link looks like. They give no guidance on response headers, content sanitization, or serving rules, so none are claimed here. They also do not say whether other file types are affected. Restricting the permission only helps on sites that do not need untrusted uploads. It does not fix the underlying flaw in unpatched versions.

fixtures.scenario: An unpatched Zope 5.8.4 site lets an untrusted community role upload images. An attacker uploads an SVG file that contains malicious code, then sends a victim a crafted link. The victim follows the link and the code runs in the context of the site.

The site runs Zope 5.8.5 or later, or 4.8.10 or later. The permission to add documents, images, and files is held only by the Manager role, so untrusted users cannot upload an SVG file. SVG images are shown only through image tags that name them as the source.

citations.quote: There is a stored cross site scripting vulnerability for SVG images.
To exploit the vulnerability, an attacker would first need to upload an image, and then trick a user into following a specially crafted link.
All versions of Zope are impacted on sites that allow untrusted users to upload images.
Patches are available in Zope 4.8.10 and 5.8.5.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through the unquoted title property in Zope Management Interface breadcrumbs
patterns.cause: The title property, available on most Zope objects, can hold script code. The Zope Management Interface (ZMI) displays it unquoted in the breadcrumbs element, so stored script runs in the browser of anyone who views the affected object.
preconditions: The deployment runs Zope 4 or Zope 5 below the patched releases 4.8.11 and 5.8.6.
Someone can store attacker-chosen text in the title property of a Zope object.
A user views that object in the ZMI, where the breadcrumbs element renders the title without quoting.
patterns.prevention: Treat the title property as untrusted text wherever the ZMI renders it, including the breadcrumbs element. Quote or escape it for the HTML context at output time, so stored markup is shown as plain text and never interpreted. Upgrade to Zope 4.8.11 or 5.8.6 or later, which the advisories name as the patched releases. As a workaround until then, keep editing and viewing of Zope objects in the ZMI limited to Manager users, which the advisory says is the default.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the patches change the code, so the exact escaping approach is not covered here. They do not say whether other properties or other ZMI views have the same flaw. They do not say how effective the Manager-only workaround is when a Manager user is the author or the viewer of the malicious title. Only breadcrumbs rendering is named as the affected output.

fixtures.scenario: A user with permission to edit an object sets its title property to text containing script code. An administrator later opens that object in the ZMI on an unpatched Zope 4 or 5 install. The breadcrumbs element prints the title unquoted, so the script runs in the administrator's browser session.

The same title text is stored, but the ZMI quotes the title when it renders the breadcrumbs, or the site runs Zope 4.8.11 or 5.8.6 or later. The administrator sees the text displayed literally and no script runs.

citations.quote: because the title property is displayed unquoted in the breadcrumbs element
The title property, available on most Zope objects, can be used to store script code
Make sure only Manager users can edit and view Zope objects in the Zope Management Interface. This is the default.

patterns.title: Recursive URL crawling must not pivot from an external server to an internal server
patterns.cause: In LangChain before 0.0.317, the recursive URL loader in document_loaders/recursive_url_loader.py allowed crawling to proceed from an external server to an internal server. This gives a server-side request forgery (CWE-918) condition.
preconditions: The application uses the recursive URL loader from LangChain before 0.0.317.
The crawl starts from or reaches a server that is external to the deployment.
An internal server is reachable from the machine running the crawler.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade LangChain to 0.0.317 or later. In any crawler of your own, do not let a crawl that began on an external server continue to an internal server. Decide which destinations a crawl may reach before any request is sent, and check every followed link against that decision, not only the starting address.
patterns.limitations: The advisories give only a one-sentence description. They do not say how the fix decides what counts as internal. They also do not say how redirects, DNS resolution or non-default URL schemes are handled, or whether other loaders are affected. Verify those points against the released code and your own deployment. Network-level egress controls are not discussed in the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A crawl starts at a page on an external server that links to a host on the internal network. The loader follows that link, so the crawler fetches content from the internal server on behalf of whoever controls the external page.

A crawl starts at a page on an external server that links to a host on the internal network. The loader refuses to proceed from the external server to the internal server, and the internal host is never requested.

citations.quote: LangChain before 0.0.317 allows SSRF via document_loaders/recursive_url_loader.py because crawling can proceed from an external server to an internal server.

patterns.title: Stored XSS via uploaded avatar served with a file-extension-derived content type
patterns.cause: Avatar upload validation only confirmed the file could be read as an image and trusted the client-supplied Content-Type. The uploaded file extension was never validated on the server and was saved as given. Avatars were served by Django's built-in serve view, which picks the response Content-Type from the URL extension, so a file named with an html extension was rendered as a web page.
preconditions: An authenticated user can upload an avatar and control its filename and declared mimetype
The server does not validate the uploaded file extension (only client-side checks exist)
Uploaded avatars are served by Django's built-in serve view, which derives Content-Type from the URL extension
A victim visits the crafted avatar URL on the application's origin
patterns.prevention: Validate the file extension on the server side, not only in client-side code, and do not trust user-controlled inputs such as the declared mimetype or filename. Stop serving uploaded avatars through Django's built-in serve view and use a purpose-built controller that sets the content type itself. Optionally store file content in the database instead of the filesystem to reduce other file-related risks.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change beyond saying version 1.9.2 fixes the issue. They do not specify the allowed extension list, the content-type handling details of a replacement controller, or whether additional response headers should be used. Other remediation options are listed only as advice.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user uploads a JPEG whose metadata comment holds script markup, renames it with an html extension, and sends an image mimetype. The server accepts it and serves it by extension as HTML, so a visiting victim runs the script.

The server checks the extension on its own side and rejects an html filename despite the image mimetype. Avatars are returned by a dedicated controller that sets an image content type, so embedded markup is never rendered as a page.

citations.quote: The issue with the Django `serve` view is that it determines the `Content-Type` of the response by the file extension in the URL path.
The only file extension validation is performed on the client-side, which can be easily bypassed.
Validate the file extension on the server side, not in client-side code.

patterns.title: SSRF filter bypass through one-time DNS check, redirects and DNS rebinding in URL import
patterns.cause: The URL import feature checked the URL once before sending the request. The check was a single DNS lookup to confirm the address was outside a few excluded subnets. It never validated the destination IP address actually contacted, so an HTTP redirect or a DNS name that changes its answer defeated the check.
preconditions: The application fetches user-supplied URLs on the server side, such as an import from URL feature.
The SSRF protection is enabled and relies only on a hostname resolution check made before the request.
The HTTP client follows redirects automatically.
The attacker controls a web server or DNS name that can redirect or return different addresses over time.
patterns.prevention: Do not treat a separate pre-request lookup as proof that the request is safe. Validate the destination IP address of the connection that is actually made against the deny list before any response is saved, so a name that resolves differently at request time is caught. Make sure redirect targets receive the same destination check. Consider also blocking internal cloud API address ranges to protect instance credentials.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, so how redirects are handled in the patched release is not covered here. They list only four IPv4 deny ranges and do not discuss IPv6 or other special-use ranges. The remediation advice is brief. The protection only applies when the SSRF_PROTECTION_ENABLED setting is turned on, and versions before 1.11.0 are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A user imports a task file from a URL on an attacker host. The name resolves to a public address during validation, then to 127.0.0.1 when the request is sent, or the host answers with a 301 redirect to an internal server.

The server checks the IP address of the connection it actually makes and applies the deny list to it, including after any redirect, so a rebinding name or a redirect to an internal address is rejected.

citations.quote: The issue here is the SSRF validation is only performed before the request is sent, and does not validate the destination IP address.
Before saving any responses, validate the destination IP address is not in the deny list.
This protection can be bypassed by either using HTTP redirection or performing a DNS rebinding attack.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through unsanitized DAG parameter descriptions in Apache Airflow
patterns.cause: A DAG author could put unbounded, unsanitized JavaScript in the parameter description field of a DAG. That text was later shown to other users in the browser, where the script ran on the client side. The sources do not name the exact template or rendering path.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version 2.6.0 through 2.7.3 is in use.
An attacker can author or edit a DAG and so control the parameter description text.
The description is stored and later displayed in the web interface without sanitization.
Another user opens the DAG or task details in a browser, which runs the injected script.
patterns.prevention: Treat DAG parameter descriptions as untrusted data. Sanitize or escape them for the HTML context in which they are displayed, so that markup in the text is shown as plain text and never executed. Bound the allowed size of the field, since the sources describe it as both unbounded and not sanitized. For Airflow deployments, upgrade to version 2.8.0 or newer, as the advisory recommends. In your own code, apply the same rule to every user-supplied descriptive field that is stored and later rendered for other users.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream change works, which views render the field, or what limits were set. They do not say whether other DAG fields were affected. They state that the issue does not allow escaping the browser sandbox or changing server-side data beyond what a DAG author can already do. The impact is described as misleading other users by changing what they see. Only the upgrade path to 2.8.0 or newer is stated as a mitigation.

fixtures.scenario: A DAG author writes a parameter description that contains script markup. Another user opens the DAG details in the browser. The description is rendered without sanitization, so the script runs in that user's session and can change what they see.

A DAG author writes a parameter description that contains script markup. The application sanitizes or escapes the text and limits its length when it renders it. The viewer sees inert text, and no script runs in the browser.

citations.quote: allows a DAG author to add an unbounded and not-sanitized javascript in the parameter description field of the DAG
This Javascript can be executed on the client side of any of the user who looks at the tasks in the browser sandbox.
Users of Apache Airflow are recommended to upgrade to version 2.8.0 or newer to mitigate the risk associated with this vulnerability

patterns.title: Unvalidated package folder on edit allows writing downloads outside the downloads directory
patterns.cause: pyLoad restricts the folder name when a package is created, so it stays inside the downloads folder. The package edit path in the web UI takes the folder value from the request and stores it with no equivalent restriction. An authenticated user can therefore point a package at any directory on the server filesystem, and the downloaded file is written there. If that directory holds pyLoad event scripts, this can lead to command execution.
preconditions: The attacker is an authenticated web UI user who can create and edit packages.
The package edit handler accepts a folder value from the request and passes it on without the restriction applied at creation.
The attacker can make the server download a file they control, for example from a link to a server they run.
The target directory is writable by the pyLoad process, such as a scripts directory that pyLoad processes and runs.
patterns.prevention: Treat the package folder as untrusted input on every path that sets it, not only at creation. The edit operation must enforce the same rule as package creation: the resulting storage location must stay within the downloads folder. Apply the check in the shared code that stores package data, so no entry point can skip it. Reject or neutralize folder values that name locations outside the downloads root, and verify the final location is inside that root before any file is written.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the missing check on the edit path and a proof of concept that abuses script directories. They do not describe the upstream fix, so the exact validation approach is not specified here. They also do not assess whether the creation-time filter is sufficient on its own. The CVE record only labels the issue as unrestricted file upload, and the sources give no affected-version range beyond 0.5.0. The scripts-based command execution depends on pyLoad settings and on how it processes script directories. This card does not cover hardening of those features.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user creates a package with a valid link, then edits it and sets the folder field to an absolute path of a pyLoad scripts directory. After the package is restarted, the downloaded file is stored in that directory instead of under the downloads folder.

An authenticated user edits a package and submits a folder value naming a location outside the downloads folder. The server rejects or neutralizes the value, and any file the package downloads stays inside the downloads folder.

citations.quote: However, when editing packages there is no prevention in place and a user can just pick any arbitrary directory in the filesystem.
a filter is applied to make sure it can't traverse directories and stays within /downloads.
A web UI user can store files anywhere on the pyLoad server and gain command execution by abusing scripts.
pyLoad 0.5.0 is vulnerable to Unrestricted File Upload.

patterns.title: Ray job submission API reachable by remote attackers allows arbitrary code execution
patterns.cause: The Ray job submission API lets a remote attacker execute arbitrary code. The vendor's position is that Ray is not intended for use outside a strictly controlled network environment, so exposing this API beyond such a network leaves it open to untrusted callers. The sources do not describe the internal request-handling flaw behind the SSRF and untrusted-input classification.
preconditions: A Ray deployment with the job submission API enabled, such as the versions named in the advisory (2.6.3 and 2.8.0).
A remote attacker can reach the job submission API over the network.
The deployment sits outside a strictly controlled network environment, or it does not use token authentication where that option exists.
patterns.prevention: Treat the job submission API as a code execution interface. Keep Ray deployments inside a strictly controlled network environment, as the vendor documentation states, and do not expose the API to untrusted networks. Where the version allows it (2.52.0 and later), enable token authentication so that only callers holding a valid token can submit jobs. Review who and what can reach the API as part of deployment hardening.
patterns.limitations: The sources are vague. They do not name the vulnerable endpoint, the SSRF mechanism, the full affected version range, or the upstream code change. They do not say how token authentication is configured or how far it mitigates the issue. The vendor disputes that this is a vulnerability and calls it an intended-use boundary, so the guidance rests on network isolation and optional token authentication rather than a described code-level fix.

fixtures.scenario: A team runs a Ray cluster and makes the job submission API reachable from a broad or public network with no token authentication. A remote attacker sends a job to the API and gets arbitrary code executed on the cluster.
A team runs Ray inside a strictly controlled network that untrusted hosts cannot reach. They run version 2.52.0 or later with token authentication enabled, so only authorized callers can submit jobs.

citations.quote: Anyscale Ray allows a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via the job submission API.
Ray, as stated in its documentation, is not intended for use outside of a strictly controlled network environment.
customers at version 2.52.0 and later can choose to use token authentication.

patterns.title: SQL injection through a user-specified quote in the Superset where_in Jinja macro
patterns.cause: The where_in Jinja macro in Apache Superset lets users specify a quote. Combined with a carefully crafted statement, that user-chosen quote allows SQL injection.
preconditions: Running Apache Superset before 2.1.3, or from 3.0.0 before 3.0.2 (the CVE record says before 2.1.2 for the 2.x line).
Jinja templating is used in queries, and the where_in macro is called.
A user can supply the quote argument together with a crafted statement.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Apache Superset to 2.1.3 or 3.0.2 or later, as the advisories recommend. In any similar templating helper, do not let a caller-chosen quote character decide how values are delimited in generated SQL. Fix the delimiting inside the helper rather than trusting user input.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the internal fix, the exact macro arguments, or any workaround short of upgrading. The CVE record lists 2.1.2 as the last affected 2.x version, while the GitHub and PYSEC advisories say before 2.1.3. This card therefore does not claim whether 2.1.2 is affected.

fixtures.scenario: A Superset 3.0.1 deployment lets users write Jinja queries. A user calls the where_in macro with a custom quote value and a crafted statement, which breaks out of the intended value list and alters the SQL.
The deployment runs Superset 3.0.2 or 2.1.3 or later, where the advisories say the issue is fixed. The same where_in call with a custom quote and crafted statement does not alter the query.

citations.quote: A where_in JINJA macro allows users to specify a quote, which combined with a carefully crafted statement would allow for SQL injection
Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.1.3 or 3.0.2, which fixes the issue.
This issue affects Apache Superset: before 2.1.2, from 3.0.0 before 3.0.2.

patterns.title: XCom pickle deserialization can be reached even when XCom pickling is disabled
patterns.cause: In Apache Airflow versions before 2.8.1, the protection provided by turning the XCom pickling setting off could be bypassed. A potential attacker could poison XCom data, and the poisoned data was then processed when the XCom value was deserialized. The sources do not describe the bypass mechanism.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version is earlier than 2.8.1
The deployment relies on the XCom pickling setting being disabled as its protection against unsafe deserialization
The attacker is able to author a DAG, which the advisory says is required to exploit the issue
XCom data written by the attacker is later deserialized
patterns.prevention: Upgrade apache-airflow to version 2.8.1 or later, which the advisory states fixes the issue. Do not treat the XCom pickling setting alone as a sufficient safeguard on older versions. More generally, an implementation should make sure that a configuration switch meant to forbid pickle deserialization is enforced on every path that reads XCom values, so that data written by a DAG author is never turned back into objects through a route that ignores the switch. Also limit who can author DAGs, since exploitation requires that role.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not explain how the bypass works, which code paths are affected, or what the upstream change does, so this card cannot give finer-grained guidance. The advisory rates the issue as low severity because it requires a DAG author. Mitigations other than upgrading are not described in the sources, and restricting DAG authorship is an inference from the stated precondition, not an advisory recommendation.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 2.8.0 deployment has XCom pickling turned off and the operator assumes XComs are therefore safe. A user with DAG authoring rights crafts a task that writes poisoned XCom data, and the data is deserialized later despite the setting.

The deployment runs Airflow 2.8.1 or later with XCom pickling turned off. The same DAG author cannot use the bypass to get poisoned XCom data deserialized, and DAG authoring rights are limited to trusted users.

citations.quote: Apache Airflow, versions before 2.8.1, have a vulnerability that allows a potential attacker to poison the XCom data
This vulnerability is considered low since it requires a DAG author to exploit it.
Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.8.1 or later, which fixes this issue.

patterns.title: Symlink in a malicious Ansible role overwrites files outside the extraction path
patterns.cause: An attacker crafts a malicious Ansible role that contains a symlink. When the victim executes the role, the symlink can be used to overwrite a file outside of the extraction path. The sources classify this as an absolute path traversal. They do not say which component or step performs the extraction.
preconditions: The victim obtains and executes an Ansible role crafted by an attacker.
The role content is extracted to a directory, and a symlink inside it can point to a location outside that extraction path.
The operation writes to a file through that symlink, so the write lands outside the intended directory.
patterns.prevention: Treat role content as untrusted and run roles only from sources you trust. When extracting role content, do not let any entry write outside the extraction directory. Resolve the final destination of each entry, including where any symlink points, and reject the entry if the resolved location is not inside the intended directory. Reject absolute destinations as well as relative ones that climb out of the directory. Upgrade to an Ansible release that contains the upstream fix for CVE-2023-5115.
patterns.limitations: The sources are brief. They do not name the affected Ansible component, the archive format, the exact extraction code path, or the fixed versions. They do not describe how the upstream fix works. The prevention direction above is a general safeguard for this class of flaw and not a description of the upstream change. Consult the vendor advisory for affected and fixed versions.

fixtures.scenario: A user downloads a role from an untrusted party. The role contains a symlink that points to a file outside the extraction directory. During extraction or execution, a write goes through the symlink and overwrites that outside file.

The same role is processed by an implementation that resolves the real destination of every entry, including symlink targets, and rejects any entry that resolves outside the extraction directory. The outside file is left unchanged and the role is refused.

citations.quote: A symlink can be used to overwrite a file outside of the extraction path.
This flaw allows an attacker to craft a malicious Ansible role and make the victim execute the role.

patterns.title: Arbitrary file read through the file route of a publicly exposed Gradio app
patterns.cause: Gradio versions before 4.11.0 had a flaw in the file route that allowed file traversal. An attacker who knew the path of a file on the host could read it. Regular browser URLs did not trigger the flaw, but programmatic tools such as curl could, so the server could not rely on the client to keep requests well formed. The same route could also be abused for server-side request forgery.
preconditions: The application runs a gradio version earlier than 4.11.0.
The app is reachable at a public URL, for example created with the share option or hosted on Hugging Face Spaces.
The attacker knows or can guess the path of a file to look for.
The attacker sends requests with a programmatic tool rather than a normal browser.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade gradio to 4.11.0 or later, which fixes both the file traversal and the server-side request forgery problems in the file route. In any similar file-serving endpoint, do not assume that clients send well-formed URLs, because a browser can behave differently from a raw HTTP tool. The server should itself check that every requested path refers only to files the application meant to expose, and it should not fetch arbitrary remote locations on behalf of a caller.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact malformed request shape or the mechanics of the upstream fix, so this card gives only the upgrade direction and general guidance. They do not say which files or deployments were actually exposed, and they give no detail on how the request forgery was carried out. Apps that are not publicly reachable are described as less exposed only by implication.

fixtures.scenario: A demo built with a gradio version before 4.11.0 is shared through a public link. A remote user with curl requests a known file path through the file route and receives the contents of a file outside the intended files.
The same demo runs gradio 4.11.0 or later. A raw request for an arbitrary host file through the file route is not served, and the route cannot be used for server-side request forgery.

citations.quote: This was not possible through regular URLs passed into a browser, but it was possible through the use of programmatic tools
an attacker could access arbitrary files on a machine running a Gradio app with a public URL
also contained a vulnerability that made it possible to use it for SSRF attacks
This issue has been patched in version 4.11.0.

patterns.title: Command injection in PaddlePaddle get_online_pass_interval (CVE-2023-52310)
patterns.cause: PaddlePaddle versions before 2.6.0 have a command injection flaw in get_online_pass_interval. The advisories say this let an attacker execute arbitrary commands on the operating system. They do not describe the internal mechanism.
preconditions: The application uses a PaddlePaddle version older than 2.6.0.
The get_online_pass_interval function is reachable in the deployment.
An attacker can influence what the function processes (the sources do not say which input).
patterns.prevention: Upgrade PaddlePaddle to 2.6.0 or later, where the advisories no longer list the issue. In code that wraps or resembles this function, do not let untrusted values become part of an operating system command. Prefer direct library calls over launching external commands. Where an external process is unavoidable, pass untrusted values only as separate, validated arguments and never as command text.
patterns.limitations: The sources are brief. They do not name the vulnerable parameter, the shell or process-launch path, the exact fix, or how an attacker reaches the function. The prevention direction beyond upgrading is general guidance for this weakness class, not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs PaddlePaddle 2.5.x and passes externally supplied values to get_online_pass_interval. A crafted value leads to execution of arbitrary operating system commands.
The service runs PaddlePaddle 2.6.0 or later. Any value that reaches an external process is validated and passed as a separate argument, so it is never interpreted as command text.

citations.quote: PaddlePaddle before 2.6.0 has a command injection in get_online_pass_interval.
This resulted in the ability to execute arbitrary commands on the operating system.

patterns.title: Command injection in PaddlePaddle _wget_download before version 2.6.0
patterns.cause: The advisories state that PaddlePaddle before 2.6.0 has a command injection in _wget_download, which allowed arbitrary commands to be executed on the operating system. They do not describe the vulnerable input or the exact mechanism.
preconditions: PaddlePaddle older than 2.6.0 is installed
The _wget_download function is reached in the application or workflow
An attacker can influence what _wget_download processes (the sources do not say which parameter)
patterns.prevention: Upgrade PaddlePaddle to 2.6.0 or later, the first version the advisories do not list as affected. When code builds a download step, keep externally supplied values as plain data and do not let them be interpreted as operating system commands. Prefer a direct download call or an argument-list process invocation over shell command strings. The sources do not describe the actual fix, so treat this as general direction.
patterns.limitations: The sources give no detail on the vulnerable parameter, the command construction, the attack vector, or the fix. They only name the function and the affected version range. Whether other functions share the flaw is not stated. The general-direction advice above is not confirmed as the upstream fix.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs PaddlePaddle 2.5.x and uses a feature that calls _wget_download with a value an outside party can influence. The attacker gets arbitrary commands executed on the host operating system.
The same service runs PaddlePaddle 2.6.0 or later, and any value that reaches a download step is handled as data and not as command text. The download does not result in arbitrary command execution.

citations.quote: PaddlePaddle before 2.6.0 has a command injection in _wget_download.
This resulted in the ability to execute arbitrary commands on the operating system.

patterns.title: PaddlePaddle command injection in convert_shape_compare (CVE-2023-52314)
patterns.cause: PaddlePaddle versions before 2.6.0 contain a command injection (CWE-78) in convert_shape_compare. The sources do not say how attacker-influenced data reaches an operating system command, so the exact mechanism is not described here.
preconditions: PaddlePaddle older than 2.6.0 is installed.
A code path that reaches convert_shape_compare is exercised in the deployment.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade PaddlePaddle to version 2.6.0 or later, which is the release the advisories name as the boundary for this flaw. Until the upgrade is done, treat any workflow that exercises convert_shape_compare in an affected version as able to run arbitrary operating system commands, and limit who can influence its input.
patterns.limitations: The sources give no detail on the vulnerable input, the call path, or the trigger conditions. They do not describe how the fix works, and they do not mention mitigations other than moving past version 2.6.0. They do not say whether any configuration makes the flaw unreachable. The interim guidance above is a precaution inferred from the impact statement, not a documented workaround.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs PaddlePaddle 2.5.x and exercises convert_shape_compare. Under the advisory, an attacker who can influence this path could execute arbitrary commands on the host operating system.
The same service runs PaddlePaddle 2.6.0 or later, which is outside the affected range named by the advisories for convert_shape_compare.

citations.quote: PaddlePaddle before 2.6.0 has a command injection in convert_shape_compare.
This resulted in the ability to execute arbitrary commands on the operating system.

patterns.title: Mercurial revision in pip VCS URL injects options into hg clone
patterns.cause: When pip installed from a Mercurial VCS URL, the revision given in that URL was passed to the hg clone call in a way that let it be read as a command-line option. An attacker-chosen revision could therefore add arbitrary Mercurial configuration options.
preconditions: pip older than version 23.3 is used
The package is installed from a Mercurial VCS URL, meaning one that starts with hg+
The revision part of the URL is controlled or influenced by an untrusted party
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to pip 23.3 or later. In code that builds version-control commands, make sure a user-supplied revision can only be interpreted as a revision value and never as an option to the clone command. Treat revisions in requirement URLs as untrusted input, and review requirement files from third parties before installing hg+ URLs.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so the exact mechanism is not covered here. They also do not say which configuration options are dangerous, or whether other version control systems are affected. They only state that users who do not install from Mercurial are not affected.

fixtures.scenario: A requirements file from an untrusted contributor lists an hg+ URL whose revision text looks like a Mercurial configuration option. pip older than 23.3 passes it to hg clone, which applies the injected configuration.
The same requirements file is installed with pip 23.3 or later, or the project has no hg+ URLs. The revision is not treated as a clone option, and installs from other sources are unaffected.

citations.quote: the specified Mercurial revision could be used to inject arbitrary configuration options to the
Controlling the Mercurial configuration can modify how and which repository is installed.

patterns.title: Arbitrary file upload via HTTP PUT to an MLflow server (path traversal class)
patterns.cause: MLflow allowed arbitrary files to be PUT onto the server. The vulnerability is classified as path traversal (CWE-22), which means a write operation was not confined to the location the server intended. The sources give no further detail on the mechanism.
preconditions: An MLflow server is reachable by a client that can send HTTP PUT requests.
The affected MLflow version is in use. The sources do not state which versions are affected.
patterns.prevention: Treat any file location derived from a client request as untrusted. Before writing, resolve the final destination to its canonical absolute form, for example with os.path.realpath(), and confirm it lies inside the directory the server is meant to write to. Reject the request if it does not. Also restrict which clients may use write endpoints, and upgrade to a release that contains the vendor fix referenced by the advisory.
patterns.limitations: The sources are brief. They do not say which parameter or endpoint was abused, which versions are affected, or how the vendor fixed the issue. The confinement approach above is general guidance for the path traversal class, not a description of the upstream change. Deployment-specific controls such as authentication and network exposure are not covered by the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A client sends an HTTP PUT request to an MLflow server with a destination that points outside the intended storage area. The server writes the supplied content to that location, so an arbitrary file is placed on the server.

A client sends an HTTP PUT request with a destination that points outside the intended storage area. The server resolves the final path, sees that it is not inside the permitted root, and rejects the request without writing any file.

citations.quote: MLflow allowed arbitrary files to be PUT onto the server.
MLflow allowed arbitrary files to be PUT onto the server.

patterns.title: Unauthenticated arbitrary file overwrite in MLflow server leading to code execution
patterns.cause: The MLflow web server allowed an unauthenticated attacker to write or overwrite any file on the host file system. Overwriting files that the system later executes, such as a user shell startup file, turns the file write into command execution.
preconditions: The MLflow web server is reachable by an attacker
The server does not require authentication for the affected operation
The server process can write to sensitive files on the host
patterns.prevention: Do not let an unauthenticated caller cause the server to write to arbitrary file system locations. Require authentication for operations that write data. Confine any server-side write to a designated storage area, and reject or neutralize any location the caller can influence that falls outside it. Run the server with the least file system privileges it needs, so that startup files and other executable locations are not writable.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the vulnerable endpoint, the parameter involved, or the exact fix. The guidance here is therefore general. It does not describe which MLflow versions are affected or how the patch works.

fixtures.scenario: An MLflow server is exposed on a network with no authentication. An anonymous remote user makes it write a file at a location of their choosing, replacing a user's shell startup file, and gets command execution on the host.

An MLflow server requires authentication for write operations and confines writes to its designated storage area. It runs under an account that cannot modify shell startup files, so an anonymous request cannot overwrite them.

citations.quote: An attacker can overwrite any file on the server hosting MLflow without any authentication.
allows to write / overwrite any file on the file system

patterns.title: Reflected XSS from echoing the Content-Type header in MLflow auth server responses
patterns.cause: The MLflow auth server code takes the user-supplied Content-Type header from a POST request and places it directly into a formatted string that is returned to the user. The value is not sanitized or escaped, so attacker-chosen JavaScript in the header can run in the victim's browser.
preconditions: The MLflow server runs with the auth component in mlflow/server/auth/__init__.py handling POST requests.
A response message is built by placing the raw Content-Type header value into a formatted string.
The reflected response is interpreted by a victim's browser in a way that lets injected script execute.
patterns.prevention: Treat every request header, including Content-Type, as untrusted data. Do not insert its raw value into response text. Prefer a fixed error message that does not repeat the header. If the value must be shown, escape or sanitize it for the output context first. Check that the response content type and encoding prevent the browser from treating reflected text as active markup. Add tests that send script-like Content-Type values and confirm the response does not contain them unescaped.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, the affected or patched versions, the specific endpoint or error path, or the response content type returned. The guidance above is general output-handling direction and is not a statement about how MLflow resolved the issue.

fixtures.scenario: A client sends a POST request to the MLflow auth-enabled server with a Content-Type header containing script content. The server builds an error message by formatting the header value into a string and returns it, so the script text appears unescaped in the response a victim's browser renders.

A client sends the same POST request with a script-like Content-Type header. The server replies with a fixed message that does not repeat the header, or with an escaped value, and no script text appears as active content in the response.
