citations.quote: An attacker can inject malicious JavaScript code into the Content-Type header, which is then improperly reflected back to the user without adequate sanitization or escaping
the user-supplied Content-Type header is directly injected into a Python formatted string and returned to the user

patterns.title: Gradio command injection and sensitive information exposure (CVE-2023-6572)
patterns.cause: The advisories classify the flaw as command injection (CWE-77) that also exposes sensitive information to an unauthorized actor (CWE-200) in the gradio-app/gradio repository, in code prior to the fix on main. They do not describe the vulnerable code path, the input involved, or how the two weaknesses relate.
preconditions: The application uses the gradio Python package at a version from before the fix landed on main.
An actor who is not authorized to see the affected information can reach the vulnerable gradio functionality.
patterns.prevention: Move to a gradio release that includes the upstream fix for this CVE and do not run builds from before it. In your own code, keep externally supplied values out of anything that is interpreted as a command, so they stay plain data. Limit what information an unauthenticated actor can retrieve from a gradio deployment.
patterns.limitations: The sources are brief and name neither the affected function, the injection vector, the data exposed, nor the exact fixed version. This card gives only general direction and cannot say which inputs are dangerous or which release is the first safe one. Check the project's release notes and the referenced fix commit for specifics.

fixtures.scenario: A team hosts a gradio app built from a version older than the fix on main. An unauthorized outside user can reach the app, and the app may allow command injection or leak sensitive information to that user.
A team runs a gradio release that contains the upstream fix. It treats externally supplied values as data rather than command text and does not expose sensitive information to unauthorized users.

citations.quote: Command Injection in GitHub repository gradio-app/gradio prior to main.
Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor in GitHub repository gradio-app/gradio prior to main.

patterns.title: Deserialization of untrusted data in transformers before 4.36.0
patterns.cause: Versions of the huggingface transformers library prior to 4.36.0 are affected by CWE-502, deserialization of untrusted data. The sources do not name the affected function, file format or class, so the exact trigger is not described here.
preconditions: The application uses a transformers release older than 4.36.0.
Data from an untrusted source can reach a deserialization step handled by the library. The sources do not say which step.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade transformers to 4.36.0 or later, which is the boundary the advisories give for the affected range. Until the upgrade is done, do not let data from untrusted sources reach any deserialization step in code that uses an older release. Treat externally supplied artifacts as untrusted input and keep them out of deserialization paths.
patterns.limitations: The advisories are very short. They do not name the vulnerable code path, the data format, the attack impact or the exact fix. The advisories also differ slightly on the boundary: one says prior to 4.36.0 and the others say prior to 4.36. Confirm the exact fixed release against the project's own release notes. This card gives no guidance beyond upgrading and avoiding untrusted deserialization.

fixtures.scenario: A service pins transformers to a release older than 4.36.0 and passes data obtained from an untrusted outside source into a step that deserializes it.
A service runs transformers 4.36.0 or later and does not pass data from untrusted sources into deserialization steps.

citations.quote: Deserialization of Untrusted Data in GitHub repository huggingface/transformers prior to 4.36.0.
Deserialization of Untrusted Data in GitHub repository huggingface/transformers prior to 4.36.

patterns.title: Path traversal in MLflow versions before 2.9.2
patterns.cause: The sources state only that MLflow, in the mlflow/mlflow repository, contains a path traversal weakness (CWE-22) in versions prior to 2.9.2. They do not name the affected component, endpoint, parameter, or code path.
preconditions: The deployment runs an mlflow release older than 2.9.2.
patterns.prevention: Run mlflow 2.9.2 or later, since the advisories describe versions prior to 2.9.2 as affected. Until the upgrade is done, treat any mlflow code path that turns externally supplied input into a file location as a path traversal candidate and review it for CWE-22.
patterns.limitations: The sources are very brief. They give no root cause, entry point, attack conditions, exploit prerequisites, or impact details, and they do not describe how the fix works. This card therefore cannot say which mlflow features are reachable, whether authentication changes exposure, or what a code-level mitigation looks like. The fix commit and the bounty report are not quoted in the sources, so nothing is claimed from them.

fixtures.scenario: A team runs an mlflow release older than 2.9.2 and has not applied the update, so it is within the version range the advisories describe as affected by path traversal.
A team runs mlflow 2.9.2 or later, which is outside the version range the advisories describe as affected.

citations.quote: Path Traversal in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.9.2.

patterns.title: Backslash-style parent directory sequences in file names (MLflow before 2.9.2)
patterns.cause: MLflow versions prior to 2.9.2 are affected by a path traversal weakness of the backslash form, where a file name contains a backslash, two dots, and another backslash before the final name (CWE-29). The sources give no further detail on which component or code path mishandled such input.
preconditions: The deployment runs mlflow at a version prior to 2.9.2.
A file name or path value containing the backslash parent-directory pattern reaches the affected code.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mlflow to 2.9.2 or later, which is the version the advisories name as the boundary for this issue. In your own code that handles file names, treat the backslash parent-directory pattern as a traversal form, the same as the forward-slash form. Do not rely on checks that look only for forward slashes.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which MLflow endpoint, function, or platform is affected, how the input is delivered, or what an attacker can read or write. They also do not describe the upstream fix, so this card cannot say how it validates paths. Details such as exploit impact and platform dependence are not established here.

fixtures.scenario: An mlflow installation older than 2.9.2 handles a file name that contains the backslash parent-directory pattern, and the name is not rejected as a traversal attempt.

Path Traversal: '\..\filename' in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.9.2.

patterns.title: Command injection in mlflow through a downloaded malicious config
patterns.cause: Per the advisories, mlflow is affected by a command injection weakness (CWE-77). Content from a malicious config that a user downloads can lead to command execution on the victim system. The sources do not name the vulnerable function, the config format, or the exact path from config content to command execution.

The user downloads a config file that an attacker has crafted.
The user takes that one interaction, after which the attacker can execute commands.
patterns.prevention: Treat any downloaded config as untrusted data, never as something to execute. An implementation should keep values read from such a config out of any command interpreter and should not build command text from them. Where a value must be used, validate it against a strict expected form first. Upgrade to an mlflow release that contains the referenced fixes. Users should also avoid downloading configs from sources they do not trust.
patterns.limitations: The sources are brief. They do not state the affected versions, the vulnerable component, the config format, or how the upstream fix works. The prevention direction is therefore general and follows from the command injection classification, not from a described code path.

fixtures.scenario: A user downloads a config file supplied by an untrusted party and loads it with a vulnerable mlflow version. Content in the config is carried into command execution, and the attacker gains full command execution on the user's system.

mlflow Command Injection vulnerability

patterns.title: MLflow server-side request forgery exposing internal HTTP(s) servers
patterns.cause: MLflow contained a server-side request forgery weakness (CWE-918). A malicious user could use it to reach internal HTTP(s) servers through the MLflow host. The sources do not name the vulnerable endpoint, parameter or code path.

Internal HTTP(s) servers are reachable from the host running MLflow.
The deployment runs a version of MLflow that predates the fix for CVE-2023-6974.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade MLflow to a release that includes the upstream fix for CVE-2023-6974. As general SSRF hygiene, treat any destination a user can influence as untrusted. Restrict what the server may contact so that internal HTTP(s) services and cloud instance resources are not reachable on a user's behalf. Limit network egress from the MLflow host to the services it actually needs.
patterns.limitations: The sources give no detail on the vulnerable feature, the affected versions, or how the fix works. They do not say how a request destination is checked, so this card cannot describe a specific validation rule. The remote code execution outcome is described only as a worst case on an AWS instance. The sources do not say how it is achieved.

fixtures.scenario: An MLflow server runs on a cloud instance with network access to internal HTTP(s) servers. A malicious user makes the server send requests to those internal services, and in the worst case this leads to remote code execution on the host.
The MLflow deployment is upgraded to a fixed release, and its network egress is limited to required services. A request aimed at an internal HTTP(s) server is not served on the user's behalf.

in the worst case (ie: aws instance) it could be abused to get a remote code execution on the victim machine

patterns.title: Deserialization of untrusted data in huggingface transformers before 4.36
patterns.cause: The transformers library, in versions prior to 4.36, is reported to deserialize untrusted data (CWE-502). The advisories give no further detail, so the specific code path and data format are not established by the sources.
preconditions: The application uses the transformers package at a version earlier than 4.36.
Data that an untrusted party can influence is deserialized by the library in the affected path.
The exact affected feature is not named in the sources, so the second condition is stated only at the level the advisories describe.
patterns.prevention: Move to transformers 4.36 or later, since the advisories mark versions prior to 4.36 as affected. Treat any serialized artifact from an untrusted or unverified origin as hostile input. Load such artifacts only from sources you trust and can verify, and avoid feeding externally supplied data into deserialization paths. Prefer data formats that carry only inert data and cannot instantiate arbitrary objects when loaded.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say that deserialization of untrusted data occurs in huggingface/transformers prior to 4.36. They do not name the vulnerable function, the serialization format, the entry point, or the impact. They also do not describe how the fix works, so this card cannot say which loading paths were changed. The advice to prefer inert data formats is general hardening guidance and is not drawn from the sources. Upgrading is derived from the affected-version range alone.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs transformers 4.35 and processes serialized data supplied by an outside party, such as a downloaded artifact from an unverified origin, without checking where it came from.
A service runs transformers 4.36 or later, and only loads serialized artifacts from sources it has verified and trusts. Externally supplied data is not passed to deserialization paths.

patterns.title: Recursive URL crawler follows links to other hosts despite the outside-link restriction
patterns.cause: The recursive URL loader in langchain is meant to stay on the starting site when its option to prevent outside links is enabled. It still downloaded a file from a link that pointed to a different host. Links come from page content, so whoever controls a crawled page can steer the crawler to other destinations.
preconditions: An application uses the langchain recursive URL loader with a depth greater than one.
The crawler is configured to prevent outside links but a vulnerable langchain version is in use.
An attacker controls the content of a page that gets crawled and can place links in it.
patterns.prevention: Treat every link extracted from a fetched page as untrusted input. Before making any request, confirm that the link really belongs to the intended site, and drop it otherwise. Do not assume the outside-link option works in vulnerable versions. Upgrade to a langchain release that includes the upstream fix referenced in the advisory.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not explain which comparison was faulty, name the fixed release, or describe impact beyond the crawler downloading files from unintended hosts. They do not cover other loaders or redirect handling. This card gives no concrete check logic.

fixtures.scenario: A crawler starts at a trusted site with outside links prevented. A page there links to a different host whose name looks similar. The crawler downloads that file anyway.
The same crawl runs on a fixed langchain version. The link to the different host is rejected before any request is sent, and only pages on the intended site are fetched.

citations.quote: the crawler would proceed to download that file as well even though
langchain Server-Side Request Forgery vulnerability

patterns.title: Path traversal via remote filename when loading HTTP dataset sources
patterns.cause: When a dataset is loaded from an HTTP source URL, the filename taken from the Content-Disposition header or the URL path is used to build the final local file path without sanitization. A remote server can therefore supply relative traversal sequences or an absolute path and control where the file is written.
preconditions: The application loads a dataset from a source URL with an HTTP scheme
The filename comes from the Content-Disposition header or the URL path, both controlled by the remote server or URL supplier
The filename is joined into the local destination path without neutralizing traversal sequences or absolute paths
patterns.prevention: Treat the remote filename as untrusted. Reduce it to a bare base name, rejecting path separators, parent-directory sequences and absolute paths. Then resolve the final destination path and confirm it stays inside the intended download directory before writing. Upgrade mlflow to version 2.9.0 or later, which the advisories list as the fixed version.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix sanitizes names, so the exact checks are not stated here. They also give no detail on how the arbitrary file write leads to command execution, and they do not cover other mlflow dataset sources or other versions beyond the one named.

fixtures.scenario: A dataset is loaded from an HTTP URL whose server sends a Content-Disposition filename containing parent-directory sequences or an absolute path. The file is written outside the download directory.
The same dataset load reduces the remote filename to a bare base name, then checks the resolved destination is inside the download directory. A traversal filename is rejected or neutralized.

citations.quote: the filename extracted from the `Content-Disposition` header or the URL path is used to generate the final file path without proper sanitization
This flaw enables an attacker to control the file path fully by utilizing path traversal or absolute path techniques
The issue is fixed in version 2.9.0.

patterns.title: Filter bypass leads to command injection in the PaddlePaddle wget download helper
patterns.cause: The download helper paddle.utils.download._wget_download in paddlepaddle 2.6.0 was affected by command injection (CWE-78). The advisory describes it as a bypass of a filter, so a filter was present but could be circumvented. The sources do not say what the filter checked or how it was bypassed.
preconditions: The application uses paddlepaddle 2.6.0, the version named in the advisories.
Execution reaches the wget-based download helper paddle.utils.download._wget_download.
The sources do not say which input is attacker-controlled, so whether outside data reaches the helper must be checked per deployment.
patterns.prevention: Do not treat a filter or blocklist as sufficient protection for data that ends up in an operating system command, because this issue was a bypass of such a filter. Keep outside-influenced values out of any command line that a shell interprets. Prefer a native download facility, or pass each argument as a separate element to the process launcher without a shell. Also validate the value strictly against an allow-list of expected forms before use. Upgrade to a release that contains the upstream fix for this CVE.
patterns.limitations: The sources only give the affected function, the version, the weakness class and the fact that a filter was bypassed. They do not describe the vulnerable input, the bypass technique, the first fixed version or the upstream change. The prevention direction is general guidance for this weakness class, not a description of what the maintainers changed.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs paddlepaddle 2.6.0 and passes a value supplied by an outside party to the wget-based download helper. It relies only on the built-in filter to make that value safe.

A service never passes outside-influenced values to the wget-based download helper unchecked. It validates them against a strict allow-list, and its downloads do not go through a shell-interpreted command line.

citations.quote: Command injection in paddle.utils.download._wget_download (bypass filter) in paddlepaddle/paddle 2.6.0
Command injection in paddle.utils.download._wget_download (bypass filter) in paddlepaddle/paddle 2.6.0

patterns.title: Command injection in the IrGraph.draw method of PaddlePaddle 2.6.0
patterns.cause: The advisories report a command injection flaw (CWE-77) in the IrGraph.draw method of paddlepaddle/paddle 2.6.0. The sources do not describe the mechanism, so the exact data flow is unconfirmed.
preconditions: The application uses paddlepaddle version 2.6.0.
The application calls IrGraph.draw.
patterns.prevention: Treat the draw path as a command execution boundary. Do not pass values that an outside party can influence into IrGraph.draw until you have confirmed they are safe. In your own code, avoid building command text from external values. Prefer fixed program names with arguments passed as separate list items, and validate or constrain any value that must reach a command. Check the advisory and the vendor fix for the patched release, and upgrade past 2.6.0 once you have confirmed which version contains the fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a one-line description. They do not name the vulnerable parameter, the command or tool invoked, the attacker-controlled input, the platform, the severity, or the first fixed version. The prevention guidance above is general and is not a description of the upstream change. Review the fix commit before relying on this card for exact remediation.

fixtures.scenario: A service running paddlepaddle 2.6.0 calls IrGraph.draw, and a value that an outside party can influence ends up in that call.
A service calls IrGraph.draw only with fixed, developer-chosen values, or runs a release confirmed to contain the vendor fix, and does not build command text from external input.

citations.quote: Command injection in IrGraph.draw in paddlepaddle/paddle 2.6.0
Command injection in IrGraph.draw in paddlepaddle/paddle 2.6.0

patterns.title: Arbitrary file overwrite via path traversal in PaddlePaddle before 2.6
patterns.cause: Versions of paddlepaddle before 2.6 are affected by a path traversal weakness (CWE-22) that lets a file be overwritten at an arbitrary location. In general, this class of flaw arises when a path that an outside party can influence is used for a file write without confirming it stays inside the intended directory. The sources do not say which Paddle component or input is involved.
preconditions: The deployment uses paddlepaddle at a version earlier than 2.6.
A path or file name that an untrusted party can influence reaches a file-writing step (inferred from the weakness class; the sources do not name the entry point).
The process has write permission to the file that the traversal reaches.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade paddlepaddle to version 2.6 or later, which is the release line the advisories identify as no longer affected. In code that builds file paths from external input, resolve the final path to its canonical absolute form, for example with os.path.realpath(), and confirm it remains inside the intended base directory before writing. Reject separators, parent-directory segments and absolute paths in untrusted names. Run the process with the least write access it needs.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a one-line description. They do not identify the vulnerable function, the input format, the attack vector or the exact patched behavior, so the general path-validation guidance above is not confirmed as Paddle's specific fix. Check the 2.6 release notes and the linked fix commit to confirm which code paths changed.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs paddlepaddle 2.5. An externally supplied name containing parent-directory segments is joined to an output directory and used for a write, so a file outside that directory is overwritten.

An application runs paddlepaddle 2.6 or later. Any externally supplied name is resolved to a canonical absolute path and rejected unless it lies inside the intended output directory, so no file outside it is written.

citations.quote: Arbitrary File Overwrite Via Path Traversal in paddlepaddle/paddle before 2.6

patterns.title: Gradio path traversal: local file include via user-supplied JSON in an API request
patterns.cause: A JSON value supplied by a remote user in an API request was not safely handled, so it could trigger a local file include on the server. The sources do not say which field or code path was affected.
preconditions: A vulnerable version of the gradio package is exposed to remote API requests.
The server accepts a user-supplied JSON value in an API request.
That value can influence which local file the server reads or includes.
patterns.prevention: Treat every JSON value from an API request as untrusted. Do not let such a value choose a local file location directly. Where a request value must refer to a file, resolve it to a canonical absolute path (for example with os.path.realpath()) and accept it only if it falls inside an explicitly allowed directory. Reject anything else. Also upgrade to a gradio release that includes the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that a local file include could be triggered remotely through a user-supplied JSON value. They do not name the vulnerable endpoint, the JSON field, the affected or fixed versions, or the exact validation the fix applies. The canonicalize-and-confine approach above is a general direction, not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A remote client sends an API request whose JSON value points at a local file path outside the intended content area, and the server reads or includes that file because it trusts the value.

A remote client sends the same kind of API request, but the server canonicalizes the path from the JSON value, finds it outside the allowed directory, and rejects the request without reading the file.

citations.quote: A local file include could be remotely triggered in Gradio due to a vulnerable user-supplied JSON value in an API request.
Gradio Path Traversal vulnerability

patterns.title: Unneutralized input in generated pages in django CMS (CVE-2024-11319)
patterns.cause: django-cms releases 3.11.7, 3.11.8, 4.1.2 and 4.1.3 improperly neutralize input during web page generation. This allows cross-site scripting (CWE-79).
preconditions: The deployment runs django-cms 3.11.7, 3.11.8, 4.1.2 or 4.1.3.
Input that an attacker can influence is used when a page is generated, and it is not neutralized for the output context.
patterns.prevention: Check which django-cms version each deployment runs and move any affected version to a release outside the listed ones. In code that generates pages, neutralize any externally influenced input for the context where it is output, instead of trusting it. Review custom templates and plugins that build page content from user-supplied data.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the vulnerable component, the input vector, the output context, the privileges needed, or the fixed release. They do not describe the upstream change. The guidance on neutralizing input is general and is not derived from the specific flaw. Version status should be confirmed against the project's own release notes.

fixtures.scenario: A site runs django-cms 4.1.3. Input that a visitor or editor can influence ends up in a generated page without proper neutralization, so a script supplied by an attacker can run in another user's browser.
A site runs a django-cms release that is not in the affected list. Custom page-generation code neutralizes externally influenced input for its output context before it appears in the page.

citations.quote: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (XSS or 'Cross-site Scripting') vulnerability in django CMS Association django-cms allows Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).
This issue affects django-cms: 3.11.7, 3.11.8, 4.1.2, 4.1.3.

patterns.title: Untrusted configuration files deserialized without validation in MobileViTV2 handling (CVE-2024-11392)
patterns.cause: The configuration file handling for MobileViTV2 in Hugging Face Transformers lacks proper validation of user-supplied data. As a result, untrusted data can be deserialized, which allows an attacker to execute arbitrary code in the context of the current user.
preconditions: The application uses Hugging Face Transformers and processes MobileViTV2 configuration files.
The configuration file or its contents are supplied by an untrusted party.
A user opens a malicious file or visits a malicious page, since the advisory says user interaction is required.
patterns.prevention: Treat every configuration file as untrusted input. Validate user-supplied configuration data before it reaches any deserialization step, and do not deserialize content that has not passed that validation. Obtain model and configuration files only from sources you trust. Upgrade to a Transformers release that includes the upstream fix for this issue.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the specific deserialization mechanism, the affected or fixed versions, or the exact validation the fix applies. They do not describe the upstream change. This card therefore gives only general direction: validate input before deserializing and avoid untrusted files. Check the upstream pull request and release notes for exact version guidance.

fixtures.scenario: A user downloads a MobileViTV2 configuration file from an untrusted source and loads it with Transformers. The configuration handling deserializes its contents without validating them, so a crafted file can run attacker-chosen code as the current user.

A user loads a MobileViTV2 configuration only from a trusted source, using a Transformers release that includes the fix. Content from any untrusted origin is validated as plain data before it is used, so no unvalidated content is deserialized.

citations.quote: The specific flaw exists within the handling of configuration files.
The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data.
User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

patterns.title: Deserialization of untrusted model files in Hugging Face Transformers MaskFormer
patterns.cause: The parsing of model files in Hugging Face Transformers, reported for the MaskFormer model, does not properly validate user-supplied data. This lets untrusted data be deserialized, so an attacker can execute code in the context of the current user.
preconditions: The application uses an affected installation of Hugging Face Transformers and parses model files, as in the MaskFormer model flaw.
The model file or its contents are supplied by an untrusted party.
A user opens a malicious file or visits a malicious page, since user interaction is required.
patterns.prevention: Treat every model file from an outside party as untrusted input. Do not let its contents reach deserialization unless the data has been validated first. Restrict loading to model files from sources you trust and control, and do not open files that users or remote parties supply without review. Keep Transformers updated to a release that includes the upstream fix for this issue. Run model-loading code with the fewest privileges available, because the attacker's code runs as the current user.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the serialization format, the specific loading function, the affected or fixed version numbers, or how the upstream fix works. This card therefore gives only general direction: validate input before deserialization and restrict trusted sources. It does not say which file formats are safe, and it does not describe the exact validation to apply.

fixtures.scenario: A service lets users submit a MaskFormer model file and parses it with an affected Transformers installation without validating its contents. A crafted file leads to deserialization of untrusted data and code execution as the service user.

A service loads MaskFormer model files only from a source the team trusts and controls, on an updated Transformers release. It rejects user-submitted model files and runs the loader with minimal privileges.

citations.quote: The specific flaw exists within the parsing of model files.
The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data.
User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

patterns.title: Untrusted Trax model files deserialized without validation in Transformers
patterns.cause: The model file handling in Hugging Face Transformers for Trax models does not properly validate user-supplied data before deserializing it. A crafted model file can therefore make the library deserialize untrusted data, which leads to arbitrary code execution in the context of the current user.
preconditions: An affected installation of Hugging Face Transformers handles a Trax model file.
The model file is supplied by an untrusted party, so its contents are attacker-controlled.
A user must interact, for example by opening a malicious file or visiting a malicious page.
patterns.prevention: Treat every model file from an outside source as untrusted input. Do not let the loading path deserialize its contents until the data has been validated. Load such files only from trusted, verified origins, and run model loading with the least privilege available, since the attacker's code runs as the current user. Upgrade to a Transformers release that includes the maintainers' fix for this issue.
patterns.limitations: The sources are vague. They do not name the vulnerable function, the serialization format, the affected or fixed versions, or the validation that the fix adds. This card therefore gives only general direction and cannot confirm that any specific check is sufficient. The sources also do not say how a file or page reaches the user beyond the need for user interaction.

fixtures.scenario: An application downloads a Trax model file from an unknown third party and loads it with an affected Transformers version. The file contains attacker-crafted data, so loading it deserializes untrusted content and runs the attacker's code with the current user's privileges.

An application loads Trax model files only from a trusted, verified source, and the loading path validates the file data before deserializing it. The same application runs a Transformers version that includes the maintainers' fix, so a crafted file does not lead to code execution.

citations.quote: The specific flaw exists within the handling of model files.
The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data.
An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current user.

patterns.title: Gradio file parameter lets attackers probe internal ports through distinguishable responses
patterns.cause: A GET request to gradio accepts a file parameter that an attacker controls. The server's response differs depending on the target. Either a Location header is present or a File not allowed error is returned. That difference lets the attacker tell which internal ports are open. The sources classify this as SSRF (CWE-601 is the assigned weakness), and they do not describe the internal code path in more detail.
preconditions: The gradio server is reachable by the attacker and accepts GET requests that carry a file parameter.
The server can reach hosts or ports on an internal network that the attacker cannot reach directly.
The attacker can read response headers and error text, so the Location header versus File not allowed difference is observable.
patterns.prevention: Do not let a client-supplied file parameter steer the server toward an arbitrary host or port. Validate the value against what the application intends to serve before any request or redirect is made, and reject everything else. Make the rejection response for disallowed targets the same regardless of whether the target is reachable, so neither a Location header nor a distinct error reveals port state. Upgrade gradio to a release that contains the fixes referenced for CVE-2024-1183.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a short description. They do not say which gradio versions are affected, which route handles the file parameter, or how the upstream fix works. The advisory text says SSRF, while the family label here is open redirect, and the sources do not explain how the two relate beyond the Location header being observable. The prevention direction is general guidance and not a statement about the exact upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: An attacker sends repeated GET requests to a gradio app, changing the file parameter to point at different internal addresses and ports. Some responses carry a Location header and others return a File not allowed error, so the attacker maps which internal ports are open.

The same requests are made, but the app checks the file parameter against what it is meant to serve and refuses all other values. Every refused request gets the same response whether or not the internal port is open, so the attacker learns nothing about the internal network.

citations.quote: By manipulating the 'file' parameter in a GET request, an attacker can discern the status of internal ports
based on the presence of a 'Location' header or a 'File not allowed' error in the response.

patterns.title: Open redirect via unvalidated next parameter in login flow
patterns.cause: The login functionality of pyload-ng handles the next parameter improperly, so an attacker-supplied value can send users to an arbitrary external site after they interact with the login page.
preconditions: The application exposes a login endpoint that accepts a next parameter indicating where to send the user afterward
The affected version is pyload 0.5.0, before the fix in pyload-ng 0.5.0b3.dev79
A victim can be induced to follow an attacker-crafted login link containing a malicious next value
patterns.prevention: Treat the next parameter as untrusted input. Before redirecting, check that the target is a local path on the same site and not an absolute URL or a URL naming another host. Reject or ignore any value that fails the check and fall back to a fixed default page. Alternatively, map allowed destinations to server-side identifiers instead of accepting raw URLs. Upgrade to pyload-ng 0.5.0b3.dev79 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact validation the upstream fix applies, which URL forms were accepted by the vulnerable code, or whether other endpoints share the same weakness. The guidance above is general redirect-handling direction and not a description of the upstream change. Whether the redirect happens before or after authentication is not stated.

fixtures.scenario: A phishing email links to the pyload login page with a next parameter pointing to an attacker-controlled external site. The user logs in and the application redirects the browser to that external site, which imitates the real interface.

The login page receives a next parameter pointing to an external site. The application detects that the target is not a local path on the same site, discards it, and redirects the user to the default home page after login.

citations.quote: The vulnerability is due to improper handling of the 'next' parameter in the login functionality.
An attacker can exploit this vulnerability to redirect users to malicious sites, which can be used for phishing or other malicious activities.
The issue is fixed in pyload-ng 0.5.0b3.dev79.

patterns.title: ReDoS in the Nougat fast tokenizer post-processing of transformers
patterns.cause: In the huggingface/transformers file tokenization_nougat_fast.py, the post_process_single() function runs a regular expression over specially crafted input. The regex can show exponential time complexity under certain conditions, which causes excessive backtracking and very high CPU usage.
preconditions: The application uses transformers version 4.46.3, the affected version named in the advisories.
The application uses the Nougat fast tokenizer code in tokenization_nougat_fast.py.
post_process_single() is called on text that an attacker can craft or influence.
patterns.prevention: Do not run a regular expression that can backtrack exponentially over untrusted or model-generated text. Review the patterns used in post-processing and rewrite any that can backtrack heavily so their running time stays predictable. Upgrade to a transformers release that includes the upstream fix once it is available for your environment. Where possible, keep untrusted text from reaching this post-processing step without checks, and keep a CPU or time limit around it so one request cannot stall the service.
patterns.limitations: The sources name the affected file, function and version, but do not describe the exact regex, the triggering input shape, or how the upstream fix changes the pattern. They also do not list fixed versions or say how the crafted input reaches the function in a given deployment. The mitigations here are general directions, not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A service uses transformers 4.46.3 and passes externally supplied text to the Nougat fast tokenizer post-processing. A crafted input makes the regex in post_process_single() backtrack excessively, so CPU stays pinned and the service becomes unresponsive.

A service uses a transformers release that includes the upstream fix, or a patched post-processing step whose pattern cannot backtrack exponentially. The same crafted input finishes in normal time, and the service keeps handling other requests.

citations.quote: The vulnerability occurs in the post_process_single() function, where a regular expression processes specially crafted input.
The issue stems from the regex exhibiting exponential time complexity under certain conditions, leading to excessive backtracking.
This can result in significantly high CPU usage and potential application downtime

patterns.title: SQL injection via prompt injection in the LlamaIndex JSON query engine
patterns.cause: The default_jsonalyzer function of JSONalyzeQueryEngine in llama-index is open to SQL injection through prompt injection. Attacker-influenced prompt content can therefore steer the SQL that is run. The advisories say this can lead to arbitrary file creation and denial of service. The advisory title also points to temporary file creation in a directory with insecure permissions.
preconditions: The application uses JSONalyzeQueryEngine with its default_jsonalyzer function.
An untrusted party can influence the prompt or the query text that reaches the engine.
The installed llama-index version is older than the fixed release named in the advisories.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade llama-index to a release that contains the fix, at least 0.12.3 per the GitHub advisory. Until then, treat all prompt-derived and model-derived query text as untrusted input. Do not let it reach the database layer as trusted SQL. Limit what the process can do if a query is subverted, for example by restricting file creation and resource use. Keep the engine away from untrusted users if you cannot upgrade.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the fix works, which SQL features are abused, or how the file creation happens, so this card gives no implementation-level guidance. The sources also disagree on the fixed version: the GitHub advisory says 0.12.3 and the CVE record says 0.5.1. The safer reading is to use the higher version and confirm against the package release notes. The sources do not say whether other query engines are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A chat application passes user questions to JSONalyzeQueryEngine on an unpatched llama-index. A user embeds instructions in the question, and the generated SQL is altered to create files or exhaust resources on the host.

The application runs a llama-index version that includes the fix, at least 0.12.3. It treats user-derived query text as untrusted and runs the engine in a process with restricted file and resource permissions. The same malicious question does not result in file creation or denial of service.

citations.quote: allows for SQL injection via prompt injection. This can lead to arbitrary file creation and Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks.
The vulnerability affects the latest version and is fixed in version 0.12.3.
The vulnerability affects the latest version and is fixed in version 0.5.1.
LlamaIndex vulnerable to Creation of Temporary File in Directory with Insecure Permissions

patterns.title: Unvalidated file paths in Gradio upload requests allow arbitrary file read
patterns.cause: The UploadButton handling of file upload paths did not properly validate user-supplied input. An attacker who intercepts and modifies the network request to the queue join endpoint can change the file path and make the server read or place files in unintended locations, such as private SSH keys.
preconditions: The Gradio application runs a version older than 4.19.2
The application is reachable by untrusted users, for example through a public link or Hugging Face Spaces
The attacker can intercept and modify the requests the Gradio front end sends to the server
patterns.prevention: Treat every file path that arrives in a client request as untrusted. Do not let the client choose which server-side file is read or where an upload lands. Check the path on the server against the directories the application is meant to expose, and reject anything outside them before any file access. Upgrade Gradio to version 4.19.2 or higher, which contains the fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact validation flaw, the request fields involved, or how the patch works. They give no detail on which directories are safe or how the check should be written. The claim that remote code execution is possible is stated only as a potential outcome.

fixtures.scenario: A public Gradio app uses an upload button. An attacker edits the request sent to the queue join endpoint so the file path points to a private SSH key on the host, and the server accepts the path and returns the file.
The server treats the submitted path as untrusted and checks it against the allowed locations. A path pointing outside them is rejected, and the app runs Gradio 4.19.2 or higher.

citations.quote: access files on the machine hosting the Gradio application
improper validation of user-supplied input in the UploadButton component
allowing attackers to redirect file uploads to unintended locations on the server
Yes, the problem has been patched in Gradio version 4.19.2 or higher.

patterns.title: ReDoS in Scrapy XML node iteration and open_in_browser from regex-based parsing of untrusted responses
patterns.cause: Scrapy used vulnerable regular expressions to parse response content in two places: the default iternodes node iterator (used by XMLFeedSpider and its subclasses, and by direct calls to scrapy.utils.iterators.xmliter), and, in Scrapy 2.6.0 to 2.11.0, open_in_browser for a response with no base tag. A crafted response makes the regular expression engine do inefficient work, which causes extreme CPU and memory usage and can hang the process.
preconditions: The application uses XMLFeedSpider or a subclass with the default iternodes iterator, or calls scrapy.utils.iterators.xmliter directly.
Alternatively, on Scrapy 2.6.0 to 2.11.0, the application calls open_in_browser on a response that has no base tag.
An attacker can influence the response content that is parsed, for example through a malicious or compromised site or feed being crawled.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Scrapy 2.11.1, or to Scrapy 1.8.4 if on 1.8 or lower and the upgrade to 2.11.1 is not possible. As an interim workaround for XMLFeedSpider, switch the node iterator from the default to the xml or html iterator. For open_in_browser, either review the response content before calling it or define the base tag manually so that the automatic definition is not triggered. In general, avoid parsing untrusted markup with regular expressions that can backtrack heavily, and prefer a real parser or bounded patterns.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the exact vulnerable patterns, the input shapes that trigger them, or the size at which the slowdown becomes severe, so this card cannot describe attack payloads. They do not say whether the xml and html iterators are free of every similar issue, only that switching to them is a listed workaround. The manual review workaround for open_in_browser is vague about what to look for. The sources do not say whether other Scrapy parsing code is affected, nor whether open_in_browser is affected in versions older than 2.6.0 (the advisory only lists 2.6.0 to 2.11.0).

fixtures.scenario: A crawler uses an XMLFeedSpider subclass with the default iternodes iterator to process feeds fetched from third-party servers. One server returns a specially crafted XML body, and the worker spends extreme CPU and memory in node iteration and stops serving other requests.

The same crawler runs Scrapy 2.11.1 or later (or 1.8.4 on the 1.8 line). If it must stay on an older release, the spider is configured to use the xml or html node iterator instead of the default, so the crafted body does not cause runaway resource use.

citations.quote: Handling a malicious response could cause extreme CPU and memory usage during the parsing of its content
Upgrade to Scrapy 2.11.1.
either manually review the response content to discard a ReDos attack or manually define the base tag
By crafting malicious XML content that exploits inefficient regular expression complexity used in the parsing process, an attacker can cause a denial-of-service (DoS) condition.

patterns.title: Server-side request forgery in TFIDFRetriever load_local (langchain-community 0.0.26)
patterns.cause: In langchain-community 0.0.26, the load_local function of the TFIDFRetriever component can be manipulated into server-side request forgery, and the advisory says this can be attacked remotely. The sources do not explain the internal mechanism.
preconditions: The application runs langchain-community version 0.0.26.
The application uses the TFIDFRetriever component and calls its load_local function.
An attacker can reach the application remotely and manipulate what load_local does, as the advisory describes.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade langchain-community to version 0.0.27 or later, which the advisory says addresses the issue. Confirm that no deployment image, lock file or vendored copy still pins 0.0.26.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which input is manipulated, what request the server makes, or how the fix in 0.0.27 works. They also do not say whether versions other than 0.0.26 are affected before the fix. Interim mitigations other than upgrading are not described, so none are claimed here.

fixtures.scenario: A service pins langchain-community 0.0.26 and uses TFIDFRetriever load_local in a way that remote users can influence. The service is exposed to server-side request forgery.
The same service is upgraded to langchain-community 0.0.27 or later, and the dependency lock file and deployed image are checked to confirm the old version is gone.

citations.quote: Affected is the function load_local in the library libs/community/langchain_community/retrievers/tfidf.py of the component TFIDFRetriever.
The manipulation leads to server-side request forgery.
Upgrading to version 0.0.27 is able to address this issue.

patterns.title: Stored XSS via attacker-controlled href on anchor elements in Dash apps
patterns.cause: Vulnerable Dash components (dash before 2.15.0, plus older dash-core-components and dash-html-components) allow script execution when the href of an anchor tag is controlled by an adversary. A saved view can carry that value to other users, whose browsers then run the attacker's script.
preconditions: The app runs an affected version, such as dash before 2.15.0.
An adversary can control the href value of an anchor tag.
The app lets users store input or views that a different user later reloads.
The attacker is an authenticated user who can save such a view.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade dash to 2.15.0 or later, and upgrade dash-core-components and dash-html-components to the fixed releases named in the advisories. Until then, do not let user-supplied or stored data set the href of an anchor tag, and treat any saved view as untrusted input when another user reloads it.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe what the upstream fix changes. They do not say which URL schemes or values are dangerous or how to validate them, so the interim advice to keep untrusted data out of href is a conservative reading of the stated trigger, not a verified mitigation. The affected version ranges differ slightly between the advisories.

fixtures.scenario: A Dash app lets signed-in users save a view and share it. The saved state sets the href of an anchor tag from user input. The app runs dash 2.14. Another user opens the shared view and the attacker's script runs in that user's session.
The app runs dash 2.15.0 or later with fixed component packages, and saved view data is never used to set an anchor href. A user opening a shared view only sees content the app itself controls.

citations.quote: are vulnerable to Cross-site Scripting (XSS) when the href of the a tag is controlled by an adversary.
This is only exploitable in Dash apps that include some mechanism to store user input to be reloaded by a different user.
versions of the package dash before 2.15.0

patterns.title: XSS in djangorestframework via the break_long_headers template filter
patterns.cause: The break_long_headers template filter splits a header value and joins the pieces with line break tags, but the input is not properly sanitized before this step. Untrusted header content can therefore end up in rendered HTML as active markup.
preconditions: The application uses a djangorestframework version before 3.15.2.
A template renders content through the break_long_headers template filter.
The value passed to the filter can be influenced by an attacker, for example a request header value.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade djangorestframework to version 3.15.2 or later. In any custom filter that inserts line break tags into text, neutralize the untrusted input first by escaping it for HTML output, and only then split and join the pieces, so that only the intended break tags are treated as markup. Avoid marking the combined result as safe before the input has been escaped.
patterns.limitations: The sources only name the break_long_headers filter, the improper sanitization before splitting and joining with line break tags, and the fixed version 3.15.2. They do not describe which inputs reach the filter in practice, how exploitation is carried out, or what the exact upstream change is, so the escaping direction above is general guidance rather than a description of the upstream fix.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs djangorestframework 3.15.1 and renders a page that passes a header value containing markup through the break_long_headers filter. The value is split and joined with line break tags without proper sanitization, so the markup reaches the page unescaped.

An application runs djangorestframework 3.15.2 or later, or uses a custom filter that escapes the header value for HTML before splitting and joining it with line break tags. Markup in the header value is shown as text and not interpreted by the browser.

citations.quote: Versions of the package djangorestframework before 3.15.2 are vulnerable to Cross-site Scripting (XSS) via the break_long_headers template filter

due to improper input sanitization before splitting and joining with
tags.

patterns.title: Unvalidated client-supplied URLs added to proxy target set enable SSRF in gradio
patterns.cause: The proxy route did not sufficiently validate user-supplied URLs. A request header (X-Direct-Url) sent to the root and config routes could add arbitrary URLs to the set of replica URLs the server treats as valid proxy targets. The proxy request builder then did not adequately check that the target was a safe URL.
preconditions: The application exposes a proxy route that forwards requests to URLs it considers valid.
Client-controlled request headers can add entries to the server-side set of trusted proxy targets.
The proxy request builder does not adequately check that the destination is a safe URL.
patterns.prevention: Do not let request headers or other client input add entries to the set of trusted proxy destinations. Treat that set as server-side configuration only. Validate the destination in the proxy request construction step against an explicit allowlist of safe targets before any outbound request, and reject anything else. Do not rely on membership in a set that clients can influence.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream validation logic, the affected or fixed version ranges, or which internal endpoints were reachable beyond a general reference to the Hugging Face space. They do not say whether other headers or routes are affected. This card gives direction only and does not specify an allowlist format.

fixtures.scenario: A client sends a request to the config route with a header naming an internal address. The server adds it to its trusted replica URL set. The client then calls the proxy route with that address, and the server fetches the internal endpoint.

The trusted proxy target set is fixed by server configuration and ignores client headers. A request naming an internal address is rejected when the proxy request is built, because the address is not on the allowlist.

citations.quote: An SSRF vulnerability exists in the gradio-app/gradio due to insufficient validation of user-supplied URLs
allowing the addition of arbitrary URLs for proxying
potential access to internal endpoints within the Hugging Face space

patterns.title: HTML attribute injection through user-controlled keys in the Jinja xmlattr filter
patterns.cause: The xmlattr filter in affected Jinja versions accepts attribute keys that contain spaces. Each space-separated part is then read by the browser as a separate attribute. When keys come from user input, an attacker can inject arbitrary attributes and keys, which bypasses autoescaping and can lead to XSS.
preconditions: The application uses the xmlattr filter on a mapping rendered into HTML or XML.
Attribute keys, not only values, come from user input.
The rendered page is viewed by other users.
A vulnerable Jinja version is in use.
patterns.prevention: Do not let untrusted input choose attribute keys passed to the xmlattr filter. Check each key against a fixed allowlist of known attribute names before rendering, and reject keys with spaces or other unexpected characters. Do not rely on a blacklist of dangerous attributes, since blacklist-based checks may be bypassed. Upgrade Jinja to a release that includes the upstream fix as defense in depth, and keep validating keys anyway.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the fixed Jinja version or describe the exact characters the fix rejects. They do not detail how blacklist checks are bypassed. Attribute values and other contexts are not covered. Accepting user keys is described as an uncommon use of the filter.

fixtures.scenario: A profile page builds an attribute mapping from user-submitted names and values and renders it with the xmlattr filter. A key containing a space adds a second attribute, such as an event handler, which runs for other viewers.
The page accepts only keys from a fixed allowlist, and user input supplies values only. A submitted key with a space or an unknown name is rejected before rendering, so no extra attribute is created.

citations.quote: XML/HTML attributes cannot contain spaces, as each would then be interpreted as a separate attribute.
an application doing so should already be verifying what keys are provided regardless of this fix.
It may also be possible to bypass attribute validation checks if they are blacklist-based.

patterns.title: Directory traversal in Salt syndic cache directory creation
patterns.cause: Syndic cache directory creation in Salt is vulnerable to a directory traversal attack. The path used to create the cache directory is not confined to its intended location, so a malicious user can cause an arbitrary directory to be created on a Salt master.
preconditions: A Salt master creates syndic cache directories.
A malicious user or attacker can influence the path used for syndic cache directory creation.
The directory creation step does not keep the final path inside the intended cache location.
patterns.prevention: Before creating a cache directory, resolve the final path and confirm it is still inside the intended cache root. Reject any value that would escape that root, such as one containing parent-directory components or path separators. Prefer treating externally supplied identifiers as a single plain name rather than as a path. Upgrade to a Salt release that contains the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources are brief. They do not say which input carries the traversal sequence, which Salt component supplies it, or whether authentication is needed. They do not list affected or fixed versions, and they do not describe how the upstream fix works. The prevention guidance is the general approach for directory traversal, not a description of the upstream change. The sources only describe arbitrary directory creation, not file read or write.

fixtures.scenario: A Salt master builds a syndic cache directory path from a name supplied by a malicious user. The name contains parent-directory components, so the directory is created outside the cache area at a location the attacker chose.

A Salt master builds the syndic cache directory path from a supplied name, resolves the full path, and checks that it stays inside the cache root. A name that would escape the root is rejected and no directory is created.

citations.quote: Syndic cache directory creation is vulnerable to a directory traversal attack in salt project
create an arbitrary directory on a Salt master

patterns.title: Directory traversal through a crafted url in the Salt file server
patterns.cause: The Salt file server accepts a url from a requester and a specially crafted url can lead to a directory traversal. The requested location is not kept inside the area the file server is meant to serve.
preconditions: A Salt master runs the file server and handles requests that carry a url chosen by the requester.
A malicious user can send a specially crafted url to the file server.
patterns.prevention: Treat the requested url as untrusted data. Before any file is opened, resolve the requested location to its canonical absolute form, for example with os.path.realpath(). Then confirm the result is still inside the intended file server root, and reject the request if it is not. Do this check on the final resolved location, not on the raw text of the url.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say that a crafted url causes a directory traversal in the file server and allows reading arbitrary files from the master. They do not name the affected code path, the exact url form, the affected or fixed versions, or the precise upstream change. The prevention steps above are a general direction and not a description of the upstream fix.

fixtures.scenario: A user sends the Salt file server a crafted url, and the server maps it to a file outside the served directories. The user reads an arbitrary file from the master filesystem.
The file server resolves each requested url to a canonical path, checks that it is under the configured file server root, and refuses any request that resolves elsewhere.

citations.quote: A specially crafted url can be created which leads to a directory traversal in the salt file server.
A malicious user can read an arbitrary file from a Salt master

patterns.title: Stored XSS through Markdown preview in JupyterLab (CVE-2024-22420)
patterns.cause: JupyterLab was vulnerable to stored cross-site scripting (described as SXSS) when it showed Markdown content from a notebook with Markdown cells or from a Markdown file in the preview feature. The workaround of disabling the table of contents extension suggests that component is involved. Attacker-controlled Markdown could then act with the victim's privileges in the JupyterLab session.
preconditions: The victim runs a JupyterLab version older than 4.0.11.
The victim opens a malicious notebook with Markdown cells, or a malicious Markdown file, using the JupyterLab preview feature.
The table of contents extension is enabled, since disabling it is the documented workaround.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade JupyterLab to version 4.0.11 or later. If an upgrade is not possible, disable the table of contents extension. When building or reviewing similar features, treat all Markdown text from notebooks and files as untrusted data in every component that displays or processes it, including preview and table of contents features. Do not let it run as active content in the application page. Open notebooks and Markdown files from untrusted sources only after the fix or workaround is in place.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact injection point, the payload form, or what the patch changed, so this card gives no code-level guidance. The role of the table of contents extension is inferred from the workaround alone. The package list includes notebook, but the sources name only JupyterLab 4.0.11 as patched and give no fixed version for notebook. The sources also do not say whether other rendering paths are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A user on JupyterLab 4.0.10 with the table of contents extension enabled opens a notebook from an untrusted source. One Markdown cell contains attacker-written content. Viewing it in the preview feature lets the attacker read data the user can access and send requests as the user.

A user on JupyterLab 4.0.11 or later opens the same notebook in the preview feature. Alternatively, a user who cannot upgrade has disabled the table of contents extension first. The Markdown content does not run as attacker-controlled active content, and the user's data and session stay protected.

citations.quote: The vulnerability depends on user interaction by opening a malicious notebook with Markdown cells, or Markdown file using JupyterLab preview feature.
A malicious user can access any data that the attacked user has access to as well as perform arbitrary requests acting as the attacked user.
JupyterLab version 4.0.11 has been patched. Users are advised to upgrade. Users unable to upgrade should disable the table of contents extension.

patterns.title: Token exposure through a malicious link in JupyterLab running with an older jupyter-server
patterns.cause: A user who clicks a malicious link may have their Authorization and XSRF tokens exposed to a third party. This happens when JupyterLab runs on an older jupyter-server that has a redirect vulnerability. The sources do not describe the internal mechanism, including how path handling contributes.
preconditions: The deployment runs a JupyterLab release that is not one of the patched versions (4.1.0b2, 4.0.11 or 3.6.7).
The deployment runs a jupyter-server release older than 2.7.2, which lacks the redirect vulnerability fix.
A user clicks a malicious link.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade JupyterLab to a patched release (4.1.0b2, 4.0.11 or 3.6.7 or later in each line). Also upgrade jupyter-server to version 2.7.2 or newer, which includes the redirect vulnerability fix. The advisory identifies no other workaround, so keep both components current rather than relying on user caution about links.
patterns.limitations: The sources give no technical detail about the vulnerable code path or the exact change made in JupyterLab. They do not say how the path traversal weakness (CWE-23) maps onto the token leak. They do not name specific jupyter-server releases before 2.7.2 beyond the fix version. The notebook package is listed for this CVE, but the sources give no patched notebook version. No workaround has been identified.

fixtures.scenario: An administrator runs a JupyterLab release older than 4.0.11 on a jupyter-server older than 2.7.2. A user clicks a link crafted by an attacker, and the user's Authorization and XSRF tokens may be exposed to a third party.

An administrator runs JupyterLab 4.0.11 or a later patched release on jupyter-server 2.7.2 or newer. The same malicious link does not expose the user's tokens, because both the JupyterLab patch and the redirect fix are present.

citations.quote: JupyterLab versions 4.1.0b2, 4.0.11, and 3.6.7 are patched.
to version 2.7.2 or newer which includes a redirect vulnerability fix.

patterns.title: Directory traversal in aiohttp static routes when symlink following is enabled
patterns.cause: When aiohttp serves static files and the follow_symlinks option is set to true, it does not validate that the requested file path stays inside the configured static root directory. A remote user can therefore read arbitrary files on the system, even when no symlinks are present.
preconditions: aiohttp is used as a web server and a static route is configured with a root directory
The follow_symlinks option on that static route is set to true
The aiohttp version is older than 3.9.2
The server accepts requests from remote users
patterns.prevention: Do not enable follow_symlinks outside a restricted local development environment. The option is not needed for symlinks that point inside the static root, only for ones that leave it. If a static route must allow symlinks that leave the root, make sure the final file path is checked against the static root before it is read. Upgrade to aiohttp 3.9.2 or later, and keep the option disabled even after upgrading. Serve static files from a reverse proxy such as nginx instead of from aiohttp in production.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact request shape that triggers the traversal, the internals of the upstream fix, or the full range of affected versions beyond the fix in 3.9.2. They say only that the issue has existed since follow_symlinks was introduced. They also warn that, even with the fix, enabling the option on a server that accepts remote requests carries a substantial risk of misconfiguration. Setups that do not enable the option are described as not vulnerable.

fixtures.scenario: A public aiohttp application registers a static route for a static directory with follow_symlinks set to true and runs a version older than 3.9.2. A remote client requests a path that resolves outside the static root, and the server returns the contents of an unrelated file on the host.

The application registers the static route without enabling follow_symlinks, runs aiohttp 3.9.2 or later, and has a reverse proxy serve static assets in production. Requests for paths outside the static root are not served.

citations.quote: When 'follow_symlinks' is set to True, there is no validation to check if a given file path is within the root directory.
This option is NOT needed to follow symlinks which point to a location _within_ the static root directory
Disabling follow_symlinks and using a reverse proxy are encouraged mitigations.
Version 3.9.2 fixes this issue.

patterns.title: Open redirect after login via URL that the parser treats as relative but the client normalizes to an external host
patterns.cause: After login, pyload-ng checks the next value with a safe-URL check inside the redirect helper before redirecting the user. The check relies on urlparse. For an unusual URL such as https:///example.com, urlparse treats it as a relative path, so it passes. The actual request then normalizes it to https://example.com, so the user is sent to an arbitrary domain. The parser and the client disagree about what the URL means.
preconditions: The application redirects the user after login to a destination taken from a user-controlled next parameter.
The safe-URL check decides whether the target is local based on how urlparse classifies it.
An attacker can get a victim to follow a login link carrying a crafted next value.
patterns.prevention: Do not trust the parser's classification of a redirect target alone. Validate it the way the client will interpret it. Treat malformed or unusual absolute-URL forms, such as a scheme followed by an empty host and extra slashes, as untrusted instead of as relative paths. Either normalize the value first and then compare its host with the application's own host, or reject anything that is not a plain local path. Fall back to a fixed default page when the check fails.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the contents of the upstream patch, the affected version range, or any bypass forms beyond the one example. This card does not claim that blocking that single form is sufficient. The sources say only that validation of the next value was incorrect.

fixtures.scenario: A user opens a login link whose next value is https:///example.com. The safe-URL check parses it as a relative path and accepts it. After login the browser normalizes it to https://example.com and lands on the attacker's site, which can be used for phishing.

A user opens a login link with the same next value. The validator rejects the malformed absolute-URL form, or normalizes it and sees that the host is not the application's own. The user is sent to the default page after login instead of the external site.

citations.quote: Open redirect vulnerability due to incorrect validation of input values when redirecting users after login.
The documentation in the urllib library shows that improper URLs are recognized as relative paths when using the
interprets it as a relative path, but in the actual request it is converted to

patterns.title: Unsanitized imported task data rendered in Choices or Labels tags enables stored XSS
patterns.cause: Data imported through the file upload feature is not properly sanitized before it is rendered within a Choices or Labels tag. Markup supplied in an imported task field is therefore treated as active page content instead of inert text, so script can run in the browser of whoever opens the task.
preconditions: Label Studio version earlier than 1.11.0 is in use
The attacker has permission to use the data import function
The project labeling config renders imported values through a Choices or Labels tag
A user opens a task whose imported data contains attacker-supplied markup
patterns.prevention: Treat every value in imported task data as untrusted, whatever the file source. Sanitize or escape it for the HTML context before it is rendered in Choices or Labels output, so markup and event handler attributes are never interpreted as live content. Apply the protection at render time as well as at import. Upgrade to Label Studio 1.11.0 or later, since the advisory names earlier versions as affected.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so the exact sanitization method and library are unknown. They do not say whether other tags or import paths are affected, or whether any mitigation exists besides upgrading. The proof of concept was reproduced only on version 1.10.1 with one template.

fixtures.scenario: A user with data import permission uploads a task file whose image field holds HTML with an event handler attribute. A labeling config using Choices or Labels renders it unsanitized, and the script runs when another user opens the task.

The same task file is uploaded, but imported values are sanitized before rendering in Choices or Labels. The markup appears as inert text or is stripped of active content, and no script runs when the task is opened.

citations.quote: On all Label Studio versions prior to 1.11.0, data imported via file upload feature is not properly sanitized prior to being rendered
Malicious scripts can be injected into the code, and when linked with vulnerabilities such as CSRF, it can cause even greater damage.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS on the Flask-AppBuilder OAuth login page via crafted URL
patterns.cause: The OAuth login page in Flask-AppBuilder 4.1.4 through 4.2.0 allowed a specially crafted URL to inject JavaScript that then ran in the victim's browser. The sources describe this as a cross-site scripting flaw (CWE-79) introduced in 4.1.4. They do not say which URL component or template caused it.
preconditions: The application runs Flask-AppBuilder version 4.1.4 up to and including 4.2.0.
The OAuth login page is reachable by users.
An attacker can get a user to follow a crafted URL to that login page.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Flask-AppBuilder to 4.2.1 or a newer release, where the issue is patched. Until the upgrade, treat any value arriving through the URL to the OAuth login page as untrusted, and make sure the page never emits it as executable script.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the vulnerable parameter, template or code path, so they cannot show which interim mitigations would be complete. They confirm only the affected range (4.1.4 to 4.2.0) and the patched version (4.2.1). Deployments that customize the login view or its templates may need their own review, which the sources do not cover.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs Flask-AppBuilder 4.2.0 with OAuth login enabled. An attacker sends a user a specially crafted link to the OAuth login page, and script code embedded in the URL runs in the user's browser.
The application runs Flask-AppBuilder 4.2.1 or newer. The same crafted link to the OAuth login page does not result in injected JavaScript executing in the user's browser.

citations.quote: An attacker could trick a user to follow a specially crafted URL to the OAuth login page.
This issue was introduced on 4.1.4 and patched on 4.2.1, user's should upgrade to 4.2.1 or newer versions.

patterns.title: Template variable XSS in MLflow recipe output escalating to client-side RCE in Jupyter
patterns.cause: MLflow did not sufficiently sanitize template variables when rendering content for a recipe. Values controlled by an untrusted recipe could therefore be emitted as active markup or script in the rendered output, producing cross-site scripting.
preconditions: A user runs an untrusted recipe with an affected MLflow version
Recipe-controlled values are inserted into a template without sanitization
For the client-side RCE impact, the recipe is run and its output rendered in a Jupyter Notebook
patterns.prevention: Treat every template variable as untrusted data and neutralize it for the output context before it is placed into rendered content, for example by relying on the template engine's automatic escaping or by explicitly escaping each value. Do not run recipes from untrusted sources, particularly in Jupyter Notebook, and upgrade to a MLflow release that contains the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say that sanitization of template variables was insufficient. They do not name the affected template, the exact output context, the affected version range, or the specific escaping method used by the fix, so this card does not cover those details.

fixtures.scenario: A user opens an untrusted recipe in a Jupyter Notebook. A value defined by the recipe is placed into a template without sanitization, and the rendered output runs attacker-chosen script in the notebook's browser context.
The same untrusted recipe is processed, but every template variable is escaped for its output context before rendering. The value is displayed as inert text and no script runs in the notebook.

citations.quote: Insufficient sanitization in MLflow leads to XSS when running an untrusted recipe.
This issue leads to a client-side RCE when running an untrusted recipe in Jupyter Notebook.
The vulnerability stems from lack of sanitization over template variables.

patterns.title: Unsanitized dataset table fields in MLflow recipes enable XSS and client-side RCE in Jupyter
patterns.cause: MLflow did not sufficiently sanitize dataset table fields. When a recipe ran on an untrusted dataset, content from those fields reached the rendered output as active content, which caused cross-site scripting.
preconditions: A recipe is run on a dataset that comes from an untrusted source.
Dataset table fields are included in the output the recipe produces without sufficient sanitization.
For the client-side RCE impact, the recipe is run inside a Jupyter Notebook.
patterns.prevention: Treat every value in a dataset table as untrusted data. Sanitize or neutralize all dataset table fields before they are rendered in any output the recipe produces, so that field content is displayed as plain text and never interpreted as active content.
