An attacker can create a watch with an attacker-chosen URL and enable webdriver mode for it.
patterns.prevention: Decide whether a URL is a local-file URL from its parsed scheme, not from a string-prefix match on the raw text. Parse the URL with a standard URL parser, normalise the scheme, and apply the local-file policy to every file URI form: no hostname, empty hostname, and with hostname. Run the same decision wherever the URL is validated and wherever the fetcher chooses how to load it, so the two checks cannot disagree. Reject file URIs by default unless local files are explicitly allowed. Upgrade to version 0.47.06 or later, which the advisory says addresses the issue.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so this card gives only the general direction. They do not discuss other bypass forms, such as case variations, other schemes, or redirects. They state that no workarounds are known. The issue is reported only for instances with a webdriver enabled and ALLOW_FILE_URI false or undefined.

fixtures.scenario: An instance has a webdriver enabled and ALLOW_FILE_URI unset. A user creates a watch whose URL is file:/etc/passwd with webdriver mode on. The prefix check for file:// does not match, so the watch is accepted, fetched, and the file contents appear in the preview.

The same instance parses each submitted URL and reads its scheme. The watch URL file:/etc/passwd is recognised as a file URI and rejected because local files are not allowed. The forms file:///etc/passwd and file://host/etc/passwd are rejected the same way.

citations.quote: The issue comes with the fact that the file URI scheme is not required to have double slashes.
It later checks if local files are permitted, but one of the preconditions for the check is that the URL starts with
This issue has been addressed in version 0.47.06 and all users are advised to upgrade.

patterns.title: SQL injection through an unvalidated api_key value concatenated into a spend logs query in litellm
patterns.cause: The /global/spend/logs endpoint in litellm built an SQL query by concatenating an unvalidated api_key parameter directly into the query text. Special elements in that value were not neutralized, so a caller could change the structure of the SQL command instead of only supplying a value.
preconditions: The application builds an SQL command as text and inserts a request parameter, here api_key, into it by concatenation.
The parameter value is not validated or neutralized before it reaches the SQL command.
An attacker can send the endpoint a request whose api_key value contains malicious data.
patterns.prevention: Never place request-supplied values such as api_key into the SQL command text by concatenation. Keep the command structure fixed and pass user-controlled values to the database separately, so special characters are treated as data and not as SQL syntax. Also validate the expected shape of the value before use. Review every endpoint that filters spend or log data by caller-supplied identifiers for the same pattern.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the actual upstream fix, the affected version range, or which other parameters or endpoints might share the flaw. They say only that the issue affects the latest version at the time of the report. The prevention direction above is the general remedy for the stated cause, not a confirmed description of the patch. The sources also do not say whether authentication limits who can reach the endpoint.

fixtures.scenario: A spend report endpoint receives an api_key query parameter and joins it into the text of a SELECT statement. A caller supplies a value containing SQL special characters and extra clauses, and the database runs the altered statement, exposing or modifying data beyond the intended key.

The same endpoint uses a fixed SELECT statement with a placeholder for the api_key filter and hands the caller's value to the database driver as a separate bound parameter. The same hostile input is matched literally as a key string, finds no rows, and does not change the statement.

citations.quote: The affected code constructs an SQL query by concatenating an unvalidated
The vulnerability arises due to improper neutralization of special elements used in an SQL command.
Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could lead to unauthorized access, data manipulation, exposure of confidential information, and denial of service (DoS).

patterns.title: Incomplete engine-specific function checks let SQL bypass Superset authorization
patterns.cause: Apache Superset checks submitted SQL against a set of disallowed engine-specific functions as part of its SQL authorization. For PostgreSQL, three functions were missing from that set: query_to_xml_and_xmlschema, table_to_xml and table_to_xml_and_xmlschema. SQL using them was not flagged, so attackers could bypass the authorization. This is a follow-up to CVE-2024-39887, which addressed the same kind of gap with other functions.
preconditions: Apache Superset version earlier than 4.1.0 is deployed.
A PostgreSQL database is reachable through Superset.
The disallowed-function configuration (DISALLOWED_SQL_FUNCTIONS) does not list the three missing PostgreSQL functions.
An attacker can submit SQL that is subject to Superset's SQL authorization check.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Superset to version 4.1.0 or later, which includes these functions in the disallowed set. If an immediate upgrade is not possible, add the three PostgreSQL functions to the DISALLOWED_SQL_FUNCTIONS configuration set. More generally, treat the per-engine list of disallowed functions as a security control that must be kept complete, and review it again whenever a bypass is reported for any engine function.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not explain how the three functions enable the bypass or what data an attacker can reach. They do not say whether other engines or other functions are affected, or whether a function list alone is sufficient to stop this class of issue. They do not describe the exact attacker privileges needed. The configuration workaround is stated only for the three named functions.

fixtures.scenario: A Superset instance older than 4.1.0 is connected to PostgreSQL and uses the default disallowed-function set. A user submits a query that calls table_to_xml. The authorization check does not flag the function, so the query passes the check that should have blocked it.

A Superset instance runs version 4.1.0 or later, or an older instance has query_to_xml_and_xmlschema, table_to_xml and table_to_xml_and_xmlschema added to its disallowed-function configuration. A query calling any of them is flagged by the authorization check.

citations.quote: certain engine-specific functions are not checked, which allows attackers to bypass Apache Superset's SQL authorization
This issue is a follow-up to CVE-2024-39887 with additional disallowed PostgreSQL functions now included
Users are recommended to upgrade to version 4.1.0, which fixes the issue or add these Postgres functions to the config set DISALLOWED_SQL_FUNCTIONS.
This issue affects Apache Superset: <4.1.0.

patterns.title: Prefix-based file URL blocklist bypassed for local file read in watch URLs
patterns.cause: The application accepted user-supplied watch URLs and tried to block local file access by checking whether the stripped URL began with the file scheme followed by a slash. Variants such as a relative form with dot-dot segments right after the scheme, or a space before the slashes, slipped past this weak check. User input could then reach file paths without adequate validation.
preconditions: The attacker can create a watch with an arbitrary URL
The instance has a webdriver configured
The only guard is a text-prefix check on the URL string
The watch preview returns fetched content to the attacker
patterns.prevention: Do not rely on matching a blocked prefix in the raw URL text. Parse the URL with a real parser, then allow only the web schemes the feature needs and reject everything else, including any form of the file scheme. Apply this check to the parsed result and on every path where a watch URL is accepted or fetched, so odd spacing or relative forms cannot change the outcome. Upgrade to 0.48.05 or later, where this issue is reported fixed.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream fix, so the allow-list and parser guidance is a general direction and not a confirmed account of the patch. They also name only the file scheme and the webdriver-backed preview path, and do not say whether other schemes or fetchers were affected.

fixtures.scenario: A user creates a watch whose URL starts with the file scheme and uses a relative path with dot-dot segments, or has a space before the slashes. The prefix check misses it, and the preview shows the contents of the system password file.
The same watch URLs are parsed first. Only permitted web schemes are accepted, so any file-scheme variant is rejected at creation and no local file content appears in the preview.

citations.quote: Improper input validation in the application can allow attackers to perform local file read (LFR) or path traversal attacks.
The attacker can still bypass this by using:
This vulnerability is fixed in 0.48.05.

patterns.title: Pickle deserialization of untrusted bytes in FAISS.deserialize_from_bytes (CVE-2024-5998)
patterns.cause: The FAISS.deserialize_from_bytes function in langchain deserializes its input with pickle. Pickle data from an untrusted source can therefore run arbitrary commands, for example through the os.system function, when the application loads it.
preconditions: The application calls FAISS.deserialize_from_bytes on a serialized vector store.
The serialized bytes can be supplied or altered by an untrusted party, for example through an upload, a shared store, or a download.
The langchain or langchain-community version is one the advisories list as affected. GHSA-f2jm-rw3h-6phg and PYSEC-2026-1514 say versions prior to 0.2.4.
patterns.prevention: Do not pass bytes from an untrusted or unauthenticated source to FAISS.deserialize_from_bytes. Treat serialized index bytes as executable input and load them only if the application itself produced them and they were stored where outsiders cannot write. Where the index must come from an outside party, avoid pickle-based loading and rebuild the index from the original documents with a trusted embedding step. Also move to a release at or after 0.2.4, since the advisories list earlier versions as affected.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so this card cannot say whether newer releases add a safety flag or change the loading format. The sources disagree on scope: the CVE and PYSEC-2024-323 text says the latest version is affected, while GHSA-f2jm-rw3h-6phg and PYSEC-2026-1514 say versions prior to 0.2.4. They do not map the fixed version to langchain versus langchain-community. They also do not say whether upgrading alone is enough when untrusted bytes are still loaded, so avoiding untrusted input remains the safer rule.

fixtures.scenario: A web service lets users upload a saved vector store file and passes the uploaded bytes straight to FAISS.deserialize_from_bytes. An attacker uploads a crafted pickle payload that runs a system command on the server when it is loaded.

A service builds its vector store from its own documents, stores the serialized bytes in a location only the service can write, and loads only those bytes. Files from outside parties are never deserialized. They are re-indexed from the source documents instead.

citations.quote: A vulnerability in the FAISS.deserialize_from_bytes function of langchain-ai/langchain allows for pickle deserialization of untrusted data.
This can lead to the execution of arbitrary commands via the os.system function.
The issue affects versions prior to 0.2.4.

patterns.title: Client-chosen api_base sends server-held API key to attacker domain in litellm
patterns.cause: In litellm 1.38.10, users could specify the api_base parameter when calling POST /chat/completions. The application then sent the request to whatever domain api_base named, and that request included the OpenAI API key. The caller, not the operator, controlled the destination of a request that carried a server-side secret.
preconditions: The deployment runs litellm 1.38.10 and exposes POST /chat/completions to users.
The endpoint accepts a user-supplied api_base parameter and uses it as the upstream destination.
The outbound request carries the OpenAI API key held by the server.
patterns.prevention: Do not let a request-supplied value choose the destination of an outbound call that carries server-held credentials. Take the upstream base address from operator-controlled configuration, or accept a user-supplied value only if it matches an operator-defined allowlist of trusted destinations. Treat any per-request override of the destination as untrusted input, and never attach the server's API key to a request sent to an address the operator did not approve.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe only the vulnerable behavior in version 1.38.10. They do not describe the upstream fix, the patched version, or any other affected parameters or endpoints. They do not say whether authentication on the endpoint changes exploitability. The allowlist approach above is a general design direction and not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A user sends a chat completions request to the litellm server and sets api_base to a domain they control. The server forwards the request to that domain with the OpenAI API key attached, and the user reads the key from their own server logs.

A user sends a chat completions request that includes an api_base pointing at their own domain. The server ignores or rejects the value because it is not on the operator-approved list, and sends the request only to the configured upstream. The API key never reaches the user's domain.

citations.quote: This request includes the OpenAI API key.
leading to unauthorized access and potential misuse of the API key.

patterns.title: Arbitrary callback names in litellm post_call_rules allow remote code execution
patterns.cause: In litellm 1.40.12, the post_call_rules configuration accepts a callback function. The supplied value is split at the final dot. The last part is treated as the function name, and the remaining part is given a .py extension and imported. Nothing restricts the value to a vetted callback, so an attacker can name a system method such as os.system as the callback. The command then runs when a chat response is processed.
preconditions: litellm 1.40.12 is in use, the version named in the advisory.
The post_call_rules configuration accepts a callback value that an attacker can influence.
The callback value is split at the last dot and resolved to an importable module and function name.
A chat response is processed, which triggers the configured callback.
patterns.prevention: Never turn a configuration string directly into an imported module and callable. Resolve each callback only against an explicit allowlist of operator-approved callback functions, or against a fixed, trusted location that holds only callback code. Reject any value that resolves to a standard library or system function such as os.system. Treat the post_call_rules setting as sensitive, so that untrusted users cannot write or change it.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe only the vulnerable behavior. They do not say how an attacker gains the ability to set post_call_rules, which versions besides 1.40.12 are affected, or exactly how upstream changed the code. The allowlist and access-control directions above are general mitigations, not a description of the upstream fix.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment on litellm 1.40.12 lets a user supply a post_call_rules entry whose value names a system method such as os.system. The value is split at the last dot and resolved, so processing a chat response runs an arbitrary command on the server.

A deployment accepts only callback names from a fixed allowlist of approved functions in operator-controlled code. A value naming os.system is rejected at configuration time, and untrusted users cannot edit post_call_rules, so no arbitrary command runs when a chat response is processed.

citations.quote: The issue exists in the handling of the 'post_call_rules' configuration, where a callback function can be added.
The provided value is split at the final '.' mark, with the last part considered the function name
This allows an attacker to set a system method, such as 'os.system', as a callback

patterns.title: Stored XSS through files uploaded in Open WebUI chat
patterns.cause: In open-webui version 0.3.8, the chat file upload feature accepts a file containing attacker-controlled malicious content. When a victim later opens that file through a URL or a shared chat, the content runs as JavaScript in the victim's browser. The uploaded content is therefore treated as active content, not as inert data.
preconditions: The application is open-webui version 0.3.8, the version named in the advisories.
An attacker can upload a file through the chat file upload functionality.
A victim accesses the stored file through a URL or through a shared chat.
patterns.prevention: Treat every uploaded file as untrusted data. When a file is delivered to a user, by direct URL or through a shared chat, make sure its content cannot execute as script in the application's browser context. Neutralize or sanitize attacker-controlled content, or serve it so the browser does not interpret it as active content. Apply this check on every path that returns uploaded content, including shared chat views.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, the exact file types or payloads involved, or which versions after 0.3.8 are fixed. They do not say which delivery mechanism, such as sanitization, response headers or content-type handling, resolves the issue. This card gives only a general direction and should be checked against the vendor's patched release.

fixtures.scenario: A user uploads a file with embedded script content in a chat and shares the chat. A second user opens the file through its URL or the shared chat, and the script runs in that user's browser session.

A user uploads the same file and shares the chat. When the second user opens the file through its URL or the shared chat, the content is handled as untrusted data and does not run as script in the application's context.

citations.quote: A Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability exists in the chat file upload functionality of open-webui/open-webui version 0.3.8.
when accessed by a victim through a URL or shared chat, executes JavaScript in the victim's browser

patterns.title: Prompt injection in GraphCypherQAChain leading to database injection
patterns.cause: In GraphCypherQAChain (reported in version 0.2.5), attacker-controlled prompt text can steer the chain into injection against the backing graph database. The chain's database access is not independently limited, so unauthorized reads and writes follow.
preconditions: The application uses the GraphCypherQAChain class from langchain or langchain-community, reported at version 0.2.5
Untrusted users can supply prompt text to the chain
The chain's database connection can perform operations beyond what the calling user is authorized to do
patterns.prevention: Treat every user prompt reaching the chain as untrusted. Enforce authorization and tenant separation in the database layer, not in the prompt or chain. Give the chain's connection only the permissions its use case needs, such as read-only access scoped to the current tenant, so injected requests cannot create, update, or delete data. Move to a patched release; the exact fixed version is not stated in the sources.
patterns.limitations: The sources only describe the impact and the affected class and version. They do not explain the exact injection mechanism, the fixed version, or how the upstream change works. The least-privilege and tenant-scoping advice is a general mitigation derived from the listed impacts, not a documented fix.

fixtures.scenario: A multi-tenant app passes end-user questions to GraphCypherQAChain using one shared, full-privilege database account. A crafted prompt makes the chain delete nodes or read another tenant's data.
The app passes end-user questions to the chain through a database account limited to read-only access on the current tenant's data. A crafted prompt cannot modify data or reach other tenants.

citations.quote: A vulnerability in the GraphCypherQAChain class of langchain-ai/langchain version 0.2.5 allows for SQL injection through prompt injection.
Attackers can create, update, or delete nodes and relationships without proper authorization, extract sensitive data, disrupt services

patterns.title: Local file read in MLflow dbfs handling when only the URL path is validated
patterns.cause: In mlflow 2.15.1 with the dbfs service configured, the URL is concatenated directly into the file protocol. Only the path part of the URL is checked. Other parts, such as the query and parameters, are not handled. This allows an arbitrary local file read (CWE-22, CWE-29).
preconditions: mlflow version 2.15.1 is in use, the version named in the advisory.
The dbfs service is configured and in use.
The dbfs service is mounted to a local directory.
The URL is concatenated directly into the file protocol, and the check covers only its path part.
patterns.prevention: Do not build a local file location by concatenating a whole URL into the file protocol. Validate every component of the URL, including the query and parameters, not just the path. Resolve the final local location and confirm it stays inside the intended mounted directory before reading. Reject any URL carrying unexpected components.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not give the exact payload shape, the fixed version, or whether versions other than 2.15.1 are affected. They also do not explain how query or parameter parts reach the local path. The prevention is therefore a general direction, not a verified description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A dbfs service is mounted to a local directory. A URL is joined into a file protocol string and only its path is checked. Query or parameter parts are left unchecked, so a crafted URL reads an arbitrary local file.

The same mounted dbfs service validates every URL component, including query and parameters. It rejects unexpected parts. It also confirms the resolved local location stays inside the mounted directory before any read.

citations.quote: only the path part of the URL is checked, while parts such as query and parameters are not handled
The vulnerability is triggered if the user has configured the dbfs service, and during usage, the service is mounted to a local directory.

patterns.title: Unvalidated user-supplied model file path allows directory traversal in MLflow Tracking Server
patterns.cause: The tracking server uses a user-supplied path for model files in file operations without proper validation. A remote attacker can supply a crafted path that escapes the intended location, and the sources state this can lead to code execution as the service account.
preconditions: The MLflow Tracking Server is reachable by a remote attacker
A model creation or model file handling operation accepts a path value supplied by the user
The supplied path is used in file operations without proper validation
Authentication is not required to reach the vulnerable flow, per the advisory
patterns.prevention: Treat every user-supplied model file path as untrusted. Before any file operation, validate the path and confirm it resolves to a location inside the intended storage root. Reject absolute paths and parent-directory segments, and resolve the final path with a canonicalizing call such as os.path.realpath() before comparing it to the allowed base directory. Apply this check at every entry point that handles model file paths, and fail closed when validation does not succeed.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the affected endpoint, parameter, or versions, and do not describe the exact validation that was missing or how the upstream change addresses it. They do not explain how a file write leads to code execution. The guidance above is general path containment practice that follows from the stated lack of validation, not a description of the upstream fix.

fixtures.scenario: A remote, unauthenticated client sends a model creation request whose model file path contains parent-directory segments. The server uses it directly in file operations, so files are written or read outside the intended model storage location.

The same request is received, but the server validates the supplied path, resolves it, and finds it falls outside the allowed model storage root. The request is rejected and no file operation occurs outside that root.

citations.quote: The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a user-supplied path prior to using it in file operations.
Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.
An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the service account.

patterns.title: ReDoS in GPT-NeoX-Japanese subword tokenizer regular expressions
patterns.cause: The SubWordJapaneseTokenizer class in the GPT-NeoX-Japanese tokenization module uses a regular expression with exponential complexity on certain inputs. When specially crafted text is processed, the regex engine performs excessive backtracking, consuming high CPU time.
preconditions: The application uses the GPT-NeoX-Japanese tokenizer from the transformers library, specifically the SubWordJapaneseTokenizer class.
The installed transformers version is affected (the advisory names v4.48.1 as affected).
Untrusted or attacker-influenced text reaches the tokenizer, so specially crafted input can trigger the vulnerable regular expression.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a transformers release that includes the upstream fix for this tokenizer. When writing or reviewing similar tokenizers, avoid regular expressions whose structure allows exponential backtracking on crafted input: prefer patterns without nested or overlapping repetition, or use a linear-time matching approach or manual scanning. As defense in depth, limit the length of text passed to the tokenizer and run tokenization of untrusted input under CPU time limits or in a separate worker so a stalled request cannot take down the service. Add regression tests with long adversarial inputs and a time budget.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify the exact vulnerable pattern, the input shapes that trigger the backtracking, the first fixed release, or the earliest affected version. They only name v4.48.1 as affected. Input length limits and timeouts reduce impact but do not remove the underlying regex weakness. The sources do not describe the upstream fix, so the safe approaches above are general guidance and not a description of that change.

fixtures.scenario: A web service accepts arbitrary user text and passes it to the GPT-NeoX-Japanese tokenizer on transformers v4.48.1. An attacker submits a specially crafted string, the regex backtracks excessively, CPU usage spikes, and the service becomes unresponsive.

The service runs a transformers version containing the upstream fix, caps the length of input text, and tokenizes untrusted input in a worker with a CPU time limit. The same crafted string is processed quickly or rejected, and the service stays responsive.

citations.quote: The issue stems from a regex exhibiting exponential complexity under certain conditions, leading to excessive backtracking.
The vulnerability occurs in the SubWordJapaneseTokenizer class, where regular expressions process specially crafted inputs.
This can result in high CPU usage and potential application downtime, effectively creating a Denial of Service (DoS) scenario.

patterns.title: Tar archive path traversal in MLflow pyfunc extraction
patterns.cause: MLflow's pyfunc extraction process handles tar archive entries improperly. It calls tarfile.extractall without path validation, so a crafted tar.gz with parent-directory components or absolute paths can write outside the intended extraction directory.
preconditions: The application extracts a tar.gz archive in the pyfunc extraction process
The archive comes from an untrusted source or from another tenant
Extraction runs without checking where each entry would be written
patterns.prevention: Before writing any archive entry, check that its final destination resolves inside the intended extraction directory. Reject entries with parent-directory components or absolute paths, and abort the extraction when a check fails. Treat archives from multi-tenant or untrusted artifact sources as hostile input.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, the affected version range beyond the latest version at disclosure, or how links inside archives are handled. They give no detail on how code execution would be reached. This card only gives the general direction of validating entry paths.

fixtures.scenario: A multi-tenant service ingests a user-uploaded tar.gz model artifact. One entry name contains parent-directory components, and extraction runs with no path check. The file lands outside the extraction directory and overwrites an existing file.

The same service resolves each entry's destination before extraction and compares it to the extraction directory. The entry with parent-directory components and any absolute-path entry are rejected, and the whole archive is refused.

citations.quote: allows for arbitrary file writes due to improper handling of tar archive entries
without path validation enables crafted tar.gz files containing
poses a high/critical risk in scenarios involving multi-tenant environments or ingestion of untrusted artifacts

patterns.title: Untrusted model dependency specs interpolated into a shell command in MLflow container setup
patterns.cause: During model serving container initialization, the _install_model_dependencies_to_env() function reads dependency specifications from the model artifact's python_env.yaml file and interpolates them directly into a shell command without sanitization. Artifact-controlled text therefore becomes part of a command line that the shell interprets.
preconditions: MLflow version 3.8.0 is in use
The model is deployed with the local environment manager mode rather than a managed isolated one
The model artifact, including its python_env.yaml file, comes from an attacker or other untrusted party
The deployment system builds and runs the dependency installation as a shell command
patterns.prevention: Treat everything in a model artifact, including python_env.yaml, as untrusted data. Do not join dependency specifications into a shell command string. Validate each entry as a plain dependency requirement and hand it to the installer as a discrete argument without shell interpretation. Upgrade to a fixed MLflow release and deploy only artifacts from trusted sources.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the code change or the validation rules used. They disagree on the fixed version: the GitHub advisory and PySEC entry say 3.8.1, while the CVE record says 3.8.2. Check which release is actually safe. The sources do not cover deployments that use other environment manager modes.

fixtures.scenario: An untrusted model artifact has a python_env.yaml with a dependency entry carrying extra shell commands. It is deployed on MLflow 3.8.0 in local environment manager mode, which builds a shell command from the entry and runs the attacker's commands.
The same artifact is deployed on a fixed release, or dependency entries are treated as plain data and never joined into a shell string, so the extra text is not executed as a command.

citations.quote: directly interpolates them into a shell command without sanitization
This allows an attacker to supply a malicious model artifact and achieve arbitrary command execution on systems that deploy the model.
The vulnerability affects versions 3.8.0 and is fixed in version 3.8.1.

patterns.title: SQL injection in DuckDBVectorStore delete via ref_doc_id
patterns.cause: The delete function of DuckDBVectorStore in llama-index v0.12.19 lets an attacker-controlled ref_doc_id manipulate the SQL statement that is run, so input is treated as SQL rather than as a plain value.
preconditions: The application uses DuckDBVectorStore from llama-index, reported in version v0.12.19
The delete function is reachable with a ref_doc_id value that an attacker can influence
patterns.prevention: Never let ref_doc_id change the structure of the SQL statement. Pass it to DuckDB only as a bound query parameter, not by joining it into the SQL text. Validate that identifiers have the expected form before calling delete, and avoid exposing delete to untrusted callers. Upgrade to a llama-index release that contains the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources only name the delete function and the ref_doc_id parameter in v0.12.19. They do not state the exact fixed version, the vulnerable query text, or the mechanics of the file access, so the guidance here is a general direction and not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A service passes a user-supplied ref_doc_id straight to the DuckDBVectorStore delete function, and a crafted value alters the SQL so that it can read or write files on the server.
A service sends ref_doc_id to the delete function only as a bound parameter after checking its format, so a crafted value is treated as data and cannot change the SQL statement.

citations.quote: An SQL injection vulnerability exists in the delete function of DuckDBVectorStore in run-llama/llama_index version v0.12.19.
This vulnerability allows an attacker to manipulate the ref_doc_id parameter, enabling them to read and write arbitrary files on the server

patterns.title: OS command injection via the files argument of the LlamaIndex CLI
patterns.cause: The CLI passed the files argument directly into os.system, so shell metacharacters in an attacker-controlled value were interpreted as shell commands and executed.
preconditions: Affected versions: LLama-Index CLI before v0.4.1, corresponding to LLama-Index before v0.12.21
The attacker controls the content of the files argument
Locally, the attacker controls the CLI arguments; remotely, a web application calls the CLI with a user-controlled filename
patterns.prevention: Do not build a shell command string from untrusted input. Do not hand the files value to os.system. Run any needed external program through an API that takes the program and its arguments as separate items and does not invoke a shell. Treat the files value strictly as data, such as a path to open. Upgrade to LLama-Index 0.12.21 or later (CLI 0.4.1 or later). Wrappers and web applications that call the CLI should also check user-supplied filenames before passing them on.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, so the exact remediation is not confirmed here. They do not say which other CLI arguments or code paths, if any, are affected. The prevention direction is general guidance, not a description of the patch.

fixtures.scenario: A web app accepts a filename from a user and starts the LlamaIndex CLI with it as the files argument. The CLI places the value into a shell command run by os.system, so a filename containing shell separators runs extra commands.
The same app uses a patched version (LLama-Index 0.12.21 or later). The filename is treated only as data, and no shell parses it, so separators or other metacharacters in it have no command effect.

citations.quote: An attacker who controls the content of this argument can inject and execute arbitrary shell commands.
and remotely if a web application calls the LLama-Index CLI with a user-controlled filename.

patterns.title: SQL injection in llama-index vector store integrations (CVE-2025-1793)
patterns.cause: Multiple vector store integrations in llama-index version v0.12.21 are vulnerable to SQL injection (CWE-89). An attacker can read and write data using SQL. The sources do not say which integrations, parameters or code paths are affected.
preconditions: The application uses llama-index version v0.12.21 with one of the vector store integrations that have the SQL injection flaw.
Attacker-influenced input reaches a vulnerable vector store integration, for example through a web application built on the library.
The application serves several users from shared vector store data, which makes cross-user data exposure possible.
patterns.prevention: Do not run the affected version v0.12.21. Move to a release that includes the upstream fix for CVE-2025-1793, and confirm the fixed version in the project's release notes because the sources do not name one. Make sure that any value coming from a user or an external caller is passed to the database only as data and never becomes part of SQL text. Keep database accounts used by vector stores limited to the access the application needs, so that a mistake exposes less data. Where several users share one store, enforce per-user separation in the application as well.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that multiple vector store integrations in v0.12.21 are affected and that attackers can read and write data. They do not name the integrations, the vulnerable parameters, the first fixed version or the exact mechanism. The least-privilege and per-user separation advice is general hardening and is not drawn from the advisory text. Check the fix commit and release notes for specifics.

fixtures.scenario: A web application on llama-index v0.12.21 lets users search a shared vector store through one of the affected integrations. A user supplies crafted input, and the SQL injection lets them read and write data, including data belonging to other users.

The same application runs a release that includes the fix for CVE-2025-1793. Caller-supplied values reach the database only as data. The database account is least-privileged, so crafted input cannot read or alter other users' records.

citations.quote: Multiple vector store integrations in run-llama/llama_index version v0.12.21 have SQL injection vulnerabilities.
These vulnerabilities allow an attacker to read and write data using SQL, potentially leading to unauthorized access to data of other users

patterns.title: ReDoS from nested quantifiers in the docstring code block regex of preprocess_string()
patterns.cause: The regular expression used by preprocess_string() in the transformers.testing_utils module to process code blocks in docstrings contains nested quantifiers. When given input with a large number of newline characters, it triggers catastrophic backtracking, which consumes excessive CPU.
preconditions: The transformers package is a version before 4.50.0
An attacker can supply input to preprocess_string() or to a code path that calls it
The supplied input contains a large number of newline characters
patterns.prevention: Upgrade transformers to 4.50.0 or later, where the regex was rewritten to avoid the inefficient pattern. When writing similar code, avoid nested quantifiers in patterns that process untrusted multi-line text, and do not pass untrusted input to preprocess_string() or code paths that call it.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which code paths outside the testing_utils module call preprocess_string(), nor how reachable it is in typical deployments. They do not describe the exact old or new regex, and they do not give input size thresholds. The CVE text names version 4.48.3 while the advisory says all versions before 4.50.0 are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A service running transformers older than 4.50.0 passes user-supplied text containing thousands of newline characters to preprocess_string(), and the regex backtracks until CPU is exhausted.
The service runs transformers 4.50.0 or later, which uses a rewritten regex, and does not route untrusted text to preprocess_string().

citations.quote: the regex used to process code blocks in docstrings contains nested quantifiers that can trigger catastrophic backtracking when given inputs with many newline characters
released in **4.50.0**, which rewrites the regex to avoid the inefficient pattern.
leading to exponential backtracking when processing input with a large number of newline characters

patterns.title: Command injection on the master through a crafted git url in on-demand pillar
patterns.cause: The on-demand pillar functionality accepts a git url that can be influenced by a holder of a minion key. A specially crafted url can cause an arbitrary command to run on the master. The sources do not explain the exact mechanism by which the url becomes a command.
preconditions: The attacker has access to a minion key.
The master exposes the on-demand pillar functionality.
A git url that the attacker can craft is processed by the master during on-demand pillar handling.
patterns.prevention: Treat any git url that arrives through an on-demand pillar request as untrusted input, even when it comes from an authenticated minion. Validate it against a strict expectation of what a repository location looks like, or against an allow-list of configured repositories. Make sure the value can never be interpreted as a command or option by a shell or by the git program. Run the master with the least privilege practical, because injected commands run with the master process privileges. Apply the vendor security update for Salt.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the injection mechanism, the affected or fixed versions, the specific code path, or the exact fix. They do not say whether the url reaches a shell or a git argument list. The validation and hardening advice above is therefore general direction, not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A master has on-demand pillar enabled. An attacker holding a valid minion key submits a specially crafted git url. The master processes it, and an arbitrary command runs on the master with the same privileges as the master process.

The master validates any git url received through on-demand pillar against an allow-list of expected repositories and rejects anything else. A crafted url from a minion key holder is refused and no command runs on the master.

citations.quote: An attacker with access to a minion key can exploit the 'on demand' pillar functionality with a specially crafted git url
run on the master with the same privileges as the master process

patterns.title: Directory traversal in Salt master minion file cache creation
patterns.cause: The master's default cache is vulnerable to a directory traversal attack. Cache file locations can escape the intended cache directory, so cache files can be written or overwritten outside of it.
preconditions: Salt master uses its default cache for minion file cache creation
A path or name used to build a cache file location can be influenced so that it leaves the cache directory
patterns.prevention: Before creating or writing any cache file, resolve the final target location (for example with os.path.realpath()) and confirm it stays inside the configured cache directory. Reject any request whose resolved target falls outside it. Also upgrade Salt to a release that includes the fix referenced in the advisory.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say the default cache allows writes or overwrites outside the cache directory. They do not name the vulnerable function, the input that is controlled, the affected versions, or the exact fix. The containment check described here is a general direction, not the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A cache entry name containing parent-directory segments is joined to the cache directory, and the master writes the file at a location outside that directory, overwriting an existing file.
The master resolves the full target path, sees it falls outside the cache directory, refuses the write, and leaves all files outside the cache directory unchanged.

citations.quote: The master's default cache is vulnerable to a directory traversal attack.
Which could be leveraged to write or overwrite 'cache' files outside of the cache directory.

patterns.title: Unvalidated tgt_env used to build a path in the Salt GitFS find_file method
patterns.cause: In the find_file method of the GitFS class, a filesystem path is built with os.path.join from the tgt_env variable without validating it. Because the input is unvalidated, an attacker can influence where the path points.
preconditions: The Salt Master uses the GitFS class and reaches its find_file method.
The tgt_env value comes from input that the code does not validate.
The Master process has permissions on the target files or directories.
patterns.prevention: Treat tgt_env as untrusted and validate it before it is used in any path construction. Reject values that are not acceptable environment names, instead of passing them to os.path.join. Apply the same check anywhere else this value feeds a filesystem path.
patterns.limitations: The sources only name the find_file method of GitFS and the tgt_env variable. They do not describe the upstream fix, the affected or patched versions, how an attacker supplies tgt_env, or whether other code paths are affected. This card therefore gives no specific validation rule beyond validating the input before it is used in a path.

fixtures.scenario: An attacker-influenced tgt_env value reaches find_file in GitFS and is joined into a filesystem path with os.path.join without validation. The Master can then create directories or delete files outside the intended location, limited only by its own permissions.

The tgt_env value is validated before find_file uses it to build a path. A value that is not an acceptable environment name is rejected, so no path is built from it and no directory is created or file deleted.

citations.quote: In the find_file method of the GitFS class, a path is created using os.path.join using unvalidated input
This can be exploited by an attacker to delete any file on the Master's process has permissions to.

patterns.title: Remote model checkpoints loaded with torch.load and default pickle settings allow code execution (CVE-2025-24357)
patterns.cause: The checkpoint iterator in vllm/model_executor/weight_utils.py, hf_model_weights_iterator, loads model files downloaded from Hugging Face by calling torch.load with the weights_only parameter left at its default value of False. In that mode, torch.load unpickles the file, and a malicious pickle can run arbitrary code during unpickling.
preconditions: The application loads a model checkpoint fetched from a remote repository that the operator does not fully control.
The checkpoint is in a pickle-based format that goes through torch.load rather than the safetensors format.
torch.load is called with the weights_only parameter at its default value of False.
The vllm version in use is older than v0.7.0.
patterns.prevention: Treat downloaded model checkpoints as untrusted input. Prefer the safetensors format, which the advisory says is not vulnerable to this issue. When a pickle-based checkpoint must be loaded, do not call torch.load with its default unrestricted behavior. Enable the restricted loading option and consult the PyTorch documentation warning on torch.load. Only fetch weights from repositories you trust. Upgrade vllm to v0.7.0 or later, where the issue is fixed.
patterns.limitations: The sources state that the fix landed in v0.7.0 but do not describe what the change does. They do not say whether the restricted loading option alone is sufficient, whether pickle checkpoints are still accepted after the fix, or which other loading paths in vllm may call torch.load. They also give no guidance on verifying repository provenance. This card does not claim that any specific torch.load configuration is fully safe.

fixtures.scenario: A service downloads a model repository from a public hub that ships a pickle-based checkpoint. The loader opens it with torch.load using the default weights_only setting. A tampered checkpoint contains a payload that runs an operating system command on the host while the file is being unpickled.

The same service loads weights from a repository that provides safetensors files, or it loads pickle-based files only with the restricted loading option enabled and from a trusted source. It runs vllm v0.7.0 or later, so a tampered checkpoint does not get arbitrary code run during loading.

citations.quote: It use torch.load function and weights_only parameter is default value False.
when torch.load load a malicious pickle data it will execute arbitrary code during unpickling.
Note that most models now use the safetensors format, which is not vulnerable to this issue.
This vulnerability is fixed in v0.7.0.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through user-uploaded images in CKAN group, organization and user profiles
patterns.cause: CKAN accepted user-supplied files for group, organization and user profile images. A specially crafted file could contain code that runs when the file is opened. The code could then send arbitrary requests to the server.
preconditions: CKAN version earlier than 2.10.7 (2.10 line) or 2.11.2 (2.11 line)
The attacker is a registered user of the site
File uploads for user or group images are enabled and the allowed types are not restricted
An administrator opens the crafted file
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to CKAN 2.10.7 or 2.11.2 or later. If an immediate upgrade is not possible, restrict the file types accepted for user and group uploads using the ckan.upload.user.mimetypes, ckan.upload.user.types, ckan.upload.group.mimetypes and ckan.upload.group.types options. Sites that do not need uploads can disable user uploads entirely by setting the user types option to none. In general, accept only the image types a profile or group image needs, and treat uploaded files as untrusted content that must not run code when opened.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the code change in the fixed releases, which file types or formats carry the payload, or how uploaded files are served to the browser. The configuration restrictions are a workaround for older versions and are not shown to be equivalent to the patch. The sources do not say whether the workaround covers every upload path.

fixtures.scenario: A registered user uploads a specially crafted file as a group, organization or user profile image on CKAN older than 2.10.7 or 2.11.2. An administrator later opens it and the embedded code sends requests to the server.
The site runs CKAN 2.10.7 or 2.11.2 or later, or limits the allowed user and group upload types, or disables uploads, so the crafted file is not a usable attack vector.

citations.quote: Using a specially crafted file, a user could potentially upload a file containing code that when executed could send arbitrary requests to the server.
If that file was opened by an administrator, it could lead to escalation of privileges of the original submitter or other malicious actions.
This vulnerability has been fixed in CKAN 2.10.7 and 2.11.2
site maintainers can restrict the file types supported for uploading

patterns.title: Reflected XSS from unsanitized label config task data rendered on a GET example endpoint
patterns.cause: The upload-example endpoint accepted a label_config query parameter on a GET request. A specially formatted XML label config could carry inline task data containing HTML or JavaScript. The endpoint rendered that user-provided HTML without proper sanitization, so script ran in the victim's browser when they visited a crafted URL.
preconditions: An endpoint accepts a label configuration from a GET query parameter
Inline task data inside the config is rendered as HTML without sanitization
The victim can be persuaded to open an attacker-crafted URL
The Content Security Policy is only in report-only mode, so it does not block script execution
patterns.prevention: Do not render user-supplied HTML from request parameters without sanitizing it. Treat inline task data inside a label config as untrusted and sanitize or escape it before it reaches the page. Avoid exposing this behavior on a GET request; the advisory suggests deprecating the GET behavior at the example-config endpoint since it is not used. As defense in depth, run the Content Security Policy in enforcement mode instead of report-only mode so unauthorized script is actively blocked. The fix is reported in version 1.16.0.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact sanitization method used in the patch, which components were changed, or whether other endpoints that render task data are affected. A Content Security Policy in enforcement mode is listed as a mitigation, but the sources do not say it fully prevents the issue or what policy would be needed. They also do not say whether the GET behavior was removed or only sanitized in version 1.16.0.

fixtures.scenario: A user opens a link to the upload-example endpoint whose label_config query parameter holds an XML config with inline task data containing an image element with an error event handler. The page renders that HTML unsanitized, the handler runs, and attacker JavaScript executes in the victim's session.

The same link is opened, but inline task data from the label config is sanitized or escaped before rendering, and the Content Security Policy is enforced. The markup appears as inert content or is stripped, and no script runs.

citations.quote: the upload-example endpoint renders user-provided HTML content without proper sanitization on a GET request
Enable the Content Security Policy in enforcement mode instead of report-only mode to actively block unauthorized script execution
Deprecate the `GET` behavior at the `example-config` endpoint since it's not used
Version 1.16.0 contains a patch for the issue.

patterns.title: SSRF through user-supplied S3 endpoint URL in storage connections
patterns.cause: The S3 storage feature lets users set a custom endpoint URL, which is passed directly to the boto3 AWS SDK with no validation or restrictions on protocol or destination. The server then sends requests to whatever host the user chose, and error messages from failed requests include the full response body.
preconditions: The attacker is an authenticated user who can create an S3 storage connection
The custom S3 endpoint URL is accepted without validation of protocol or destination
A storage sync is triggered so the server makes calls to the chosen endpoint
Error messages from failed requests expose the response body to the user
patterns.prevention: Validate the S3 endpoint URL strictly so that only legitimate S3 service endpoints are accepted. Use an allowlist of permitted endpoint domains and protocols rather than accepting arbitrary hosts. Sanitize error messages so failed requests never return response content from the target. Add network-level controls limiting outbound connections from the application server. Upgrading to version 1.16.0 or later applies the vendor patch.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact validation rules in the patched release, nor how redirects, hostname resolution changes, or alternate address encodings are handled. The listed mitigations are general recommendations and may not cover every bypass. Legitimate self-hosted S3-compatible endpoints may need explicit allowlisting.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user creates an S3 storage connection whose custom endpoint points at an internal web service over plain HTTP, then triggers sync. The server calls that host, and the resulting S3 parsing error echoes the internal response body.

The endpoint is checked against an allowlist of approved domains and protocols before use. An internal hostname is rejected when the connection is created, and sync failures return a generic message without any response body.

citations.quote: This endpoint URL is passed directly to the boto3 AWS SDK without proper validation or restrictions on the protocol or destination.
error messages from failed requests contain the full response body, allowing data exfiltration from internal services.
Add an allowlist of endpoint domains and protocols

patterns.title: Unsafe pickle deserialization of HTTP request payloads in BentoML serde
patterns.cause: In BentoML 1.4.2, the deserialization routine in serde.py passes payload bytes to pickle loading when the payload metadata has no buffer-lengths entry. The payload comes from an HTTP request the client fully controls, and nothing validates it first. Crafted serialized data therefore runs code on the server during deserialization, with no authentication needed.
preconditions: A BentoML service version 1.4.2 or earlier is reachable over HTTP by the attacker
The request body is turned into a payload object that the serde deserialization routine handles
The payload metadata lacks a buffer-lengths entry, so the pickle loading path is taken
The request declares the BentoML pickle content type
patterns.prevention: Never pass bytes taken from a network request to a pickle-style deserializer. Treat the request body and its declared content type as untrusted, and do not select a code-executing deserialization path based on client-supplied metadata. Accept only data-only formats with explicit validation on network-facing endpoints. Upgrade to BentoML 1.4.3 or later, where the vulnerability is reported fixed.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how version 1.4.3 changes the code, so this card does not claim which formats or checks the fix uses. They also do not describe the code path taken when buffer-lengths metadata is present, nor other entry points that might reach deserialization. The proof of concept covers one API endpoint only.

fixtures.scenario: A BentoML 1.4.2 service listens on port 3000. An unauthenticated client posts a crafted pickle body with the BentoML pickle content type, and the server unpickles it, running attacker-chosen code.
The service runs BentoML 1.4.3 or later, and request bodies are never fed to a pickle loader. A crafted pickle body is rejected or parsed only as plain validated data, so no attacker code runs.

citations.quote: It allows any unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the server.
Due to the lack of validation in the code, maliciously crafted serialized data can execute harmful actions during deserialization.
This vulnerability is fixed in 1.4.3.

patterns.title: SSRF in langchain-community RequestsToolkit from unrestricted request destinations
patterns.cause: The RequestsToolkit component (langchain_community.agent_toolkits.openapi.toolkit.RequestsToolkit) did not enforce restrictions on which addresses it could send requests to. A toolkit meant to reach remote internet addresses could also reach local addresses.
preconditions: The application uses RequestsToolkit from the langchain-community package, reported as affected in version 0.0.27.
The toolkit issues outbound requests without any restriction on the destination address.
An attacker can influence which address the toolkit requests.
Local services, cloud instance metadata endpoints, or other internal hosts are reachable from the host running the toolkit.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade langchain-community to version 0.0.28 or later, where the sources say the issue is fixed. In any code that issues requests on behalf of untrusted input, restrict destinations so that only intended remote internet addresses are allowed and local or internal addresses are refused. Apply the restriction at the point where the request is made, not only to the text that was supplied.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how version 0.0.28 implements the fix. They do not say which address ranges are blocked, whether an allowlist or denylist is used, or whether redirects and DNS resolution are covered. They also do not state how an attacker supplies the target address. Verify those details against the released code and test them yourself. Network-level egress controls are not discussed in the sources.

fixtures.scenario: An agent built with RequestsToolkit at version 0.0.27 is asked to fetch a URL chosen by an untrusted user. The URL points at a local service or a cloud instance metadata endpoint, and the toolkit sends the request and returns the response.
The same agent runs on langchain-community 0.0.28 or later. A request aimed at a local or internal address is refused, and only requests to intended remote internet addresses go through.

citations.quote: the toolkit does not enforce restrictions on requests to remote internet addresses, allowing it to also access local addresses.
an attacker could exploit this flaw to perform port scans, access local services, retrieve instance metadata from cloud environments
This issue has been fixed in version 0.0.28.

patterns.title: Untrusted network bytes passed to pickle in the vLLM Mooncake KV transfer pipe
patterns.cause: When vLLM is configured to use Mooncake for disaggregated KV transfer, the receive path in the Mooncake pipe takes raw bytes from a ZMQ/TCP connection and hands them directly to pickle.loads(). Pickle deserialization can run attacker-chosen code, so whoever can deliver bytes to that path can execute code on the distributed host.
preconditions: vLLM is configured to use Mooncake to distribute KV across distributed hosts.
The Mooncake pipe receives data over ZMQ/TCP, which is exposed over the network by design to enable disaggregated prefilling.
The received bytes are deserialized with pickle without validation.
No network or authentication controls stop arbitrary senders from reaching the affected service.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade vLLM to version 0.8.0 or later, where the issue is fixed (see pull request 14228). More generally, an implementation should never pass bytes read from a network socket to pickle.loads(). Data arriving from other hosts must be treated as untrusted, even when the transport is intended only for cluster-internal use.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so this card does not prescribe a specific replacement format. The advisory also gives conflicting information on exposure: one passage is struck through (claiming the sockets listen on all interfaces), while the CVE text still says all network interfaces. The advisory says only the sender socket and the receiver ack socket are publicly accessible, and that the pickled data comes from the receive path using a locally configured decode host address. The sources do not say whether network restrictions alone would be adequate mitigation.

fixtures.scenario: A vLLM deployment on a version before 0.8.0 uses Mooncake for disaggregated prefilling across hosts. The receive routine reads raw bytes from the ZMQ/TCP link and deserializes them with pickle. A party who can send a crafted payload to the service gets code execution on the decode host.

A vLLM deployment runs version 0.8.0 or later, which contains the fix for this issue. Bytes received from other hosts are never passed to pickle.loads(), so a crafted payload cannot trigger code execution through the Mooncake pipe.

citations.quote: unsafe deserialization exposed directly over ZMQ/TCP on all network interfaces will allow attackers to execute remote code on distributed hosts
Additionally, it does not appear that there are any controls (network, authentication, etc) to prevent arbitrary users from sending this payload
This vulnerability is fixed in 0.8.0.

patterns.title: Symlinks in an Obsidian vault let the reader open files outside the vault
patterns.cause: The ObsidianReader in LlamaIndex did not resolve symbolic links to their real paths and did not check whether the resolved paths were inside the intended vault directory. A symlink in the vault that pointed elsewhere was therefore treated as an ordinary Markdown file and read.
preconditions: The application uses the ObsidianReader from the LlamaIndex Obsidian reader integration. The sources name versions 0.12.23 to 0.12.28 of the repository and a fixed reader release of 0.5.1.
An attacker can place symbolic links inside the vault directory that is being read.
The symlinks point to files outside the vault directory, and the reader processes them as valid Markdown files.
patterns.prevention: Before reading any entry found while walking a vault, resolve it to its real path so symlinks are followed to their actual target. Then confirm that the resolved path lies within the resolved vault root, and skip or reject any entry that does not. Make this containment check on the resolved path rather than on the name as listed. Upgrade to a fixed release of the Obsidian reader integration (0.5.1 or later, per the advisory).
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the flaw and the affected versions but not how the upstream fix works, so this card gives only the general direction. They do not say whether other readers or loaders in the project have the same weakness. They do not cover platform-specific link types or how vault contents are stored. They do not discuss concurrent changes to the vault between the check and the read. The impact is described only as potentially exposing sensitive information.

fixtures.scenario: A vault directory contains a note whose name ends in the Markdown extension but is really a symbolic link to a sensitive file outside the vault. The reader lists the entry, does not resolve it, and loads the external file's contents as if it were a note.

The same vault is loaded, but each entry is resolved to its real path and compared against the real path of the vault root. The symlinked entry resolves outside the vault, so it is skipped or rejected and its contents are never loaded. Regular notes inside the vault are still read.

citations.quote: fails to resolve symlinks to their real paths and does not validate whether the resolved paths lie within the intended directory
This flaw enables attackers to place symlinks pointing to files outside the vault directory, which are then processed as valid Markdown files

patterns.title: Billion laughs XML entity expansion in the llama-index sitemap parser (CVE-2025-3225)
patterns.cause: The sitemap parser in the run-llama/llama_index repository, affecting the Papers Loaders package before version 0.3.2, is vulnerable to XML entity expansion, also called a billion laughs attack. A malicious Sitemap XML can make it consume excessive system memory.
preconditions: The application uses an affected release: the Papers Loaders package before version 0.3.2, or llama-index from v0.10.0 through v0.12.29.
The application parses a Sitemap XML document through the llama-index sitemap parser.
An attacker can supply or influence the Sitemap XML that gets parsed.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to the fixed releases: Papers Loaders 0.3.2, which ships with llama-index 0.12.29. Until the upgrade is done, treat any Sitemap XML from a source you do not control as hostile input to the sitemap parser.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so this card cannot say which parser setting or code path was changed. They do not say whether other XML parsing paths in llama-index are affected. The advisories differ on versions: some name v0.12.21 and others give a range from v0.10.0 through v0.12.29. Confirm your exact version against the advisory. The stated impact is denial of service by memory exhaustion, and no other impact is claimed.

fixtures.scenario: A service built on an affected llama-index release loads a sitemap from a URL an outside party controls. The document is a billion laughs payload, so parsing exhausts system memory and may crash the host.

The same service runs Papers Loaders 0.3.2 or later, which ships with llama-index 0.12.29 or later. It loads the same hostile sitemap and does not suffer the memory exhaustion described in the advisories.

citations.quote: allows an attacker to supply a malicious Sitemap XML, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) by exhausting system memory
specifically affecting the Papers Loaders package before version 0.3.2 (in llama-index v0.10.0 and above through v0.12.29)
The issue is resolved in version 0.3.2 (in llama-index 0.12.29).

patterns.title: Pickle-based ZeroMQ receive on exposed sockets in vLLM Mooncake integration allows remote code execution
patterns.cause: The vLLM Mooncake integration exchanged data using pickle based serialization over unsecured ZeroMQ sockets. The advisory says the receive call recv_pyobj() contains an implicit pickle.loads(), so bytes from any peer that reaches the socket are deserialized as objects. The sockets were also set to listen on all network interfaces, which made them easier for an attacker to reach.
preconditions: vLLM version from 0.6.5 up to but not including 0.8.5
The Mooncake integration is in use; instances that do not use it are not vulnerable
The ZeroMQ sockets use pickle based serialization with no security on the channel
An attacker can reach the sockets over the network, which is more likely because they listen on all interfaces
patterns.prevention: Never deserialize network input with pickle. Do not use socket helpers that implicitly unpickle, such as recv_pyobj(), on any socket a peer outside the trust boundary could reach. Exchange data in a plain data-only format and validate it on receipt. Bind sockets only to the interface that is actually needed rather than all interfaces. Upgrade vLLM to 0.8.5 or later, or disable the Mooncake integration if it is not required.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change, so they do not say which serialization format or binding policy replaced the old behavior. They do not say whether authentication or encryption was added to the sockets. They only confirm that version 0.8.5 patches the issue. Narrowing the bind interface reduces exposure but does not make unpickling untrusted data safe.

fixtures.scenario: A vLLM 0.8.4 deployment enables the Mooncake integration. Its ZeroMQ sockets listen on all interfaces and read incoming messages with recv_pyobj(). A host on the same network sends a crafted pickle payload, which is deserialized and runs attacker code.

A vLLM deployment runs 0.8.5 or later, or does not enable the Mooncake integration. Any socket that carries data between hosts accepts only a data-only format that is validated on receipt, and it is not bound to all interfaces.

citations.quote: vulnerable to remote code execution due to using pickle based serialization over unsecured ZeroMQ sockets.
The vulnerable sockets were set to listen on all network interfaces
vLLM instances that do not make use of the mooncake integration are not vulnerable.

patterns.title: ReDoS from backtracking-prone regular expression in transformers chat command
patterns.cause: The SETTING_RE pattern in transformers/commands/chat.py contains repetition groups and non-optimized quantifiers. Input that almost matches the pattern makes the regex engine backtrack exponentially, which consumes CPU time and can degrade or deny service.
preconditions: The deployment uses huggingface/transformers version 4.49.0, the version named in the advisories.
Input strings reach the SETTING_RE pattern in the chat command module.
An attacker can supply specially crafted strings that almost match the pattern.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade transformers to version 4.51.0 or later, where the issue is fixed. When writing or reviewing similar patterns, avoid repetition groups combined with non-optimized quantifiers, because these allow exponential backtracking on almost-matching input. Test such patterns against near-miss payloads, not only valid input, and treat any text from users as untrusted before it reaches a backtracking regex engine.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the code change in the fix, the exact shape of the pattern, or how much input is needed to cause a noticeable slowdown. They also do not say how remote an attacker's access to the chat command is, or whether other patterns in the library are affected. Only version 4.49.0 is named as vulnerable, so the full range of affected versions is unclear.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs transformers 4.49.0 and passes user-supplied text to the chat command's settings parsing. A user sends a long string that almost matches the expected settings format. The regex engine backtracks exponentially and the process stalls on CPU, degrading the application for other users.
A service runs transformers 4.51.0 or later, which contains the fix. The same near-miss string is handled without exponential backtracking, and the application stays responsive.

citations.quote: The regex contains repetition groups and non-optimized quantifiers, leading to exponential backtracking when processing 'almost matching' payloads.
This can degrade application performance and potentially result in a denial-of-service (DoS) when handling specially crafted input strings.
The issue is fixed in version 4.51.0.

patterns.title: Catastrophic regex backtracking in Transformers get_configuration_file
patterns.cause: The get_configuration_file() function in transformers.configuration_utils uses a regular expression with an unbounded wildcard between a config prefix and a json suffix. Crafted input strings can force catastrophic backtracking and excessive CPU consumption.
preconditions: The application uses the Hugging Face Transformers library at version 4.49.0, the version named as affected.
The get_configuration_file() function in transformers.configuration_utils is reached during configuration lookup.
An attacker can influence the strings that this matching is applied to, though the sources do not say exactly which inputs are attacker-reachable.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Transformers to version 4.51.0 or later, where the issue is reported as resolved. When writing similar matching logic, avoid patterns that put an unbounded wildcard between fixed literal parts and run them on untrusted strings. Instead, use a narrow, explicit match for the expected file name shape, or non-regex string handling. Where inputs come from outside the trust boundary, also limit their length and treat unexpected names as invalid.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix changed the matching logic, so the exact replacement approach is not stated here. They also do not give the input lengths or shapes that trigger the worst case, or the routes by which untrusted strings reach the function. Only version 4.49.0 is named as affected, and versions before it are not addressed.

fixtures.scenario: A model serving application runs Transformers 4.49.0 and passes externally influenced file name strings through configuration lookup. A crafted string makes the matching consume excessive CPU, which raises latency and disrupts serving for other requests.
The same application runs Transformers 4.51.0 or later. Crafted configuration-related strings no longer cause catastrophic backtracking, so CPU use and latency stay normal.

citations.quote: The affected version is 4.49.0, and the issue is resolved in version 4.51.0.
can be exploited to cause excessive CPU consumption through crafted input strings, leading to catastrophic backtracking.
This can result in model serving disruption, resource exhaustion, and increased latency in applications using the library.

patterns.title: ReDoS in get_imports() when filtering try/except blocks from loaded module source
patterns.cause: The get_imports() function in dynamic_module_utils.py in Hugging Face Transformers used a regular expression to filter out try/except blocks from Python code. The pattern matches a try keyword and colon, then lazily consumes arbitrary text up to an except keyword and colon. Crafted input strings trigger catastrophic backtracking and excessive CPU consumption.
preconditions: Transformers version 4.49.0 is in use, which is the affected version named in the advisories
get_imports() processes Python source text that an attacker can influence, such as code for a remotely loaded model
The try/except filtering regular expression runs on that text without any bound on matching effort
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Transformers to version 4.51.0 or later, where the issue is fixed. In your own code, do not use regular expressions with lazy, unbounded wildcards to strip or detect structured constructs such as try/except blocks in untrusted text. Prefer a method whose running time grows linearly with input size. Treat dynamically loaded code as untrusted when it is analyzed.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix changed the code, so this card does not say which replacement technique was used. They also do not give input sizes or timings that trigger the slowdown, or say whether versions before 4.49.0 are affected. Impact is described only in general terms.

fixtures.scenario: A service loads a model repository with custom code. Its import scanner applies a regex with lazy wildcards between try and except to a crafted file, backtracks catastrophically, and pins a CPU core.
The service runs Transformers 4.51.0 or later. Its import scanner handles the same crafted file in time proportional to its size, so loading finishes and the service stays responsive.

citations.quote: can be exploited to cause excessive CPU consumption through crafted input strings due to catastrophic backtracking.
This vulnerability affects versions 4.49.0 and is fixed in version 4.51.0.

patterns.title: Open redirect in Flask-AppBuilder via Host header manipulation
patterns.cause: Flask-AppBuilder versions before 4.6.2 let an unauthenticated actor trigger an open redirect by manipulating the Host header of an HTTP request. The Host value supplied by the client could therefore influence where the application redirected the user, and no explicit list of safe redirect domains was available to restrict it.
preconditions: The application runs a Flask-AppBuilder version earlier than 4.6.2.
An attacker can send HTTP requests with a manipulated Host header; no authentication is needed.
No reverse proxy or other layer enforces trusted Host header values in front of the application.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Flask-AppBuilder 4.6.2 or later. Then set the FAB_SAFE_REDIRECT_HOSTS configuration variable so that only domains the administrator explicitly lists, including subdomain patterns if needed, are accepted as redirect targets. As a workaround or defense in depth, put a reverse proxy in front of the application that enforces trusted Host header values and rejects requests carrying any other host. In general, never derive a redirect destination from a client-controlled Host header without checking it against an explicit allowlist.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which endpoints or login flows are affected, how the Host header reaches the redirect logic, or how the allowlist is matched internally. They also do not describe the behavior when the allowlist is left unset. The reverse proxy workaround is named without configuration detail. Check the vendor release notes and the fix commit for exact behavior before relying on this card.
