patterns.prevention: Evaluate the URL scheme on the decoded form of the URL, so percent-encoded characters in the scheme cannot hide a harmful protocol from the check. Upgrade to Mistune 3.3.0 or later, which is reported as fixed. Until then, add application-level URL sanitization that decodes before checking.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how version 3.3.0 changes the check. They do not say whether other encodings, such as double encoding or entity encoding, are handled. They also do not state whether image URLs and link URLs are covered identically beyond a brief mention of both.

fixtures.scenario: A comment system renders user Markdown with Mistune 3.2.0. An attacker posts a link whose target starts with the word javascript followed by a percent-encoded colon. The filter misses it, and a viewer who clicks it runs script.
The same system runs Mistune 3.3.0 or later. The same link target is neutralized, or the check decodes the URL before testing the scheme, so clicking the link does not run script.

citations.quote: However, the input URL is not URL-decoded before this check.
When rendered in a browser, the URL is decoded, resulting in execution of arbitrary JavaScript upon user interaction.
Prior to 3.3.0, HTMLRenderer.safe_url() does not block percent-encoded javascript URIs, allowing attacker-supplied Markdown links or images to bypass URL protections

patterns.title: Path traversal in mistune Include directive when reading markdown files
patterns.cause: In versions before 3.3.0, Include.parse() joins a user-supplied include path to the directory of the source markdown file and normalizes it. It never checks that the result stays inside an intended directory. Traversal sequences such as parent-directory segments can therefore point at files outside that location.
preconditions: The application uses mistune before version 3.3.0.
The Include directive is enabled, for example through the RST directive plugin.
Markdown files are processed with md.read(), so include paths are resolved relative to the source file.
The markdown content, and therefore the include path, can be influenced by an untrusted party.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to mistune 3.3.0 or later. In any code that resolves include paths, convert the final path to its resolved form, for example with os.path.realpath(). Compare it against a trusted base directory and refuse to open it if it falls outside. Do this check before opening the file. If untrusted markdown is processed, consider leaving the Include directive disabled.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream fix or how it treats symbolic links. They do not say which base directory the fix enforces, or whether other directives or code paths are affected. Impact depends on how the feature is used and which files the process can read.

fixtures.scenario: A markdown file contains an include directive whose path climbs several parent directories to reach a file outside the content folder. It is processed with md.read() on mistune before 3.3.0, and the outside file is read.

The same markdown file is processed on a version with the fix, or with path validation. The resolved include path falls outside the allowed directory, so the request is rejected and the file is not opened.

citations.quote: Include.parse() joins and normalizes user-supplied include paths without verifying that the result remains within the intended markdown directory
Validate the resolved path and ensure it remains within an allowed directory before opening the file.
This issue is fixed in version 3.3.0.

patterns.title: Quadratic emphasis parsing in mistune inline parser on long runs of strong-emphasis pairs
patterns.cause: The inline parser treats every opening run of one to three asterisks as a possible start and scans forward for a matching close marker from each one. Each scan is bounded per call, but the scan is repeated from every potential start position. A long input of many well-formed double-asterisk or triple-asterisk pairs therefore costs quadratic work, even in the default configuration with no plugins.
preconditions: The application uses a mistune version prior to 3.3.0 to render markdown.
The markdown comes from an untrusted party, such as a network user who needs no authentication.
The input contains a long sequence of well-formed double-asterisk or triple-asterisk emphasis pairs around a character.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mistune to 3.3.0 or later, which the advisories list as the fixed version. When writing or reviewing an inline parser, do not rescan forward to the end of the input from every opening marker. Process delimiters in a single pass with a delimiter stack, as CommonMark reference implementations do, so each marker is handled a bounded number of times. The advisory also suggests, as a weaker alternative, capping how many unmatched opening markers are tracked at once and treating the rest as literal text. Add a regression test that renders a very large run of emphasis pairs and checks that it finishes quickly.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe what the 3.3.0 change actually does, so this card does not claim a specific upstream approach. The cap on open markers is only a suggestion in the advisory, and its effect on rendering of real documents is not verified here. The reported timings come from one PoC on one machine and version, and the sources give no safe input size limit. Related bracket and formatting-plugin denial-of-service reports are mentioned but not detailed.

fixtures.scenario: A comment service renders user markdown with default mistune before 3.3.0. An attacker posts about 40 KB made of thousands of short strong-emphasis pairs, and one request keeps a worker busy for several seconds.
The service runs mistune 3.3.0 or later. The same large input of repeated emphasis pairs renders in time roughly proportional to its size, and a regression test guards this.

citations.quote: long sequences of well-formed double-asterisk or triple-asterisk emphasis pairs around a character cause quadratic work
Each scan is bounded per call, but the parser invokes the scan from every potential start position.
The CommonMark reference parser handles emphasis in linear time using a delimiter-stack algorithm

patterns.title: Attribute injection XSS via unescaped class option in mistune Admonition directive
patterns.cause: The render_admonition() function in the Admonition directive concatenates the user-supplied class option directly into the HTML class attribute without escaping. The option comes from raw user input, so it can break out of the attribute and inject new attributes or script.
preconditions: The application uses a mistune version prior to 3.2.1
The Admonition directive is enabled in the Markdown renderer
Untrusted users can author Markdown containing the class option on an admonition
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mistune to version 3.2.1 or later. In an implementation, treat the class option as untrusted input and escape it for the HTML attribute context before placing it in the class attribute, or validate it against a strict allowlist of class names. Do not assume that enabling escape mode on the HTML renderer covers directive options, because it does not.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact fix, the full set of directives or options that may be affected, or which characters are accepted in the class option. They state only that the directive name is validated against a whitelist. Whether other directives handle options safely is not covered.

fixtures.scenario: A site renders user Markdown with an old mistune and the Admonition directive. An author supplies a class option containing a quote that closes the attribute and adds an event handler, and it appears in the output HTML despite escape mode.

The site runs mistune 3.2.1 or later, so the class option is escaped before it enters the class attribute. A quote in the option cannot close the attribute, and no injected attribute or script reaches the page.

citations.quote: concatenates the `:class:` option directly into the HTML class attribute without escaping
This allows attribute injection and XSS even when `HTMLRenderer(escape=True)` is used.
This issue is fixed in version 3.2.1.

patterns.title: Quadratic parse time from many reference-link definitions in mistune
patterns.cause: The block parser handles each reference-link definition by scanning forward from each candidate position and revisiting the stored definition list while it decides between paragraph and definition. The advisory reports that total work grows with the square of the number of definitions, even though the label lookup dictionary itself is constant time.
preconditions: The application uses a mistune version before 3.3.0.
The application renders attacker-supplied Markdown, and the advisory reports the default create_markdown() configuration is enough with no plugins.
The attacker can submit a document with thousands of repeated or distinct reference-link definitions.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mistune to 3.3.0 or later, where the issue is reported fixed. An implementation should avoid rescanning the definition list for every definition. It should classify each line once and record each definition once, so total work stays linear in the number of definitions. The advisory says the patched build keeps parse time linear.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change, so this card gives only the direction. They do not cover other mitigations such as input size caps or timeouts, and they report timings only for one test setup on version 3.2.1. They also do not say whether versions earlier than 3.2.1 are affected beyond the statement that all versions before 3.3.0 are.

fixtures.scenario: An application renders attacker-supplied Markdown with default mistune create_markdown() on a version before 3.3.0. A document of thousands of short repeated reference definitions followed by one reference link pegs the CPU for seconds.

The same application runs mistune 3.3.0 or later. The same document of repeated definitions is parsed in time that grows linearly with the number of definitions, so doubling the input roughly doubles the time.

citations.quote: Prior to 3.3.0, a Markdown document containing many repeated or distinct reference-link definitions causes quadratic work
Doubling input quadruples time.
The patched build (with the surrounding parser amortised to O(N)) keeps the time linear.

patterns.title: Mistune safe_url denylist lets legacy and chained URL schemes reach href and src
patterns.cause: The safe_url filter in the mistune HTML renderer blocks only four schemes: javascript:, vbscript:, file: and data:. Legacy or chained schemes such as feed:, view-source:, jar:, livescript:, mocha:, ms-its:, mk: and res: pass through unchanged into rendered href and src attributes. The root cause is that a short fixed denylist cannot cover the open-ended set of schemes a user agent might honour. Some of these schemes execute script directly, and others wrap a javascript: payload.
preconditions: The application renders attacker-influenced Markdown with a mistune version earlier than 3.3.0.
The link or image target uses one of the unlisted legacy or chained schemes, through a direct link, reference link, autolink or image.
A victim's user agent still recognises that scheme, for example an older Firefox build, Edge Legacy, an in-app WebView, or a browser with a custom protocol handler.
The caller has not disabled filtering, and no other control rewrites or rejects the URL.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to mistune 3.3.0 or later, where the issue is fixed. For custom URL handling, replace the denylist with an allowlist. Allow only the few schemes a Markdown renderer really needs, such as http, https and mailto, plus fragment-only and relative references and a small set of image-only data types. Replace every other target with an inert placeholder. Normalise case and leading whitespace before comparing, and apply the same check to direct links, reference links, autolinks and image sources. Require callers to opt in explicitly to any extra scheme.
patterns.limitations: The sources confirm the fix version but do not describe how 3.3.0 implements it, so the allowlist contents here are only the direction suggested in the advisory. Exploitability depends on the user agent, and modern Chrome, Chromium Edge and Safari ignore most of these schemes. Callers who opt in to harmful protocols re-open the risk. This card covers URL scheme filtering only and does not address other XSS vectors.

fixtures.scenario: An application renders user-submitted Markdown with mistune before 3.3.0 using default settings. A link whose target begins with feed: followed by javascript: is emitted unchanged into an anchor href, so a legacy browser may run script on click.

The application uses mistune 3.3.0 or later, or a URL check that accepts only listed schemes. The same feed: chained link is not emitted as a live link, while ordinary http, https and mailto links still render normally.

citations.quote: the safe_url filter in src/mistune/renderers/html.py blocks only javascript:, vbscript:, file:, and data: schemes
Switch from denylist to allowlist. The set of schemes a markdown renderer needs to allow is small and well-known
This issue is fixed in version 3.3.0.

patterns.title: Symlink in corpus root bypasses path validation in IPIPANCorpusReader
patterns.cause: Several public reader methods pass fileids to an internal routine that opens the file with the builtin open() on a plain string. A string replace on the path pointer discards the PathPointer wrapper, so nltk.pathsec validation is skipped. A symlink with a plain name, with no separators or parent references, is then opened directly.
preconditions: nltk version before 3.10.2 with IPIPANCorpusReader in use
An attacker can place a symlink inside the corpus root directory, for example in a shared or tampered corpus
The application calls channels(), domains(), categories() or fileids(channels=...) with the symlink filename
The target file is readable by the process
patterns.prevention: Do not hand a plain string derived from a path pointer to the builtin open(). Route file access through nltk.pathsec.validate_path() with the corpus root as the required root, or through CorpusReader.open(), so the symlink target is checked before reading. Avoid string operations on path pointers before validation, since they drop the wrapper. Use nltk 3.10.2 or later, as earlier versions are listed as affected.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how validate_path() evaluates symlinks internally, nor the exact upstream change. Literal parent-directory traversal in a fileid is reported as already blocked, so this is only the symlink case. Impact is read-only, and local symlink placement is required. Other readers are not assessed here beyond the two mentioned as fixed earlier.

fixtures.scenario: A shared corpus directory holds a file named evil_link.xml that is a symlink to a file outside the root. An application on an nltk version before 3.10.2 calls channels() on the IPIPAN reader with that fileid, and the outside file content is returned.

The same directory and symlink exist, but file access goes through validated path handling with the corpus root as the required root, so the symlink pointing outside the root is rejected instead of being read.

citations.quote: Attackers can place a symlink in the corpus root directory and read arbitrary files accessible to the process
Symlink-based arbitrary file read in IPIPANCorpusReader, bypasses nltk.pathsec entirely

patterns.title: Symlink inside FrameNet corpus subdirectory escapes the corpus root in NLTK
patterns.cause: FramenetCorpusReader checks caller- or corpus-supplied names only for literal separators, parent-directory markers and drive prefixes. It then builds the path with a plain lexical join and opens it without a root-scoped, symlink-resolving check. A symlink with a separator-free name passes the name check and is followed to a file outside the corpus root.
preconditions: An attacker can place a symlink inside the frame, lu or fulltext subdirectory of a FrameNet corpus directory, for example a shared or tampered corpus.
The application calls frame_by_name(), _lu_file() or doc() with a name that matches the symlink.
The NLTK version is earlier than 3.10.2.
patterns.prevention: Do not rely on name filtering alone. Resolve the final path, including symlinks, and confirm it stays inside the corpus root before opening it. Open corpus files through the reader's scoped open routine, which does this check, rather than a lexical join followed by a raw pointer open. Upgrade NLTK to 3.10.2 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the fix direction only in general terms. They do not say how the patched release handles symlinks that point to files inside the corpus root, or how it behaves when strict sandbox enforcement is off. The read target is described as XML files, and the sources do not say whether other file types are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A shared FrameNet corpus directory has a symlink in its frame subdirectory pointing to an XML file outside the corpus root. The symlink name has no separators. A routine frame lookup by that name returns the outside file's content.

The same corpus and lookup, but the reader resolves symlinks and checks the result against the corpus root before opening. The lookup is refused because the target lies outside the root, and no outside content is returned.

citations.quote: NLTK versions before 3.10.2 contain a symlink-based sandbox bypass in FramenetCorpusReader that allows attackers to read arbitrary XML files outside the corpus root.
It never resolves symlinks.
A symlink placed inside the corpus's own subdirectory, with a name containing no separators at all, passes the guard cleanly

patterns.title: Corpus-root escape in NLTK FrameNet and NKJP readers via unsafe selectors or index state
patterns.cause: The FrameNet and NKJP corpus readers build XML filenames from caller-controlled selectors (frame names, document filenames, LU ids, NKJP file identifiers) or from index state without keeping the resulting path inside the corpus root. The reader then parses XML located outside the root and returns its content through normal public calls.
preconditions: The application uses an NLTK release before 3.10.0 (version 3.9.4 was reproduced).
The application exposes FramenetCorpusReader frame_by_name, doc or lu, or NKJPCorpusReader header, and relies on NLTK to keep parsing inside the corpus root.
An attacker can influence the selector values or the index state those readers use to build filenames.
An attacker-chosen XML file exists outside the corpus root and is readable by the application.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to NLTK 3.10.0 or later. An implementation avoids the problem by keeping these reader paths on the same root-confinement model as the generic corpus file-opening path, and by rejecting unsafe path components before it builds any filename from a frame name, document filename, LU id or NKJP file identifier. Values read from index files should be treated as untrusted in the same way as caller-supplied selectors, and a rejected value should produce an explicit path-safety error instead of a parse.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not list which path components or patterns the patched release rejects, so this card cannot say how complete that rejection is. Only 3.9.4 was reproduced; the CVE text says versions before 3.10.0 are affected without naming the earliest one. The sources describe only parsing of XML files outside the root and do not discuss other file types. They give no interim mitigation for applications that cannot upgrade.

fixtures.scenario: An application on NLTK 3.9.4 passes a user-supplied frame name containing parent-directory segments to the FrameNet frame_by_name method. An XML file placed outside the corpus root is parsed and its definition text is returned to the caller.
The same application runs NLTK 3.10.0 or later. The same frame name, or a poisoned LU id or NKJP file identifier, is rejected with an explicit path-safety error and no outside-root file is parsed.

citations.quote: allows attackers to parse XML files outside the corpus root by supplying unsafe selectors or poisoned index state.
Stable reader paths still construct raw XML filenames from unsafe selectors, poisoned index state, or unsafe file identifiers.
Reject unsafe path components before constructing filenames from frame names, document filenames, LU ids, or NKJP file identifiers.

patterns.title: SSRF URL validation fails open when DNS resolution fails
patterns.cause: The URL validator in nltk/pathsec.py relies on a helper that catches OSError and ValueError during hostname resolution and returns an empty list. The validation loop then has no addresses to check, the function returns normally, and the request proceeds with no IP validation at all.
preconditions: NLTK 3.9.4 or earlier (before 3.10.0) is in use
Network fetches pass through validate_network_url() before urlopen() is called
An attacker can influence the requested URL
The attacker can cause DNS resolution failures or use DNS rebinding
patterns.prevention: Treat an empty resolution result as a validation failure. If no addresses could be resolved and checked, reject the URL with an explicit error instead of returning normally. Never let a request proceed when IP validation was impossible. Move to a release newer than 3.9.4.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the bug and suggest an explicit empty-result check that raises an error. They do not detail how resolved addresses are checked against blocked ranges, and they do not say how the gap between validation and the actual request is closed. Failing closed on empty results may not by itself stop DNS rebinding, which the sources link to cache expiry.

fixtures.scenario: The DNS lookup for the host of a user-supplied URL raises an error, the helper returns an empty list, and the validator returns normally. The request to a cloud metadata address such as 169.254.169.254 then goes ahead unchecked.
When the lookup yields no addresses, the validator raises an error and the URL is rejected before any request is made. Only URLs whose resolved addresses were all checked are fetched.

citations.quote: when DNS resolution fails, the validation loop executes no IP checks and the function fails open
The correct behavior is fail-closed: if DNS resolution fails, the URL should be REJECTED (not allowed).
Never allow a URL request to proceed when IP validation was impossible.

patterns.title: NLTK StreamBackedCorpusView skips pathsec.ENFORCE path validation
patterns.cause: StreamBackedCorpusView opens and stats string file paths directly with the builtin open and os.stat calls. It never goes through the pathsec validation wrapper. Setting pathsec.ENFORCE to true therefore does not restrict reads made through this class. XMLCorpusView and corpus reader subclasses that pass a raw string fileid to it are also affected.
preconditions: NLTK version earlier than 3.10.0 is in use
An attacker can influence the fileid string passed to StreamBackedCorpusView or a corpus reader built on it
The operator relies on pathsec.ENFORCE as the control that limits file access to allowed NLTK data directories
patterns.prevention: Upgrade NLTK to 3.10.0 or later. In custom code, do not pass untrusted strings as fileid to corpus views or readers. Map user input to a fixed allowlist of known corpus file identifiers instead. Any code path that opens or stats a user-influenced path should go through the same pathsec validation as other NLTK file access, and should not call the builtin open directly. Do not treat pathsec.ENFORCE as a guarantee for corpus readers on affected versions.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change or list every reader class affected beyond XMLCorpusView and subclasses that pass a raw string fileid. They do not say whether non-string fileids are safe. Check the vendor release notes for 3.10.0 before relying on this card for full coverage.

fixtures.scenario: A web service sets pathsec.ENFORCE to true, then builds a StreamBackedCorpusView from a file name taken from a JSON request body. A client submits a system password file path and the service returns its first line, despite enforcement being enabled.

A service runs NLTK 3.10.0 or later. It accepts only a short corpus name from a fixed allowlist and resolves it to a known file inside the NLTK data directory. A request naming a system password file is rejected before any file is opened.

citations.quote: NLTK before 3.10.0 contains an arbitrary local file read vulnerability in StreamBackedCorpusView that bypasses pathsec.ENFORCE
Attackers who control the fileid argument can read arbitrary local files regardless of the ENFORCE setting

patterns.title: Webhook delivery SSRF via unvalidated redirects and unpinned DNS resolution
patterns.cause: The webhook URL guard resolved the hostname and rejected non-public addresses, but only for the original URL. Delivery then followed HTTP redirects and re-resolved the hostname without pinning the validated address, so redirect targets and rebinding answers were never checked. The test endpoint returned the upstream status and body to the caller.
preconditions: The server exposes the webhook API without authentication; the sources say webhook authorization lives only in an optional auth plugin that is not loaded by default
The URL check runs only on the original webhook URL, before the request is sent
Delivery follows redirects and resolves the hostname again at connect time without reusing the validated address
The attacker can host a public HTTPS endpoint that passes the check and redirects to an internal target
patterns.prevention: Validate the address a connection actually reaches, not just the result of an earlier name lookup. Check the peer IP of every established connection against public-address rules right after connect and before any TLS or HTTP exchange. Route redirect hops through the same protected connections so each new target is checked. Otherwise stop following redirects, or re-validate every hop. Normalize IPv6 forms that embed an IPv4 address (IPv4-mapped, 6to4, NAT64) before classifying an address as public. Do not return upstream response bodies to unauthenticated callers.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the full fix internals. The CVE record says affected versions start at 3.3.0 and are fixed in 3.15.0, while the advisory says the guard shipped in 3.10.0; this mismatch is unresolved. The advisory also reports later IPv6-transition bypasses of the first fix, fixed in 3.16.0, so 3.15.0 alone may not cover IPv6 or NAT64 networks. Redirects with status 307 or 308 allow blind POST writes to internal endpoints as well as reads.

fixtures.scenario: A default no-auth tracking server accepts a webhook whose URL is an attacker public HTTPS host. At delivery that host redirects to a link-local metadata address, the server follows it, and the test endpoint returns the body.

Delivery checks the peer IP of every established connection, including each redirect hop, against public-address rules before sending any request, so a redirect to a metadata or loopback address is refused.

citations.quote: follows redirects and re-resolves the hostname without pinning the validated address
the peer IP of each connected socket is validated against public-IP rules immediately after
each redirect opens a new connection through the protected pool
The original is_global classifier did not decode IPv6 addresses embedding an IPv4 address

patterns.title: Scheduler deserializes human-in-the-loop next_kwargs without an allow-list
patterns.cause: In Apache Airflow 3.3.0, human-in-the-loop tasks moved from the triggerer to an awaiting_input task state swept by the scheduler. The sweep deserializes the task instance's next_kwargs without an allow-list. A Dag author controls that value through the task execution API, so author-supplied data can drive module imports and object instantiation inside the scheduler process.
preconditions: Apache Airflow 3.3.0 is deployed (versions before 3.3.0 are not affected, and the fix is in 3.3.1)
Human-in-the-loop tasks use the awaiting_input state, which the scheduler sweeps
The attacker is a Dag author who can set next_kwargs through the task execution API
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later. Applying the earlier fix for CVE-2026-58076 does not cover this code path. In general, a privileged process such as the scheduler should not deserialize author-controlled values unless the set of allowed classes is restricted by an allow-list. Treat next_kwargs as untrusted input at every place it is deserialized.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the code of the fix or how the allow-list is built. They do not say whether the default allowed_deserialization_classes setting is consulted after the fix, or whether any workaround exists short of upgrading. The exact impact beyond arbitrary import and instantiation, or terminating the scheduler job, is not detailed.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 3.3.0 deployment runs a human-in-the-loop task in the awaiting_input state. A Dag author sets next_kwargs through the task execution API, and the scheduler sweep deserializes it with no allow-list.

An Airflow 3.3.1 or later deployment runs the same human-in-the-loop task. The scheduler sweep no longer deserializes author-supplied next_kwargs without an allow-list, so arbitrary imports are not triggered.

citations.quote: can cause an arbitrary module import and object instantiation inside the scheduler process, or terminate the scheduler job.
No non-default configuration is required: the sweep runs unconditionally every 15 seconds
Versions before 3.3.0 are not affected, because human-in-the-loop tasks deferred onto the triggerer instead.
Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later.

patterns.title: GitPython option injection via keyword arguments and dash-leading revisions
patterns.cause: The unsafe-option check that blocks upload-pack and exec style options is only called from fetch, pull, push and clone_from. Repo.archive() and git.ls_remote() turn caller keyword arguments into Git options without it, so attacker-chosen options can run commands. Repo.iter_commits() and Repo.blame() place the revision before the separator and do not reject a leading dash, so a revision can act as an option that makes Git open and truncate a file.
preconditions: An application passes attacker-controlled keyword arguments or option dictionaries to Repo.archive() or git.ls_remote().
An application passes attacker-controlled revision strings to Repo.iter_commits() or Repo.blame().
GitPython is a version before 3.1.51.
patterns.prevention: Never forward untrusted dictionaries as keyword arguments to Repo.archive(), git.ls_remote() or dynamic git command calls. Accept only a fixed allowlist of option names and values you define, and reject command-selecting options such as exec and upload-pack. Reject any revision that starts with a dash before it reaches Repo.iter_commits() or Repo.blame(), and validate it as a real ref or object name. Upgrade to 3.1.51 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so it is unclear which other Git subcommands reached through the dynamic command interface are covered. The advisory text says the dynamic surface never got the earlier fix. Allowlisting remains the application's job.

fixtures.scenario: A web service exports repository archives and forwards a user-supplied options dictionary to Repo.archive(). The user adds a remote option and an exec option naming a command, and the server runs it.
The service builds archive options itself from a fixed allowlist of format and prefix values, ignores other user keys, rejects revisions starting with a dash, and runs GitPython 3.1.51 or later.

citations.quote: GitPython before 3.1.51 fails to guard against dangerous Git options passed as keyword arguments in Repo.archive() and git.ls_remote()
Repo.iter_commits() and Repo.blame() do not check for leading-dash revision arguments
Exploitation requires an application that passes attacker-controlled arguments to these methods.

patterns.title: Option blocklist bypass through git long-option prefix abbreviation in GitPython
patterns.cause: The unsafe-options guard normalizes option names only by converting underscores to hyphens, then does an exact-match lookup against a blocklist. Git accepts any unambiguous prefix of a long option, so an abbreviated key misses the blocklist but is still resolved by git to the blocked option, such as upload-pack, and executes an attacker-chosen command.
preconditions: The host application passes attacker-controlled keyword argument keys into a GitPython clone, fetch, pull or push call.
The allow_unsafe_options setting is left at its default of false, so the blocklist is the only defense.
The installed GitPython version carries the blocklist fix but is older than 3.1.51.
patterns.prevention: Do not rely on exact-match blocklists when the downstream parser accepts a wider grammar than the guard models. Treat any option name that is a prefix of a blocked long option as blocked, after the same normalization that is used when building the command line. Better, use an allowlist of permitted option names for security-sensitive subcommands, or invoke git so that long-option abbreviation is disabled. Also validate keyword keys against a fixed, developer-chosen set before they reach the library, and upgrade GitPython to 3.1.51 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which approach the released fix uses; the remediation options come from the report's suggestions. Abbreviations of the config option bypass the blocklist, but the report says weaponizing them through an ext:: URL is separately blocked by the protocol allowlist. Exploitation requires the host to forward attacker-controlled keys, so applications that use only fixed keys are not reachable. The sources do not discuss other git subcommands beyond clone, fetch, pull and push.

fixtures.scenario: A web service forwards user-supplied option names and values into a repository clone call with default safety settings. The user supplies an abbreviated upload-pack option name and a program path, and git runs that program.
The service accepts only a fixed set of option names chosen by the developer and rejects any abbreviated or unknown name before it reaches git.

citations.quote: Git accepts any unambiguous prefix of a long option
It does not account for git's unambiguous long-option prefix abbreviation.
Where the host passes only fixed/validated keys, this is not reachable
GitPython before 3.1.51 contains an incomplete command injection blocklist that fails to account for git's long-option prefix abbreviation feature.

patterns.title: Callback deserialization imports attacker-named modules in the Airflow scheduler
patterns.cause: The Task SDK rebuilt a Callback object from serialized data by re-running its constructor. That constructor imports the module named by the stored callback path. SyncCallback is an Airflow class, so it passes the default allowed_deserialization_classes allow-list, and the allow-list does not stop the import. A Dag author controls a task instance's next_kwargs through the task execution API, so that author can choose the module path. The scheduler deserializes the value during its awaiting_input timeout sweep, and the chosen module is then imported inside the scheduler process.
preconditions: apache-airflow at version 3.3.0 or later but before 3.3.1 (versions before 3.3.0 lack the scheduler sweep that reaches the class)
An attacker can act as a Dag author and set a task instance's next_kwargs through the task execution API
The scheduler's awaiting_input timeout sweep deserializes that stored value, which runs unconditionally with default configuration
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later. In general, do not rebuild objects from stored data by running constructors that import a module or class named inside that data. Treat values that task code can write, such as next_kwargs, as untrusted input in privileged processes like the scheduler. Check any stored import path against a fixed set of expected targets before importing, and do not rely on a class-name allow-list alone when the allowed class itself triggers imports.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream change in detail, so the exact validation it adds is not covered here. They do not say what an imported module can do beyond being imported in the scheduler process. They do not state whether 3.3.0 itself is affected beyond saying only earlier versions are not. Tightening allowed_deserialization_classes is stated not to help. Fixes for CVE-2026-58076 and CVE-2026-67260 are stated not to cover this path.

fixtures.scenario: A Dag author submits a next_kwargs value containing a serialized SyncCallback whose stored callback path names an arbitrary module. When the scheduler's awaiting_input timeout sweep deserializes it, the constructor imports that module inside the scheduler process, even with a tightened allow-list.

A deployment runs apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later. The same crafted next_kwargs value is deserialized by the sweep, and no arbitrary module named in the stored data is imported into the scheduler process.

citations.quote: can therefore cause an arbitrary module to be imported inside the scheduler process, when the scheduler's
so tightening that setting does not help.
No non-default configuration is required; the sweep runs unconditionally.
Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later.

patterns.title: SSRF through unvalidated sub-resource requests in a browser-based web loader
patterns.cause: The Playwright web loader in Open WebUI checked the destination address only for the top-level document request. The request interceptor returned early for every other resource type. Once the validated page loaded, its own scripts could issue further requests to blocked internal addresses, and the loader returned the final page DOM to the user, so data read from those addresses appeared in web-search or RAG output.
preconditions: The Playwright web loader engine is selected instead of the default loader, on a version from 0.9.6 up to but not including 0.11.0.
A Playwright browser is reachable, either local or through a remote websocket endpoint.
An authenticated user, with no administrator role needed, can submit a URL for ingestion or trigger a web search.
The browser process has a network route to something worth reading, such as cloud instance metadata, other containers or internal APIs.
patterns.prevention: Apply address validation to every request a headless browser makes, not just top-level navigation. Fetch each intercepted request with automatic redirects disabled, re-validate the destination on every redirect hop, and fulfill the request only if the address is global. Also close the paths that bypass request interception: block service-worker requests and handle WebSocket connections so they never connect upstream. Upgrading to 0.11.0 resolves the issue without configuration changes.
patterns.limitations: The sources say the flaw gives read access only, with no write or availability impact, and only within the browser's existing network position. They do not describe how the address check resolves hostnames or handles DNS rebinding, so those points are not covered here. Deployments on the default loader are reported as unaffected. The proof of concept exercised the interceptor with stand-in objects rather than a full browser.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment on version 0.10.2 uses the Playwright loader. An authenticated user submits a page whose script requests a cloud metadata address, and the response is returned in the page DOM in search or RAG output.

Every browser request, including scripts, redirects, service workers and WebSockets, must resolve to a global address. The same page's metadata request is blocked and no internal data appears in the output.

citations.quote: the Playwright web loader validates only the top-level page request and lets sub-resource requests pass unvalidated
Every intercepted request is now validated, fetched with redirects disabled, re-validated on each redirect hop and then fulfilled
The same change blocks the two paths that never reached the interceptor at all

patterns.title: Client-side SSRF through the default Vega loader in chat chart rendering
patterns.cause: The chart renderer treated a chart spec as trusted authored content rather than untrusted chat text, so it accepted Vega's default loader. That loader fetches data url and topojson or geo sources at view construction. It also lets image mark URLs into the output SVG, where the browser fetches them on display.
preconditions: Vega or vega-lite fenced blocks in chat content are rendered in the viewer's browser with the default loader.
An attacker can place a block where another user will see it, such as a shared chat, a channel message, or model, RAG or tool output the attacker can influence.
The victim must open the message, so exploitation is not zero-click.
patterns.prevention: Treat chart specs from chat text as untrusted. Build the Vega view with a restricted loader whose load operation always fails and whose sanitize step resolves each URI with the browser's own URL parser and permits only data: and same-origin results. Cover both exits: data and geo sources fetched at view construction, and image mark URLs written into the SVG as href and fetched on display. Charts then work only with inline data values. Downstream SVG sanitization alone is not enough, because the URL is a legitimate attribute value. For Open WebUI, upgrading to 0.11.0 is sufficient.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the fix only at a high level and do not list every Vega feature that could load resources. Requests are GET only and no server-side data is exposed directly. Impact depends on what the victim's browser can reach. The CVE record gives the affected range as 0.6.34 up to 0.11.0.

fixtures.scenario: A user posts a vega-lite block in a shared chat whose data section uses a url pointing at an attacker or internal host. When the victim opens it, the victim's browser fetches that URL at view construction.
The same block is rendered with a loader that always fails loading and permits only data: and same-origin URIs. No outbound request is made, and charts with inline data values still render.

citations.quote: Any user who can place such a block where another user will see it can make that user's browser issue attacker-chosen outbound GET requests
The renderer treated a chart spec as trusted authored content rather than as untrusted chat text, so it accepted Vega's default loader.
The second path survives downstream SVG sanitization because the URL is a legitimate attribute value, not markup.

patterns.title: SSRF filter bypass via IPv4 addresses embedded in NAT64 IPv6 literals
patterns.cause: The server decided whether a user-supplied URL destination was allowed by applying the ipaddress is_global test to the literal IPv6 address, without looking at the IPv4 address embedded inside it. The NAT64 well-known prefix is a global prefix that can carry any IPv4 destination, so an internal or cloud-metadata target wrapped in it passed the check. The same test backed the pre-fetch URL validation and the connect-time re-checks, so no later layer caught it.
preconditions: The attacker has any verified user account; no admin role is needed.
The deployment network provides NAT64 translation for the well-known 64:ff9b::/96 prefix.
The application fetches user-supplied URLs server-side (RAG URL ingestion, URL-to-markdown conversion, web-search content retrieval) and returns the response body to the caller.
The default local-fetch setting is off and the default hostname blocklist is in place; neither stops the attack because the blocklist matches hostname strings.
patterns.prevention: Do not judge a destination by the literal IPv6 address alone. Before deciding whether an address is global, unwrap the IPv4 address embedded in IPv6 transition encodings and classify that embedded address. Cover every standardized transition encoding, not just the NAT64 prefix, since the same reasoning error applies to each. Apply the same classification at every checkpoint: the pre-fetch URL check and each connect-time re-check that guards against DNS rebinding. Public destinations wrapped in these encodings should still be allowed, to avoid over-blocking.
patterns.limitations: The sources only demonstrate the NAT64 well-known prefix; they do not list the other transition encodings the fix covers. The proof of concept modelled NAT64 by binding translated addresses locally, not through a real gateway. Impact is described only for GET responses. Deployments without NAT64 translation are reported as unaffected. The sources do not describe other SSRF vectors or other filter weaknesses.

fixtures.scenario: A verified user submits a URL whose host is an IPv6 literal in the NAT64 well-known prefix wrapping a cloud metadata IPv4 address, on a network with a NAT64 gateway. The filter accepts it and the internal response body is returned.
The same URL is rejected because the embedded IPv4 address is unwrapped and classified as non-global, while a NAT64-wrapped public address is still allowed to be fetched.

citations.quote: Open WebUI checked whether a user-supplied URL destination was globally routable by applying ipaddress.is_global to the literal IPv6 address
Address classification now unwraps the IPv4 embedded in IPv6 transition encodings before deciding whether a destination is global
Deployments on IPv4-only networks, or on any network without a NAT64 gateway, are not affected: the address has nowhere to route.

patterns.title: Sandboxed preview iframe must not combine script execution with same-origin access for files served from the app origin
patterns.cause: In Open WebUI 0.9.0 through 0.10.2, the terminal file-preview branch that loads HTML from a served URL used a fixed iframe sandbox that always granted both allow-scripts and allow-same-origin. The terminal proxy is mounted under the application's own origin, and the response carries no Content-Security-Policy unless the operator configured one. The sandbox was therefore the only isolation boundary, and it granted the permission that removed that isolation. The other preview path, which uses inline document content, already made same-origin access opt-in and injected a policy. The served-URL branch ignored that setting.
preconditions: An admin has configured at least one terminal server that the victim can reach. Deployments with none are not affected.
The attacker has a normal authenticated account with access to that terminal server and needs no admin rights.
No restrictive Content-Security-Policy is applied through the terminal proxy header setting, which is unset by default.
A malicious HTML file gets written and displayed. A display_file tool call opens the preview automatically, but producing the file needs a prompt injection or a social step.
patterns.prevention: Do not hardcode allow-same-origin in the sandbox of any iframe that renders HTML from a user- or tool-controlled source. Build the sandbox value from the same opt-in user setting for every preview path, so the default is an opaque origin that cannot reach the parent window or its stored session token. Keep the two preview paths consistent so a hardened path cannot be bypassed through a newer one. Where operators can set response headers on proxied content, a restrictive Content-Security-Policy adds a second layer.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the opt-in setting behaves when users enable it. They do not say whether serving previews from a separate origin was considered. They do not give a default Content-Security-Policy for the proxy. With the setting turned on, the same exposure presumably returns, though the sources do not state this. The advisory notes that no global policy is set and that the file reaches the app only through a prompt injection or a social step.

fixtures.scenario: A user with terminal access has a tool write an HTML file that reads the parent window's stored session token. The chat auto-opens it in an iframe with scripts and same-origin both allowed, so the script runs at the app origin and leaks the token.
The same file opens in an iframe whose sandbox omits same-origin access unless the user opted in. The page loads at an opaque origin, cannot reach the parent window, and cannot read the token.

citations.quote: the terminal file-preview serveUrl iframe branch always granted allow-same-origin together with allow-scripts for HTML files served from the application origin.
the sandbox was the only isolation boundary left, and it was granting precisely the permission that dissolved it.
so by default the preview loads at an opaque origin and cannot reach the parent context.

patterns.title: Unbounded recurrence walk from a fixed far-past anchor stalls the event loop
patterns.cause: Automation recurrence parsing anchored minutely and hourly rules at the fixed date 2000-01-01 and walked forward one interval at a time to find the next run. The walk therefore covered roughly a quarter-century of occurrences, synchronously, on the event loop that also serves the scheduler, HTTP and WebSocket traffic. The distance between the anchor and the present is attacker-influenced work that grows with real time, and it was never bounded or moved off the loop.
preconditions: The attacker can create or update an automation. This is admin-only by default, but ordinary users can do it on deployments that granted the automations feature.
The recurrence rule is minutely, with no start date or with a start date well in the past.
The deployment runs a single worker (the default), so no other worker absorbs the stall.
The automation is stored, so the scheduler recomputes the next run on each poll and repeats the walk.
patterns.prevention: Do not use a literal far-past date as the reference point for sub-daily rules. Snapping to clock boundaries only needs a reference of the right phase, so anchor the rule to the current clock instead, and the walk starts at the next occurrence. Honour a caller-supplied start date only when the number of occurrences it implies stays under a fixed bound, and otherwise replace it with the clock-aligned anchor. Treat the cost of computing the next run as work that needs a bound, because the scheduler repeats it for every stored automation on each poll.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not give the numeric occurrence bound used by the fix. They do not say whether the computation was also moved off the event loop; they only state that originally nothing did so. Hourly rules alone cost about 0.34 s and are not materially exploitable by themselves. Measurements were taken at function level, not end to end. Only the fix in version 0.11.0 is described, and no other mitigation is documented.

fixtures.scenario: A user permitted to create automations submits a minutely recurrence rule with no start date or one far in the past. The parser walks from a fixed year-2000 anchor on the event loop, and the scheduler repeats the walk on every poll.

The same minutely rule is anchored to the current clock, so the next run is found at once. A supplied start date is used only when the occurrences it implies stay under a fixed bound; otherwise the clock anchor replaces it.

citations.quote: Nothing bounds the walk, and nothing moves it off the loop.
Sub-daily rules are now anchored to the current clock instead of the year-2000 date, so the walk starts at the next occurrence
This causes availability impact for every other user of the instance.

patterns.title: Escape KaTeX fallback output so failed math renders as text, not HTML
patterns.cause: In Open WebUI 0.10.0 up to 0.11.0, the KaTeX renderer component caught any rendering failure and fell back to showing the original math source. It put that untouched source into the page through the HTML insertion directive. Deeply nested math input makes KaTeX fail with a stack overflow rather than a parse error, so the fallback runs. The Markdown math tokenizer keeps everything between the delimiters verbatim, including complete tags, so the author of a message controls the inserted string exactly. Script in it runs in the viewer's browser.
preconditions: The application renders user-supplied math with KaTeX and has an error fallback that shows the original source.
The fallback inserts that source as HTML, not as text.
An attacker can store a message with deeply nested math, using a normal user account, and a victim opens it in a chat, shared chat, or channel.
patterns.prevention: Treat the original math source on the error path as untrusted text. HTML-escape it before it reaches the DOM, or insert it as plain text, so a failed render shows the formula as text and never as markup. Do not assume the renderer's option for suppressing parse errors covers every failure. Stack overflows from deeply nested input surface as a different exception class, so the catch branch must be safe for any failure. Upgrading to 0.11.0 resolves the issue and needs no configuration change.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe only the escaping of the fallback source in this one component. They do not say whether other renderers or the successful KaTeX output were reviewed, and they do not describe any input depth or size limit. Affected versions are 0.10.0 through 0.10.2, per the advisory. Exploitation needs the victim to open the content, but no interaction with the message itself.

fixtures.scenario: A user posts a message with one inline math block: nested opening braces, an image tag with an error handler, then matching closing braces. KaTeX overflows the stack, and the fallback inserts the raw source as HTML, so the handler runs in the viewer's session.
The same message is posted, KaTeX still fails, but the fallback HTML-escapes the source first. The viewer sees the formula and tag as literal text, and no script runs.

citations.quote: the renderer falls back to inserting the original math source into the page as HTML rather than as text
The error path now HTML-escapes the math source before it reaches the DOM
makes KaTeX fail with a stack overflow instead of a parse error

patterns.title: Unbounded backtracking regex in knowledge file search stalls the worker
patterns.cause: The knowledge search tool let a chat participant choose the pattern used to grep knowledge files. Any pattern containing regex metacharacters was compiled with a backtracking regex engine and run over every line of every reachable file. Nothing limited matching time. Existing caps on results returned and files scanned did not bound the time one line could take. Because the search ran synchronously inside the event loop, one slow match blocked the whole worker.
preconditions: The knowledge builtin tool group is enabled, which is the default, and the model is given the grep-style knowledge file tool
The attacker is any authenticated user who can read at least one file, such as their own upload, so both the pattern and the searched text are attacker-controlled
A model is willing to call the tool with the attacker's literal pattern, which the advisory says is reliable in practice but not guaranteed on every turn
The affected versions run from 0.9.6 up to but not including 0.11.0
patterns.prevention: Do not run user-influenced patterns through a regex engine that has no time limit. Use an engine that supports a per-search timeout and give each tool call one overall matching budget. When the budget is exhausted, stop and return an error instead of continuing to match. Do not rely on capping pattern length, line length, match count or file count, because backtracking cost grows exponentially with the length of the matched text rather than with the pattern. Treat any pattern with regex metacharacters as untrusted input to the matcher.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say whether other code paths accept user-chosen patterns. They do not say whether the search still runs inside the event loop after the fix, so a timeout may still hold the worker for up to the budget. The advisory states only that upgrading to 0.11.0 is sufficient and does not describe any other mitigation for older versions.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user uploads a file with one short line of repeated characters. They ask the model to call the knowledge grep tool with a nested-alternation pattern that cannot match. The worker spins at full CPU and other users on it get no responses.

The same request runs under a timeout-capable engine and a roughly 2 second matching budget for the whole tool call. The search aborts and the tool returns an error, so the worker stays responsive to other users.

citations.quote: Cost scales exponentially with the length of the matching text
neither of which bounds the time a single line can consume
Backtracking cost is exponential in the length of the matched text rather than in the pattern
every tool call now runs its searches under a single 2 second matching budget

patterns.title: Gateway secret api_base stored and fetched without SSRF validation
patterns.cause: The AI Gateway stores the auth_config.api_base value of a gateway secret verbatim, with no check of scheme, host, or IP range. The gateway proxy endpoint later sends an HTTP request to that stored base plus a caller-supplied path and returns the full response body. The existing SSRF guard for webhook URLs is never called on this path.
preconditions: The attacker can authenticate to the MLflow server, and read-only accounts are enough
The attacker can create a gateway secret with a chosen api_base, since that action needs only basic authentication and no specific scope
The attacker can reach the gateway proxy endpoint, which requests the stored api_base plus a caller-chosen path
An internal address such as a cloud metadata service is reachable from the MLflow server
patterns.prevention: Validate any user-supplied api_base before it is stored and before the proxy uses it. Check the scheme, host, and resolved IP range, and reject non-global and metadata addresses. Reuse the existing webhook URL guard on the gateway secret and proxy code path instead of leaving it uncalled. Also give the secret-creation action an explicit permission check so that basic authentication alone is not enough.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix in detail. They do not say how redirects, DNS rebinding, or later changes to a stored value are handled, or which permission scope is required. Applying the existing guard at both save time and request time is a reasonable direction, but the sources do not confirm it. Related issue CVE-2026-4035 concerns a separate mechanism and is not covered here.

fixtures.scenario: A read-only user creates a gateway secret whose api_base points at an internal metadata address. The server saves it unchecked. The user then calls the proxy endpoint with a chosen path and receives the internal response body.

A user submits a secret with an internal or metadata api_base. The server validates scheme, host, and IP range with the existing SSRF guard and rejects it. Nothing is stored, so the proxy never contacts the internal address.

citations.quote: MLflow's AI Gateway accepts an auth_config.api_base value when creating a gateway secret (mlflow/server/handlers.py, _create_gateway_secret) with no validation of scheme, host, or IP range
MLflow's existing SSRF guard, _validate_webhook_url (which blocks non-global and metadata IPs), is never invoked anywhere in this gateway secret/proxy code path.
subsequently issues an HTTP request to that stored api_base plus a caller-supplied path and returns the full response body

patterns.title: Dotted-name bypass in NLTK AllowlistUnpickler enables code execution via untrusted parser models
patterns.cause: The allowlist unpickler checked only the pickle module string and not the global name. A dotted global name could then be resolved by attribute traversal to a callable outside the allowlisted namespace, so a crafted model file could run arbitrary commands when loaded.
preconditions: NLTK version earlier than 3.10.3 is in use
The application loads a transition-parser model through allowlisted_pickle_load, for example via TransitionParser.parse
The model file comes from an untrusted or attacker-influenced source
patterns.prevention: Upgrade NLTK to 3.10.3 or later. When writing an allowlist for deserialization, validate both the module and the global name together, and do not let dotted names resolve through attribute traversal to objects outside the approved set. Treat model files from untrusted sources as unsafe to load.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change or how names are checked after the fix. They do not say whether other loaders in NLTK are affected. Only the transition-parser model loading path is named as an attack route.

fixtures.scenario: A service downloads a transition-parser model from a third party and calls TransitionParser.parse on it with NLTK 3.10.2. The model file holds a dotted global name that escapes the allowlist and runs a command.
The service runs NLTK 3.10.3 or later and loads only models from trusted, verified origins. The loader checks the full global name against the allowlist, so the dotted-name trick is rejected.

citations.quote: validates only the pickle module string and not the global name, allowing attackers to resolve dotted names by attribute traversal
Attackers can craft untrusted transition-parser models that execute arbitrary commands when TransitionParser.parse loads the model through allowlisted_pickle_load.

patterns.title: Absolute path in Crubadan table.txt escapes the corpus root in NLTK
patterns.cause: In NLTK 3.9.4 through 3.10.2, CrubadanCorpusReader joins the corpus root with the column-0 value read from the table.txt mapping file. When that value is absolute, os.path.join discards the root. The file is then opened with the builtin open() instead of the pathsec-validated opener, so the containment check that nltk.pathsec applies when ENFORCE is set never runs.
preconditions: The application loads a corpus package whose contents an attacker controls.
The table.txt mapping file has an absolute path as its column-0 value.
The language n-gram file is opened with the builtin open() rather than the pathsec-validated opener.
The target file name ends in -3grams.txt and its contents parse as token count lines.
patterns.prevention: Treat the column-0 value from table.txt as untrusted input. Open corpus files through the pathsec-validated opener so the containment check is applied, not through the builtin open(). Reject absolute values and confirm that the resolved path stays inside the corpus root before reading. Do not load corpus packages from untrusted sources.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name a patched release or describe the upstream fix. They do not say whether ENFORCE is on by default. They also do not cover other corpus readers. Disclosure is limited to paths ending in -3grams.txt whose contents parse as token count lines, so other file types are outside what the sources describe.

fixtures.scenario: A corpus package ships a table.txt whose first column holds an absolute path ending in -3grams.txt outside the corpus directory. Calling lang_freq on that language reads the outside file and returns its parsed contents.
The same table.txt entry is rejected or confined to the corpus root by the validated opener, so lang_freq cannot read any file outside the corpus directory.

citations.quote: os.path.join discards the root when that value is absolute and the read escapes the corpus directory
opens the result with the builtin open() rather than the pathsec-validated opener
limited to paths ending in -3grams.txt whose contents parse as token count lines

patterns.title: Catastrophic regex backtracking in NLTK TweetTokenizer naked-domain URL matching
patterns.cause: The URL expression in nltk/tokenize/casual.py, compiled into TweetTokenizer.WORD_RE, has a naked-domain branch whose domain-label prefix repeats without a bound. Input with many alternating label separators can be split into labels in exponentially many ways. The branch also requires a trailing top-level domain that such input never supplies, so the engine tries those splits and fails at each offset. The HANG_RE substitution applied before matching does not collapse this pattern.
preconditions: The application runs a version of nltk that predates 3.10.1.
The application calls TweetTokenizer.tokenize or the module-level casual_tokenize.
The text being tokenized comes from untrusted users, such as submitted social-media text.
The input contains long runs of alternating label separators with no valid top-level domain after them.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade nltk to 3.10.1 or later, which bounds the label repetition in the domain-label prefix. When writing or reviewing similar tokenizer patterns, avoid unbounded repeated groups whose pieces can be split in more than one way, especially when a required suffix may be missing. Check such patterns against long inputs that nearly match but lack the required ending.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say that version 3.10.1 bounds the label repetition. They do not give the exact bound, the full affected version range, or any other mitigation, such as input size limits or timeouts. They also do not say whether other branches of the tokenizer pattern are affected. Exact input sizes and timings vary by environment.

fixtures.scenario: A web service passes user-submitted text to casual_tokenize on an nltk version older than 3.10.1. A request of a few kilobytes made of alternating label separators with no top-level domain ties up one CPU for seconds to minutes.

The service runs nltk 3.10.1 or later, where the label repetition is bounded. The same separator-heavy input is rejected by the pattern quickly and tokenization completes without stalling the request.

citations.quote: Input consisting of many alternating label separators can be partitioned in exponentially many ways
A few kilobytes of input therefore consumes seconds to minutes of single-threaded CPU
Version 3.10.1 bounds the label repetition.

patterns.title: Image viewer blob URL lifetime allows same-origin script from crafted SVG in JupyterLab
patterns.cause: JupyterLab's image viewer displays a specially crafted SVG image through a blob URL created with URL.createObjectURL. The blob URL is revoked too early. As a result the image keeps an executable same-origin context when it is opened through the image viewer and then opened in a new browser tab. This is cross-site scripting (CWE-79), and the sources state it can lead to arbitrary code execution on the JupyterLab server.
preconditions: JupyterLab version earlier than 4.5.10 (4.5 line) or earlier than 4.6.2 (4.6 line).
The image viewer plugin is enabled.
A specially crafted SVG image file is opened through the image viewer.
The image is then opened in a new browser tab.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to JupyterLab 4.5.10 or 4.6.2, which contain the patch. If upgrading is not yet possible, disable the image viewer plugin and confirm it is disabled by listing the installed lab extensions. For similar code, treat user-supplied SVG as active content. Do not let a blob URL created for it keep a same-origin, script-capable context when the image is reopened in a new tab. Review when the blob URL is revoked relative to how the image can be reached.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not explain why the early revocation yields an executable context, which browsers are affected, or what exact change the patch makes, so this card does not describe the upstream fix. The prevention for similar code is a general direction inferred from the stated cause, not a documented patch detail. The sources describe the plugin workaround only by its effect of disabling the image viewer.

fixtures.scenario: A user of a JupyterLab 4.5.9 server opens a crafted SVG file in the image viewer and then opens the image in a new browser tab. The blob URL has already been revoked, the image retains a same-origin executable context, and its script runs against the JupyterLab server.

The same crafted SVG is opened in JupyterLab 4.5.10 or 4.6.2, or on a server where the image viewer plugin is disabled. Opening it in a new tab does not give the image an executable same-origin context.

citations.quote: JupyterLab's ImageViewer uses URL.createObjectURL for a specially crafted SVG image and revokes the blob URL too early
allowing the image to retain an executable same-origin context when it is opened through the image viewer
This XSS issue can be used to cause remote code execution (RCE) on the JupyterLab server.
This issue is fixed in versions 4.5.10 and 4.6.2.

patterns.title: Unvalidated notebook margin settings from overrides.json allow script injection through style content in JupyterLab
patterns.cause: The sideBySideLeftMarginOverride and sideBySideRightMarginOverride notebook settings were not properly validated before being inserted into style content. A crafted overrides.json could therefore carry instructions that run as code in the JupyterLab page instead of only changing a display preference.
preconditions: JupyterLab version in the affected range (the CVE record says from 3.3.0 until 4.5.10 and 4.6.2)
A crafted overrides.json is applied, either imported by the user with the Import button in the Settings Editor or loaded automatically from a settings location
For the automatic path, the attacker can write to a directory JupyterLab loads settings from, such as on a shared or multi-tenant file system
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to JupyterLab 4.5.10 or 4.6.2 or later, as no workaround is listed. When implementing similar features, treat every setting value as untrusted data. Validate it strictly against the narrow form it is meant to have before it is placed into style content, and do not rely on a settings file being limited to display preferences. Operationally, restrict write permissions on the application settings directory and other Jupyter configuration paths on shared file systems. Distribute configuration through a trusted process instead of ad-hoc importing of shared files.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact validation rules or the code change in the fix. They do not give the exact payload form either. They are inconsistent on the first affected version: the advisory says 4.5+ while the CVE record says 3.3.0. Directory permissions only reduce cross-user planting and do not fix the flaw, and the user-import path still needs a patched version.

fixtures.scenario: A user imports a shared overrides.json through the Settings Editor Import button. Its left margin override holds crafted text instead of a plain margin value, and the unvalidated text goes into style content and runs as code with the user's access.

The same import on a patched JupyterLab (4.5.10 or 4.6.2 or later) is checked first, so margin overrides that are not valid display values do not reach style content. Settings directories are also not writable by other users.

citations.quote: the sideBySideLeftMarginOverride and sideBySideRightMarginOverride settings are not properly validated before being inserted into style content
a crafted settings file to contain instructions that execute as code instead of only changing display preferences
restrict write permissions on the application settings directory and other Jupyter configuration paths

patterns.title: Unbounded regex compile in vLLM lm-format-enforcer backend enables ReDoS
patterns.cause: The lm-format-enforcer structured-output backend passes the user-supplied regex to lmformatenforcer.RegexParser, which builds an interegular FSM synchronously. No timeout or buildability check applies, and request validation returns immediately when a regex is present. The sibling xgrammar and outlines backends had already been guarded by compile_regex_with_timeout. A catastrophic pattern therefore pegs a CPU core and stalls the engine path.
preconditions: vLLM version earlier than 0.26.0 is running.
The operator selected the lm-format-enforcer backend through the structured outputs configuration; the default auto setting resolves to xgrammar.
A client can send a structured_outputs.regex value in a completions request; vLLM has no authentication by default.
patterns.prevention: Treat every user-supplied regex as untrusted input to an expensive compile step. Run the lm-format-enforcer regex compile under a bounded timeout, as the xgrammar and outlines backends do with compile_regex_with_timeout. Also validate the pattern at request-validation time, rejecting un-buildable or oversized patterns before they reach the engine. Return a clean error instead of blocking the structured-output path. Apply the same guard to every backend that compiles user regexes, so none is left as a missed sibling. Upgrading to 0.26.0 or later also resolves this issue.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not give the timeout value, the size limits, or the buildability rules. They do not say whether a timed-out compile is cancelled or merely abandoned. The reproduction covers one nested bounded-repetition pattern and does not characterize all patterns that trigger the hang. The upstream fix is not described in the sources beyond the version in which it landed.

fixtures.scenario: A vLLM server older than 0.26.0 uses the lm-format-enforcer backend. An unauthenticated completions request sets a structured output regex made of deeply nested bounded repetitions. The compile never finishes, one core is pegged, and other requests stall.

The same deployment compiles the regex under a timeout, and request validation rejects un-buildable or oversized patterns. The nested-repetition request returns a clean error quickly, and other requests continue to be served.

citations.quote: it compiles the attacker-supplied regex with no timeout and no buildability check.
One request pegs a CPU core and blocks the structured-output engine path.
This issue is fixed in version 0.26.0.

patterns.title: Model processor fetches user media strings directly, bypassing the media connector's SSRF and local-file checks
patterns.cause: The MiMoV2Omni multimodal processor in vLLM passed attacker-controlled image and audio strings to a direct HTTP GET call and to a local image-open call instead of the shared MediaConnector. Earlier hardening lived only in MediaConnector, so this later-added code path skipped the domain allowlist, the local-path allowlist and the size caps. The result was server-side requests and reads of any file the vLLM process can access.
preconditions: vLLM version earlier than 0.26.0 serving the MiMoV2OmniForCausalLM architecture
An attacker controls a string value supplied as image or audio multimodal input
The string reaches the model processor directly, for example through library use or batch processing, rather than only through the protected chat path
The vLLM host can reach internal services or cloud metadata endpoints, or holds sensitive readable files
patterns.prevention: Send every externally sourced media string through one hardened loader that enforces a URL scheme and domain allowlist, a local-path allowlist and size limits before any network request or file open. Model-specific processors should not make their own HTTP or file calls on user strings. Alternatively, keep string inputs from reaching processors at all and require all media fetching to happen in the shared loader first. Upgrading to version 0.26.0 or later applies the vendor fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change, so this card does not say how the fix is implemented. They do not say how redirects or DNS rebinding are handled inside the shared loader. Only this model's processor is described as affected; other processors would need their own review. The advisory text suggests the audio loader was affected in the same way, but the fixed-version statement is the only confirmation given.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment serves MiMoV2OmniForCausalLM and passes a user-supplied image string, such as an internal metadata URL or a local file path, straight into multimodal input; the processor fetches or opens it with no allowlist.
The same deployment, on version 0.26.0 or later, has every user-supplied image or audio string fetched through the shared media connector, so disallowed domains and local paths are rejected.

citations.quote: bypassing allowed_media_domains and allowed_local_media_path protections and allowing server-side requests and reads of arbitrary files accessible to the vLLM process
route every external resource fetch through
This issue is fixed in version 0.26.0.

patterns.title: Stored XSS in django CMS edit-mode plugin exception heading
patterns.cause: In django CMS 5.0.8 until 5.0.9, when plugin rendering fails in edit mode, the exception renderer builds a cms-rendering-exception heading from the exception message, placeholder, placeholder source and plugin short description. These values are interpolated without escaping, and the output is returned as safe markup. Stored HTML therefore runs in the editor's browser.
preconditions: An editor can store HTML in data used by a plugin's get_short_description(), or in other values interpolated into the exception message.
A plugin raises an exception during edit-mode rendering and placeholder rendering catches it.
The custom heading is returned as safe markup, so Django template autoescaping does not apply.
patterns.prevention: Escape every value placed into the custom exception heading before the placeholder output is marked safe, for example by building the heading with Django's format_html helper so the message is escaped. Keep Django's traceback HTML separate from the custom heading, because its escaping does not cover extra markup assembled by django CMS. Upgrade to 5.0.9 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources give 5.0.8 until 5.0.9 as the affected range and say only that older code was affected, so earlier releases are not clearly covered. Restricting plugin editing to fully trusted staff is only a partial mitigation. Setting DEBUG to false does not help. The sources do not describe other rendering paths.

fixtures.scenario: An editor saves HTML markup in a plugin field used by its short description. The plugin then raises during edit-mode rendering, and the exception heading includes that text unescaped, so a script runs in another staff user's browser.
The same plugin fails in edit mode, but the heading is built with escaping. The stored markup appears as plain text in the error block and no script runs in the staff user's browser.

citations.quote: Values from get_short_description(), the exception message, the placeholder, or placeholder.source are interpolated into a cms-rendering-exception heading and later returned through mark_safe.
Escape the custom exception heading before returning it as safe placeholder markup.
does not mitigate the issue: it only controls whether Django's traceback HTML is appended.
