patterns.title: GitPython rm and checkout forward pathspec file options, letting callers read arbitrary files via error text
patterns.cause: IndexFile.remove() and Head.checkout() pass caller-supplied keyword arguments straight into git rm and git checkout with no option guard. If a caller supplies a pathspec-from-file option together with the NUL-delimited pathspec option, Git treats the whole named file as one pathspec. When nothing matches, Git's error message quotes that pathspec, and GitPython returns it in GitCommandError.stderr. The full contents of the file are therefore disclosed to the caller.
preconditions: Application code calls IndexFile.remove() or Head.checkout() with keyword arguments that an untrusted party can influence
The GitPython version is older than 3.1.58
The chosen file is readable by the process running GitPython
The caller can see the error output, for example GitCommandError.stderr
patterns.prevention: Do not forward untrusted keyword arguments into git rm or git checkout. Validate options before the command runs, and reject the pathspec-from-file option and the NUL-delimited pathspec option, preferably with an allowlist of expected options. Upgrade to GitPython 3.1.58 or later. Where the application builds these calls itself, keep file-reading options out of any caller-controlled input, and do not show raw Git error output to untrusted users.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix in detail, so the exact set of rejected options is unknown. The report says git reset and git mv did not disclose file contents in testing, and that git status and the guarded checkout-index did not either. Whether other call sites or Git versions behave differently is not covered. The disclosure relies on how Git quotes unmatched pathspecs in its error text.

fixtures.scenario: A web service lets users pass extra options to a wrapper around IndexFile.remove(). A user sends a pathspec-from-file option naming a sensitive file plus the NUL pathspec option, and the error text returned in the response contains the whole file.

The wrapper accepts only a fixed set of known options and rejects pathspec-related options before calling IndexFile.remove() or Head.checkout(). The same request is refused and no file content appears in any error.

citations.quote: GitPython versions before 3.1.58 fail to validate options passed to git rm and git checkout commands in IndexFile.remove() and Head.checkout()
makes Git treat the whole file as a single NUL-delimited pathspec, and the unmatched-pathspec error quotes it verbatim.
to read arbitrary files accessible to the process, with full file contents returned in GitCommandError.stderr.

patterns.title: Unguarded option forwarding in GitPython Repo.init allows hook planting via template
patterns.cause: Repo.init forwards its keyword arguments verbatim to git init, with no unsafe-option check and no allow_unsafe_options parameter. The git init template option copies the hooks directory of the template into the new repository's hooks directory. An attacker-controlled template value therefore plants an executable hook that runs on a later git operation, such as a commit.
preconditions: The application passes externally influenced keyword arguments, in particular a template value, into Repo.init.
The attacker can stage an executable hooks directory at a path known to the host process.
The GitPython version is earlier than 3.1.58; the advisory lists 3.1.57 and earlier as affected.
A later git operation, such as a commit, runs in the newly initialized repository.
patterns.prevention: Never forward untrusted option names or values to Repo.init. Build the init options inside the application from a fixed allowlist, and reject template and separate-git-dir. Any option check should run before git is invoked and should cover path-taking and hook-installing options. Upgrade to GitPython 3.1.58 or later, which the CVE text implies is the first non-vulnerable release.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix itself, so its exact behavior is unconfirmed. The denylist in the advisory is only a suggestion and names just template and separate-git-dir; the full set of dangerous git init options is not given. The separate-git-dir option is described only as a redirect vector with value control. The sources do not say how the hook directory gets staged on the host.

fixtures.scenario: A service accepts a caller-supplied options mapping and passes it to Repo.init. The caller sets template to a directory holding an executable post-commit hook, and the next commit in the new repository runs it.
The service ignores caller-supplied option names and builds init options from a fixed allowlist that excludes template and separate-git-dir, so no hook is copied from an outside directory.

citations.quote: GitPython before 3.1.58 contains a remote code execution vulnerability in Repo.init that forwards unsafe git options without validation.
Arbitrary code execution (hook fires on next git op) at the privileges of the host process.
path-taking / hook-installing options

patterns.title: Option injection into git read-tree via treeish arguments in GitPython IndexFile methods
patterns.cause: IndexFile.from_tree, IndexFile.reset (which delegates to from_tree) and IndexFile.merge_tree pass caller-influenced treeish strings positionally to git read-tree. They apply no unsafe-option check and add no argument separator. A treeish that looks like the path-taking index-output option is therefore read as an option, and because the last occurrence wins, it overrides the method's own temporary output path.
preconditions: The application passes attacker-influenced treeish values to IndexFile.from_tree, IndexFile.reset or IndexFile.merge_tree
GitPython is a version before 3.1.58
The host process can write to the attacker-chosen target path
patterns.prevention: Do not let untrusted text reach the treeish positions unchecked. Reject values that start with a dash, or validate them as real revisions before use. Put an argument separator before positional treeish values where git allows it, and block the path-taking index-output option on this call. Upgrade GitPython to 3.1.58 or later. The advisory suggests an unsafe-option guard with an opt-in parameter, a separator before the positional arguments, or both.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the fix only as a suggestion and do not detail the upstream change. Only the index-output option is shown to be exploitable. They do not say whether other read-tree options are dangerous here, so a broad dash-prefix rejection is a conservative choice, not a documented requirement. The written content is a git-index blob the attacker does not choose, so the impact is file overwrite or destruction, not code execution. The advisory text names the affected versions inconsistently (up to 3.1.57 versus before 3.1.58).

fixtures.scenario: A web service takes a revision string from a request and passes it to IndexFile.from_tree. A caller supplies a string naming the index-output option with a path to an existing config file, and that file is replaced by a git-index blob.
The service checks that the revision string does not begin with a dash and resolves to a real commit before calling IndexFile.from_tree. An option-shaped string is rejected and no file is touched.

citations.quote: Attackers can inject the --index-output option to overwrite arbitrary files with a valid git-index blob
append caller-influenced treeish strings to git read-tree without option validation or argument separation
Arbitrary file overwrite / destruction at the privileges of the host process.

patterns.title: GitPython unsafe-option guard bypass through joined short-option token when single-char splitting is disabled
patterns.cause: The check_unsafe_options guard checks a candidate list of option names built from the kwargs. When split_single_char_options is False, that list holds only the single-character key and omits the value-derived option. The argv builder still emits a joined token of the short flag plus its value. Git clusters short flags and reads the tail of that token as the upload-pack option, so the guard never sees what git executes. This is an incomplete fix for an earlier bypass that handled only the split case.
preconditions: The application forwards a user-controlled kwargs dictionary to a guarded GitPython method such as clone_from, fetch, pull, push, ls_remote, iter_commits, blame or archive.
The attacker can include the split_single_char_options switch set to False together with a single-character key whose value carries the payload.
GitPython is older than 3.1.58, with unsafe options left disallowed by default.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to GitPython 3.1.58 or later. When building or reviewing such a guard, make it judge the same tokens git will receive. Either derive candidate options from the joined short-option form as well as the split form, or run the unsafe-option check over the fully transformed argument list instead of a reconstructed name-only list. Do not forward untrusted kwargs dictionaries to these methods without reviewing them.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change in 3.1.58 or confirm which approach it uses. They do not say whether other short options besides the upload-pack one are reachable the same way. The impact depends on the application forwarding attacker-controlled kwargs, and the report gives no guidance on filtering such input.

fixtures.scenario: A web service passes a client-supplied options dictionary straight into a clone call. The client sets the single-character-splitting switch to False and adds a one-letter option whose value starts with a short flag for upload-pack followed by a shell command. The guard passes and the command runs.
The service runs GitPython 3.1.58 or later, and the unsafe-option check sees the joined token that git will parse. The upload-pack option is detected and the call is rejected before any command runs.

citations.quote: Attackers can supply a crafted kwargs dictionary to guarded methods like clone_from to emit a joined token parsed as --upload-pack
git clusters value-less short flags then parses
The guard's candidate list omits the smuggled option

patterns.title: Untrusted .gitmodules include directive leaks local file content through GitPython submodule enumeration
patterns.cause: The parser used to read .gitmodules for submodule enumeration inherits the default behavior of merging include directives. A .gitmodules file shipped in a cloned repository can therefore name any local file in an include section. The include resolver follows absolute paths and unchecked relative paths, and its only gate is a readability check. When the target is not valid git-config syntax, the parser raises MissingSectionHeaderError, whose message embeds the file's first line verbatim. Submodule enumeration does not catch this error type, so the text reaches the caller, logs or error pages.
preconditions: The application opens a repository whose .gitmodules file is controlled by an untrusted party, such as a cloned third-party repository.
The application uses a GitPython version before 3.1.59 and accesses the repository submodules list, a read-only operation.
The target file is readable by the process and its first line is not a valid git-config section header.
Exception text from GitPython is visible to the attacker, for example through CI logs, error pages, or exception trackers.
patterns.prevention: Never let content from an untrusted repository pull in other files through include or includeIf directives. When parsing .gitmodules, construct the submodule config parser with include merging disabled, as the config writer path already does. Upgrade GitPython to 3.1.59 or later. As defense in depth, reject resolved include paths that fall outside the repository tree, and avoid echoing raw file content in parse errors for files the caller did not explicitly choose to open. Treat parser exceptions from submodule enumeration as untrusted-input failures and do not forward their text to users.
patterns.limitations: Only the first line of the target file leaks, because parsing aborts at the first error, but the same behavior works as a file-existence oracle. The sources do not describe the exact upstream change, so the path containment and error message hardening are advisory suggestions rather than confirmed parts of the fix. Include conditions (includeIf) are only followed when a repository is supplied to the parser, and the sources do not say whether other callers are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A service clones an untrusted repository whose .gitmodules adds an include section pointing at a local credentials file, then lists the repository submodules. The resulting parse error text, containing the file's first line, is written to a shared log.
The same service lists submodules with include merging disabled for .gitmodules, so the include section is ignored, no foreign file is opened, and no file content appears in any error message.

citations.quote: GitPython before 3.1.59 fails to disable merge_includes when parsing .gitmodules, allowing attackers to disclose local file content by including arbitrary file paths via [include] directives.
when repo.submodules is accessed, GitConfigParser raises MissingSectionHeaderError embedding the target file's first line verbatim in the exception message
a readability check, not a path restriction.

patterns.title: GitPython clone_from allows --separate-git-dir to place git metadata outside the destination
patterns.cause: The clone denylist, unsafe_git_clone_options, does not list --separate-git-dir, although the init denylist does and the clone docstring says allow_unsafe_options should gate it. The check only compares option names against the denylist and does not validate the path value. A separate_git_dir keyword therefore reaches the real git clone command with allow_unsafe_options at its default of False. Git then writes the full repository metadata tree to the given path and leaves a gitlink file at the intended destination.
preconditions: The host application forwards a caller-influenced value as the separate_git_dir keyword of Repo.clone_from() or Repo.clone(), or as a raw --separate-git-dir token in multi_options.
The application does not validate or reject that value and does not intentionally set allow_unsafe_options to True.
The process has permission to create directories at the attacker-chosen path.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to GitPython 3.1.59 or later. Do not pass untrusted keyword arguments or multi_options entries into clone calls, and keep allow_unsafe_options at False. An implementation should treat --separate-git-dir as unsafe on the clone path, as the init path already does, so that the same option-name guard used for --template, --upload-pack and --config also rejects it. Applications should also reject any caller-supplied repository-metadata location themselves.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change or its handling of option aliases. The guard inspects option names only, so it does not validate path values. Hook execution needs a later git operation on the redirected or colliding directory. Impact is bounded by the filesystem permissions of the process running GitPython.

fixtures.scenario: A service forwards a client-supplied separate_git_dir value into Repo.clone_from() with allow_unsafe_options left at its default. No error is raised, and git writes the repository metadata outside the clone destination.

The service never forwards client-controlled separate_git_dir values and runs GitPython 3.1.59 or later. Clone options come from a fixed set, so repository metadata stays inside the intended destination.

citations.quote: GitPython before 3.1.59 omits --separate-git-dir from unsafe_git_clone_options, allowing attackers to create arbitrary git directories outside the intended clone destination.
Parity gap between two sibling denylists that guard the same underlying primitive (arbitrary redirection of git metadata storage)
redirect repository metadata to an attacker-controlled filesystem path, enabling arbitrary directory creation and potential hook execution.

patterns.title: SSRF bypass in NLTK pathsec when an HTTP proxy is configured
patterns.cause: The URL helper validates the requested hostname locally. When proxy handlers are inherited, the safe HTTP and HTTPS handlers that pin the validated destination are disabled. The proxy then performs the real fetch against a destination that is never re-validated, so the validated hostname no longer matches the actual egress target.
preconditions: NLTK version before 3.10.3 using nltk.pathsec.urlopen or its callers (nltk.data.load, Downloader.index, Downloader.download)
An HTTP proxy is configured in the runtime
The application relies on pathsec as its SSRF barrier
An attacker can choose a public URL that the proxy forwards to an internal loopback-only service
patterns.prevention: Do not treat local hostname validation as sufficient when a proxy performs the fetch. Either validate the destination the proxy will actually reach, or fail closed and refuse the request when it would fall back to an unpinned proxied path. Apply this to every kind of proxy, including environment-configured proxies and explicitly added proxy handlers. Allow proxied fetches only through a deliberate operator opt-in for a proxy that is trusted. Upgrade to NLTK 3.10.3 or later. Add regression tests covering pathsec.urlopen, nltk.data.load and downloader fetches with a proxy configured.
patterns.limitations: The sources conflict on patch status: the advisory text says not yet patched, while the CVE record says versions before 3.10.3 are affected. The sources do not describe the exact commit contents. The operator opt-in restores the exposure, so the proxy's own network controls then decide what can be reached. Direct, non-proxied fetches were described as still protected by destination pinning. Published 3.9.4 did not reproduce the issue.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs an affected NLTK with an HTTP proxy configured and loads a public URL that passes hostname validation. The proxy forwards it to a loopback-only internal service, and the internal content is returned to the caller.

The same service runs a patched NLTK with a proxy configured and enforcement on. The proxied fetch is refused unless operators deliberately opted in to trust the proxy, so the internal service is not reached.

citations.quote: proxy-handler inheritance disables the safe HTTP/HTTPS handlers so the actual fetch is performed by the proxy against a destination that is never re-validated
NLTK cannot pin the egress through a proxy, so it stops pretending to
NLTK before 3.10.3 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability

patterns.title: Unrestricted pickle loading of NLTK TransitionParser model files allows code execution
patterns.cause: In NLTK 3.9.4 and earlier, TransitionParser.parse() loads a model file through the library's pickle_load() helper with its restricted option left at the default of off. That routes the data through WarningUnpickler, which only warns and does not override find_class(). Any class or function named in the file can therefore be resolved during unpickling, so a crafted model file runs arbitrary Python code. NLTK ships a RestrictedUnpickler that blocks this, but the sources say no production code path uses it. The same default is reported at call sites in the chart parser application.
preconditions: The application runs NLTK 3.9.4 or earlier (fixed in 3.10.0).
The application calls TransitionParser.parse() with a model file path.
An attacker can supply or replace the model file that gets loaded.
The pickle loading helper is used without its restricted option turned on.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to NLTK 3.10.0 or later, where the same malicious file is rejected because its global is not in a pickle allowlist. Treat every model file as executable content: load only files from trusted, integrity-controlled locations and never from user-supplied or world-writable paths. In code that calls the pickle loading helper, choose the restricted deserialization mode so unpickling resolves only allowlisted globals. Where stricter control is needed, prefer an allowlist of permitted modules over trusting file names or paths.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe exactly what 3.10.0 changed or what its allowlist contains. They note that restricted loading may break older sklearn-based models and that a module allowlist would be more robust. Chart parser application call sites are listed as using the same unsafe default, but the sources do not say whether 3.10.0 changes them. The sources do not cover other NLTK loaders or verification of model file provenance.

fixtures.scenario: A data pipeline on NLTK 3.9.4 accepts a model file path from an upload form and passes it to TransitionParser.parse(). An attacker uploads a pickle whose reduce hook invokes a system command. Unpickling runs it with the privileges of the pipeline user.

The pipeline runs NLTK 3.10.0 or later and loads models only from a read-only directory controlled by the operator. A crafted pickle naming a system call is rejected with an error saying the global is not in the allowlist, and no command runs.

citations.quote: WarningUnpickler, which does not override find_class() and therefore permits arbitrary class resolution.
NLTK provides a RestrictedUnpickler for safe deserialization, but it is not used by production code paths.
embedded pickle gadget chains execute arbitrary Python code with the privileges of the user running the application.
A more robust approach would implement a module allowlist in `RestrictedUnpickler.find_class()`.

patterns.title: Allowlisted pickle loaders that trust whole module namespaces allow code execution
patterns.cause: The allowlisted pickle loaders in NLTK trusted entire module namespaces instead of exact safe callables. A crafted pickle can use the REDUCE opcode to call dangerous functions inside an allowed namespace, such as the REPP tokenizer execute method or a numpy f2py helper that evaluates attacker-controlled input. The code runs during unpickling.
preconditions: The application loads a tokenizer or model artifact from an untrusted source.
The artifact is loaded through an allowlisted loader such as the punkt loader or the transition parser parse method.
The loader's allowlist permits a whole module or namespace prefix rather than exact names.
patterns.prevention: Allow only exact pairs of module and qualified name for the few classes or functions that are genuinely needed. Never allow whole namespaces such as the tokenize package or numpy. Reject dotted attribute names during class lookup. Deny dangerous modules (os, subprocess, sys, builtins, numpy.f2py, the REPP tokenizer module) as a backstop even when a broad allowlist exists. Name safe primitives such as int individually. Treat post-load type checks as a secondary defense only, because code runs before they happen. Upgrade NLTK to 3.10.3 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not give the full 3.10.3 fix. The GHSA text says not yet patched, while the CVE text says versions before 3.10.3 are affected. The transition parser still allows numpy, scipy and sklearn because array unpickling needs their submodules, so it relies on the deny guards. A denylist is only a backstop. Some other loaders read user-selected files and rely on warnings.

fixtures.scenario: A loader allowlists the whole tokenize namespace. A pickle that names the REPP tokenizer execute method as its REDUCE callable runs a command while the artifact is loaded.
A loader allows only exact named globals, rejects dotted names and denies dangerous modules. The same pickle is refused at class lookup, and a legitimate punkt round trip still loads.

citations.quote: The allowlist trusts whole module namespaces instead of exact safe globals, so crafted pickles can invoke dangerous in-namespace callables through pickle REDUCE.
keep post-load type validation only as a secondary defense.
NLTK versions before 3.10.3 contain a remote code execution vulnerability in allowlisted pickle loaders that trust entire module namespaces instead of specific safe callables.

patterns.title: Corpus reader constructors bypass the pathsec sandbox on caller-supplied roots
patterns.cause: A string corpus root is turned into a path pointer without pathsec validation. Some readers then call the builtin file open or the sqlite3 connect function directly on paths derived from that root. These calls never reach the sandbox check that the pathsec file API applies, so files and SQLite databases outside the intended data root can be read even with enforcement enabled.
preconditions: The application passes a caller-influenced corpus root path to a reader constructor such as LinThesaurusCorpusReader or PanLexLiteCorpusReader
The NLTK version is older than 3.10.3
The target file or SQLite database is readable by the process but lies outside the intended NLTK data root
patterns.prevention: Treat every corpus root as untrusted input. Validate raw string roots against the allowed data roots before building a reader. Route all root and derived-path handling through pathsec or a validated path pointer, and avoid direct builtin file opens and direct SQLite connections on constructor-derived paths. Upgrade to NLTK 3.10.3 or later. Until then, do not pass user-controlled roots to corpus readers.
patterns.limitations: The sources name only LinThesaurusCorpusReader and PanLexLiteCorpusReader as demonstrated entry points. They do not say whether other readers are affected. They do not describe the exact upstream fix. The advisory describes read access only, and the proof of concept patches the allowed-roots set to simulate a sandbox with no permitted roots.

fixtures.scenario: An app builds a LinThesaurusCorpusReader or PanLexLiteCorpusReader from a user-supplied directory string on an NLTK version before 3.10.3. The reader opens a file or SQLite database outside the data root, although direct pathsec access to that location is blocked.

The app upgrades to NLTK 3.10.3 or later and checks the root against the allowed data roots before constructing any reader. An outside-root path is rejected, and only validated roots reach the reader.

citations.quote: NLTK versions before 3.10.3 contain a path sandbox bypass vulnerability in corpus-reader constructors that allows attackers to read files outside the intended data root.
The constructor path therefore never hits the sandbox guard that
Required privileges: none beyond the ability to supply a corpus root path to a consumer call site

patterns.title: Unvalidated per-call JVM options in NLTK Stanford wrappers allow JVM flag injection
patterns.cause: NLTK added validation of JVM options only on the global configuration path (config_java). The java() function's per-call options parameter was passed straight into the JVM command line without validation. All four Stanford wrapper classes (parser, tagger, tokenizer, segmenter) store user-supplied java_options and send them through this unvalidated path. This bypasses the earlier fix for CVE-2026-12841.
preconditions: NLTK before 3.10.3 is in use with a Stanford wrapper class or a direct call to java() with its per-call options parameter
The java options value is influenced by an attacker, for example through user input, configuration files or environment variables
A Java runtime is available so the JVM command is actually launched
patterns.prevention: Apply the same option validation on every path that can add options to the JVM command line, including the per-call path, not only the global configuration setter. Reject agent-loading flags (agentlib, agentpath, javaagent), the remote debugging flag (Xrunjdwp) and argument-file references that start with the at sign. Upgrade NLTK to 3.10.3 or later. Do not build java options from untrusted input; prefer a fixed set of options chosen by the application.
patterns.limitations: The sources name only a few dangerous flags and do not give the full block list or describe how the shipped fix handles edge cases such as unusual quoting or option spelling. They do not describe the upstream commit beyond saying the per-call path lacked validation. Validation by block list may miss other risky flags, and the sources do not say whether an allow list was adopted.

fixtures.scenario: A web service builds a Stanford parser wrapper and fills its java options argument from a request field. A caller submits an option that loads a native agent from a path they control, and the flag reaches the JVM unchecked.

The service uses NLTK 3.10.3 or later and passes only fixed, application-chosen java options. Any per-call option with an agent, debug or argument-file flag is rejected before the JVM command is built.

citations.quote: NLTK before 3.10.3 fails to validate JVM options passed through the per-call options parameter in the java() function
All four Stanford Java wrapper classes accept user-supplied

patterns.title: Corpus readers reopening root-derived paths with built-in open let symlinks escape the trusted root
patterns.cause: Several NLTK corpus readers (ipipan, crubadan, lin) derive file paths from trusted corpus state, convert them back to plain strings, and reopen them with built-in open() instead of nltk.pathsec.open(). The symlink-aware trusted-root check is skipped, so a symlink inside the root can point outside it and still be parsed.
preconditions: The application uses an NLTK version before 3.10.3 with an affected corpus reader.
An attacker can stage corpus files or symlinks under a trusted NLTK data root or trusted corpus directory.
The reader opens a root-derived file such as header.xml, table.txt, or a simN.lsp file through built-in open().
Parsed results are returned to a caller through public reader methods such as channels(), domains(), or synonyms().
patterns.prevention: Every file open that starts from a root-derived path must go through the root-aware check. Use nltk.pathsec.open(), or validate the path with the pathsec validation helper scoped to the reader's own corpus root, before opening. Keep the trusted-root information attached to derived paths instead of reducing them to plain strings. Where a reader has a concrete corpus root, scope the check to it. Audit all raw file opens in the corpus readers, not only the three named ones. Upgrade to NLTK 3.10.3 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources give conflicting patch status: the advisory text says not yet patched, while the CVE record says versions before 3.10.3 are affected. They describe the fix only at a high level. The audit notes say the path validation does not block hardlinks, which are tracked separately, and does not close the race between validating and opening. Readers without a concrete root fall back to a global sandbox whose allowed-roots list includes the system temp directory, so that fallback is weaker. The sources do not say whether other readers outside those listed are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A shared corpus directory is the trusted root. A contributor adds a symlink named table.txt or header.xml pointing to a file outside it. The reader opens it with built-in open, and public methods return content from outside the root.

Same directory and symlink, but the reader opens each derived path through the root-aware pathsec check scoped to the corpus root. The escaping symlink is rejected, while ordinary regular files inside the root still load normally.

citations.quote: NLTK versions before 3.10.3 contain a path traversal vulnerability in corpus readers that reopen root-derived paths using built-in open()
Attackers who stage symlinked corpus files under a trusted data root can disclose outside-root content through normal corpus reader methods
The global-sandbox fallback (toolbox, named_entity, xmldocs-view) is only as tight as the allowed-roots list

patterns.title: ReDoS in NLTK Text.findall and TokenSearcher.findall from unvalidated user-supplied regular expressions
patterns.cause: The findall methods of Text and TokenSearcher take a caller-supplied regular expression and run it with the Python re engine, with no validation and no timeout. The only preprocessing rewrites the angle-bracket syntax and does not inspect or reject patterns that backtrack catastrophically. A nested-quantifier pattern run against a token that cannot match forces exhaustive backtracking and pins the CPU.
preconditions: NLTK version is earlier than 3.10.0
Text.findall or TokenSearcher.findall is called with a pattern that an external party controls
The pattern contains constructs that cause catastrophic backtracking, such as nested quantifiers, and the searched text does not match it
patterns.prevention: Upgrade NLTK to a patched release (3.10.0 or later). Until then, treat any regular expression from outside the trust boundary as hostile and do not pass it to the findall methods of Text or TokenSearcher. If user patterns must be supported, an implementation should check them before use and bound how long matching can run, so one request cannot monopolize the Python process. Prefer fixed, developer-written patterns.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the patch works, so the exact validation or timeout behavior in the fixed release is unknown. They say only that commit d8e4753 resolved the issue and that versions before 3.10.0 are affected. They do not say whether other NLTK modules that accept regular expressions are affected, and they do not give a safe-pattern policy.

fixtures.scenario: A web service takes a pattern from a request and passes it to the findall method of an NLTK Text object on a version before 3.10.0. A crafted nested-quantifier pattern run against a token that cannot match pins the CPU for all users.

The service runs NLTK 3.10.0 or later, and pattern strings from outside callers are never passed to findall. Only fixed, developer-written patterns are used, so a request cannot trigger runaway backtracking.

citations.quote: accept user-supplied regular expressions without validation or timeout
resulting in indefinite CPU saturation and denial of service to all users of the Python process.
Users should update to the patched version.

patterns.title: ReDoS in NLTK tgrep via user-supplied regex nodes
patterns.cause: The tgrep module compiles regular expressions embedded in pattern nodes and runs them with re.search against tree node labels, with no validation and no timeout. A pattern chosen by an attacker can trigger catastrophic backtracking, which saturates the CPU and blocks the Python process.
preconditions: Application uses nltk.tgrep, for example tgrep_positions() or tgrep_compile()
The tgrep pattern, or a regex node inside it, comes from an external or untrusted source
NLTK version is earlier than 3.10.3
patterns.prevention: Do not let untrusted callers choose tgrep patterns that contain regex nodes. Accept only trusted or fixed patterns, or reject regex nodes in external input. Upgrade to NLTK 3.10.3 or later. Where regex execution on external input remains, bound its run time, for example by isolating it in a separate process that can be terminated. This matches the timeout-guarded direction the maintainers described.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the final upstream fix, so its exact mechanism is unknown. They give no validation rules for regex nodes and do not say whether 3.10.3 validates patterns, limits time, or does both. The timeout approach is described only as a planned patch. Risk grows with pathological patterns and non-matching node labels, but no precise thresholds are given.

fixtures.scenario: A web API passes a client-supplied tgrep pattern to tgrep_positions(). The pattern has a regex node with nested quantifiers, and a tree label of repeated characters cannot match it, so the worker spins on backtracking.

The service runs NLTK 3.10.3 or later and accepts only tgrep patterns from trusted authors or a fixed allowlist. Untrusted callers cannot supply regex nodes, so no attacker-chosen regex reaches the engine.

citations.quote: compiles user-supplied regular expressions embedded in /regex/ pattern nodes and executes them via re.search against tree node labels without any validation or timeout.
Maintainers are currently collaborating on a patch to wrap the regex execution in a timeout-guarded mechanism.
NLTK before 3.10.3 contains a regular expression denial of service (ReDoS) vulnerability in the tgrep module.

patterns.title: Quadratic ReDoS in NLTK Pl196xCorpusReader on malformed TEI blocks
patterns.cause: Pl196xCorpusReader parses whole TEI text blocks with several lazy regular expressions. When a block holds many opening tags with no matching closing tags, each match attempt scans toward the end of the block and fails, then restarts at the next opening tag. This repeated rescanning gives quadratic CPU growth.
preconditions: The application parses attacker-influenced PL196X or TEI-like corpus files with Pl196xCorpusReader
The file contains a text block with many unmatched opening tags such as paragraph tags
A public reader API such as words() or tagged_words() is called on the file
The NLTK version is earlier than 3.10.3
patterns.prevention: Upgrade NLTK to 3.10.3 or later. Where upgrading is not possible, do not parse untrusted corpus files with this reader. A safe implementation avoids lazy whole-block regular expressions that restart from every opening tag, and instead uses a linear parser or a bounded tokenizer that reads the block once. Regression tests should check near-linear runtime on malformed inputs with many unmatched tags.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change in 3.10.3, so the precise parsing approach of the fix is unconfirmed. The advisory timings come from one reproduction and will vary by machine. The sources give no guidance on input size limits or timeouts as mitigations.

fixtures.scenario: A service accepts uploaded PL196X corpus files and calls words() on each. An upload has a valid header and a text block with thousands of opening paragraph tags and no closers. Runtime roughly quadruples each time the tag count doubles, stalling the parser thread.

The service runs a patched NLTK release (3.10.3 or later) whose reader parses blocks in a single linear pass. The same malformed upload is rejected or yields no content, and runtime grows roughly in proportion to input size.

citations.quote: Lazy `.*?` whole-block regexes rescan untrusted XML-like blocks from each opening-tag position.
Replace the whole-block lazy-regex parser with a linear parser or bounded tokenizer
NLTK before 3.10.3 contains a regular expression denial of service vulnerability in Pl196xCorpusReader

patterns.title: Model-artifact APIs in NLTK bypass pathsec containment by using raw file open on caller-chosen paths
patterns.cause: Several NLTK model import and export helpers, including TransitionParser train and parse, AveragedPerceptron save and load, PerceptronTagger save to JSON, and the maxent parameter saver, open caller-controlled paths with the built-in open function. They do not use pathsec-aware helpers, so paths outside the allowed roots are read or written even though guarded sibling helpers reject the same paths.
preconditions: The application enables pathsec enforcement and restricts allowed roots to a sandbox directory.
Untrusted workflows or users can choose model import or export paths.
The application calls one of the affected model-artifact APIs in NLTK through 3.10.3.
patterns.prevention: Send every model-path file read and write through the pathsec-aware open helper or the existing guarded helpers, never the built-in open function. Treat any caller-supplied model path as untrusted until pathsec has checked it. Add regression tests that pair each model API with a negative control, such as a guarded helper, on the same outside-root path.
patterns.limitations: The sources say the issue affects 3.9.4, 3.10.0-rc2 and, per the CVE text, versions through 3.10.3. One advisory says not yet patched, so the fixed version is unclear. The sources do not describe how symlinks are handled, and they only describe exposure when pathsec is enabled. They do not describe the upstream fix in detail.

fixtures.scenario: Pathsec enforcement is on with one sandbox root. A workflow lets users pick a path for saving or loading a parser or perceptron model, and a path outside the root is read or written even though the guarded open helper rejects it.
Same setup, but model load and save go through the pathsec-aware open helper, so an outside-root path is rejected. A test checks each API against a negative control on the same path.

citations.quote: path traversal vulnerability in model-artifact APIs that bypass pathsec enforcement by using raw file operations on caller-controlled paths.
Several model-artifact APIs still treat caller-controlled model paths as ordinary filenames even when NLTK path security is enforced.

patterns.title: Pre-existing hardlinks in the install tree let NLTK downloader overwrite outside files
patterns.cause: The NLTK downloader checks for path traversal and symlink escapes during ZIP extraction, but it treats a pre-existing hardlink in the install tree as an ordinary in-root file. Extracted member data is then written through the hardlink and changes the outside inode.
preconditions: The downloader root is writable by an attacker, for example a shared downloader directory.
The attacker can create a hardlink inside that root pointing to a target file outside it on the same filesystem.
A normal package install via Downloader.download or Downloader.incr_download extracts a member onto the hardlink path.
The NLTK version is earlier than 3.10.3.
patterns.prevention: Treat a pre-existing hardlink at an extraction target as unsafe and refuse to write through it, as is already done for a symlink at the same location. Verify at the inode level that each write path stays within the intended install tree, since a path-name check alone does not reveal a hardlink alias. Add regression tests that pair hardlink cases with existing symlink negative controls. Upgrade to NLTK 3.10.3 or later, and avoid shared or attacker-writable downloader directories.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream patch detects hardlinks or which exact checks it uses, so this card gives only the direction. The attack needs the target file on the same filesystem as the downloader root. The sources do not say whether other extraction paths are affected, or whether other file types besides hardlinks and symlinks are involved.

fixtures.scenario: A downloader root on a shared writable volume holds a pre-existing hardlink at a path where a package member will extract. It points to a same-filesystem file outside the root. A normal install writes through it and the outside file changes.

Same layout, but the installer detects the pre-existing hardlink at the extraction target, as it already does for a symlink, and refuses to write through it. The outside file keeps its original content.

citations.quote: The downloader validates traversal and symlink conditions but does not reject pre-existing hardlink aliases inside the install tree.
Attackers with write access to a shared downloader directory can create hardlinks pointing to outside-root files that are then overwritten during normal package extraction
Treat pre-existing hardlinks as unsafe in extraction targets, verify that each write path stays within the intended install tree at the inode level

patterns.title: Client-supplied routing and credential parameters redirect proxy provider calls and leak stored keys
patterns.cause: The proxy checked request bodies with an incomplete denylist. It did not cover every sensitive parameter and did not inspect equivalent values nested in other request fields, in path values, or in bracket-notation form data. A caller could therefore supply a routing or credential value, such as api_base, base_url, model_list, fallbacks, or litellm_credential_name, and the proxy applied it without clearing the operator's stored key.
preconditions: The caller is an authenticated user of the LiteLLM proxy, including a holder of a low-privilege proxy key.
The proxy is running a version older than the patched releases, for example older than 1.88.6 or 1.96.2 on those lines.
The proxy has provider credentials configured, and client-side overrides of connection parameters are not disabled.
The proxy can reach internal services, which makes server-side requests to them possible.
patterns.prevention: Do not rely on a partial denylist to protect routing and credential parameters. Apply the checks to every sensitive parameter and to equivalent values wherever they can appear: nested request fields, path values, and bracket-notation form data. Make sure a client-supplied routing or credential value is never applied while the operator's stored key stays attached to the outbound call. Upgrade to a patched release. Until then, set the general_settings option allow_client_side_credentials to false, restrict proxy keys to trusted callers, and block the affected parameters at a reverse proxy or API gateway.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the internals of the fix, so the exact validation design is unspecified. They name the affected files but not the individual checks changed. The listed workarounds reduce exposure but are not a substitute for upgrading. The sources do not say whether other deployments or configurations are affected.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated proxy user sends a request whose body includes an api_base value pointing to a server they control. The proxy applies it and calls that server with the operator's stored provider key, so the key is leaked.
The same request is rejected or the override is ignored, because the sensitive parameter is checked wherever it appears, including nested fields, and client-side credential overrides are disabled.

citations.quote: any authenticated LiteLLM proxy user could redirect an outbound provider call to a destination the user controls
The proxy's request-body validation was a denylist that did not cover every sensitive parameter and did not inspect parameters nested inside other request fields
restrict proxy keys to trusted callers

patterns.title: Path traversal via console_scripts and gui_scripts entry point names in pip
patterns.cause: pip treated console_scripts and gui_scripts entry point names as paths instead of plain file names, and did not sanitize the resolved absolute path against the installation directory. Entry points could therefore be written outside the intended directory.
preconditions: A package being installed declares console_scripts or gui_scripts entry points
An entry point name contains path components that resolve outside the installation directory
The affected pip version generates scripts from those names without validating the resolved path
patterns.prevention: Treat each entry point name strictly as a file name, not a path. Reject names containing directory separators or parent-directory components. Resolve the final absolute script path, for example with os.path.realpath(), and confirm it is inside the target scripts directory before writing anything. Upgrade to a pip release that includes the fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not list affected or fixed pip versions, exploit details, or the exact validation rules used upstream. They also do not say which platforms or install modes are impacted. Check the upstream advisory and pull request for specifics.

fixtures.scenario: A package declares a console_scripts entry whose name contains parent-directory components. The installer joins it to the scripts directory without checking, so the launcher lands outside the install location.

The installer treats the entry name as a bare file name, rejects separators and parent-directory parts, and verifies the resolved path is inside the scripts directory. A traversing name causes the install to fail.

citations.quote: pip would treat console_scripts and gui_scripts as paths instead of file names without sanitizing the resolved absolute path to the installation directory
leading to entry points being installed outside the installation directory.

patterns.title: ReDoS in GitPython actor parsing of commit author and committer headers
patterns.cause: GitPython before 3.1.60 parses the author and committer header of a commit object with a pattern that has an unbounded greedy name group followed by a literal space and opening angle bracket. When the header has a long string and an opening angle bracket with no closing one, the regex engine backtracks quadratically. The header text comes straight from the raw commit bytes, with no length limit, character restriction or timeout before it reaches the regex engine.
preconditions: The application uses GitPython before 3.1.60 and reads the author or committer of a commit, directly or through iteration or blame.
The commit object comes from a source the application does not fully control, such as a third-party repository, pull request, bundle or archive.
The author or committer header holds a very long string with an unterminated opening angle bracket, which can be written at the object level without git's write-side sanity checks.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade GitPython to 3.1.60 or later. In any actor-line parser, do not let the name group match angle brackets, so a missing closing bracket fails in linear time instead of quadratic time. As defense in depth, reject author and committer lines above a modest length before any regex runs. Where untrusted repositories are processed, also run commit parsing under a time limit or in a separate worker so one crafted commit cannot stall the whole pipeline.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, only an advisory suggestion, so its exact shape is not confirmed here. The advisory gives a 4096-byte limit only as an example, not a vetted threshold. Timings were measured on GitPython 3.1.59 with Python 3.12.3 and may differ elsewhere. The sources do not say whether other parsing patterns in the library are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A repository holds a commit whose author header has a 200000-byte name followed by an opening angle bracket with no closing one. A CI worker reads the commit author with GitPython 3.1.59 and stalls for about 150 seconds.

The same crafted commit is read with GitPython 3.1.60 or later, or with a parser whose name and email groups exclude angle brackets and which rejects oversized header lines first, so parsing finishes or fails promptly.

citations.quote: the Python regex engine enters quadratic backtracking, causing complete single-threaded CPU exhaustion proportional to the square of the input length.
no length limit, character restriction, or timeout
GitPython before 3.1.60 contains a regular expression denial of service vulnerability in Actor.name_email_regex that processes commit author and committer fields.

patterns.title: Same-origin sandbox grant in proxied terminal port preview iframe enables account takeover
patterns.cause: The port preview iframe used a fixed sandbox that combined script execution with same-origin access. The terminal proxy serves previewed port content from the application's own origin and adds no Content-Security-Policy by default. The sandbox was therefore the only isolation boundary, and it granted the permission that removes that isolation. Script on a previewed port could reach the parent window and read the session token.
preconditions: An admin has configured at least one shared terminal server that both attacker and victim can reach
The attacker has an ordinary authenticated account and can start a listening process on that terminal
The victim opens the port list and clicks the attacker's port
No restrictive Content-Security-Policy or terminal proxy header setting is applied to the proxied response
patterns.prevention: Do not combine script execution with same-origin access for iframes that show untrusted content served from your own origin. Make same-origin access an explicit per-user opt-in that is off by default, so the preview loads at an opaque origin and cannot reach the parent context. Apply this to every iframe, not just some. Where possible, serve proxied untrusted content from a separate origin, or add a restrictive Content-Security-Policy to the proxied response. Upgrade to 0.11.1 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact sandbox attribute handling beyond the opt-in setting. Users who enable the same-origin setting regain the vulnerable behavior. Sources do not cover separate-origin hosting or header hardening in detail. Personal terminals with external URLs and deployments with no terminal server were not affected.

fixtures.scenario: An admin configures a shared terminal server. A normal user starts a web service on a port there that serves a script. A victim clicks that port in the preview, and the iframe runs the script in the application origin with parent access.

The same shared terminal setup, but the preview iframe lacks same-origin permission unless the user explicitly enabled the opt-in setting, which is off by default. The attacker's page loads at an opaque origin and cannot reach the parent.

citations.quote: src/lib/components/chat/FileNav/PortPreview.svelte rendered terminal port content in an iframe sandbox containing both allow-scripts and allow-same-origin.
Because the terminal proxy serves that content from the Open WebUI origin, an authenticated user with access to a shared terminal server
so the preview loads at an opaque origin and cannot reach the parent context.

patterns.title: DNS rebinding SSRF from double hostname resolution in the Open WebUI Playwright web loader
patterns.cause: The loader validated the address of a user-submitted hostname in Python, then handed the request to the Playwright browser. The browser resolved the hostname a second time and connected to an answer that was never checked. The check and the connection used two different resolvers in two different processes, so the check could not constrain where the browser connected.
preconditions: The web loader engine is set to the Playwright option, which is not the default.
A Playwright browser is reachable, either local or remote.
An authenticated user, with no administrator role needed, can submit a URL for ingestion or trigger a web search.
The attacker controls authoritative DNS for the submitted hostname and answers the two lookups differently, and the browser can reach internal services.
patterns.prevention: Resolve the hostname once, validate that result, and make the connection to that same validated address. Do not hand the network request to a component that resolves names on its own after validation. Re-validate every redirect hop the same way. If a browser must be involved, give it only the response that the application's own safe HTTP client fetched. The sources report the issue as fixed in version 0.11.1.
patterns.limitations: The sources name the affected range as 0.9.6 until 0.11.1 and describe the fix only in general terms. They say the path from the HTTP endpoint to the loader was traced in source, not driven end to end. They report a read primitive only, with no modification or availability impact demonstrated. They do not discuss other mitigations, such as network egress restrictions for the browser process.

fixtures.scenario: A user submits a URL on an attacker-run domain. Python validation sees a public address, then the Playwright browser resolves the name again, gets an internal or metadata address, and the response appears in the search or ingestion result.

The hostname is resolved once, the address is validated, and the application's own HTTP client connects to that same address. Each redirect hop is re-validated, and the browser is given only the response that was received.

citations.quote: The browser resolved the hostname a second time, on its own, and that answer was never checked.
It issues the request from the SSRF-safe HTTP client instead, which resolves the hostname once and connects to that same validated address
From 0.9.6 until 0.11.1, SafePlaywrightURLLoader in backend/open_webui/retrieval/web/utils.py validated a user-controlled hostname in Python

patterns.title: Server-side URL fetch treats globally routable as proof a destination is external
patterns.cause: The address screen for server-side URL fetches (RAG URL ingestion and web search) treated Python's globally routable classification as proof that a destination was external. Some internal-purpose addresses, such as the Azure platform channel 168.63.129.16, are allocated from ordinary public space and pass that test. The earlier hardening that unwrapped IPv6 addresses carrying an IPv4 address left this test unchanged.
preconditions: The attacker is an authenticated, verified user who can reach RAG URL ingestion or web search; no administrator role or special workspace permission is needed.
Local web fetch is at its default of disabled, so the address screen is the only control in place.
No operator-supplied filter list entry covers the reserved addresses; the list is empty by default in affected versions.
For the Azure platform channel, the host must run on Azure. Elsewhere that address routes nowhere.
patterns.prevention: Do not equate globally routable with external. Apply an explicit default block list of reserved and internal-purpose ranges to every resolved address, at URL validation and again at connection time on every HTTP transport, so redirect hops and DNS rebinding are also covered. Let operators extend the list but not remove the defaults. Also reject alternative spellings of blocked addresses, such as IPv4-mapped, IPv4-translated, 6to4 and NAT64 forms and obfuscated decimal, octal or hexadecimal notation.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not list the full default block list. No credential or secret was shown to be retrieved from the Azure platform channel, and no request was issued to a live one. The read-back was confirmed only through the ingestion endpoint's response. Deployments with local web fetch enabled were never protected by this screen. Only the fetch paths named in the sources were analyzed.

fixtures.scenario: A verified user submits a URL containing the Azure platform channel address to the RAG URL ingestion endpoint on an Azure-hosted instance with default settings. The screen passes it and the response body is returned to the caller.

The same URL is rejected because a block list of reserved ranges is checked on each resolved address at validation and at connection time, including redirect hops. Ordinary public addresses still pass.

citations.quote: That screen decided whether a destination was external by asking Python's standard library whether the address is globally routable.
a default block list of reserved and internal-purpose ranges is applied to every resolved address, at URL validation and again at connection time
No specific credential or secret was retrieved from the Azure platform channel during this investigation, and this advisory does not claim one.

patterns.title: SSRF via unvalidated HTTP redirect destinations in server-side fetches
patterns.cause: The excluded-host list was checked only during validation of the URL the user submitted. The private-address check sat in the aiohttp resolver, which aiohttp skips for hosts written as IP literals. When redirect following was added as an option, neither control was applied to the redirect destination.
preconditions: Redirect following is enabled through the AIOHTTP_CLIENT_ALLOW_REDIRECTS setting, which defaults to false, on an Open WebUI build from 0.9.5 up to before 0.11.1.
The attacker has an authenticated account of any role.
The account can use a feature that makes the server fetch a URL, such as web search, URL ingestion, the page fetch tool, or chat image URLs.
patterns.prevention: Apply the excluded-host list to every request on each HTTP client, at the point where the real destination is known, so that it covers every redirect hop and reused connections. Keep the private-address check at connection time and hook it where aiohttp resolves hosts, so that hosts written as IP literals are covered too. Upgrade to 0.11.1 or later. If outbound fetches go through a forward proxy, enforce destination restrictions on the proxy itself.
patterns.limitations: Behind a forward proxy, the private-address check sees the proxy address instead of the final destination, so the upgrade alone does not constrain it. Only the excluded-host list still applies to the destination on that path. The sources do not show that an aiohttp path can return an attacker-chosen response verbatim to the requester. They also do not address other versions or other settings.

fixtures.scenario: Redirect following is on. A user submits a public URL that is not excluded. The page redirects to an excluded host or to a loopback IP literal, and the server connects to it with no check applied at the redirect hop.
Redirect following is on, on version 0.11.1 or later. The same redirect is blocked at the hop before any connection, because both checks run on the destination. Ordinary public fetches still work.

citations.quote: Neither control was applied to the destination of an HTTP redirect.
aiohttp answers a host written as an IP address itself without consulting a resolver
Where the server reaches the internet through a forward proxy, the private-address check sees the proxy's address rather than the final destination
From 0.9.5 until 0.11.1, server-side web fetches did not reapply WEB_FETCH_FILTER_LIST or private-address controls to HTTP redirect destinations

patterns.title: KMS endpoint ending in .sock is treated as a Unix domain socket path in PyMongo field level encryption
patterns.cause: PyMongo passed the masterKey.endpoint value from a key vault document into its host parsing helper without validating it. That helper returns any string ending in .sock unchanged, skipping the hostname and port validation applied to other inputs. The connection code then treated the string as a filesystem path and connected to it with AF_UNIX, although the custom KMS endpoint feature is documented to support TCP hosts only.
preconditions: The application uses client-side field level encryption or Queryable Encryption.
An attacker can write to the key vault collection, for example by editing masterKey.endpoint on a data key.
The driver makes a KMS request for the altered key, which happens on the next request once the key cache entry (about 60 seconds) expires.
patterns.prevention: Treat the KMS endpoint read from the key vault as untrusted input. Validate it as a hostname and port, and reject any endpoint ending in .sock with a configuration error before any connection is attempted, on both synchronous and asynchronous paths. Do not let a stored endpoint string select a Unix domain socket path. Upgrade to PyMongo 4.18.2 or later. As defense in depth, restrict write access to the key vault collection to trusted principals, validate masterKey.endpoint on keys you create, and audit existing key vault documents for endpoints ending in .sock.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe limited impact: the socket is wrapped in a verifying TLS context, insecure KMS TLS options are rejected, and the handshake always fails, so only a fixed TLS ClientHello start is sent and the attacker does not choose the bytes. The sources do not state the first affected PyMongo version or whether other side effects of connecting to a local socket are possible. Restricting key vault write access is a mitigation, not a fix.

fixtures.scenario: An application using CSFLE on an unpatched PyMongo reads a data key whose masterKey.endpoint was changed to a value ending in .sock. The driver treats it as a local socket path and opens an AF_UNIX connection from inside the application process.

The same application runs a patched PyMongo. The .sock endpoint is rejected with a configuration error before any connection is attempted, and only the key vault's trusted principals can write data keys.

citations.quote: can cause an application using the driver to open connections to local sockets on the application host
The documented custom KMS endpoint feature supports TCP hosts only
Applications whose key vault is not writable by untrusted parties are not affected.

patterns.title: Chat template names used as filenames in save_pretrained allow path traversal
patterns.cause: The save_pretrained() methods of PreTrainedTokenizerBase and ProcessorMixin use keys from the chat_template dictionary directly as filenames without proper validation. Those keys come from a tokenizer_config.json file that an attacker can control, so they can escape the intended save directory.
preconditions: The victim loads a tokenizer or processor from an attacker-published Hugging Face Hub repository with a crafted tokenizer_config.json
The chat_template value is a dictionary whose keys are attacker-controlled
The victim then calls save_pretrained() on the loaded tokenizer or processor
The installed transformers version is earlier than 5.10.0
patterns.prevention: Treat every chat template name as untrusted data and never use it as a path component as received. Validate each name before writing: accept only a plain file-name-like value with no directory separators or parent-directory segments, and reject anything else. As a second check, resolve the final target path (for example with os.path.realpath()) and confirm it stays inside the intended save directory before any file is created. Upgrading to transformers 5.10.0 or later is the stated fixed range.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact validation rules the upstream fix applies, so the allowed character set and the handling of rejected names (error versus skip) are not specified here. They do not list other code paths that might use template names as filenames. The affected-version bounds differ between the sources: one says earlier than 5.10.0, the other says up to 5.8.0.dev0.

fixtures.scenario: A tokenizer_config.json from a Hub repo has a chat_template dictionary with a key containing parent-directory segments. The victim calls save_pretrained(), and the key is used as a filename, so the write lands outside the save directory.

The save routine checks each chat template name, rejects any containing separators or parent-directory segments, and confirms the resolved path is inside the save directory. The crafted key is refused and no file is written outside.

citations.quote: keys from the `chat_template` dictionary are used directly as filenames without proper validation
the attacker-controlled keys can escape the intended save directory, enabling arbitrary file writes with attacker-controlled content
An attacker can exploit this by publishing a malicious Hugging Face Hub repository with a crafted `tokenizer_config.json` file.
